Slide 54
  • The notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to differentiate into neuroectoderm & form the neural plate.
  • The notochord forms the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral disc in the adult.
  • The neural plate folds to give rise to the neural tube, which is open at both ends at the anterior and posterior neuropores. The anterior and posterior neuropores connect the lumen of the neural tube with the amniotic cavity.
  • The anterior neuropore closes during week 4 (day 25). Failure of the anterior neuropore to close results in upper neural tube defects.
  • The posterior neuropore closes during week 4 (day 27). Failure of the posterior neuropore to close results in lower NTDs (e.g., spina bifida).
  • As the neural plate folds, some cells differentiate into neural crest cells.
  • The rostral part of the neural tube becomes the adult brain.
  • The caudal part of the neural tube becomes the adult spinal cord.
  • Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP): AFP levels in maternal blood and amniotic fluid are used to screen for neural tube defects, Down syndrome, and other chromosomal abnormalities.
  • Development of the Neural tube
Slide 56
  • Neural crest cells will migrate and differentiate into distinct neurons, such as cranial nerve sensory ganglion cells and dorsal root ganglion cells, postganglionic autonomic ganglion cells (sympathetic & parasympathetic), chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, Schwann cells, and melanocytes. In addition, mesodermal cells alongside the neural tube begin to form somites, which will form skeletal muscle, vertebrae and the dermis.

Slide 60: Cephalocaudal Folding

Notes:

With growth of the brain vesicles, brain bulges into the amniotic cavity and then cranial and caudal folding ventrally. Endoderm is brought inside the embryo to form the gut tube

Slide 61: Results of Folding
  • With growth of the brain, cephalocaudal folding results- head and tail move ventrally, embryo is C-shaped
  • The endoderm become enclosed inside the embryo forming the gut-tube and the body wall closes except at the connecting stalk.
  • The ectoderm covers the embryo from outside & the amniotic sac expand to surround embryo.
  • The oral membrane and the cloacal membrane become ventral.
  • The heart, pericardium and the septum transversum (future diaphragm) become ventral.
  • Heart is here (rostral)
  • Heart is now here (ventral)
  • Moore and Persaud, The Developing Human 9th ed
Slide 62: Lateral Folding Creates the Intraembryonic Body Cavity and Surrounds the Embryo in the Amnion
  • Langman's Medical Embryology 14th ed

Notes:

The amnionic cavity is on the dorsum of the embryo. The dorsum of the embryo is covered with surface ectoderm (skin). The ventral side of the embryo is open to the yolk sac. Remember the lateral plate mesoderm and it has 2 layers, the somatic layer which will form the body wall and the visceral layer that covers the viscera/internal organs. The objective is to enclose the embryo in the amniotic cavity and close the ventral body wall. To do that, the layer of lateral plate mesoderm, the somatic mesoderm(body wall) is going to grow ventrally, along with the amniotic cavity, and surround the embryo. A space is formed between the somatic mesoderm and the splanchnic mesoderm that is the other (inside)layer of the lateral plate mesoderm. This space is the peritoneal cavity and the thoracic cavity. The somatic mesoderm will create the ventral body wall and enclose the developing gut tube within the intraembryonic body cavity, leaving in one area only, a connection between the gut tube and the yolk sac that will be part of the umbilical cord.

Slide 66: Early cardiovascular development

Notes:

The heart tube continues dorsally into a dorsal aorta that passes caudally. Branches of the aortae are (1) umbilical arteries establishing connections with vessels in the chorion, (2) vitelline arteries to the umbilical vesicle, and (3) dorsal intersegmental arteries to the body of the embryo. Vessels on the umbilical vesicle form a vascular plexus that is connected to the heart tubes by vitelline veins. The cardinal veins return blood from the body of the embryo. The umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood and nutrients to the chorion, which, in turn, provides nourishment to the embryo. The arteries carry poorly oxygenated blood and waste products to the chorionic villi for transfer to the mother's blood.

Slide 67
  • Fetal circulation & Vascular Shunts
  • Ductus venosus shunts blood from umbilical vein to inferior vena cava (bypass the liver)
  • Foramen Ovale shunts blood from the right atrium to left atrium
  • Ductus arteriosus shunts blood from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta.
Slide 68
  • Fetal circulation & Vascular Shunts
Slide 69: Umbilical cord (connecting stalk)
  • Allantois→ a small endodermal lined diverticulum off the hindgut. Urachus is Allantois’s fibrous element, which later forms the median umbilical ligament (obliterated Urachus).
  • Vitelline duct: it is a tube connecting the Midgut to the yolk sac (ventrally endodermal lined structure).
  • Umbilical vessels (2 umbilical arteries + left umbilical vein)
  • Two ducts (allantois + vitelline duct) will both be atrophied.
Slide 70
  • Single Umbilical Artery (SUA)
  • Single umbilical artery (SUA) cords occur in approximately 0.5-1% of pregnancies and are combined with congenital malformations in 11-30% of all cases.
  • Isolated single umbilical artery (iSUA) is the term used if no other malformation is observed.
  • It is associated with a risk of adverse perinatal outcome (perinatal death, preterm birth, small for gestational age, low Apgar score, transfer to the intensive care unit.
Slide 71: Clinical Consideration: Amnion and Amniotic Fluid
  • Fluid provides protection and allows for free movement
  • Fetus swallows about 400 mls (½ total volume) daily
  • Increase or decreased fluid volume can be associated with the presence of birth defects
  • Polyhydramnios-excess amniotic fluid volume associated with esophageal atresia
  • Oligohydramnios-decrease fluid volume associated with renal agenesis
  • Amniotic bands - tears in amnion that encircle and constrict developing limbs, can cause deformities

Primary Ovarian Insufficiency

Structural Causes of AUB

  • Polyps – benign localized overgrowth of endometrial glands & stroma
  • Adenomyosis – benign presence of endometrial glands & stroma w/in

the myometrium of the uterus (not where they are supposed to be)

  • Leiomyoma (aka fibroids) – benign smooth muscle tumors of the

myometrium

(precancer) – abnormal proliferation of

endometrial tissue

  • Usually due to unopposed estrogen
  • Must be ruled out for post menopausal

bleeding

Page 18

Non-structural Causes of AUB

  • Coagulopathy – a disorder of one of the components of coagulation
  • Ovulatory dysfunction – a disorder of hormonal secretion from the

ovary (ie Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome, etc) or other

hormonal disorder that affects ovarian function (ie thyroid

disorders, diabetes, prolactinomas, etc)

  • Endometrial – a dysfunction of the endometrial lining despite

normal hormonal secretion

  • Iatrogenic – causes related to medications or medical procedures

(ie hormonal contraceptive therapies, anticoagulants, etc)

  • Not Otherwise Classified – causes are poorly understood or rare

(AV malformations, surgical scars, etc)

  • Post Menopausal Bleeding

  • Primary or Secondary Amenorrhea; Oligomenorrhea

affecting 13% of this population

  • Symptoms – Facial Hair, Acne, Male Pattern Baldness, Central

Obesity, Menstrual Abnormalities, Acanthosis Nigricans

  • Causes – multifactorial (genetic, environmental,

testosterone exposure in utero)

Differential Diagnosis

for AUB

menopausal, hymenal

  • Pelvic

Page 34

Dysmenorrhea

  • Painful menstruation
  • Incidence – 50-90%, only about 45% will present
  • Usually starts 6-12 mon following menarche
  • Risk Factors – age <30, BMI <20, smoking, younger menarche,

longer cycles, heavier flow, and h/o sexual abuse

  • Protective Factors – age >30, increasing parity, exercise, hormonal

usage like OCPs

  • MOA – Elevated Prostaglandin & Leukotriene levels with

inflammation causing uterine contractions & cramping

Page 35

Dysmenorrhea - Secondary Causes

  • Endometriosis
  • Adenomyosis
  • Fibroids
  • Congenital Anomaly (ie mullerian malformations)
  • Pelvic Adhesions (ie prior surgery)
  • Pelvic Inflammatory Disease
Page 36

Dysmenorrhea Eval & Treatment

  • Symptoms – cramping pain in the lower abdomen/pelvis beginning at

onset of menstrual flow & lasting 8-72 hours

  • Primary associated symp: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headaches, muscle

cramps, low back pain, fatigue, sleep disturbance

  • Secondary associated symp: abnormal uterine bleeding, vaginal discharge,

dyspareunia

  • Diagnosis – history, abdominal/pelvic exam
  • Labwork (ie urine, STI/Vaginosis testing, pregnancy, etc)
  • Pelvic ultrasound
  • Laparoscopy
  • Treatment – NSAIDs, Hormonal Therapy (OCP, leuprolide acetate),

Exercise (45-60 min 3x/wk), TENs, Heat, Acupuncture, Surgery

  • Complications – Mood disorders, Missed Work/School, Infertility
Page 37

Endometriosis

  • Presence of endometrial glands & stroma in extrauterine locations
  • Estrogen promotes implantation of endometrial tissue & stimulates

inflammation

  • Neurogenesis, which is indicated by high levels of nerve growth factors that

alter & increase sensory and sympathetic nerve fibers, is observed in

endometriotic tissue.

  • Prevalence – peak is 25-35 yo
  • Incidence – most common gyne disorder,

affecting 10% repro age pts

  • Risk Factors – increased flow, low BMI, FH,

nulliparity, short cycles, early menarche

Is it Endometriosis?: Evergreen Women's Health, PC.: Board Certified Gynecologists

Page 38

Endometriosis Eval & Treatment

  • Symptoms
  • Dysmenorrhea (painful) & Menometrorrhagia (heavy/irregular)
  • Dyspareunia
  • Chronic pelvic pain
  • Infertility
  • Cyclical GI symp (ie painful bowel movements)
  • Cyclical urinary symp
  • Diagnosis – delayed 4-10 yrs
  • History & Physical exam – abdominal/pelvic
  • Imaging limitations
  • Pelvic Ultrasound (85% specificity, 50-84% sensitivity)
  • MRI of pelvis +/- abdomen w/o contrast
  • Laparoscopy
  • Management
  • Medications
  • Hormonal – suppress estrogen (OCPs, Depo/Nexplanon, etc but less so IUDs), leuprolide acetate
  • Analgesics – NSAIDs
  • Aromatase inhibitors – Letrozole, etc
  • Alternative treatments – acupuncture, exercise, dietary changes (avoid gluten & dairy)
  • Laparoscopy – ablation of lesions

Page 43

Contraceptive Mechanism: Estrogen vs Progestin

Estrogen component

  • Negative feedback at

hypothalamus/pituitary

  • Blunts FSH release
  • Prevents development of a

dominant follicle

  • Stabilizes endometrium and

improves cycle control

Progestin component

  • Inhibits LH surge → prevents

ovulation

  • Thickens cervical mucus → slows

sperm transport

  • Suppresses/atrophies endometrium
  • alters/suppresses the endometrium

Combined Oral Contraceptives (COCs)

Formulation and schedule

  • Contain estrogen, most often

ethinyl estradiol, plus a progestin.

  • Monophasic: constant

estrogen/progestin dose.

  • Triphasic or multiphasic: changing

hormone doses across cycle-

varying progestin does to mimic

cycle

  • Typical cycle: active hormone pills

followed by hormone-free interval.

Notes

  • Suppress gonadotropins → prevent

ovulation.

  • Withdrawal bleeding occurs during

placebo/hormone-free interval.

  • Extended-cycle or continuous use

reduces frequency of withdrawal

bleeding.

  • Useful for cycle regulation as well

as contraception.

Page 49

Progestin-Only Contraception

Shared progestin effects

Suppress LH and ovulation to variable

degrees.

Thicken cervical mucus.

Suppress/alter endometrium.

Do not carry the same estrogen-

related thrombotic risk pattern.

Shared adverse-effect pattern

Irregular bleeding is common,

especially early.

Headache, mood symptoms, weight

gain, and libido changes can occur.

Androgenic progestins can worsen

acne/hirsutism.

Choice often depends on adherence

needs and bleeding preferences.

Page 50

Adverse Effects: Split by Hormonal Driver

Hormonal

component

Common effects

Serious / distinctive risks

Estrogen

Nausea, breast tenderness,

headache, fluid retention

Thromboembolism,

hypertension, MI/stroke risk

pattern

Progestins

Headache, mood

symptoms/depression, weight

gain, libido changes, irregular

bleeding

Androgenic effects with some

progestins; DMPA bone loss;

drospirenone hyperkalemia risk

Most high risk “avoid this patient” warnings are driven by estrogen; most method-specific

nuisance effects are driven by progestin delivery.

Page 51

Progestin-Only Pills (POPs)

Useful when estrogen is undesirable

Pharmacology

Daily: Usually norethindrone in classic

“mini-pill” formulations.

Low continuous dose.

Mechanism relies heavily on cervical

mucus and variable ovulation

suppression.

Drospirenone POP is an alternative

formulation.

Clinical use and cautions

May be used in breastfeeding patients

or those with estrogen

contraindications.

Daily adherence matters.

Irregular bleeding is more frequent.

Rapid return to fertility after stopping

classic POPs is a useful vignette clue.

Page 52

Depot Medroxyprogesterone Acetate (DMPA)

High sustained progestin exposure

Mechanism and delivery

  • IM/SC Medroxyprogesterone

acetate injection every 3 months.

  • Sustained progestin levels strongly

suppress ovulation.

  • Many users develop amenorrhea

over time.

Distinctive adverse effects

  • Weight gain is common.
  • Return to fertility can be delayed for

several months after stopping.

  • Bone mineral density loss is the key

long-term adverse effect.

Page 53

Etonogestrel Implant

Long-acting reversible contraception (LARC)

Mechanism

  • Subdermal

etonogestrel release.

  • Strong ovulation

suppression.

  • Thickened cervical

mucus contributes.

Why it is high efficacy

  • Lasts up to 3 years
  • Efficacy does not rely

on daily or weekly

adherence.

  • Reversible when

removed.

Adverse-effect clue

Irregular

menstrual

bleeding

+ headache

Page 54

Levonorgestrel-Releasing IUD

Local progestin effect with high efficacy

Mechanism

IUD-Levonorgestrel released inside

uterus.

Thickens cervical mucus.

Alters endometrium and sperm

function/survival.

Ovulation may continue in some

users.

Clinical profile

Long-acting reversible contraception (3-8 yrs)

Appropriate when patient desires long-term

contraception.

Highly useful for heavy menstrual bleeding.

Initial spotting can occur; bleeding often

becomes lighter/amenorrheic.

Page 59

Medications used for

induced abortion

Page 60

Mifepristone-Progesterone antagonist

Mechanism

Competitive progesterone-receptor

antagonist.

Interferes with progesterone needed to

maintain pregnancy.

Causes decidual

breakdown/separation and cervical

softening.

Increases uterine responsiveness to

prostaglandins.

Adverse effects

Abdominal pain and uterine bleeding are

expected pharmacologic consequences.

Treatment Failure

Incomplete termination can occur.

Mechanistic contraindication:

ectopic pregnancy is not treated by this

regimen.

Also antagonizes glucocorticoid

receptors → explains contraindication in

chronic adrenal failure / long-term

corticosteroid therapy.

Page 61

Misoprostol-Prostaglandin analog

Mechanism

Prostaglandin E1 analog.

Stimulates myometrial contraction.

Promotes cervical ripening.

Used after mifepristone to actively

expel pregnancy tissue.

Adverse effects

Cramping / abdominal pain.

Uterine bleeding.

Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea.

Fever/chills can occur due to

prostaglandin effects.

A 30-year-old woman undergoing evaluation for infertility has an endometrial biopsy performed. Histologic

examination reveals a thickened endometrium with sacculated glands containing secretory material and coiled

spiral arteries. The glands show a saw-tooth appearance and are distended with glycogen-rich secretions.

Which of the following best describes the phase of the ovarian cycle and the corresponding days of the

menstrual cycle?

Page 6

Ovary: Structure and Function

LO: Describe the microscopic organization of the ovary, uterine tube, and uterus

Relate histological changes to the ovarian cycle, menstrual cycle, and pregnancy

Microscopic organization:

Cortex: Contains follicles at various stages of development,

the corpus luteum, and corpora albicantia, embedded in a

cellular stroma.

Medulla: Loose connective tissue carrying blood vessels,

lymphatics, and nerves.

Tunica albuginea: Dense connective tissue layer beneath the

surface epithelium.

Surface epithelium: Simple cuboidal to squamous

mesothelium (historically misnamed "germinal epithelium").

Oogenesis:

Begins in fetal life (~11–12 weeks' gestation); oogonia enter

meiosis I and arrest as primary oocytes in prophase I until

puberty.

The LH surge resumes meiosis I, yielding a secondary oocyte

plus first polar body; the secondary oocyte is released at

ovulation and arrests in metaphase II.

Meiosis II completes only if fertilization occurs, extruding the

second polar body.

Page 7

Folliculogenesis:

  • Primordial follicles: Primary oocyte surrounded by a

single layer of flat (squamous) pregranulosa cells. These

represent the largest pool of oocytes, formed in fetal

life and held dormant until recruited or lost to atresia.

Primary follicles: Cuboidal granulosa cells; zona pellucida

forms.

Secondary (preantral) follicles: Multiple granulosa layers;

antrum begins to form; theca interna and externa

differentiate.

Tertiary (antral/Graafian) follicles: Large antrum; oocyte

surrounded by corona radiata on the cumulus oophorus;

ready for ovulation.

LO: Describe the microscopic organization of the ovary, uterine tube,

and uterus, and relate histological changes to the ovarian cycle,

menstrual cycle, and pregnancy

Endometriosis

LO: Explain how altered structure/function leads to clinical consequences (e.g., follicular cysts, tubal infertility, endometriosis,

abnormal uterine bleeding, menopause).

Endometriosis is defined by the presence of endometrial glands and stroma in a location outside the uterus

Multifocal and involves pelvic structures (e.g., ovaries, pouch of Douglas, uterine ligaments, fallopian tubes)

  • Less frequently, involves distant areas of the peritoneal cavity, periumbilical tissues, or laparotomy scars
  • There are three types of endometriosis:
  • superficial peritoneal endometriosis
  • ovarian endometriosis
  • deep infiltrating endometriosis
  • Risk of malignant transformation is mainly confined to deep infiltrating endometriosis

lesions that penetrate more than 5 mm beneath the peritoneal surface, often involving structures like the

bowel, bladder, and uterosacral ligaments.

More prone to genetic mutations and cellular changes that may lead to malignancy

Page 13

LO: Explain how altered structure/function leads to clinical consequences (e.g., follicular cysts, tubal infertility, endometriosis,

abnormal uterine bleeding, menopause).

Endometriosis-Pathogenesis

Pathogenesis

1. origin from the uterine endometrium

2. origin from cells outside the uterus giving rise to endometrial tissue

The leading theories are as follows:

•The regurgitation theory: endometrial tissue implants at ectopic sites via retrograde

flow of menstrual endometrium through the opening of the fallopian tube

•The benign metastasis theory: endometrial tissue can “spread” to distant sites (e.g.,

bone, lung, and brain) via blood vessels and lymphatic channels

•The metaplastic theory: endometrium arises directly from coelomic epithelium

(mesothelium of pelvis or abdomen), from which the müllerian ducts and ultimately

the endometrium originate during embryonic development. Mesonephric remnants

may undergo endometrial differentiation and give rise to ectopic endometrial tissue.

•The extrauterine stem/progenitor cell theory: stem/progenitor cells from the bone

marrow differentiate into endometrial tissue.

Implants have different characteristics than eutopic uterine endometrium

Endometriotic tissue exhibits increased levels of proinflammatory and angiogenic

factors, including prostaglandin E 2, vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), and

matrix metalloproteinases (MMP), some of which are released by macrophages

that are recruited to endometriotic implants by proinflammatory factors

Endometriotic stromal cells make high levels of aromatase, leading to increased

local production of estrogen from androgens

Adenomyosis

LO: Explain the pathophysiology and clinicopathologic features of functional disorders, including polycystic ovary syndrome, endometrial

hyperplasia, adenomyosis, and endometriosis.

Definition

Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the

myometrium (uterine muscle wall)

Pathophysiology

Endometrial tissue becomes embedded deep within the myometrium

between muscle bundles

This ectopic tissue induces reactive hypertrophy of surrounding smooth

muscle

Results in a globular, enlarged uterus with a thickened uterine wall

Clinical Features

Menorrhagia (heavy menstrual bleeding)

Dysmenorrhea (painful menstruation)

Pelvic pain, especially pre-menstrual

May coexist with endometriosis, but they are distinct entities.

Gross and Imaging Findings

Uterus appears enlarged and boggy

Wall may be diffusely thickened

Diagnosed via MRI or ultrasound, though definitive diagnosis may

require histology

LO: Explain the pathophysiology and clinicopathologic features of functional disorders, including polycystic ovary syndrome, endometrial

hyperplasia, adenomyosis, and endometriosis

Endometrial Hyperplasia

Definition & Pathogenesis

Endometrial hyperplasia is an abnormal proliferation of endometrial glands due to excess estrogen unopposed by

progesterone

It is a precursor lesion for Type I endometrial carcinoma (endometrioid type).

Etiologies of Estrogen Excess

Obesity (peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogens in adipose tissue)

Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)

Estrogen-producing ovarian tumors (e.g., granulosa cell tumors)

Exogenous estrogen therapy without progestin

Classification

1. Hyperplasia without atypia

Increased gland-to-stroma ratio

Glands may be cystically dilated

Low risk of progression to carcinoma (1–3%)

2. Hyperplasia with atypia (also called Endometrial Intraepithelial Neoplasia, EIN)

Complex glandular architecture

Nuclear atypia: enlarged, vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli

High risk of progression to carcinoma

Associated with PTEN mutations

Endometrial Carcinoma-Endometrioid

Type I Endometrial Carcinoma (Endometrioid Type)

Risk Factors:

Mutations in mismatch repair genes and the tumor suppressor gene PTEN are early

events in the stepwise development of endometrioid carcinoma.

Estrogen excess: obesity, PCOS, estrogen-producing tumors, unopposed estrogen

therapy

Associated conditions: endometrial hyperplasia with atypia (EIN)

Age group: perimenopausal women (peak 55–65 years)

Molecular Basis:

PTEN mutations (Cowden syndrome)

Mismatch repair gene mutations (e.g., Lynch syndrome)

Occasional TP53 mutations (late event)

Morphology:

Glandular architecture resembling proliferative endometrium

Graded 1–3 based on differentiation:

Grade 1; A: well-differentiated glands

Grade 3; B: solid growth, marked atypia

Clinical Features:

Presents with postmenopausal bleeding

Slow progression, often localized

Good prognosis if detected early (90% 5-year survival in early stages)

LO: Differentiate between type I and type II endometrial carcinomas in terms of risk factors, molecular basis, morphology, and outcomes, and

Type II Endometrial Carcinoma (Serous Type):

Risk Factors:

Endometrial atrophy, not estrogen-related

Older age: typically 65–70 years

Not associated with obesity or hyperplasia

Molecular Basis:

TP53 mutations (early and central event)

Serous tumors are preceded by serous endometrial intraepithelial carcinoma

(SEIC), in which TP53 mutations are often detected, indicating a central role for

altered p53 function in the development of this form of endometrial carcinoma,

which shows significant morphologic and biologic overlap with ovarian serous

carcinoma.

Morphology:

Papillary structures, marked cytologic atypia; C: High-grade by definition

Diffuse p53 immunostaining due to mutant protein accumulation; D

Clinical Features:

Aggressive behavior

Often presents at advanced stage

Poor prognosis, dependent on staging

Uterine Leiomyoma (Fibroid)

LO: Compare benign and malignant uterine tumors (e.g., leiomyomas vs. leiomyosarcomas), including morphology, clinical course, and prognosis.

  • Most common tumors in women
  • Benign smooth muscle neoplasms; single or multiple
  • Estrogen and progesterone stimulate leiomyoma growth; tumors shrink after menopause
  • Associated with recurrent chromosomal abnormalities, including rearrangements of

chromosomes 6 and 12 found in other benign neoplasms (e.g., endometrial polyps and

lipomas)

  • Mutations in the MED12 gene; encodes a protein that regulates RNA polymerase II-mediated

transcription, have been identified in up to 70% of leiomyomas

  • The mechanism by which MED12 mutations contribute to the development of leiomyomas is

not understood.

Uterine Leiomyoma (Fibroid)-Morphology

LO: Compare benign and malignant uterine tumors (e.g., leiomyomas vs. leiomyosarcomas), including morphology, clinical course, and prognosis.

Gross:

Sharply circumscribed, firm gray-white masses with a characteristic whorled cut surface

Ranging from small nodules to large tumors

Types: embedded within the myometrium (intramural), lie beneath the endometrium (submucosal) or the

serosa (subserosal; may extend out on attenuated stalks (pedunculated)

Subserosal may become attached to surrounding organs and develop a blood supply (parasitic leiomyomas

Submucosal leiomyomas may ulcerate and cause abnormal uterine bleeding (menometrorrhagia)

Submucosal leiomyomas are associated with increased risk for spontaneous abortion

Malignant transformation to leiomyosarcoma is extremely rare

Histologic examination:

Bundles of intersecting uniform smooth muscle cells (elongated nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm) similar in

appearance to typical myometrium

Foci of fibrosis, calcification, and degenerative softening may be present

Page 26

LO: Compare benign and malignant uterine tumors (e.g., leiomyomas vs. leiomyosarcomas), including morphology, clinical course, and prognosis.

Leiomyosarcoma

Uncommon malignant neoplasms

Arise from the myometrium or endometrial stromal precursor cells

Almost always solitary and most often occur in postmenopausal women, in contrast to leiomyomas;

leiomyomas are frequently multiple and usually arise before menopause

They have complex, highly variable karyotypes including chromosomal deletions

Like leiomyomas, they contain MED12 mutations but in a smaller subset (30%).

Morphology

Soft, hemorrhagic, necrotic masses

The histopathology is highly variable; from tumors resembling leiomyoma to wildly anaplastic neoplasms

The diagnostic features of leiomyosarcoma include tumor necrosis, cytologic atypia, and mitotic activity

Because increased mitotic activity is sometimes seen in benign smooth muscle tumors, particularly in young

women, an assessment of all three features is necessary to make a diagnosis of malignancy

Page 31

Serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma

1. Site of Origin for High-Grade Serous Carcinoma

STIC lesions in the fallopian tube, particularly at the fimbriated end, are now recognized as the precursor lesions for many high-grade serous

carcinomas previously thought to originate in the ovary.

This has shifted the paradigm from “ovarian origin” to fallopian tube origin for these aggressive tumors.

2. Molecular Features

>90% of STICs harbor TP53 mutations, similar to uterine serous carcinoma.

These mutations are a hallmark of high-grade serous neoplasia.

3. Association with BRCA Mutations

STICs are frequently found in prophylactically removed fallopian tubes from women with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations.

Less commonly seen in women without known genetic risk factors.

4. Clinical Implications

Prophylactic salpingo-oophorectomy in BRCA mutation carriers can detect STICs before invasive carcinoma develops.

Early identification may prevent progression to high-grade serous carcinoma involving the ovary, omentum, and peritoneal cavity.

5. Histological Features

Atypical epithelial cells with:

High nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio

Strong p53 immunostaining

No evidence of stromal invasion in STIC.

A complex endocrine disorder

Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)-Pathophysiology

LO: Explain the pathophysiology and clinicopathologic features of functional disorders, including polycystic ovary syndrome, endometrial

hyperplasia, adenomyosis, and endometriosis.

Pathophysiology: (↑LH, ↓ FSH, ↑ androstenedione, ↓estradiol, ↑estrone)

1. Underlying Neuroendocrine Dysregulation

The hypothalamic-pituitary axis in PCOS is intrinsically dysregulated, possibly due to genetic and environmental factors.

This leads to increased GnRH pulse frequency, which favors LH secretion over FSH; LH:FSH ratio (often >2:1)

2. Androgen Feedback Loop

LH stimulates theca cells → ovarian thecal overactivity--↑ androgen production (e.g., testosterone, androstenedione)--- ↓ FSH

(negative feedback loop)

↓ FSH → Impaired Granulosa Cell Function (↓ aromatase activity in granulosa cells); Androgens are not efficiently converted to

estrogens → follicular arrest (first meiosis) and anovulation

This selective feedback maintains or further increases GnRH pulse frequency, reinforcing LH dominance.

3. Peripheral Conversion of Androgens to Estrogens

Androgens →estrone via aromatization in adipose tissue

Leads to chronic low-level estrogen without progesterone →endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma

4. Insulin Resistance and Hyperinsulinemia

Insulin acts synergistically with LH to stimulate theca cells →more androgen production.

Insulin also reduces SHBG (Sex Hormone Binding Globulin) → ↑free androgens, which perpetuate the feedback loop.

5. Absence of Progesterone Feedback

Due to anovulation, there is no corpus luteum →no progesterone---- menstrual irregularity and unopposed estrogen effects.

Progesterone normally slows GnRH pulses; its absence allows faster GnRH pulsate

A 28-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of 8 months of amenorrhea. She reports hot flashes, night

sweats, and vaginal dryness. She has no significant past medical history and takes no medications. Her menarche

was at age 13, and her cycles had been regular until the past year. She denies hirsutism or acne. BMI is 22 kg/m².

Pelvic exam shows normal external genitalia with reduced vaginal rugae. A pregnancy test is negative. Laboratory

studies show:

Serum FSH: markedly elevated

Serum LH: elevated

Serum estradiol: decreased

Serum testosterone: normal

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

A. Premature ovarian failure (primary ovarian insufficiency)

B. Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS)

C. Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea

D. Asherman syndrome

E. Hyperprolactinemia

Question 10:

Page 37

A.

Premature ovarian failure:

Ovarian failure before age 40, characterized by amenorrhea, hypoestrogenic symptoms (hot flashes, vaginal atrophy), elevated FSH/LH

(hypergonadotropic hypogonadism), and low estradiol [ovarian (hypergonadotropic) cause]

Normal BMI and absence of androgen excess further support the diagnosis.

B. Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS):

Typically presents with obesity, hirsutism, acne, infertility, and oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea.

Lab findings include elevated LH/FSH ratio (>2:1), increased androgens, and normal/low estrogen

This patient lacks hyperandrogenic features and has low estrogen with high FSH, not typical of PCOS

C. Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea:

Seen in patients with low BMI, excessive exercise, or stress.

Characterized by low or normal FSH, LH, and estrogen due to suppressed GnRH secretion.

D. Asherman syndrome: Outflow-tract/endometrial scarring

Intrauterine adhesions following curettage or infection cause amenorrhea, but systemic hypoestrogenic symptoms (hot flashes, vaginal

atrophy) are absent

Gonadotropins and estradiol are normal; SH/LH would not be markedly elevated.

E. Hyperprolactinemia:

Causes galactorrhea, headaches, or visual field defects due to pituitary adenoma

Labs would show low/normal FSH/LH, low estrogen due to GnRH suppression, not the high FSH/LH seen here

  • Ovarian malignancy is the second most common gynecologic malignancy (following

endometrial carcinoma)

  • Tumors of the ovary arise from any of the three cell types in the normal ovary: (1)

multipotent surface/fallopian tube epithelium; (2) pluripotent germ cells; and (3) sex cord–

stromal cells.

  • The great majority of malignant ovarian tumors are of epithelial cell origin; 90%
  • Germ cell and sex cord–stromal cell tumors are less frequent, 10% of malignant tumors of

the ovary

Ovarian Tumors-Classification

LO: Describe the embryologic/histologic components of the ovary (surface epithelium, germ cells, sex cord–stromal cells) as the basis for tumor

classification.

Most primary ovarian neoplasms arise from müllerian epithelium:

Classified based on differentiation and extent of proliferation of the

epithelium

Three major histologic types: serous, mucinous, and endometrioid

Benign:

80% of surface epithelial tumors

occur in young women between 20 and 45 years of age

Frequently cystic and may have an accompanying stromal

component

Borderline:

Occur at older ages

Majority behave in a benign manner, some recur, and a few progress

to carcinoma

Malignant tumors:

Between 45 and 65 years of age and may be cystic

(cystadenocarcinoma) or solid (carcinoma).

Types I and II

•Type I carcinoma: low-grade tumor; in association with borderline tumors

or endometriosis and includes low-grade serous, endometrioid, and

mucinous tumors

•Type II carcinoma : high-grade serous carcinoma that arises from serous

tubal intraepithelial carcinoma

Page 42

Ovarian Tumors-Risk Factors

LO: Identify risk factors, hereditary cancer syndromes, and molecular mechanisms underlying epithelial, sex cord–stromal, and germ cell ovarian

tumors.

Important risk factors:

  • increasing age
  • early menarche/late menopause
  • Nulliparity
  • family history
  • germline mutations in certain tumor suppressor genes
  • Prolonged use of oral contraceptives reduces the risk due to suppression of ovulation.
  • Around 5% to 10% of ovarian cancers are familial, associated with mutations in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 tumor

suppressor genes (also mutated in a subset of hereditary breast cancer).

Page 43

Ovarian Tumors: Serous Tumors

LO: Identify risk factors, hereditary cancer syndromes, and molecular mechanisms underlying epithelial, sex cord–stromal, and germ cell ovarian

tumors.

Serous Tumors

  • Most common of the ovarian epithelial tumors
  • Benign and borderline tumors are most common between 20 and 45 years of age
  • Serous carcinomas generally occur later in life except in familial cases.
  • Low-grade tumors arise from benign or borderline lesions and progress slowly in a stepwise manner to

become invasive carcinoma.

  • Low-grade tumors have mutations in the KRAS, BRAF, or ERBB2 oncogenes and wild-type TP53 alleles
  • High-grade serous tumors arise in the fimbriated end of the fallopian tube via serous tubal intraepithelial

carcinoma

High-grade serous tumors have TP53 mutations; 95% of cases

  • Almost all ovarian carcinomas arising in women with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations are high-grade serous

carcinomas with TP53 mutations

Page 44

Ovarian Tumors: Serous Tumors- Gross Pathology

LO: Describe the embryologic/histologic components of the ovary (surface epithelium, germ cells, sex

cord–stromal cells) as the basis for tumor classification.

Morphology:

  • large, spherical to ovoid, cystic structures up to 30 to 40 cm in diameter.
  • About 25% of benign tumors are bilateral.
  • In benign tumors, the serosal covering is smooth and glistening.
  • By contrast, the surface of adenocarcinoma has nodular irregularities where

tumor has invaded the serosa.

  • Single cavity, or multiple cavities divided by multiple septa into

multiloculated masses

  • The cystic spaces are filled with a clear, serous fluid.
  • Protruding into the cystic cavities are papillary projections (malignant)

Ovarian Tumors: Mucinous Tumors

LO: Identify risk factors, hereditary cancer syndromes, and molecular mechanisms underlying epithelial, sex cord–stromal, and germ cell ovarian

tumors.

Mucinous Tumors

  • Two features distinguish them from serous tumors:
  • Mucin-secreting cells
  • Mucinous tumors are less likely to be malignant
  • Overall, only 10% of mucinous tumors are malignant; another 10% are borderline, and

80% are benign.

  • Occur in middle adult life and are rare before puberty and after menopause
  • Mutation of the KRAS proto-oncogene is a consistent genetic alteration in all

mucinous tumors of the ovary.

Ovarian Tumors: Endometrioid and Clear Cell

LO: Describe the embryologic/histologic components of the ovary (surface epithelium, germ cells, sex cord–stromal cells) as the basis for tumor

classification. Identify risk factors, hereditary cancer syndromes, and molecular mechanisms underlying epithelial, sex cord–stromal, and germ

cell ovarian tumors.

Endometrioid Tumors

solid or cystic

In association with endometriosis

Microscopic examination: tubular glands, similar to those of the endometrium, within the lining of cystic spaces

Usually malignant; benign and borderline forms exist

They are bilateral in about 20% of cases, and 15% to 20% of women with these ovarian tumors have a concomitant

endometrial carcinoma.

Similar to endometrioid-type carcinoma of the endometrium, endometrioid carcinomas of the ovary frequently have

mutations in the PTEN tumor suppressor gene and other genes that act to upregulate PI3K-AKT signaling

Clear Cell Carcinoma

A rare subtype of epithelial ovarian tumors

Benign and borderline are rare

Clear cell carcinomas are composed of large epithelial cells with abundant clear cytoplasm (similar to gestational

endometrium)

In association with endometriosis or endometrioid carcinoma of the ovary

Most commonly mutated genes ( PIK3CA, ARID1A, KRAS, PTEN, and TP53 ) are shared with endometrioid carcinoma

Ovarian Teratomas

LO: Describe the embryologic/histologic components of the ovary (surface epithelium, germ cells, sex cord–stromal cells) as the basis for tumor

classification. Identify risk factors, hereditary cancer syndromes, and molecular mechanisms underlying epithelial, sex cord–stromal, and germ

cell ovarian tumors.

Teratomas account for 15–20% of ovarian tumors; >90% are benign, most commonly found in young women.

They are classified into:

Mature (benign);

Immature (malignant)

Monodermal or highly specialized

Mature (Benign) Teratomas (dermoid cysts):

Mature tissues from all three germ layers:

Ectoderm: skin, hair, neural tissue

Mesoderm: bone, cartilage, muscle

Endoderm: respiratory or gastrointestinal epithelium

Gross features:

Cystic structure filled with sebaceous material and hair

May contain teeth, bone, cartilage

Usually unilateral (90%), more common on the right side

Rarely exceeds 10 cm

Complications:

Ovarian torsion (10–15% of cases)

Malignant transformation (∼1%, usually to squamous cell carcinoma)

Paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis (rare, associated with neural tissue)

Granulosa Cell Tumor

Granulosa cell tumor (GCT) of the ovary belongs to the

category of sex cord-stromal tumors that show differentiation

towards granulosa cells of the ovarian follicle. There

are two subtypes - adult GCT and juvenile GCT.

Adult GCT, mostly seen in peri- and postmenopausal

women, accounts for 95% of all GCTs and makes up 1-2% of

all ovarian tumors--Postmenopausal bleeding, breast

tenderness, pelvic mass

Juvenile GCT, which occurs in children and younger women

(<30 yrs), makes up the remainder 5% of all GCTs--

precocious puberty, breast development and vaginal bleeding

in toddlers

Small, bland, cuboidal to polygonal cells arranged in

various patterns. Call-Exner bodies (Red Arrow): small

follicle-like structures, filled with eosinophilic material.

The cells may show nuclear grooves (coffee bean

nuclei).

Slide 4: Objectives:
  • Describe the microscopic organization of the ovary, uterine tube, and uterus
  • Relate histological changes to the ovarian cycle, menstrual cycle, and pregnancy.
  • Explain how altered structure/function leads to clinical consequences (e.g., follicular cysts, tubal infertility, endometriosis, abnormal uterine bleeding, menopause).
  • Recognize congenital and developmental anomalies of the uterus and their clinical implications (Self study).
  • Explain the pathophysiology and clinicopathologic features of functional disorders, including polycystic ovary syndrome, endometrial hyperplasia, adenomyosis, and endometriosis.
  • Discuss pelvic inflammatory disease and infections of the uterine tubes and endometrium: common pathogens, pathogenesis, morphology, and complications.
  • Compare benign and malignant uterine tumors (e.g., leiomyomas vs. leiomyosarcomas), including morphology, clinical course, and prognosis.
  • Differentiate between type I and type II endometrial carcinomas in terms of risk factors, molecular basis, morphology, and outcomes, and relate type I to hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal carcinoma (Lynch syndrome).
  • Recognize the features and molecular alterations of uterine carcinosarcoma (malignant mixed Müllerian tumor).
  • Describe the embryologic/histologic components of the ovary (surface epithelium, germ cells, sex cord–stromal cells) as the basis for tumor classification.
  • Identify risk factors, hereditary cancer syndromes, and molecular mechanisms underlying epithelial, sex cord–stromal, and germ cell ovarian tumors.

Slide 6: Question 1: Answer and Explanation
  • A 30-year-old woman undergoing evaluation for infertility has an endometrial biopsy performed. Histologic examination reveals a thickened endometrium with sacculated glands containing secretory material and coiled spiral arteries. The glands show a saw-tooth appearance and are distended with glycogen-rich secretions.
  • Which of the following best describes the phase of the ovarian cycle and the corresponding days of the menstrual cycle?
  • A. Follicular phase; days 6–13
  • B. Ovulatory phase; days 13–15
  • C. Luteal phase; days 15–28
  • D. Menstrual phase; days 1–5
  • E. Proliferative phase; days 6–14
  • The luteal phase of the ovarian cycle begins after ovulation (around day 14) and lasts until menstruation begins
  • During this phase, progesterone from the corpus luteum induces secretory transformation of the endometrium:
  • Sacculated glands with secretory product
  • Coiled spiral arteries
  • Saw-tooth glandular appearance
  • These changes are consistent with days 15–28 of the menstrual cycle
Slide 7: Ovary: Structure and Function
  • LO: Describe the microscopic organization of the ovary, uterine tube, and uterus
  • Relate histological changes to the ovarian cycle, menstrual cycle, and pregnancy
  • Microscopic organization:
  • Cortex: Contains follicles at various stages of development, the corpus luteum, and corpora albicantia, embedded in a cellular stroma.
  • Medulla: Loose connective tissue carrying blood vessels, lymphatics, and nerves.
  • Tunica albuginea: Dense connective tissue layer beneath the surface epithelium.
  • Surface epithelium: Simple cuboidal to squamous mesothelium (historically misnamed "germinal epithelium").
  • Oogenesis:
  • Begins in fetal life (~11–12 weeks' gestation); oogonia enter meiosis I and arrest as primary oocytes in prophase I until puberty.
  • The LH surge resumes meiosis I, yielding a secondary oocyte plus first polar body; the secondary oocyte is released at ovulation and arrests in metaphase II.
  • Meiosis II completes only if fertilization occurs, extruding the second polar body.
Slide 8: Folliculogenesis:
  • Primordial follicles: Primary oocyte surrounded by a single layer of flat (squamous) pregranulosa cells. These represent the largest pool of oocytes, formed in fetal life and held dormant until recruited or lost to atresia.
  • Primary follicles: Cuboidal granulosa cells; zona pellucida forms.
  • Secondary (preantral) follicles: Multiple granulosa layers; antrum begins to form; theca interna and externa differentiate.
  • Tertiary (antral/Graafian) follicles: Large antrum; oocyte surrounded by corona radiata on the cumulus oophorus; ready for ovulation.
  • LO: Describe the microscopic organization of the ovary, uterine tube, and uterus, and relate histological changes to the ovarian cycle, menstrual cycle, and pregnancy

Notes:

The zona pellucida is a thick glycoprotein-rich extracellular layer that surrounds the oocyte (egg cell). It forms during follicular development and lies between the oocyte plasma membrane and the surrounding granulosa cells (corona radiata). Functions of the Zona Pellucida

1. Sperm Binding

The zona pellucida contains glycoproteins (ZP1, ZP2, ZP3, and ZP4) that allow sperm to recognize and bind to the oocyte. This is the first step in fertilization.

2. Triggers the Acrosome Reaction

After sperm binding, the zona pellucida induces the acrosome reaction, during which enzymes are released from the sperm head to digest a pathway through the zona pellucida.

3. Prevents Polyspermy

Once fertilization occurs, cortical granules from the oocyte modify the zona pellucida (the zona reaction), preventing additional sperm from entering the egg.

4. Protects the Early Embryo

The zona pellucida remains around the embryo during the first few cell divisions as it travels through the uterine tube. The blastocyst later "hatches" from the zona pellucida before implantation.

Slide 9: LO: Describe the microscopic organization of the ovary, uterine tube, and uterus, and relate histological changes to the ovarian cycle, menstrual cycle, and pregnancy

| Cycle Phase | Days | Key Events | Histological Features | Hormonal Control | Ovarian Phase |

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| Menses | 1–5 | Progesterone withdrawal → spiral artery constriction → ischemia → shedding of stratum functionalis | Sloughing tissue, extravasated blood | ↓ Progesterone due to corpus luteum degeneration; ↑ FSH & LH | Late Luteal → Follicular Start / corpus luteum → corpus albicans |

| Proliferative Phase | 6–14 | Estrogen-driven regeneration of stratum functionalis | Straight glands, mitotic activity, thin endometrium | FSH stimulates follicle growth → Estrogen production | Follicular Phase / (variation of menstrual cycle) |

| Ovulation | ~Day 14 | LH surge triggered by high estrogen → release of secondary oocyte | Transition between proliferative and secretory phases | High estrogen → LH surge | Ovulation |

| Secretory Phase | 14–28 | Progesterone from corpus luteum → glandular secretion, spiral artery coiling | Sacculated glands, saw-tooth appearance, predecidual cells | Corpus luteum secretes progesterone; if no fertilization → ↓ progesterone → menstruation | Luteal Phase |

Notes:

The follicular phase begins on the first day of menstruation and ends with ovulation.

Its length depends on how quickly the dominant follicle matures in response to FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone).

Factors like stress, illness, weight changes, and hormonal fluctuations can delay follicular development, thus delaying ovulation.

In contrast, the luteal phase is relatively fixed, usually lasting 14 days in most women.

Clinical Relevance:

Irregular cycles are often due to variability in the follicular phase, not the luteal phase.

In reproductive medicine, tracking ovulation helps pinpoint the follicular phase length and assess cycle regularity.

Slide 10: LO: Describe the microscopic organization of the ovary, uterine tube, and uterus, and relate histological changes to the ovarian cycle, menstrual cycle, and pregnancy-Continued

| Ovarian cycle stage | Ovarian histology | Matching menstrual (endometrial) phase | Endometrial histology | Dominant hormonal control |

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| Early follicular phase (primordial → primary follicles recruited) | Primordial follicles (flat granulosa) activate to primary follicles (cuboidal granulosa, zona pellucida forming); coincides with menses | Menstrual phase (days ~1–5), then early proliferative | Functional layer shed; ischemia/apoptosis with spiral-artery vasospasm, then basal-layer regeneration | Rising FSH (loss of negative feedback as prior corpus luteum regresses); low estrogen/progesterone |

| Mid-follicular phase (secondary/antral follicle growth, dominant follicle selection) | Antrum enlarges; theca interna secretes androstenedione; granulosa aromatize to estradiol; one dominant follicle emerges | Proliferative phase | Glandular and stromal proliferation, mitoses; straight tubular glands; spiral arteries lengthen | FSH stimulates aromatase; rising estradiol (negative feedback on FSH) |

| Late follicular phase (preovulatory Graafian follicle) | Large Graafian follicle; oocyte with corona radiata on cumulus oophorus | Late proliferative phase | Maximal glandular proliferation; subnuclear glycogen vacuoles appear; pseudostratified epithelium | Peak estradiol → positive feedback triggering LH surge |

| Ovulation (~day 14) | LH surge → follicle rupture; oocyte completes meiosis I to secondary oocyte (arrests in metaphase II) and is released | Transition to secretory phase | Onset of secretory transformation | LH surge (with FSH surge) |

| Early–mid luteal phase (corpus luteum) | Ruptured follicle luteinizes into corpus luteum; luteinized granulosa/theca cells | Early–mid secretory phase | Tortuous, sacculated glands; subnuclear then luminal secretion; stromal edema; coiled spiral arteries; decidualization near implantation window | LH-driven corpus luteum secretes progesterone + second estradiol rise; progesterone dominant |

| Late luteal phase (corpus luteum regression, if no pregnancy) | Corpus luteum → corpus albicans (scar) | Late secretory / premenstrual | Glandular breakdown, stromal apoptosis, decreased endometrial height, spiral-artery constriction | Falling estrogen and progesterone; rising FSH begins next cycle |

| Luteal rescue (if fertilization/implantation) | Corpus luteum maintained (corpus luteum of pregnancy) | Decidualized secretory endometrium sustained | Full decidualization; no shedding | hCG from trophoblast sustains corpus luteum → continued progesterone |

Notes:

The follicular phase begins on the first day of menstruation and ends with ovulation.

Its length depends on how quickly the dominant follicle matures in response to FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone).

Factors like stress, illness, weight changes, and hormonal fluctuations can delay follicular development, thus delaying ovulation.

In contrast, the luteal phase is relatively fixed, usually lasting 14 days in most women.

Clinical Relevance:

Irregular cycles are often due to variability in the follicular phase, not the luteal phase.

In reproductive medicine, tracking ovulation helps pinpoint the follicular phase length and assess cycle regularity.

Slide 11: Uterine Histological Changes in the Menstrual Cycle
  • LO: Describe the microscopic organization of the ovary, uterine tube, and uterus, and relate histological changes to the ovarian cycle, menstrual cycle, and pregnancy
  • Proliferative endometrium. Straight, non-secretory endometrial glands
  • Early secretory phase endometrium with secretory products starting to accumulate in some glands (arrows)
  • Late secretory phase endometrium; glands are widely sacculated, with characteristic saw-tooth appearance, and lumens distended with secretions (X).

Notes:

For the uterine tube, the mucosa is lined by a simple columnar epithelium of ciliated and secretory (peg) cells that peak in ciliation and secretory activity in the late follicular/periovulatory phase under estrogen, then deciliate and atrophy in the luteal phase under progesterone.

Slide 12: Question 2
  • A 30-year-old woman has had recurring pelvic pain with dysuria and dysmenorrhea for the past 5 years. On pelvic examination there are no abnormal findings. Magnetic resonance imaging shows focal, less than 3 mm, bright lesions in the anterior cul-de-sac along with adhesions. She receives therapy with a combination of oral contraceptive agent along with an aromatase inhibitor, and her condition improves. Her lesions are most likely to have which of the following microscopic appearances?
  • Endometrial glands with stroma
  • Enlarged, avascular chorionic villi
  • Neutrophilic abscesses
  • Noncaseating granulomata
  • Poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma
Slide 13: Question 2: Answer and Explanation
  • A 30-year-old woman has had recurring pelvic pain with dysuria and dysmenorrhea for the past 5 years. On pelvic examination there are no abnormal findings. Magnetic resonance imaging shows focal, less than 3 mm, bright lesions in the anterior cul-de-sac along with adhesions. She receives therapy with a combination of oral contraceptive agent along with an aromatase inhibitor, and her condition improves. Her lesions are most likely to have which of the following microscopic appearances?
  • Endometrial glands with stroma
  • Enlarged, avascular chorionic villi
  • Neutrophilic abscesses
  • Noncaseating granulomata
  • Poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma
  • Endometrial glands with stroma (correct): Endometriosis is histologically defined as ectopic endometrial glands and stroma, often accompanied by hemosiderin-laden macrophages.
  • Enlarged, avascular chorionic villi: Describes hydatidiform mole/hydropic villi, a gestational trophoblastic process — unrelated.
  • Neutrophilic abscesses: Suggest acute pyogenic infection (e.g., tubo-ovarian abscess), not endometriosis, which shows chronic inflammation and hemosiderin.
  • Noncaseating granulomata: Point to sarcoidosis or a granulomatous salpingitis (e.g., foreign-body/Crohn), not endometriosis.
  • Poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma: Endometriosis is benign; this describes malignancy.

Notes:

The presentation is classic endometriosis: chronic cyclic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dysuria, and small (<3 mm) hyperintense peritoneal implants with adhesions in the cul-de-sac in a reproductive-age woman, improving on a combined oral contraceptive plus an aromatase inhibitor. Endometriotic lesions are estrogen-dependent, and aromatase inhibitors work by blocking local estrogen production within the lesions.

Slide 14: Endometriosis
  • LO: Explain how altered structure/function leads to clinical consequences (e.g., follicular cysts, tubal infertility, endometriosis, abnormal uterine bleeding, menopause).
  • Endometriosis is defined by the presence of endometrial glands and stroma in a location outside the uterus
  • Multifocal and involves pelvic structures (e.g., ovaries, pouch of Douglas, uterine ligaments, fallopian tubes)
  • Less frequently, involves distant areas of the peritoneal cavity, periumbilical tissues, or laparotomy scars
  • There are three types of endometriosis:
  • superficial peritoneal endometriosis
  • ovarian endometriosis
  • deep infiltrating endometriosis
  • Risk of malignant transformation is mainly confined to deep infiltrating endometriosis
  • lesions that penetrate more than 5 mm beneath the peritoneal surface, often involving structures like the bowel, bladder, and uterosacral ligaments.
  • More prone to genetic mutations and cellular changes that may lead to malignancy
Slide 15: Endometriosis-Pathogenesis
  • LO: Explain how altered structure/function leads to clinical consequences (e.g., follicular cysts, tubal infertility, endometriosis, abnormal uterine bleeding, menopause).
  • Pathogenesis
  • 1. Origin from the uterine endometrium
  • 2. origin from cells outside the uterus giving rise to endometrial tissue
  • The leading theories are as follows:
  • The regurgitation theory: endometrial tissue implants at ectopic sites via retrograde flow of menstrual endometrium through the opening of the fallopian tube
  • The benign metastasis theory: endometrial tissue can “spread” to distant sites (e.g., bone, lung, and brain) via blood vessels and lymphatic channels
  • The metaplastic theory: endometrium arises directly from coelomic epithelium (mesothelium of pelvis or abdomen), from which the müllerian ducts and ultimately the endometrium originate during embryonic development. Mesonephric remnants may undergo endometrial differentiation and give rise to ectopic endometrial tissue.
  • The extrauterine stem/progenitor cell theory: stem/progenitor cells from the bone marrow differentiate into endometrial tissue.
  • Implants have different characteristics than eutopic uterine endometrium.
  • Endometriotic tissue has increased expression of proinflammatory and angiogenic mediators: prostaglandin E₂ (PGE₂), vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), and matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs). These promote inflammation, angiogenesis, invasion, and survival of ectopic endometrial tissue.
  • Macrophages and other inflammatory cells recruited to lesions produce many inflammatory and angiogenic mediators.
  • Endometriotic stromal cells express aromatase, leading to increased local conversion of androgens to estrogens and creating an estrogen-rich microenvironment that promotes lesion growth and persistence.
  • Female Genital System and Breast

Kumar, Vinay, MBBS, MD, FRCPath, Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 17, 602-635

Pathogenesis of endometriosis. Depicted is the interplay between factors expressed in endometriotic implants and activated macrophages that are hypothesized to play a role in the establishment and maintenance of endometriotic implants. COX2, Cyclo...

Notes:

Endometriosis is maintained by a self-perpetuating inflammatory-estrogenic cycle: inflammatory cells increase PGE₂ production, PGE₂ upregulates aromatase expression, aromatase increases local estrogen production, and estrogen further stimulates lesion growth and inflammation.

Slide 16: Endometriosis-Morphology
  • LO: Explain how altered structure/function leads to clinical consequences (e.g., follicular cysts, tubal infertility, endometriosis, abnormal uterine bleeding, menopause)
  • Explain the pathophysiology and clinicopathologic features of functional disorders, including polycystic ovary syndrome, endometrial hyperplasia, adenomyosis, and endometriosis.
  • Morphology
  • Consists of functioning endometrium; undergoes cyclic bleeding
  • Collection of blood in aberrant foci---appear red-brown nodules or implants, ranging in size from microscopic to 1 to 2 cm in diameter, that lie on or just under the affected serosal surface
  • When lesions are widespread, organizing hemorrhage can cause extensive fibrous adhesions between fallopian tubes, ovaries, and other structures and obliterate the pouch of Douglas
  • The ovaries may become markedly distorted by large cystic masses (3 to 5 cm in diameter) filled with brown fluid resulting from previous hemorrhage; chocolate cysts or endometriomas
  • Diagnosis depends on finding both endometrial glands and stroma at sites external to the endometrium
  • Endometrial stromal cells: hormone-responsive spindle mesenchymal cells; support the endometrium and differentiate into decidual cells during pregnancy.
  • Kumar, Vinay, MBBS, MD, FRCPath, Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 17, 602-635
  • https://webpath.med.utah.edu/FEMHTML/FEM115.html
  • https://ilovepathology.com/endometriosis/

Notes:

Clinical Features

Clinical signs and symptoms usually include severe dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and pelvic pain due to intrapelvic bleeding and periuterine adhesions. Menstrual irregularities are common, and infertility is the presenting issue for 30% to 40% of patients. Effective treatments include COX-2 inhibitors and aromatase inhibitors. Although uncommon, malignancies can develop within endometriotic tissue.

Slide 17: Question 3:
  • A 42-year-old woman presents with heavy menstrual bleeding and pelvic pain that worsens just before menstruation. Physical examination reveals a mildly enlarged, tender uterus. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a thickened uterine wall with a globular contour. Histologic examination of the uterine wall reveals endometrial glands and stroma embedded within the myometrium.
  • Which of the following best explains the pathophysiology underlying this patient’s presentation?
  • A. Ectopic endometrial tissue induces myometrial hypertrophy
  • B. Unopposed estrogen stimulation of the endometrium
  • C. Ovulatory dysfunction leading to anovulation
  • D. Endometrial hyperplasia due to chronic inflammation
  • E. Submucosal fibroid disrupting endometrial architecture
Slide 18: Question 3: Answer and Explanation
  • A 42-year-old woman presents with heavy menstrual bleeding and pelvic pain that worsens just before menstruation. Physical examination reveals a mildly enlarged, tender uterus. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a thickened uterine wall with a globular contour. Histologic examination of the uterine wall reveals endometrial glands and stroma embedded within the myometrium.
  • Which of the following best explains the pathophysiology underlying this patient’s presentation?
  • A. Ectopic endometrial tissue induces myometrial hypertrophy
  • B. Unopposed estrogen stimulation of the endometrium
  • C. Ovulatory dysfunction leading to anovulation
  • D. Endometrial hyperplasia due to chronic inflammation
  • E. Submucosal fibroid disrupting endometrial architecture
  • A. Ectopic endometrial tissue induces myometrial hypertrophy: This describes adenomyosis, where endometrial glands and stroma are located within the myometrium, causing reactive hypertrophy and resulting in abnormal uterine bleeding and dysmenorrhea
  • B. Unopposed estrogen stimulation of the endometrium: This mechanism is typical of endometrial hyperplasia, often seen in anovulatory cycles or estrogen-producing tumors, not adenomyosis.
  • C. Ovulatory dysfunction leading to anovulation: This describes dysfunctional uterine bleeding due to hormonal imbalance, not structural abnormalities like adenomyosis.
  • D. Endometrial hyperplasia due to chronic inflammation: Chronic inflammation may lead to hyperplasia, but this is not the mechanism in adenomyosis.
  • E. Submucosal fibroid disrupting endometrial architecture: While fibroids can cause abnormal bleeding, the histologic finding of endometrial tissue within the myometrium is specific to adenomyosis.
Slide 19: Adenomyosis
  • LO: Explain the pathophysiology and clinicopathologic features of functional disorders, including polycystic ovary syndrome, endometrial hyperplasia, adenomyosis, and endometriosis.
  • Definition
  • Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium (uterine muscle wall)
  • Pathophysiology
  • Endometrial tissue becomes embedded deep within the myometrium between muscle bundles
  • This ectopic tissue induces reactive hypertrophy of surrounding smooth muscle
  • Results in a globular, enlarged uterus with a thickened uterine wall
  • Clinical Features
  • Menorrhagia (heavy menstrual bleeding)
  • Dysmenorrhea (painful menstruation)
  • Pelvic pain, especially pre-menstrual
  • May coexist with endometriosis, but they are distinct entities.
  • Gross and Imaging Findings
  • Uterus appears enlarged and boggy
  • Wall may be diffusely thickened
  • Diagnosed via MRI or ultrasound, though definitive diagnosis may require histology
  • https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/uterusadenomyosis.html
  • https://ilovepathology.com/pathology-of-adenomyosis/
Slide 20: Question 4:

These neoplasms are most common in women aged 55–65 with obesity, hypertension, or diabetes mellitus. Histologic examination shows glandular architecture resembling proliferative endometrium. Molecular analysis reveals frequent PTEN mutations and occasional mismatch repair gene mutations. The tumors are typically well-differentiated and remain localized for years before spreading via lymphatics.
  • Which of the following neoplasms is most consistent with these findings?
  • A. Clear cell carcinoma
  • B. Endometrioid carcinoma
  • C. Leiomyosarcoma
  • D. Müllerian mixed tumor (carcinosarcoma)
  • E. Serous carcinoma
  • F. Stromal sarcoma
Slide 21: Question 4: Answer and Explanation
  • A study of patients with postmenopausal uterine bleeding reveals that some have malignant neoplasms arising from prior atypical hyperplastic lesions. These neoplasms are most common in women aged 55–65 with obesity, hypertension, or diabetes mellitus. Histologic examination shows glandular architecture resembling proliferative endometrium. Molecular analysis reveals frequent PTEN mutations and occasional mismatch repair gene mutations. The tumors are typically well-differentiated and remain localized for years before spreading via lymphatics.
  • Which of the following neoplasms is most consistent with these findings?
  • A. Clear cell carcinoma
  • B. Endometrioid carcinoma
  • C. Leiomyosarcoma
  • D. Müllerian mixed tumor (carcinosarcoma)
  • E. Serous carcinoma
  • F. Stromal sarcoma
  • A. Clear cell carcinoma: Rare, aggressive Type II carcinoma. Not associated with PTEN mutations or hyperplasia.
  • B. Endometrioid carcinoma: This is a Type I endometrial carcinoma, associated with: Estrogen excess (obesity, PCOS, granulosa cell tumors), Endometrial hyperplasia with atypia (EIN), PTEN and mismatch repair gene mutations, Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer), Well-differentiated glandular morphology, Slow progression and favorable prognosis if detected early
  • C. Leiomyosarcoma: A mesenchymal tumor, not associated with endometrial hyperplasia or PTEN mutations.
  • D. Müllerian mixed tumor (carcinosarcoma): Aggressive tumor with both epithelial and mesenchymal components. May arise from prior carcinoma but not typically linked to PTEN or hyperplasia. Associated with TP53 mutations.
  • E. Serous carcinoma: Type II endometrial carcinoma, associated with TP53 mutations, endometrial atrophy, and older age. Not linked to estrogen excess or hyperplasia. Morphology shows papillary structures and marked atypia.
  • F. Stromal sarcoma: Rare mesenchymal tumor, not associated with the described clinical or molecular features.
Slide 22: Endometrial Hyperplasia
  • LO: Explain the pathophysiology and clinicopathologic features of functional disorders, including polycystic ovary syndrome, endometrial hyperplasia, adenomyosis, and endometriosis
  • Definition & Pathogenesis
  • Endometrial hyperplasia is an abnormal proliferation of endometrial glands due to excess estrogen unopposed by progesterone
  • It is a precursor lesion for Type I endometrial carcinoma (endometrioid type).
  • Etiologies of Estrogen Excess
  • Obesity (peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogens in adipose tissue)
  • Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
  • Estrogen-producing ovarian tumors (e.g., granulosa cell tumors)
  • Exogenous estrogen therapy without progestin
  • Classification
  • 1. Hyperplasia without atypia
  • Increased gland-to-stroma ratio
  • Glands may be cystically dilated
  • Low risk of progression to carcinoma (1–3%)
  • 2. Hyperplasia with atypia (also called Endometrial Intraepithelial Neoplasia, EIN)
  • Complex glandular architecture
  • Nuclear atypia: enlarged, vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli
  • High risk of progression to carcinoma
  • Associated with PTEN mutations
Slide 23: Endometrial Hyperplasia-Morphology
  • LO:Explain the pathophysiology and clinicopathologic features of functional disorders, including polycystic ovary syndrome, endometrial hyperplasia, adenomyosis, and endometriosis
  • Histological Features
  • Without atypia; A: mild glandular crowding, preserved stroma
  • With atypia; B and C: crowded glands, reduced stroma, cytologic atypia
  • PTEN mutation is a shared molecular feature with endometrioid carcinoma
  • Clinical Implications
  • Presents with abnormal uterine bleeding, especially in perimenopausal or postmenopausal women
  • Requires careful evaluation to exclude invasive carcinoma
  • Management:
  • Hysterectomy for patients not desiring fertility
  • High-dose progestins for fertility preservation in younger patients
  • Kumar, Vinay, MBBS, MD, FRCPath, Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 17, 602-635
Slide 24: Endometrial Carcinoma-Endometrioid
  • LO: Differentiate between type I and type II endometrial carcinomas in terms of risk factors, molecular basis, morphology, and outcomes, and relate type I to hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal carcinoma (Lynch syndrome).
  • Type I Endometrial Carcinoma (Endometrioid Type)
  • Risk Factors:
  • Mutations in mismatch repair genes and the tumor suppressor gene PTEN are early events in the stepwise development of endometrioid carcinoma.
  • Estrogen excess: obesity, PCOS, estrogen-producing tumors, unopposed estrogen therapy
  • Associated conditions: endometrial hyperplasia with atypia (EIN)
  • Age group: perimenopausal women (peak 55–65 years)
  • Molecular Basis:
  • PTEN mutations (Cowden syndrome)
  • Mismatch repair gene mutations (e.g., Lynch syndrome)
  • Occasional TP53 mutations (late event)
  • Morphology:
  • Glandular architecture resembling proliferative endometrium
  • Graded 1–3 based on differentiation:
  • Grade 1; A: well-differentiated glands
  • Grade 3; B: solid growth, marked atypia
  • Clinical Features:
  • Presents with postmenopausal bleeding
  • Slow progression, often localized
  • Good prognosis if detected early (90% 5-year survival in early stages)
  • Type I (endometrioid) endometrial carcinoma may arise in patients with Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) due to inherited mismatch repair gene mutations → microsatellite instability (MSI).
Slide 25: Endometrial Carcinoma-Serous
  • LO: Differentiate between type I and type II endometrial carcinomas in terms of risk factors, molecular basis, morphology, and outcomes, and relate type I to hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal carcinoma (Lynch syndrome).
  • Type II Endometrial Carcinoma (Serous Type):
  • Risk Factors:
  • Endometrial atrophy, not estrogen-related
  • Older age: typically 65–70 years
  • Not associated with obesity or hyperplasia
  • Molecular Basis:
  • TP53 mutations (early and central event)
  • Serous tumors are preceded by serous endometrial intraepithelial carcinoma (SEIC), in which TP53 mutations are often detected, indicating a central role for altered p53 function in the development of this form of endometrial carcinoma, which shows significant morphologic and biologic overlap with ovarian serous carcinoma.
  • Morphology:
  • Papillary structures, marked cytologic atypia; C: High-grade by definition
  • Diffuse p53 immunostaining due to mutant protein accumulation; D
  • Clinical Features:
  • Aggressive behavior
  • Often presents at advanced stage
  • Poor prognosis, dependent on staging
