Slide 27: Question 6:
  • A 52-year-old woman presents with abnormal uterine bleeding and pelvic pain that has progressively worsened over the past six months. On physical examination, an irregularly shaped mass is palpated in the lower abdomen. Pelvic ultrasound reveals a large, heterogeneous uterine mass. A biopsy is performed, and histologic examination shows spindle-shaped cells with marked nuclear atypia, high mitotic activity, and areas of necrosis.
  • Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
  • A. Endometrial hyperplasia B. Adenomyosis C. Leiomyoma D. Leiomyosarcoma E. Endometrial carcinoma
Slide 28: Question 5: Answer and Explanation
  • A 52-year-old female is having her annual physical examination. Her only complaint is occasional heavy menstrual periods. Her gynecologist palpated a mass in the uterus. She underwent a hysterectomy. Examination of the resected uterus revealed the pathologic lesion illustrated in the figure. Of the following, which is most characteristic of this condition?
  • Malignant transformation is common.
  • It is a very rare cause of infertility.
  • Microscopic examination would reveal interlocking fascicles of skeletal muscle
  • The condition is estrogen sensitive.
  • The condition is almost exclusively present in white females.
  • The condition is estrogen-sensitive (correct): Leiomyomas express estrogen (and progesterone) receptors; estradiol drives smooth-muscle proliferation, and they typically regress after menopause.
  • Malignant transformation is common: False — benign leiomyomas are not thought to transform into leiomyosarcoma; leiomyosarcoma is found in only ~0.5% of hysterectomies for presumed fibroids and arises independently.
  • It is a very rare cause of infertility: False — submucosal/intramural fibroids can impair implantation and fertility and increase pregnancy loss.
  • Microscopic examination would reveal interlocking fascicles of skeletal muscle: False — leiomyomas are composed of interlacing fascicles of smooth (not skeletal) muscle.
  • Almost exclusively present in white females: False — incidence is 2–3× higher in Black than white women.
Slide 29: Question 6: Answer and Explanation
  • A 52-year-old woman presents with abnormal uterine bleeding and pelvic pain that has progressively worsened over the past six months. On physical examination, an irregularly shaped mass is palpated in the lower abdomen. Pelvic ultrasound reveals a large, heterogeneous uterine mass. A biopsy is performed, and histologic examination shows spindle-shaped cells with marked nuclear atypia, high mitotic activity, and areas of necrosis.
  • Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
  • A. Endometrial hyperplasia B. Adenomyosis C. Leiomyoma D. Leiomyosarcoma E. Endometrial carcinoma
  • A. Endometrial hyperplasia: Glandular (epithelial) proliferation with increased gland-to-stroma ratio, not an atypical spindle-cell mass.
  • B. Adenomyosis: Benign endometrial glands/stroma within myometrium; no atypia or mitoses.
  • C. Leiomyoma: Benign — lacks significant atypia, has low mitotic activity, and no coagulative tumor-cell necrosis.
  • D. Leiomyosarcoma (correct): Matches all three malignant criteria.
  • E. Endometrial carcinoma: An epithelial (glandular) malignancy, not a spindle-cell tumor.

Notes:

The triad of spindle cells with marked nuclear atypia, high mitotic activity, and coagulative tumor-cell necrosis is diagnostic of leiomyosarcoma; the WHO/NCCN threshold is a spindle-cell proliferation with ≥2 of moderate–severe atypia, tumor cell necrosis, or mitotic index ≥10/10 HPF.

Slide 30: Uterine Leiomyoma (Fibroid)
  • LO: Compare benign and malignant uterine tumors (e.g., leiomyomas vs. leiomyosarcomas), including morphology, clinical course, and prognosis.
  • Most common tumors in women
  • Benign smooth muscle neoplasms; single or multiple
  • Estrogen and progesterone stimulate leiomyoma growth; tumors shrink after menopause
  • Associated with recurrent chromosomal abnormalities, including rearrangements of chromosomes 6 and 12 found in other benign neoplasms (e.g., endometrial polyps and lipomas)
  • Mutations in the MED12 gene; encodes a protein that regulates RNA polymerase II-mediated transcription, have been identified in up to 70% of leiomyomas
  • The mechanism by which MED12 mutations contribute to the development of leiomyomas is not understood.
Slide 31: Uterine Leiomyoma (Fibroid)-Morphology
  • LO: Compare benign and malignant uterine tumors (e.g., leiomyomas vs. leiomyosarcomas), including morphology, clinical course, and prognosis.
  • Gross:
  • Sharply circumscribed, firm gray-white masses with a characteristic whorled cut surface
  • Ranging from small nodules to large tumors
  • Types: embedded within the myometrium (intramural), lie beneath the endometrium (submucosal) or the serosa (subserosal; may extend out on attenuated stalks (pedunculated)
  • Subserosal may become attached to surrounding organs and develop a blood supply (parasitic leiomyomas
  • Submucosal leiomyomas may ulcerate and cause abnormal uterine bleeding (menometrorrhagia)
  • Submucosal leiomyomas are associated with increased risk for spontaneous abortion
  • Malignant transformation to leiomyosarcoma is extremely rare
  • Histologic examination:
  • Bundles of intersecting uniform smooth muscle cells (elongated nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm) similar in appearance to typical myometrium
  • Foci of fibrosis, calcification, and degenerative softening may be present

Notes:

Panel A shows a bisected uterus containing multiple well-circumscribed tan-white nodules distributed throughout the uterine wall. These nodules represent leiomyomas and are located submucosally, intramurally, and subserosally. Each mass displays a firm, whorled cut surface typical of smooth muscle tumors. Panel B presents a microscopic view of a leiomyoma composed of intersecting bundles of uniform, spindle-shaped smooth muscle cells with elongated nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm. There is minimal nuclear atypia and an absence of mitotic activity, confirming the benign nature of the tumor. These findings together illustrate the classic macroscopic and microscopic features of uterine fibroids, the most common benign tumors of the female reproductive tract.

Slide 32: Leiomyosarcoma
  • LO: Compare benign and malignant uterine tumors (e.g., leiomyomas vs. leiomyosarcomas), including morphology, clinical course, and prognosis.
  • Uncommon malignant neoplasms
  • Arise from the myometrium or endometrial stromal precursor cells
  • Almost always solitary and most often occur in postmenopausal women, in contrast to leiomyomas; leiomyomas are frequently multiple and usually arise before menopause
  • They have complex, highly variable karyotypes including chromosomal deletions
  • Like leiomyomas, they contain MED12 mutations but in a smaller subset (30%).
  • Morphology
  • Soft, hemorrhagic, necrotic masses
  • The histopathology is highly variable; from tumors resembling leiomyoma to wildly anaplastic neoplasms
  • The diagnostic features of leiomyosarcoma include tumor necrosis, cytologic atypia, and mitotic activity
  • Because increased mitotic activity is sometimes seen in benign smooth muscle tumors, particularly in young women, an assessment of all three features is necessary to make a diagnosis of malignancy
Slide 33: Leiomyoma vs Leiomyosarcoma
  • LO: Compare benign and malignant uterine tumors (e.g., leiomyomas vs. leiomyosarcomas), including morphology, clinical course, and prognosis.
  • Female Genital System and Breast

Kumar, Vinay, MBBS, MD, FRCPath, Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 17, 602-635

  • Leiomyomas
  • Leiomyosarcoma

Notes:

(A) A large hemorrhagic tumor distends the lower corpus and is flanked by two leiomyomas. (B) The tumor cells are irregular in size and have hyperchromatic nuclei. Numerous mitotic figures are present (arrows).

Gross image and histological section show hemorrhagic uterine leiomyosarcoma with irregular, hyperchromatic spindle cells and numerous mitotic figures. Gross image and histological section demonstrate features of uterine leiomyosarcoma. Left panel shows a large, infiltrative, hemorrhagic tumor distending the uterine corpus, with necrotic and blood-filled regions. It is flanked by two well-circumscribed, pale, firm, whorled nodules consistent with leiomyomas, indicating coexistence of benign and malignant smooth muscle tumors. Right panel presents a high-power microscopic view revealing densely packed spindle cells with elongated, pleomorphic, and hyperchromatic nuclei embedded in a fibrous stroma. Numerous mitotic figures, highlighted by arrows, are scattered throughout the field, indicative of high proliferative activity. The cytologic atypia, nuclear irregularity, and frequent mitoses are diagnostic hallmarks of leiomyosarcoma, distinguishing it from benign smooth muscle tumors like leiomyomas.

These tumors often recur following surgery and more than one-half eventually metastasize hematogenously to distant organs, such as the lungs, bone, and brain. Dissemination throughout the abdominal cavity is also encountered.

Slide 35: Question 7: Answer and Explanation
  • A 24-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with fever, lower abdominal pain, and vaginal discharge. Pelvic examination reveals cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness. Ultrasound shows bilateral adnexal masses with complex fluid collections. A laparoscopic examination reveals hemorrhagic, friable tissue and adhesions between the fallopian tubes and ovaries. A Gram stain of the cervical discharge is provided.
  • Which of the following is the most likely long-term complication of this patient’s condition?
  • A. Ovarian torsion B. Tubal ectopic pregnancy C. Endometrial hyperplasia D. Cervical carcinoma E. Polycystic ovary syndrome
  • This patient has pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) due to N. gonorrhoeae, leading to suppurative salpingitis.
  • The inflammation and subsequent adhesions between tubal plicae increase the risk of tubal ectopic pregnancy due to impaired ovum transport
  • Other options do not directly relate to tubal damage from PID

Notes:

Microscopic image the presence of intracellular Neisseria gonorrhoeae amongst numerous white blood cells (WBCs) known as polymorphonuclear leukocytes, or PMNs. N. Gonorrhoeae cells are pink diplococcal.

Slide 36: Inflammation of Fallopian Tubes
  • Discuss pelvic inflammatory disease and infections of the uterine tubes and endometrium: common pathogens, pathogenesis, morphology, and complications.
  • It is almost always caused by infection.
  • Suppurative salpingitis caused by any pyogenic organism
  • N. gonorrhoeae is the causative organism in more than 60% of cases
  • C. trachomatis is responsible for the remaining cases.
  • Tuberculous; rare in the USA, more common in endemic areas---- infertility.
  • C/P: fever, lower abdominal or pelvic pain, and pelvic masses due to distention of the tubes with exudate, inflammatory debris, or tuboovarian abscess
  • Adhesions form between the ovary and the tubes
  • Adhesions between the ovary and the tubal pilcae---increased risk of tubal ectopic pregnancy
  • Damage to or obstruction of the tubal lumina results in permanent sterility
  • Bilateral and asymmetric PID. A hemorrhagic inflammatory mass totally obscures the tube and ovary to the left of the uterus. The tube is adherent to the adjacent ovary on the other side.
  • Female Genital System and Breast

Slide 37: Question 8:
  • A 38-year-old woman with a BRCA1 mutation undergoes prophylactic salpingo-oophorectomy. Histological examination of the fimbriated end of the fallopian tube reveals atypical epithelial cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and strong p53 immunostaining. No invasive carcinoma is found.
  • Which of the following best describes the lesion identified?
  • A. Endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia B. Serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma C. Tuberculous salpingitis D. Follicular cyst E. Adenomyosis
Slide 38: Question 8: Answer
  • A 38-year-old woman with a BRCA1 mutation undergoes prophylactic salpingo-oophorectomy. Histological examination of the fimbriated end of the fallopian tube reveals atypical epithelial cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and strong p53 immunostaining. No invasive carcinoma is found.
  • Which of the following best describes the lesion identified?
  • A. Endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia B. Serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma C. Tuberculous salpingitis D. Follicular cyst E. Adenomyosis
  • A. Endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia: A precursor in the endometrium, not the tube.
  • B. Serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (correct): Fimbrial location, cytologic atypia, aberrant p53, no invasion.
  • C. Tuberculous salpingitis: Granulomatous inflammation with caseation, not atypical p53-positive epithelium.
  • D. Follicular cyst: A benign ovarian functional cyst lined by granulosa/theca cells.
  • E. Adenomyosis: Endometrial tissue within myometrium — wrong site and morphology.

Notes:

In a BRCA1 carrier undergoing risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy, atypical epithelial cells at the fimbriated end with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and strong (mutation-pattern) p53 staining, without invasion, define serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC) — the earliest recognizable precursor of high-grade serous carcinoma, driven by TP53 mutation.

Slide 39: Serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma
  • 1. Site of Origin for High-Grade Serous Carcinoma
  • STIC lesions in the fallopian tube, particularly at the fimbriated end, are now recognized as the precursor lesions for many high-grade serous carcinomas previously thought to originate in the ovary.
  • This has shifted the paradigm from “ovarian origin” to fallopian tube origin for these aggressive tumors.
  • 2. Molecular Features
  • >90% of STICs harbor TP53 mutations, similar to uterine serous carcinoma.
  • These mutations are a hallmark of high-grade serous neoplasia.
  • 3. Association with BRCA Mutations
  • STICs are frequently found in prophylactically removed fallopian tubes from women with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations.
  • Less commonly seen in women without known genetic risk factors.
  • 4. Clinical Implications
  • Prophylactic salpingo-oophorectomy in BRCA mutation carriers can detect STICs before invasive carcinoma develops.
  • Early identification may prevent progression to high-grade serous carcinoma involving the ovary, omentum, and peritoneal cavity.
  • 5. Histological Features
  • Atypical epithelial cells with:
  • High nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio
  • Strong p53 immunostaining
  • No evidence of stromal invasion in STIC.
  • Describe the embryologic/histologic components of the ovary (surface epithelium, germ cells, sex cord–stromal cells) as the basis for tumor classification.
  • Identify risk factors, hereditary cancer syndromes, and molecular mechanisms underlying epithelial, sex cord–stromal, and germ cell ovarian tumors.
Slide 40: Question 9:
  • A 22-year-old woman presents with irregular menstrual cycles, acne, and increased facial hair. BMI is 32 kg/m². Pelvic ultrasound reveals bilaterally enlarged ovaries with multiple subcortical cysts. Laboratory studies show elevated LH:FSH ratio and increased serum testosterone.
  • Which of the following best explains the pathophysiology of this patient’s condition?
  • A. Increased aromatase activity in granulosa cells B. Excessive androgen production due to dysregulated steroidogenesis C. Estrogen deficiency due to premature ovarian failure D. Autoimmune destruction of ovarian follicles E. Excessive FSH stimulation of theca cells
Slide 41: Question 9: Answer and Explanation
  • A 22-year-old woman presents with irregular menstrual cycles, acne, and increased facial hair. BMI is 32 kg/m². Pelvic ultrasound reveals bilaterally enlarged ovaries with multiple subcortical cysts. Laboratory studies show elevated LH:FSH ratio and increased serum testosterone.
  • Which of the following best explains the pathophysiology of this patient’s condition?
  • A. Increased aromatase activity in granulosa cells B. Excessive androgen production due to dysregulated steroidogenesis C. Estrogen deficiency due to premature ovarian failure D. Autoimmune destruction of ovarian follicles E. Excessive FSH stimulation of theca cells
  • A. Increased aromatase activity in granulosa cells: Aromatase converts androgens to estrogens; PCOS is associated with androgen excess, not increased estrogen synthesis.
  • B. Excessive androgen production due to dysregulated steroidogenesis: PCOS involves dysregulation of enzymes in androgen biosynthesis, leading to hyperandrogenism, anovulation, and polycystic ovaries.
  • C. Estrogen deficiency due to premature ovarian failure: PCOS patients often have normal or elevated estrogen levels.
  • D. Autoimmune destruction of ovarian follicles: This describes premature ovarian insufficiency, not PCOS.
  • E. Excessive FSH stimulation of theca cells: Theca cells respond to LH, not FSH, and LH is elevated in PCOS.
Slide 42: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)
  • LO: Explain the pathophysiology and clinicopathologic features of functional disorders, including polycystic ovary syndrome, endometrial hyperplasia, adenomyosis, and endometriosis.
  • Clinicopathological Features:
  • A complex endocrine disorder
  • Characterized by signs and symptoms of androgen excess and ovulatory dysfunction (e.g., menstrual abnormalities, hirsutism, polycystic ovaries, chronic anovulation, and decreased fertility)
  • The most common endocrine/metabolic disorders of women
  • First present at puberty
  • The etiology of PCOS involves both environmental and genetic factors
  • Dysregulation of enzymes involved in androgen biosynthesis, resulting in excessive androgen production
  • Patients are at increased risk for metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, cerebrovascular accidents, and endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma
  • The ovaries are twice the normal size, and studded with subcortical cysts (double the no of follicles in normal ovaries); size is 0.5 to 1.5 cm in diameter
  • Ovaries contain numerous ‘cysts’; these are not cysts but egg-containing follicles that did not develop normally due to hormonal imbalances.
  • Thickened, fibrotic ovarian capsule overlying cystic follicles lined by granulosa cells with a hyperplastic luteinized theca interna
  • Absence of corpora lutea due to anovulation
Slide 43: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)-Clinicopathological-Cont
  • LO: Explain the pathophysiology and clinicopathologic features of functional disorders, including polycystic ovary syndrome, endometrial hyperplasia, adenomyosis, and endometriosis.
  • Clinicopathological Features:
  • The ovaries are twice the normal size, and studded with subcortical cysts (double the no of follicles in normal ovaries); size is 0.5 to 1.5 cm in diameter
  • Ovaries contain numerous ‘cysts’; these are not cysts but egg-containing follicles that did not develop normally due to hormonal imbalances.
  • Thickened, fibrotic ovarian capsule overlying cystic follicles lined by granulosa cells with a hyperplastic luteinized theca interna
  • Absence of corpora lutea due to anovulation

Slide 44: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)-Pathophysiology
  • LO: Explain the pathophysiology and clinicopathologic features of functional disorders, including polycystic ovary syndrome, endometrial hyperplasia, adenomyosis, and endometriosis.
  • Pathophysiology: (↑LH, ↓ FSH, ↑ androstenedione, ↓estradiol, ↑estrone)
  • 1. Underlying Neuroendocrine Dysregulation
  • The hypothalamic-pituitary axis in PCOS is intrinsically dysregulated, possibly due to genetic and environmental factors.
  • This leads to increased GnRH pulse frequency, which favors LH secretion over FSH; LH:FSH ratio (often >2:1)
  • 2. Androgen Feedback Loop
  • LH stimulates theca cells → ovarian thecal overactivity--↑ androgen production (e.g., testosterone, androstenedione)--- ↓ FSH (negative feedback loop)
  • ↓ FSH → Impaired Granulosa Cell Function (↓ aromatase activity in granulosa cells); Androgens are not efficiently converted to estrogens → follicular arrest (first meiosis) and anovulation
  • This selective feedback maintains or further increases GnRH pulse frequency, reinforcing LH dominance.
  • 3. Peripheral Conversion of Androgens to Estrogens
  • Androgens → estrone via aromatization in adipose tissue
  • Leads to chronic low-level estrogen without progesterone → endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma
  • 4. Insulin Resistance and Hyperinsulinemia
  • Insulin acts synergistically with LH to stimulate theca cells → more androgen production.
  • Insulin also reduces SHBG (Sex Hormone Binding Globulin) → ↑ free androgens, which perpetuate the feedback loop.
  • 5. Absence of Progesterone Feedback
  • Due to anovulation, there is no corpus luteum → no progesterone---- menstrual irregularity and unopposed estrogen effects.
  • Progesterone normally slows GnRH pulses; its absence allows faster GnRH pulsate
Slide 45: Question 10:
  • A 28-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of 8 months of amenorrhea. She reports hot flashes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. She has no significant past medical history and takes no medications. Her menarche was at age 13, and her cycles had been regular until the past year. She denies hirsutism or acne. BMI is 22 kg/m². Pelvic exam shows normal external genitalia with reduced vaginal rugae. A pregnancy test is negative. Laboratory studies show:
  • Serum FSH: markedly elevated
  • Serum LH: elevated
  • Serum estradiol: decreased
  • Serum testosterone: normal
  • Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
  • A. Premature ovarian failure (primary ovarian insufficiency) B. Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) C. Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea D. Asherman syndrome E. Hyperprolactinemia
Slide 46: Question 10: Answer
  • A 28-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of 8 months of amenorrhea. She reports hot flashes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. She has no significant past medical history and takes no medications. Her menarche was at age 13, and her cycles had been regular until the past year. She denies hirsutism or acne. BMI is 22 kg/m². Pelvic exam shows normal external genitalia with reduced vaginal rugae. A pregnancy test is negative. Laboratory studies show:
  • Serum FSH: markedly elevated
  • Serum LH: elevated
  • Serum estradiol: decreased
  • Serum testosterone: normal
  • Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
  • A. Premature ovarian failure (primary ovarian insufficiency) B. Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) C. Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea D. Asherman syndrome E. Hyperprolactinemia
Slide 47: Question 10: Explanation
  • Premature ovarian failure:
  • Ovarian failure before age 40, characterized by amenorrhea, hypoestrogenic symptoms (hot flashes, vaginal atrophy), elevated FSH/LH (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism), and low estradiol [ovarian (hypergonadotropic) cause]
  • Normal BMI and absence of androgen excess further support the diagnosis.
  • B. Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS):
  • Typically presents with obesity, hirsutism, acne, infertility, and oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea.
  • Lab findings include elevated LH/FSH ratio (>2:1), increased androgens, and normal/low estrogen
  • This patient lacks hyperandrogenic features and has low estrogen with high FSH, not typical of PCOS
  • C. Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea:
  • Seen in patients with low BMI, excessive exercise, or stress.
  • Characterized by low or normal FSH, LH, and estrogen due to suppressed GnRH secretion.
  • D. Asherman syndrome: Outflow-tract/endometrial scarring
  • Intrauterine adhesions following curettage or infection cause amenorrhea, but systemic hypoestrogenic symptoms (hot flashes, vaginal atrophy) are absent
  • Gonadotropins and estradiol are normal; SH/LH would not be markedly elevated.
  • E. Hyperprolactinemia:
  • Causes galactorrhea, headaches, or visual field defects due to pituitary adenoma
  • Labs would show low/normal FSH/LH, low estrogen due to GnRH suppression, not the high FSH/LH seen here
Slide 48: POF vs PCOS

| Feature | Premature Ovarian Failure (POF/Primary Ovarian Insufficiency) | Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS) |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Age | <40 (pathologic) | Usually reproductive age |

| Symptoms | Amenorrhea, hot flashes, vaginal dryness, infertility | Oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea, infertility, obesity, hirsutism, acne |

| Hormones | ↑ FSH, ↑ LH, ↓ Estrogen, normal testosterone | ↑ LH/FSH ratio (>2:1), ↑ Androgens, normal/low Estrogen |

| Pathophysiology | Loss of ovarian follicles → ovarian failure | Chronic anovulation + hyperandrogenism |

| Long-term risk | Osteoporosis, CVD | Metabolic syndrome, endometrial hyperplasia/carcinoma |

| Ovarian morphology | Atrophic ovaries | Enlarged, polycystic ovaries |

Slide 49: Question 11:
  • A 58-year-old woman presents with abdominal bloating, early satiety, and increasing abdominal girth. Physical exam reveals ascites and a palpable adnexal mass. CA-125 is elevated. Imaging shows bilateral complex ovarian masses with peritoneal implants. Biopsy reveals high-grade serous carcinoma.
  • Which of the following features is most characteristic of this malignancy?
  • A. KRAS mutation and unilateral cystic mass B. TP53 mutation and bilateral solid-cystic masses C. Estrogen-secreting tumor with endometrial hyperplasia D. Mature tissues from all three germ layers E. Mucin-secreting cells with pseudomyxoma peritonei
Slide 50: Question 11: Answer and Explanation
  • A 58-year-old woman presents with abdominal bloating, early satiety, and increasing abdominal girth. Physical exam reveals ascites and a palpable adnexal mass. CA-125 is elevated. Imaging shows bilateral complex ovarian masses with peritoneal implants. Biopsy reveals high-grade serous carcinoma.
  • Which of the following features is most characteristic of this malignancy?
  • A. KRAS mutation and unilateral cystic mass B. TP53 mutation and bilateral solid-cystic masses C. Estrogen-secreting tumor with endometrial hyperplasia D. Mature tissues from all three germ layers E. Mucin-secreting cells with pseudomyxoma peritonei
  • A. KRAS mutation and unilateral cystic mass: KRAS mutations are typical of low-grade serous or mucinous tumors, not high-grade serous carcinoma.
  • B. TP53 mutation and bilateral solid-cystic masses: High-grade serous carcinoma is the most common and aggressive ovarian cancer. It often presents bilaterally, with TP53 mutations in >95% of cases.
  • C. Estrogen-secreting tumor with endometrial hyperplasia: Describes granulosa cell tumors, not epithelial ovarian carcinoma.
  • D. Mature tissues from all three germ layers: Describes mature teratoma, a benign germ cell tumor.
  • E. Mucin-secreting cells with pseudomyxoma peritonei: Most cases of pseudomyxoma peritonei originate from appendiceal tumors, not primary ovarian mucinous carcinoma.
Slide 51: Ovarian Tumors-Overview
  • LO: Describe the embryologic/histologic components of the ovary (surface epithelium, germ cells, sex cord–stromal cells) as the basis for tumor classification.
  • Ovarian malignancy is the second most common gynecologic malignancy (following endometrial carcinoma)
  • Tumors of the ovary arise from any of the three cell types in the normal ovary: (1) multipotent surface/fallopian tube epithelium; (2) pluripotent germ cells; and (3) sex cord–stromal cells.
  • The great majority of malignant ovarian tumors are of epithelial cell origin; 90%
  • Germ cell and sex cord–stromal cell tumors are less frequent, 10% of malignant tumors of the ovary
Slide 52: Ovarian Tumors-Classification
  • LO: Describe the embryologic/histologic components of the ovary (surface epithelium, germ cells, sex cord–stromal cells) as the basis for tumor classification.
  • Most primary ovarian neoplasms arise from müllerian epithelium:
  • Classified based on differentiation and extent of proliferation of the epithelium
  • Three major histologic types: serous, mucinous, and endometrioid
  • Benign:
  • 80% of surface epithelial tumors
  • occur in young women between 20 and 45 years of age
  • Frequently cystic and may have an accompanying stromal component
  • Borderline:
  • Occur at older ages
  • Majority behave in a benign manner, some recur, and a few progress to carcinoma
  • Malignant tumors:
  • Between 45 and 65 years of age and may be cystic (cystadenocarcinoma) or solid (carcinoma).
  • Types I and II
  • Type I carcinoma: low-grade tumor; in association with borderline tumors or endometriosis and includes low-grade serous, endometrioid, and mucinous tumors
  • Type II carcinoma : high-grade serous carcinoma that arises from serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma
  • Female Genital System and Breast

Slide 53: Ovarian Tumors-Risk Factors
  • LO: Identify risk factors, hereditary cancer syndromes, and molecular mechanisms underlying epithelial, sex cord–stromal, and germ cell ovarian tumors.
  • Important risk factors:
  • increasing age
  • early menarche/late menopause
  • Nulliparity
  • family history
  • germline mutations in certain tumor suppressor genes
  • Prolonged use of oral contraceptives reduces the risk due to suppression of ovulation.
  • Around 5% to 10% of ovarian cancers are familial, associated with mutations in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 tumor suppressor genes (also mutated in a subset of hereditary breast cancer).
Slide 54: Ovarian Tumors: Serous Tumors
  • LO: Identify risk factors, hereditary cancer syndromes, and molecular mechanisms underlying epithelial, sex cord–stromal, and germ cell ovarian tumors.
  • Serous Tumors
  • Most common of the ovarian epithelial tumors
  • Benign and borderline tumors are most common between 20 and 45 years of age
  • Serous carcinomas generally occur later in life except in familial cases.
  • Low-grade tumors arise from benign or borderline lesions and progress slowly in a stepwise manner to become invasive carcinoma.
  • Low-grade tumors have mutations in the KRAS, BRAF, or ERBB2 oncogenes and wild-type TP53 alleles
  • High-grade serous tumors arise in the fimbriated end of the fallopian tube via serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma
  • High-grade serous tumors have TP53 mutations; 95% of cases
  • Almost all ovarian carcinomas arising in women with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations are high-grade serous carcinomas with TP53 mutations
Slide 55: Ovarian Tumors: Serous Tumors- Gross Pathology
  • LO: Describe the embryologic/histologic components of the ovary (surface epithelium, germ cells, sex cord–stromal cells) as the basis for tumor classification.
  • Morphology:
  • large, spherical to ovoid, cystic structures up to 30 to 40 cm in diameter.
  • About 25% of benign tumors are bilateral.
  • In benign tumors, the serosal covering is smooth and glistening.
  • By contrast, the surface of adenocarcinoma has nodular irregularities where tumor has invaded the serosa.
  • Single cavity, or multiple cavities divided by multiple septa into multiloculated masses
  • The cystic spaces are filled with a clear, serous fluid.
  • Protruding into the cystic cavities are papillary projections (malignant)

These papillary projections are non-invasive and consistent with low-grade tumor growth. A metric scale beside the specimen indicates a cyst diameter of approximately 5 cm. Slide 56: Ovarian Tumors: Serous Tumors- Histopathology
  • LO: Describe the embryologic/histologic components of the ovary (surface epithelium, germ cells, sex cord–stromal cells) as the basis for tumor classification.
  • Microscopic:
  • Benign tumors (serous cystadenoma; A):
  • A single layer of columnar epithelial cells that line the cyst(s)
  • Cells are ciliated
  • Concentric calcifications (psammoma bodies) are common; not specific
  • High-grade carcinoma; C:
  • The cells are markedly atypical
  • Papillary formations are complex and multilayered
  • Malignant cells invade the ovarian stroma
  • low-grade carcinoma: less cytologic atypia
  • Borderline tumors (B): less cytologic atypia, no stromal invasion; peritoneal implants are “noninvasive”
  • Ovarian serous tumors, both low and high grade spread to the peritoneal surfaces and omentum-----commonly associated with ascites

Notes:

Panel A shows a serous cystadenoma composed of fibrous stroma supporting thin, branched papillae lined by a single layer of non-stratified columnar epithelium with minimal cytologic atypia. Panel B displays a borderline serous tumor with increased architectural complexity including more numerous and densely packed papillae. The lining epithelium is stratified, with multilayered nuclei and mild cytologic atypia, but without stromal invasion. Panel C shows high-grade serous carcinoma, characterized by marked nuclear pleomorphism, high mitotic activity, and destructive stromal invasion. Tumor cells appear in complex papillary and solid arrangements, and adjacent desmoplastic stroma shows inflammatory response. The images reflect a histologic continuum from benign to borderline to malignant serous neoplasia of the ovary.

Slide 57: Question 12:
  • A 45-year-old woman undergoes surgery for a large ovarian mass. The gross picture of the mass is provided. Histology shows epithelial stratification, nuclear atypia, and stromal invasion. Genetic testing reveals a KRAS mutation.
  • Which of the following best describes the tumor type?
  • A. High-grade serous carcinoma B. Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma C. Endometrioid carcinoma D. Mature teratoma E. Clear cell carcinoma
Slide 58: Question 12: Answer and Explanation
  • A 45-year-old woman undergoes surgery for a large ovarian mass. The gross picture of the mass is provided. Histology shows epithelial stratification, nuclear atypia, and stromal invasion. Genetic testing reveals a KRAS mutation.
  • Which of the following best describes the tumor type?
  • A. High-grade serous carcinoma B. Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma C. Endometrioid carcinoma D. Mature teratoma E. Clear cell carcinoma
  • A. High-grade serous carcinoma: Typically bilateral, associated with TP53 mutations and STIC lesions.
  • B. Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma: Characterized by mucin-secreting epithelium, KRAS mutations, and multiloculated cysts.
  • C. Endometrioid carcinoma: Shows glandular structures resembling endometrium; often associated with PTEN mutations.
  • D. Mature teratoma: Contains differentiated tissues from all germ layers; usually benign.
  • E. Clear cell carcinoma: Rare, associated with endometriosis; histology shows clear cytoplasm.
Slide 59: Ovarian Tumors: Mucinous Tumors
  • LO: Identify risk factors, hereditary cancer syndromes, and molecular mechanisms underlying epithelial, sex cord–stromal, and germ cell ovarian tumors.
  • Mucinous Tumors
  • Two features distinguish them from serous tumors:
  • Mucin-secreting cells
  • Mucinous tumors are less likely to be malignant
  • Overall, only 10% of mucinous tumors are malignant; another 10% are borderline, and 80% are benign.
  • Occur in middle adult life and are rare before puberty and after menopause
  • Mutation of the KRAS proto-oncogene is a consistent genetic alteration in all mucinous tumors of the ovary.
Slide 60: Ovarian Tumors: Mucinous Tumors-Morphology
  • LO: Describe the embryologic/histologic components of the ovary (surface epithelium, germ cells, sex cord–stromal cells) as the basis for tumor classification.
  • Morphology:
  • Less bilateral; DDX Krukenberg tumor
  • Well-circumscribed multicystic masses with smooth inner surface, and abundant mucinous content (yellow tan)
  • Mucin-producing epithelial cells line the cysts; a single layer of columnar epithelium with basal nuclei and apical mucin; no stratification, atypia, or stromal invasion
  • Malignant tumors are characterized by solid areas of growth, stratification of lining cells, cytologic atypia, and stromal invasion
  • Implantation of mucinous tumor cells in the peritoneum---copious amounts of mucin is called pseudomyxoma peritonei; caused by metastases from the gastrointestinal tract, usually the appendix
  • Female Genital System and Breast

Notes:

Krukenberg tumor is a metastatic ovarian tumor, classically bilateral, characterized by mucin-producing signet-ring cells and most commonly arising from diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma.

Slide 61: Ovarian Tumors: Endometrioid and Clear Cell
  • LO: Describe the embryologic/histologic components of the ovary (surface epithelium, germ cells, sex cord–stromal cells) as the basis for tumor classification. Identify risk factors, hereditary cancer syndromes, and molecular mechanisms underlying epithelial, sex cord–stromal, and germ cell ovarian tumors.
  • Endometrioid Tumors
  • solid or cystic
  • In association with endometriosis
  • Microscopic examination: tubular glands, similar to those of the endometrium, within the lining of cystic spaces
  • Usually malignant; benign and borderline forms exist
  • They are bilateral in about 20% of cases, and 15% to 20% of women with these ovarian tumors have a concomitant endometrial carcinoma.
  • Similar to endometrioid-type carcinoma of the endometrium, endometrioid carcinomas of the ovary frequently have mutations in the PTEN tumor suppressor gene and other genes that act to upregulate PI3K-AKT signaling
  • Clear Cell Carcinoma
  • A rare subtype of epithelial ovarian tumors
  • Benign and borderline are rare
  • Clear cell carcinomas are composed of large epithelial cells with abundant clear cytoplasm (similar to gestational endometrium)
  • In association with endometriosis or endometrioid carcinoma of the ovary
  • Most commonly mutated genes ( PIK3CA, ARID1A, KRAS, PTEN, and TP53 ) are shared with endometrioid carcinoma
Slide 62: Question 13:
  • A 20-year-old woman presents with acute pelvic pain. Imaging reveals a 6 cm ovarian mass with calcifications and fat. Surgical removal reveals a cyst filled with hair and sebaceous material. Histology shows skin, cartilage, and respiratory epithelium.
  • Which of the following best describes this tumor?
  • A. Immature teratoma B. Dysgerminoma C. Mature cystic teratoma D. Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor E. Endometrioid carcinoma
Slide 63: Question 13: Answer and Explanation
  • A 20-year-old woman presents with acute pelvic pain. Imaging reveals a 6 cm ovarian mass with calcifications and fat. Surgical removal reveals a cyst filled with hair and sebaceous material. Histology shows skin, cartilage, and respiratory epithelium.
  • Which of the following best describes this tumor?
  • A. Immature teratoma B. Dysgerminoma C. Mature cystic teratoma D. Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor E. Endometrioid carcinoma
  • A. Immature teratoma: Contains embryonic tissue, especially neuroepithelium; malignant.
  • B. Dysgerminoma: Uniform germ cells; radiosensitive; lacks differentiated tissues.
  • C. Mature cystic teratoma: Benign germ cell tumor with mature tissues from ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm.
  • D. Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor: Sex cord–stromal tumor; may cause virilization.
  • E. Endometrioid carcinoma: Glandular epithelial tumor resembling endometrium.
Slide 64: Ovarian Teratomas
  • LO: Describe the embryologic/histologic components of the ovary (surface epithelium, germ cells, sex cord–stromal cells) as the basis for tumor classification. Identify risk factors, hereditary cancer syndromes, and molecular mechanisms underlying epithelial, sex cord–stromal, and germ cell ovarian tumors.
  • Teratomas account for 15–20% of ovarian tumors; >90% are benign, most commonly found in young women.
  • They are classified into:
  • Mature (benign);
  • Immature (malignant)
  • Monodermal or highly specialized
  • Mature (Benign) Teratomas (dermoid cysts):
  • Mature tissues from all three germ layers:
  • Ectoderm: skin, hair, neural tissue
  • Mesoderm: bone, cartilage, muscle
  • Endoderm: respiratory or gastrointestinal epithelium
  • Gross features:
  • Cystic structure filled with sebaceous material and hair
  • May contain teeth, bone, cartilage
  • Usually unilateral (90%), more common on the right side
  • Rarely exceeds 10 cm
  • Complications:
  • Ovarian torsion (10–15% of cases)
  • Malignant transformation (∼1%, usually to squamous cell carcinoma)
  • Paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis (rare, associated with neural tissue)
  • Female Genital System and Breast

Slide 65: Ovarian Teratomas: Immature (Malignant Teratomas)
  • LO: Describe the embryologic/histologic components of the ovary (surface epithelium, germ cells, sex cord–stromal cells) as the basis for tumor classification. Identify risk factors, hereditary cancer syndromes, and molecular mechanisms underlying epithelial, sex cord–stromal, and germ cell ovarian tumors.
  • Immature (Malignant) Teratomas
  • Found in prepubertal adolescents and young women (mean age: 18)
  • Solid and bulky on gross examination
  • Composed of immature fetal-like tissues, especially:
  • Neuroepithelium
  • Cartilage
  • Bone
  • Histological features:
  • Primitive neuroepithelial tubules
  • Hyperchromatic, densely packed cells
  • Rosette-like structures
  • Prognosis:
  • Risk of metastasis correlates with the amount of immature neuroepithelium

Slide 68: Question 15:
  • A 55-year-old woman presents with vaginal bleeding. Pelvic ultrasound reveals a unilateral ovarian mass. A photomicrograph of an endometrial biopsy is provided. Histologic examination of the ovarian mass reveals Call-Exner bodies and cells with coffee-bean nuclei.
  • Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
  • A. Granulosa cell tumor
  • B. Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor
  • C. Serous cystadenocarcinoma
  • D. Immature teratoma
  • E. Dysgerminoma
Slide 69: Question 15: Answer and Explanation
  • A 55-year-old woman presents with vaginal bleeding. Pelvic ultrasound reveals a unilateral ovarian mass. A photomicrograph of an endometrial biopsy is provided. Histologic examination of the ovarian mass reveals Call-Exner bodies and cells with coffee-bean nuclei.
  • Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
  • A. Granulosa cell tumor
  • B. Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor
  • C. Serous cystadenocarcinoma
  • D. Immature teratoma
  • E. Dysgerminoma
  • A. Granulosa cell tumor (correct): Call-Exner bodies + coffee-bean grooved nuclei + estrogen effect.
  • B. Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor: Sex cord–stromal but typically androgen-secreting (virilization); shows tubules/Leydig cells with Reinke crystals, not Call-Exner bodies.
  • C. Serous cystadenocarcinoma: Epithelial tumor with papillae/psammoma bodies, no Call-Exner bodies or nuclear grooves.
  • D. Immature teratoma: Germ cell tumor with immature (usually neuroectodermal) tissue; occurs in young patients.
  • E. Dysgerminoma: Germ cell tumor with uniform cells, fibrous septa, and lymphocytic infiltrate — no Call-Exner bodies.

Notes:

An ovarian mass with Call-Exner bodies (microfollicular structures with eosinophilic material) and cells with grooved "coffee-bean" nuclei is diagnostic of an adult granulosa cell tumor. These are estrogen-secreting sex cord–stromal tumors, explaining the postmenopausal bleeding and endometrial changes (hyperplasia/carcinoma) on biopsy

Slide 70: Granulosa Cell Tumor
  • Granulosa cell tumor (GCT) of the ovary belongs to the category of sex cord-stromal tumors that show differentiation towards granulosa cells of the ovarian follicle. There are two subtypes - adult GCT and juvenile GCT.
  • Adult GCT, mostly seen in peri- and postmenopausal women, accounts for 95% of all GCTs and makes up 1-2% of all ovarian tumors--Postmenopausal bleeding, breast tenderness, pelvic mass
  • Juvenile GCT, which occurs in children and younger women (<30 yrs), makes up the remainder 5% of all GCTs--precocious puberty, breast development and vaginal bleeding in toddlers
  • Call-Exner bodies are to granulosa cell tumors what keratin pearls are to squamous cell carcinoma: they are a morphologic clue showing the tumor is attempting to recapitulate its tissue of origin (follicular differentiation.
  • Small, bland, cuboidal to polygonal cells arranged in various patterns. Call-Exner bodies (Red Arrow): small follicle-like structures, filled with eosinophilic material. The cells may show nuclear grooves (coffee bean nuclei).
  • https://ilovepathology.com/granulosa-cell-tumor-ovary/

Slide 2: Learning Objectives

Slide 3: Perineum
  • The urogenital triangle is the anterior triangular region of the diamond-shaped perineum.
  • In anatomical position, it is oriented in a horizontal plane & contains the urethra and external genitalia.
  • The anal triangle is the posterior triangular region
  • In anatomical position, It is oriented in a plane that is almost vertical and contains the anal canal, anus, external anal sphincter, inferior rectal nerve (branch of pudendal nerve), and the fat-filled ischiorectal fossa.
Slide 4: Urogenital Triangle: Perineal Membrane
  • Perineal membrane: thin fibromuscular horizontal layer with fibers running parallel to pelvic diaphragm (i.e., levator ani), divides urogenital triangle into a deep (superior to membrane) & superficial (inferior to membrane) pouch
Slide 5: Perineum Overview
Slide 6: Perineum Overview (cont.)
Slide 7: Ischioanal (Ischiorectal) Fossa
  • Fossa filled with fat, poorly vascularized.
  • Allows for expansion of the anal canal during defecation & accommodates the fetus during childbirth.
  • Infections from one of the fossae can spread to the other & into the urogenital triangle.
  • Contents: Fat, pudendal nerves and vessels giving the inferior rectal nerve & vessels
Slide 8: Male Surface Anatomy

Notes:

This is a circumcised penis

Slide 9: Female Surface Anatomy

Notes:

Remember the round ligament inserts into the skin of the labia.

Slide 10: Female & Male Superficial Pouch
  • Male: Bulb & crura (attached) of the penis give rise to erectile sinuses of the penis – corpus spongiosum & corpora cavernosa (free), respectively.
  • Female: Bulb of the vestibule & crura (attached) give rise to erectile sinuses of clitoris – glans clitoris & corpora cavernosa (free) respectively.
Slide 11: Female & Male Superficial Pouch: Erectile Tissue
  • Root/attached components: sit/attach to the perineal membrane & are the bulb and crus.
  • Free components: corpora cavernosa - body of the clitoris (F) & body of the penis (M), and corpus spongiosum –glans clitoris (F) and glans penis (M).
Slide 12: Male Superficial Pouch
  • Superficial pouch contains external genitalia & associated skeletal muscles: bulbospongiosus, ischiocavernosus, & superficial transverse perineal muscles. Because of their action during urination/erection, these muscles are generally more developed in males.
  • Sup. transverse perineal muscles: provide a firm base for the penis during erection
  • Bulbospongiosus: aids in emptying of urine/semen.
  • Ishiocavernosus: force blood from crura to corpora cavernosa, increasing turgidity of penis.
Slide 13: Female Superficial Pouch
  • Superficial pouch contains external genitalia & associated skeletal muscles, including bulbospongiosus, ischiocavernosus, & superficial transverse perineal muscles. Muscles cover erectile tissue.
  • Sup. transverse perineal muscle: support pelvic floor, fix perineal body
  • Bulbospongiosus: “sphincter” of vagina aids in erection, compresses greater vestibular gland.
  • Ishiocavernosus: forces blood from crura to corpora cavernosa, maintains erection of clitoris.
Slide 14: Male & Female Deep Pouch
  • Fat of the ischioanal fossae
  • Dorsal vessels of penis/clitoris from the internal pudendal a.
  • Dorsal nerve of penis/clitoris from the pudendal nerve
  • Deep transverse perineal m
  • Sphincter urethrae
  • Membranous urethra
  • Bulbourethral glands
  • openings for urethra & vagina
  • Urethrovaginal sphincter
Slide 15: Nerves of the Perineum

Notes:

Observe that the pudendal nerve splits in Alcock's canal(pudendal canal) into the inferior rectal, perineal, and dorsal nerve of the penis (clitoris). The perineal further splits into deep muscular branches and superficial cutaneous branches.

Slide 16: Arteries of the Perineum
  • Inferior rectal a. to the anal canal inferior to the pectinate line, anal sphincter & peri-anal skin
  • Perineal a. to superficial perineal muscles
  • Posterior labial a. to skin of posterior labia
  • A. of bulb of vestibule to bulb of vestibular bulbs and greater vestibular glands
  • Deep a of clitoris to crura of clitoris
  • Dorsal a of clitoris to glans of clitoris
  • Posterior scrotal a to skin of posterior scrotum
  • A. of bulb of penis to supply bulb, penile urethra, corpus spongiosum, bulbourethral glands
  • deep a of penis - travels through the center of each corpus cavernosum; gives off straight and helicine aa, which open directly into the sinusoids of the corpora.
  • dorsal a of penis to corpora
  • superficial external pudendal a to anterior scrotum
Slide 17: Innervation of Pelvis & Perineum
  • Sensory & motor innervation of skin, skeletal muscle
  • Somatic division of PNS: sacral plexus (L4-S4)
  • Nerve to obturator internus (L5-S1)
  • Nerve to piriformis (S1-S2)
  • Nerve to levator ani (S4, S5)
  • Nerve to coccygeus (S4, S5 )
  • Pudendal nerve (S2-S4) (perineum)
  • Motor innervation of viscera
  • Autonomic division of PNS: inferior hypogastric plexus
  • Sympathetic innervation
  • Lumbar & sacral splanchnics: effects – vasoconstriction, contraction of internal urethral (male) & anal sphincters, stimulate glandular secretion, ejaculation (male)
  • Parasympathetic innervation
  • Pelvic splanchnics (S2-S4): effects – vasodilation, contraction of the detrusor, engorgement of erectile tissue.
Slide 18: Autonomic Regulation of Sexual Function
  • Erection: parasympathetic (S2-4 via pelvic splanchnic nn)
  • Emission: sympathetic (L1-2)
  • Smooth muscle contraction of the ductus deferens to move sperm into the urethra. Contractions of seminal vesicles, prostate, and bulbourethral glands secrete seminal fluid into the urethra.
  • Ejaculation:
  • Sympathetic (L1-2): rhythmic contraction of smooth muscle in the ductus deferens & urethra; closure of internal urethral sphincter. Somatic (S2-4, pudendal n): contraction of bulbospongiosus & ischiocavernosus muscles compress the bases of the penile erectile tissue.
  • Point = Parasympathetic = Erection
  • Shoot = Sympathetic = Ejaculation
Slide 19: Pudendal Nerve Block
  • Pudendal nerve:
  • Passes out of the pelvis via the greater sciatic foramen & around the sacrospinous ligament into the lesser sciatic foramen, where it enters the pudendal (Alcock's) canal; provides somatic innervation (S2-S4) to the skin & skeletal muscles of the perineum & gives rise to inferior rectal (anal), perineal, labial, & dorsal clitoral nerve branches.
  • To relieve perineal pain during childbirth, pudendal nerve block anesthesia may be performed by injecting a local anesthetic agent into the tissues surrounding the pudendal nerve.
  • To abolish sensation from the anterior part of the perineum, an ilioinguinal nerve block is performed.
Slide 20: Male Urethral Rupture
  • Straddle injury: rupture of the spongy urethra below the perineal membrane. Urine extravasates to the scrotum, penis, superficial perineum, and lower anterior abdominal wall.
  • Pelvic fractures: rupture of the membranous (intermediate part) of the urethra. Urine extravasates to the deep perineal pouch.

Pelvic Infections TBL reading (1).pdf TBL-STI · Week 3

Canvas course 70351, file 23741671 (pdf, 0.6 MB); session TBL-STI (Week 3, 9/4/2026: TBL: Sexually Transmitted Infections). Text extracted verbatim on 2026-09-26 for REPRO-PLAN P1.2 (12 pages; 0 image-only or title/disclosure pages omitted).

Page 1

Ulcerative Infections:

Genital ulcer disease manifests as a breach in the skin or mucosa of the genitalia, usually

caused by a sexually transmitted infection. Of these infections, herpes simplex virus type 2

(HSV-2) is the most common etiology in most geographic areas, followed by syphilis and

chancroid.

Herpes Simplex Virus

Genital herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection is common ulcerative lesion, and may involve the vulva, vagina, or

cervix. HSVs are DNA viruses that include two serotypes, HSV-1 and HSV-2. HSV-1 typically results in perioral

infection, whereas HSV-2 usually involves genital mucosa and skin; however, depending on sexual practices, HSV-1

may be detected in the genital region and HSV-2 may cause oral infections as well.

By 40 years of age, approximately 30% of women are seropositive for antibodies against HSV-2.

Primary outbreaks are often asymptomatic, however about one-third of newly infected individuals are

symptomatic. Lesions typically develop 3 to 7 days after transmission and are often associated with systemic

symptoms such as fever, malaise, and tender inguinal lymph nodes. The earliest lesions usually consist of red

papules that progress to vesicles and then to painful coalescent ulcers with an erythematous base. The lesions are

easily visible on vulvar skin and mucosa, while cervical and vaginal lesions present with purulent discharge and

pelvic pain. Lesions around the urethra may cause painful urination and urine retention. The vesicles and ulcers

contain numerous viral particles, accounting for the high transmission rate during active infection. The mucosal

and cutaneous lesions heal spontaneously in 1 to 3 weeks, but during the acute infection, the virus migrates to the

regional lumbosacral nerve ganglia and establishes a latent infection. Because of viral latency, HSV infections

persist indefinitely, and any decrease in immune function due to stress, trauma, concurrent viral infection, or

hormonal changes can trigger reactivation of the virus and a secondary outbreak of the skin and mucosal lesions.

As expected, recurrences are much more common in immunosuppressed individuals.

Transmission of HSV takes place mainly during the active phase but occasionally may occur during the latent phase

due to subclinical virus shedding. Condoms and antiviral therapies reduce the risk of transmission, but do not

prevent it completely. As with other sexually transmitted diseases, the virus is more readily transmitted to women

than to men.

Page 2

The diagnosis is based on typical clinical findings and HSV detection. Lesions are unroofed and the viral exudate

collected. A Tzanck smear can be performed immediately, by spreading the material onto a slide and staining with

Giesma. The viral cytopathic effect of multinucleated giant cells with intranuclear “ground-glass” appearance

(Cowdry A inclusions) can be seen:

In addition, some laboratories offer more sensitive polymerase chain reaction tests, direct fluorecent antibody

testing, nucleic acid amplification tests, and viral culture for detection. Individuals with primary, acute HSV

infection do not have serum anti-HSV antibodies. Detection of anti-HSV antibodies in the serum is indicative of

recurrent/latent infection.

There is no effective treatment for HSV; however, antiviral agents like acyclovir or famciclovir shorten the length of

the initial and recurrent symptomatic phases.

Herpesvirus can be transmitted to neonates during passage through the birth canal of infected mothers. Although

HSV-2 infection in the neonate may be mild, more commonly it is fulminating with generalized lymphadenopathy,

splenomegaly, and necrotic foci throughout the lungs, liver, adrenals, and CNS. This risk is highest if the infection is

active during delivery and particularly if it is a primary (initial) infection in the mother. Cesarean delivery is

warranted in such cases to prevent transmission to the neonate.

Syphilis

Syphilis is a chronic sexually transmitted disease with varied clinical and pathologic manifestations. The causative

spirochete, Treponema pallidum, can be visualized on silver stains, dark field microscopy, and immunofluorescence

techniques. It is too slender to be seen on Gram stain and cannot easily be grown in culture.

Page 3

Syphilis is divided into 3 stges

1. Primary: Approximately 3 weeks after infection. Characterized by a single localized,

painless, ulcer known as a chancre. It is indurated with a clean base and rolled edge.

Because it is painless, it may go unnoticed.

2. Secondary: 1-3 months later. Characterized by a maculopapular rash on palms and soles

of feet, and painless lymphadenopathy (lymph nodes may feel rubbery). Condylomata

lata are smooth, painless, wart-like lesions that appear on genitals.

Page 4

3. Latent: Can last years. No symptoms occur, but positive serologic tests indicate

continuing infection.

4. Tertiary: characterized by gummas (chronic granulomas), aortitis (vasa vasorum

destruction resulting in aneurysms and aortic regurgitation), neurosyphilis (tabes

dorasalis, general paresis), and Argyll Robertson pupils (constricts with accommodation

but is not reactive to light).

Diagnosis is generally made serologically. Nonspecific serologic tests involve the use of nontreponemal antigens.

These extracts react with antibodies in the serum samples of patients with syphilis. VDRL (Venereal Disease

Research Laboratory) and RPR (rapid plasma regain) tests detect the presence of the antibodies. These tests are

positive in most cases of primary syphilis and are almost always positive in secondary syphilis. False positives can

occur with other infections and various autoimmune diseases, therefore positive results must be confirmed with

treponemal specific tests. Fluorescent treponemal antibody absorbed test (FTA-ABS) is the most common specific

treponemal antibody test. These tests remain positive for life even after effective treatment.

Penicilliin G is the effective treatment for syphilis. More than half of patients with secondary syphilis will

experience the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction with treatment. This is characterized by fever, chills, myalgias, and

other flu-like symptoms due to the lysis of treponemes and release of endotoxin-like substances.

Transplacental transmission occurs readily, and active disease during pregnancy results in congenital syphilis. In

the infected neonates, skin and bone lesions, such as Hutchinson’s teeth, mulberry molars, saber shins, saddle

nose, snuffles, frontal bossing, and CN VIII deafness are common. Fetal infection can also result in stillbirth. All

pregnant women should be tested in the first trimester and third trimester for syphilis, and treated with Penicillin

promptly.

Chancroid

Chancroid is an acute, ulcerative STI caused by a small gram-negative rod called Haemophilus ducreyi. It is most

common in tropical and subtropical areas among lower socioeconomic groups. It is one of the most common

causes of genital ulcers in Africa, Southeast Asia, and the Caribbean, however is uncommon in the United States.

Page 5

Clinically, chanroid presents as multiple, very painful, nonindurated ulcers with a gray or yellow exudate on the

base. It is characterized by smaller, tender unilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy, which may rupture.

Diagnosis is difficult because it requires a special culture media and PCR tests are not widely available. Treatment

is with Azithromycin

Lymphogranuloma venereum

An infection of lymphatics, this disease is caused by Chlamydiae trachomatis. C. trachomatis has more than 15

immunotypes (A-L). Types D-K cause genital tract infections. Lymphogranuloma venereum is caused by

immunotype L1-L3, and it presents as bilateral large and painful lymph nodes with fluctuant “buboes” and sinus

tracts. It is accompanied by small, painless, shallow ulcers that are usually not observed.

It is diagnosed with NAAT and treated with doxycycline.

Granuloma inguinale

Page 6

Also known as donovanosis, Granuloma Inguinale is caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. It is also uncommon in the

United States, but is endemic in some rural tropical areas. It begins as a painless, beefy red ulcer with

granulomatous appearance and rolled edges, that bleeds easily on contact. “Pseudobuboes” may occur in inguinal

lymph nodes. Microscopy will show Donovan bodies on Giesma staining (dark staining oval organisms).

It is treated with doxycycline.

Page 7

SUMMARY OF ULCERATIVE INFECTIONS

Page 8

Vaginitis

Vaginitis is inflammation of the vagina that can result in discharge, itching, and pain. These

symptoms occur primarily in three diseases: bacterial vaginosis (BV), candidiasis, and

trichomoniasis.

Bacterial Vaginosis

BV is caused by an overgrowth of Gardnerella vaginalis. It is a gram-variable rod that presents as vaginal

discharge. It is associated with sexual activity, but is not sexually transmitted. Diagnosis can be made by Amsel’s

criteria:

1. Characteristic discharge: thin, off-white, with fishy odor

2. Vaginal pH >4.5

3. Amine whiff test: mixing discharge with KOH enhances the fishy odor

4. Microscopy: showing clue cells, which are epithelial cells covered with Gardnerella

causing a stippled appearance along the edge of the cell.

Treatment is with metronidazole. Of note, metronidazole can give a disulfram-like reaction when taken with

alcohol. It can present as nausea/vomiting, facial flushing, and abdominal pain.

Candidiasis

Vaginal candidiasis is caused by an overgrowth of Candida albicans. It traditionally presents as a clumpy, white,

“cottage cheese” discharge that is odorless. It can be accompanied by vaginal itching and burning. It is associated

with an acidic vaginal pH (<4.5). On microcopy, budding yeast and pseudohyphae will be visible.

Page 9

Treatment is with fluconazole (oral) or miconazole (vaginal suppository)

Trichomonas

Trichomonas is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoa Trichomonas vaginalis. It often presents

with a malodorous, frothy, yellow-green vaginal discharge, a vaginal pH >4.5, and punctate “strawberry” lesions on

the cervix.

Microscopy will show motile protozoa.

Treatment is also treated with metronidazole.

Page 10

SUMMARY OF VAGINITIS INFECTIONS

Page 11

Cervicitis

Gonorrhea

Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative intracellular diplococcus that results in a muculopurulent discharge with

abundant neutrophils. Signs and symptoms develop within 3-5 days of infection, but asymptomatic infections are

common in both men and women. Specimens can be tested by culture or NAAT. Untreated gonococcal infections

can lead to pelvic inflammatory disease (discussed later), and disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI), with clinical

signs and symptoms such as fever/chills, arthritis/arthralgias, tenosynovitis, skin lesions, endocarditis, and

meningitis.

CDC just released updated treatment guidelines for 2021, which recommends ceftriaxone as monotherapy

recommended treatment. It was previously recommended to treat with both ceftriaxone and azithromcyin.

N.Gonorrhea can also be passed from mother to baby during birth, which can cause neonatal blindness.

Erythromycin ointment is prophylactically placed in neonatal eyes as standard of care.

Chlamydia

Chlamydia trachomatis is a small gram-negative bacterium that is an obligate intracellular pathogen, because it

cannot make it’s own ATP. As mentioned before, has more than 15 immunotypes (A-L). Types D-K cause genital

tract infections. Genital infections by C. trachomatis are the most common bacterial STIs in the world. They are

associated with similar clinical features as those caused by N.gonorrhoeae (muculopurulent discharge containing a

predominance of neutrophils).

CDC just released updated treatment guidelines for 2021, which recommends doxycycline as monotherapy

recommended treatment. Azithromycin can be used in pregnancy (this was previously the recommended

treatment for all cases).

C. trachomatis can also be passed from mother to baby during birth, which can cause neonatal blindness.

Erythromycin ointment is prophylactically placed in neonatal eyes as standard of care.

Pelvic Inflammatory Disease

PID is a polymycrobial infection of the upper genital tract (endometrium, fallopian tubes, ovaries, and pelvic

peritoneum), as a result of direct spread of pathogenic organisms along mucosal surfaces after initial infection of

the cervix. This can result in endometritis, salpingitis, and tubo-ovarian abscess.

The predominant organisms responsible for PID are C.trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae. This can lead the way for

other anaerobes to create a polymycrobial infection. Other organisms that have been isolated include

Mycoplasmia, Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, Haemophilus, E.coli, bacteroides, peptostreptococcus, clostridium,

and actinomyces.

Page 12

The greatest risk factor for PID is prior PID. Adolescence, having multiple sexual partners, not using condoms, and

infection with any of the causative organisms are important risk factors.

Patients with PID may present with purulent cervical discharge, pelvic pain, fever/chills, elevated white blood cell

count. Cervical motion tenderness is often found, characterized by the “chandelier sign” (where the patient

“jumps to the ceiling” with palpation of the cervix).

Significant effects of PID include scarring of the tubes, which can result in a hydrosalpinx, tubal factor infertility,

and risk of ectopic pregnancy. There can also be perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome), which results in

inflammation leading to localized fibrosis and “violin string” adhesions of the anterior surface of the liver to the

adjacent peritoneum. It is probably caused by chlamydial infection more often.

Mild symptoms can be treated with ceftriaxone or cefoxitin x1 dose followed by 14 days of oral doxycycline +/-

metronidazole. If the patient fails outpatient treatment, is septic, or is unable to tolerate PO, then IV cefoxitin or

cefotetan with doxycyclin +/- metronidazole.

Sources:

Robbins and Cotran, Pathology

Medical Microbiology and Immunology

Slide 4: Objectives:
  • Describe the microscopic structure of the testis.
  • Correlate the structure, location, and function of germ cells (spermatogonia, spermatocytes, spermatids, spermatozoa), Sertoli cells, and Leydig cells.
  • Explain the processes and regulation of spermatogenesis and spermiogenesis.
  • Correlate the microscopic organization and function of the rete testis, ductuli efferentes, epididymis, and ductus deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate gland, and bulbourethral glands.
  • Predict how structural alterations in the male reproductive duct system and accessory glands (rete testis, ductuli efferentes, epididymis, ductus deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate gland, and bulbourethral glands) affect reproductive function.
  • Relate the microscopic structure of the penis to its function
  • Discuss the morphology, consequences, and type of management (pharmacologic, non-pharmacologic, surgical) of phimosis, hypospadias, and epispadias.
  • List the common causes of penile infections, both sexually transmitted and acquired through other routes.
  • Describe the underlying abnormality causing Peyronie disease, the clinical consequences, and its treatment type (pharmacologic, non-pharmacologic, surgical)
  • Name the structure through which the testes descend during fetal development and what is brought with the testes in the descent.
  • Describe the complications associated with cryptorchidism.
  • Describe the clinical features and pathologic findings in the testis that occur due to torsion of the spermatic cord.
  • Discuss several inflammatory conditions affecting the testis and epididymis and the clinicopathologic features associated with each.
  • Compare and contrast the pathogenesis and clinical consequences of disorders related to the tunica vaginalis.
  • Explain the molecular and hormonal origins of prostatic nodular hyperplasia, the area of the gland affected, the natural history of the disease, various treatment strategies, and anticipated outcomes of treatment.
  • Describe the pathophysiologic basis for inflammatory conditions affecting the prostate, including the causative organisms.
  • Explain the spectrum of squamous neoplasia affecting the penis, ranging from condyloma acuminata to invasive squamous cell carcinoma, describing the risk factors, pathogenesis, morphologic features, complications, and treatment strategies.
  • Describe the most important risk factors, genetic associations, molecular basis, and clinicopathologic features for the development of testicular tumors and the different morphologic patterns seen.
  • Describe the cellular phenotype of the typical prostate adenocarcinoma and its molecular and immunohistochemical characteristics.
  • Define the histopathological diagnostic criteria for the diagnosis of prostatic adenocarcinoma.
  • Explain the epidemiology of prostate cancer with respect to age and family history.
  • Compare and contrast the significance of “histological” prostatic adenocarcinoma versus a “clinically significant” adenocarcinoma.
Slide 5: Question 1:
  • A 28-year-old man experiences orchitis after trauma to the scrotum. Which histologic structure was most likely disrupted, allowing immune recognition of sperm antigens?
  • A. Desmosomes between Sertoli cells B. Tight junctions between Sertoli cells C. Basement membrane of seminiferous tubules D. Gap junctions between Leydig cells E. Smooth muscle of myoid cells
Slide 6: Microscopic Structure of the Testis
  • Describe the microscopic structure of the testis.
  • Correlate the structure, location, and function of germ cells (spermatogonia, spermatocytes, spermatids, spermatozoa), Sertoli cells, and Leydig cells.
  • Seminiferous Tubules: Functional units of the testes (sperm production)
  • Cells:
  • Sertoli: secrete antimullerian hormone in fetal testis (8-10) w--regression of the paramesonephric (Müllerian) duct; support developing sperm cells and spermatogenesis regulation; Androgen-binding hormone secretion—concentrates testosterone; phagocytosis of excess cytoplasm during spermatogenesis; form the testicular-blood barrier (prevents autoimmunity against sperm)
  • Germ cells: spermatogenesis
  • Leydig cells: in the interstitium between seminiferous tubules; production and secretion of testosterone; abundant SER (steroidogenic cells).
  • Myoid cells: contractile cells surrounding the seminiferous tubules; facilitate the sperm movement into the epididymis
  • Supportive blood vessels, nerves, and connective tissues
  • Tunica albuginea; testicular capsule (Right Pointing Arrow). Numerous seminiferous tubules filling the capsule (Upward Pointing Arrows)
  • https://histologyprimer.abpath.org/Modules/Mod_TheMaleReproductiveSystem
Slide 7: Microscopic Structure of the Testis-Sertoli Cells and Spermatogonia
  • Describe the microscopic structure of the testis.
  • Correlate the structure, location, and function of germ cells (spermatogonia, spermatocytes, spermatids, spermatozoa), Sertoli cells, and Leydig cells.
  • Sertoli or Sustentacular Cells (Downward Arrows); clearer nucleoplasm & a prominent nucleolus. The myoid cells (Left Pointing Arrows); smooth muscle like cells.
  • https://histologyprimer.abpath.org/Modules/Mod_TheMaleReproductiveSystem
  • Spermatogonia (1) that develop into primary spermatocytes (2), followed by early spermatids (3) and late spermatids (4). Leydig cells are present in the interstitium between the seminiferous tubules (5).

Slide 9: Question 2:
  • A 20-year-old man’s biopsy shows abundant primary spermatocytes, but few or no secondary spermatocytes or spermatids. Which step is defective?
  • A. Mitosis of spermatogonia B. Meiosis I C. Meiosis II D. Spermiogenesis E. Fertilization
Slide 10: Cells Involved in Spermatogenesis
  • Describe the microscopic structure of the testis.
  • Correlate the structure, location, and function of germ cells (spermatogonia, spermatocytes, spermatids, spermatozoa), Sertoli cells, and Leydig cells.

| Cell Type | Location in Seminiferous Tubule | Ploidy | Histologic Appearance | Key Concepts |

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| Spermatogonia | Directly on basement membrane (basal compartment) | 2N, 2C | Small round cells with dark nuclei | Stem cells; undergo mitosis to form primary spermatocytes |

| Primary Spermatocytes | Just above spermatogonia (adluminal compartment) | 2N, 4C (DNA replicated) | Largest germ cells, coarse/clumped chromatin; most prominent cells seen in sections | Undergo Meiosis I. Most commonly observed meiotic cell because prophase I is long. |

| Secondary Spermatocytes | Between primary spermatocytes and spermatids | 1N, 2C | Smaller than primary spermatocytes; rarely seen | Undergo Meiosis II rapidly, so they are seldom identified on slides. |

| Spermatids | Closest to lumen | 1N, 1C | Smallest germ cells; round dense nuclei (early) or elongated nuclei (late) | Undergo spermiogenesis (no division; only morphological transformation). |

  • https://embryology.med.unsw.edu.au/embryology/index.php/Spermatozoa_Development
Slide 11: Spermatogenesis-Definition and Phases
  • LO: Explain the processes and regulation of spermatogenesis and spermiogenesis.
  • Spermatogenesis is the process of producing haploid sperm cells from diploid germ cells in the seminiferous tubules
  • Three main phases: Spermatocytogenesis, Spermatidogenesis, and Spermiogenesis
  • A final step, spermiation, involves the release of mature sperm
  • Spermatocytogenesis
  • Begins with spermatogonia (stem cells) located in the basal compartment of seminiferous tubules
  • Types of spermatogonia:
  • Type A dark (AD): stem cell maintenance
  • Type A pale (AP): differentiates into Type B
  • Type B: undergoes mitosis to form primary spermatocytes
  • Primary spermatocytes undergo meiosis I to form secondary spermatocytes.
  • Spermatidogenesis
  • Secondary spermatocytes undergo meiosis II to produce haploid spermatids
  • Spermiogenesis
  • Aniebo Umoh, E. (2024). Spermatogenesis. IntechOpen. doi: 10.5772/intechopen.1007771
Slide 12: Spermatogenesis: Spermiogenesis, maturation, and spermiation
  • LO: Explain the processes and regulation of spermatogenesis and spermiogenesis.
  • Spermiogenesis
  • Transformation of spermatids into mature spermatozoa.
  • Golgi phase: acrosome formation begins
  • Cap phase: acrosomal cap forms
  • Tail formation: development of flagellum
  • Maturation phase:
  • cytoplasm removal by Sertoli cells
  • Key organelles involved: Golgi apparatus, mitochondria, nucleus, centrioles
  • Spermiation
  • Final release of mature spermatozoa into the lumen of seminiferous tubules.
  • Facilitated by Sertoli cells.
  • Aniebo Umoh, E. (2024). Spermatogenesis. IntechOpen. doi: 10.5772/intechopen.1007771
  • Structure of Sperm - Sperm cells are divided into a head, containing DNA; a midpiece, containing mitochondria; and a tail, providing motility. The acrosome is oval and flattened
Slide 13: Spermatogenesis: Regulation and Clinical Relevance
  • LO: Explain the processes and regulation of spermatogenesis and spermiogenesis.
  • Regulation of Spermatogenesis
  • FSH stimulates Sertoli cells
  • LH stimulates Leydig cells to produce testosterone
  • Testosterone is essential for all stages.
  • Calcium signaling also plays a role in regulation.
  • Influenced by temperature, toxins, medications, and genetic factors.
  • Clinical Relevance
  • Disruption in spermatogenesis can lead to:
  • Infertility
  • Genetic disorders (e.g., Klinefelter syndrome, Down syndrome)
  • Spontaneous abortion
  • Aniebo Umoh, E. (2024). Spermatogenesis. IntechOpen. doi: 10.5772/intechopen.1007771

  • A histologic section from the epididymis shows pseudostratified columnar epithelium with long apical processes. These structures are most accurately described as which of the following?
  • A. Cilia that sweep sperm along the tubule B. Stereocilia that absorb fluid and aid maturation C. Microvilli that increase surface area for diffusion D. Flagella that provide motility for spermatozoa E. Secretory vesicles for seminal plasma proteins
Slide 15: Histology of Epididymis
  • LO: Correlate the microscopic organization and function of the rete testis, ductuli efferentes, epididymis, and ductus deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate gland, and bulbourethral glands.
  • Location: Posterior side of each testis.
  • Connection: Receives sperm from the rete testis via efferent ductules.
  • Function: Site of sperm maturation, fluid absorption, and storage.
  • Regions of the Epididymis:
  • Head (Caput); Connected to the upper testis; Receives immature, non-motile sperm
  • Body (Corpus): Highly convoluted tubule; Site of sperm maturation and motility development
  • Tail (Cauda): Connects to the vas deferens; Stores fully mature, motile sperm
  • Histology of the Epididymis: Pseudostratified columnar:
  • Principal Cells: Have stereocilia (long, non-motile microvilli); Absorb excess fluid; Secrete glycerophosphocholine (supports sperm motility)
  • Basal cells: Stem cells for epithelial renewal
  • Clear (halo) cells: May assist in fluid reabsorption
  • Numerous sperm in the lumen. The Principal cells demonstrate apical, giant microvilli known as stereocilia. Basal cells (Upward Pointing Arrow) are present at the base of the epithelium. A thin layer of smooth muscle cells (Left Pointing Arrow) aids in the forward movement of sperm
  • https://histologyprimer.abpath.org/Modules/Mod_TheMaleReproductiveSystem
  • Image attribution: "Michigan - Website Histology and Virtual Microscopy" at AnatomyTOOL.org by Michael Hortsch, UMich MedSchool, Kent Christensen, UMich MedSchool, J. Matthew Velkey, UMich MedSchool et al, license: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike.

  • EPITHELIUM | CELL BIOLOGY
  • Kierszenbaum, Abraham L., M.D., Ph.D., Histology and Cell Biology: An Introduction to Pathology, 1, 1-65
  • Cilia and ciliogenesis
  • Copyright © 2020 Copyright © 2020 by Elsevier, Inc. All rights reserved
  • A cilium has:
  • Nine pairs of peripheral microtubules surrounding two central microtubules; this 9 + 2 arrangement is called an axoneme.
  • Dynein proteins are the molecular motor proteins of this system, driving the beat of the cilia.
Slide 17: Stereocilia
  • EPITHELIUM | CELL BIOLOGY
  • Kierszenbaum, Abraham L., M.D., Ph.D., Histology and Cell Biology: An Introduction to Pathology, 1, 1-65
  • Microvilli and stereocilia (stereovilli)
