Slide 18: Microvilli, Cilia, Stereocilia

| Feature | Microvilli | Cilia (Motile) | Cilia (Primary/Non-motile) | Stereocilia |

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| Core structure | Actin filaments (bundled) | Microtubules (9+2 axoneme) | Microtubules (9+0 axoneme) | Actin filaments (bundled) |

| Motor protein | None | Dynein (ATPase) | None | None |

| Size | Short (~1 μm) | Long (~5–10 μm) | Variable | Very long (up to 120 μm); tallest actin-based projections |

| Number per cell | Thousands (brush border) | ~200 per ciliated cell | One per cell | Dozens, arranged in staircase pattern |

| Motility | Non-motile | Motile (rhythmic beating) | Non-motile | Non-motile |

| Key cross-linkers | Villin, fimbrin, espin | N/A | N/A | Fimbrin, espin, fascin (no villin) |

| Function | Increase absorptive surface area | Mucociliary clearance; move fluid | Sensory/signaling (Hedgehog, flow sensing) | Mechanotransduction (hearing/balance); absorption (epididymis) |

| Key locations | Small intestine, proximal tubule | Respiratory epithelium, fallopian tubes, ependyma | Nearly all cell types | Inner ear hair cells, epididymis |

| Associated disease | Microvillus inclusion disease (MYO5B mutation → congenital diarrhea) | Primary ciliary dyskinesia / Kartagener syndrome (dynein arm defects → sinusitis, bronchiectasis, situs inversus) | Polycystic kidney disease (PKD1/PKD2); ciliopathies | Sensorineural hearing loss (mutations in espin, stereocilin, myosin VIIa → Usher syndrome) |

| Basal body | No (anchored to terminal web) | Yes (derived from centriole) | Yes (derived from mother centriole) | No (anchored to cuticular plate) |

Slide 23: BPH: Overview-Pathogenesis
  • LO: Explain the molecular and hormonal origins of prostatic nodular hyperplasia, the area of the gland affected, the natural history of the disease, various treatment strategies, and anticipated outcomes of treatment.
  • Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH):
  • Most common benign prostatic disease in men >50 years.
  • Prevalence increases with age; affects up to 90% of men by age 80.
  • Pathogenesis
  • Androgen-dependent proliferation of stromal and glandular elements.
  • Dihydrotestosterone (DHT) is the key mediator:
  • Synthesized from testosterone via 5α-reductase type 2.
  • Binds androgen receptors to promote growth and survival of prostate cells.
  • Estrogens may enhance DHT effects, especially as testosterone declines with age.
  • Hormonal Influence: Does not occur in:
  • Males castrated before puberty.
  • Males with genetic defects in androgen signaling.
  • DHT increases stromal cell proliferation and reduces epithelial cell apoptosis.
  • Kumar, Vinay, MBBS, MD, FRCPath, Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 16, 582-601
Slide 24: BPH: Morphology and C/P
  • LO: Explain the molecular and hormonal origins of prostatic nodular hyperplasia, the area of the gland affected, the natural history of the disease, various treatment strategies, and anticipated outcomes of treatment.
  • Morphology
  • Prostate weight increases 3–5× (up to 100 g or more).
  • BPH primarily affects the transition zone, leading to:
  • Urethral compression → urinary obstruction.
  • Nodules may be solid or cystic, depending on cellular content.
  • Clinical Consequences
  • Urinary symptoms include:
  • Nocturia
  • Hesitancy
  • Weak stream
  • Incomplete emptying
  • Kumar, Vinay, MBBS, MD, FRCPath, Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 16, 582-601
Slide 25: Prostatitis
  • LO: Describe the pathophysiologic basis for inflammatory conditions affecting the prostate, including the causative organisms.
  • Types of Prostatitis
  • 1. Acute Bacterial Prostatitis
  • Sudden onset: fever, chills, dysuria, perineal pain, urinary obstruction
  • Caused by common uropathogens (e.g., E. coli)
  • Digital rectal exam is contraindicated due to risk of bacteremia
  • Diagnosis: urine culture, clinical features
  • Treated with antibiotics
  • 2. Chronic Bacterial Prostatitis
  • Recurrent UTIs with asymptomatic intervals
  • Symptoms: low back pain, dysuria, suprapubic/perineal discomfort
  • Diagnosis: leukocytes in expressed prostatic secretions, positive cultures
  • Treated with antibiotics
  • 3. Chronic Abacterial Prostatitis (Pelvic Pain Syndrome); Most common form
  • Similar symptoms to chronic bacterial prostatitis
  • No history of recurrent UTIs
  • Cultures are negative, but secretions show >10 leukocytes/HPF
  • Etiology unknown; diagnosis of exclusion
  • Treatment is empirical, based on symptoms
  • 4. Granulomatous Prostatitis
  • May mimic prostate cancer due to induration
  • Most common cause in the U.S.: BCG therapy for bladder cancer
  • Other causes: fungal infections (in immunocompromised), nonspecific foreign-body reactions
Slide 26: Prostatitis-Cont
  • LO: Describe the pathophysiologic basis for inflammatory conditions affecting the prostate, including the causative organisms.
  • Diagnosis Considerations
  • Biopsy is not routine due to nonspecific findings and risk of sepsis
  • Reserved for cases like granulomatous prostatitis or to rule out cancer
Slide 27: PCA: Epidemiology and Pathogenesis
  • Explain the epidemiology of prostate cancer with respect to age and family history.
  • Outline the cellular phenotype of the typical prostate adenocarcinoma cell and describe its molecular and immunohistochemical characteristics.
  • Epidemiology & Clinical Significance
  • Most common cancer in men and second leading cause of cancer death (after lung cancer).
  • Incidence increases with age:
  • ~20% in men in their 50s
  • ~70% in men aged 70–80
  • Most cases are asymptomatic, nonpalpable, and detected via needle biopsy following elevated PSA.
  • Pathogenesis
  • Androgens (especially DHT) are central to tumor growth and progression.
  • Tumors may initially respond to androgen deprivation, but often develop resistance via:
  • Androgen receptor (AR) gene amplification or mutation
  • Activation of alternative signaling pathways
  • Hereditary factors:
  • First-degree relatives → 2× increased risk
  • Germline mutations (e.g., BRCA2, MYC, mismatch repair genes) linked to aggressive disease
  • Environmental factors:
  • Western diet (charred meats, animal fats), estrogens, oxidants may contribute
  • Genetic alterations:
  • TMPRSS2–ETS fusion: common driver mutation
  • MYC amplification, PTEN deletion, TP53 loss, RB deletion
  • Epigenetic silencing of GSTP1, RB, MLH1, MSH2, APC
Slide 28: PCA: Morphology
  • LO: Define the histopathological diagnostic criteria for the diagnosis of PCA
  • Morphology & Histology:
  • 70% arise in the peripheral zone, often posteriorly → may be palpable on DRE
  • Gross appearance: firm, solid, gritty, pale, lacking normal spongy texture (circle)
  • Histologic features:
  • Small, crowded glands with single-layer epithelium
  • No basal cell layer (vs. BPH)
  • Enlarged nuclei with prominent nucleoli
  • HGPIN (high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia) seen in ~80% of cases
Slide 29: PCA: Gleason Grading System
  • LO: Define the histopathological diagnostic criteria for the diagnosis of PCA
  • Morphology & Histology:
  • Gleason grading system: Based on glandular architecture, not cytologic atypia.
  • Grades 1–5:
  • Grade 1: Well-differentiated, uniform glands
  • Grade 5: Undifferentiated sheets, cords, or nests of cells
  • Gleason Score = Primary grade + Secondary grade
  • Most treatable cancers: Score 6–7
  • Advanced/aggressive cancers: Score 8–10
  • Gleason scores are now grouped into Grade Groups 1–5, each with distinct prognostic implications.
  • Used alongside pathologic staging to guide treatment decisions.
  • Low-grade prostate adenocarcinoma (Gleason score 1 + 1 = 2) consisting of back-to-back uniform-sized malignant glands lined by a single layer of epithelial cells.
  • A focus of Gleason grade 4 prostatic adenocarcinoma displays large cribriform glands with multiple cellular bridges crossing the central lumina.
  • Grade group 5 adenocarcinoma (Gleason score 5 + 5 = 10) composed of sheets of malignant cells with no identifiable gland formation.
Slide 30: PCA: Diagnosis, Management, and Prognosis
  • LO: Compare and contrast the significance of “histological” prostatic adenocarcinoma versus a “clinically significant” adenocarcinoma.
  • Diagnosis
  • PSA testing: Widely used but has limited sensitivity and specificity
  • Elevated in BPH, prostatitis, and after instrumentation
  • MRI can help detect nonpalpable cancers
  • Serial PSA levels helpful in monitoring recurrence or progression
  • Bone metastases:
  • Common in late-stage disease
  • Typically osteoblastic (bone-forming), seen on radionuclide bone scans
  • Management & Prognosis
  • Surgery, radiation, ± hormonal therapy
  • 90% of treated patients have 15-year survival
  • Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT): Effective short-term, but androgen-independent clones often emerge
  • Achieved via LHRH agonists
  • Initially stimulates LH → then suppresses it → ↓ testosterone
  • Prognosis depends on:
  • Pathologic stage
  • Surgical margin status
  • Gleason grade
Slide 31: Histologic (Incidental) vs Clinically Significant Prostate Adenocarcinoma
  • LO: Compare and contrast the significance of “histological” prostatic adenocarcinoma versus a “clinically significant” adenocarcinoma.

| Feature | Histological PCA | Clinically Significant PCA |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Detection | Incidental (biopsy, PSA) | Symptomatic or palpable |

| Symptoms | None | Dysuria, obstruction, metastases |

| Gleason Score | Often ≤6 | Often ≥7 |

| Management | May be monitored | Requires treatment |

| Risk | Low progression | High morbidity/mortality |

Slide 36: Peyronie disease:
  • LO: Describe the underlying abnormality causing Peyronie disease, the clinical consequences, and its treatment.
  • An acquired condition in middle-aged or older men.
  • Characterized by fibrous plaque formation in the tunica albuginea (the fibrous sheath surrounding the corpora cavernosa). Leads to asymmetric erection, abnormal curvature, painful erections, and difficulty with intercourse.
  • Clinical Consequences
  • Penile curvature, especially during erection
  • Painful erections
  • Erectile dysfunction
  • Difficulty with intercourse
  • Psychological distress, including anxiety and depression
  • Diagnosis
  • Based on clinical history and physical exam
  • Palpable plaque on the shaft of the penis
  • Imaging (e.g., penile ultrasound) may be used to assess plaque size and calcification
  • Treatment Options
  • Treatment depends on severity, duration, and impact on function:
  • Non-surgical options:
  • Oral medications: Pentoxifylline (anti-fibrotic)
  • Intralesional injections: Collagenase Clostridium histolyticum (FDA-approved)
  • Verapamil or interferon (off-label)
  • Shockwave therapy: (limited evidence)
  • Surgical options (for severe or refractory cases)
Slide 37: LO: Discuss the morphology, consequences, and management of phimosis, hypospadias, and epispadias.
  • Hypospadias
  • Urethral opening on the ventral surface of the penis; may be glanular, penile, or perineal.
  • Incomplete fusion of urethral folds
  • Associated anomalies: Inguinal hernia, cryptorchidism
  • Abnormal urine stream, difficulty with urination and sexual function; Fertility issues if severe
  • Complications: Constricted urethral orifice may lead to Urinary tract obstruction and Increased risk of urinary tract infections (UTIs)
  • Surgical correction, typically performed between 6–18 months of age
  • Avoid circumcision before repair (foreskin may be used in reconstruction)
  • Epispadias
  • Urethral opening on the dorsal surface of the penis
  • Defective positioning of the genital tubercle
  • Often associated with: Bladder exstrophy
  • May cause urinary incontinence
  • Complex surgical repair
  • Phimosis
  • Inability to retract the foreskin over the glans
  • Congenital or acquired (e.g., inflammation, scarring): Balanitis: inflammation of the glans; Balanoposthitis: inflammation of the glans and prepuce, due to poor hygiene in uncircumcised males or accumulation of smegma (desquamated cells, sweat, debris)
  • Results in hygiene issues: Increased risk of infection
  • Painful erections
  • Topical steroids
  • Circumcision if severe or recurrent
Slide 38: Testicular Torsion:
  • LO: Describe the clinical features and pathologic findings in the testis that occur due to torsion of the spermatic cord
  • Twisting of the spermatic cord
  • Typically results in obstruction of testicular venous drainage while the thick-walled and more resilient arteries remain patent
  • If untreated---engorgement and infarction
  • Two types of testicular torsion:
  • Neonatal torsion ( in utero or shortly after birth); no associated anatomic defect
  • Adult torsion results from a bilateral anatomic defect in the anchoring of the testis in the scrotal sac that leads to its increased mobility; it typically occurs in adolescence and manifests with the sudden onset of testicular pain.
  • A urologic emergency
  • Manual untwisting within 6 hours of onset---testis remains viable.
  • Contralateral orchiopexy is performed to prevent recurrence in the unaffected testis.
  • Male Genital System and Lower Urinary Tract

Kumar, Vinay, MBBS, MD, FRCPath, Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 16, 582-601

Testicular torsion. The dark discoloration is the result of hemorrhage and infarction that occurs when twisting of the spermatic cord cuts off venous drainage. (From Klatt EC: Robbins and Cotran Atlas of Pathology, ed 4, Fig. 12.18, Philadelphia, ...

Slide 44: Cryptorchidism
  • LO:
  • Describe the complications observed for failure of the testes to descend (cryptorchidism).
  • Describe the most important risk factors, genetic associations, and molecular basis for the development of testicular tumors and outline the clinicopathologic features for the different morphologic patterns seen.
  • Cryptorchidism is a complete or partial failure of the intraabdominal testes to descend into the scrotal sac
  • It is associated with testicular dysfunction and an increased risk of testicular cancer
  • Cryptorchidism is found in approximately 1% of 1-year-old boys
  • Normally, the testes descend from the abdominal cavity into the pelvis by the third month of gestation and then through the inguinal canals into the scrotum during the last 2 months of intrauterine life.
  • The diagnosis of cryptorchidism is only established with certainty after 1 year of age particularly in premature infants
  • Undescended testes become atrophic, bilateral cryptorchidism results in sterility.
  • Even unilateral cryptorchidism may be associated with atrophy of the contralateral descended gonad.
  • Patients with unilateral cryptorchidism are also at increased risk for the development of cancer in the contralateral, normally descended testis ( intrinsic abnormality, rather than simple failure of descent)
  • Cryptorchid testes are small and firm.
  • The histologic changes include thickening of the basement membrane, loss of spermatogonia, increased interstitial stroma, and relative prominence of Leydig cells.
  • Germ cell neoplasia in situ may be present in cryptorchid testes; precursor of subsequent germ cell tumors.
  • Current recommendations are for surgical repositioning (orchiopexy), to be performed at 6 to 12 months of age.
Slide 45: Leydig Cell Tumor
  • LO: Describe the most important risk factors, genetic associations, and molecular basis for the development of testicular tumors and outline the clinicopathologic features for the different morphologic patterns seen.
  • Leydig Cell Tumor
  • Most common sex cord-stromal tumor in children.
  • Can occur at any age (children and adults)
  • Presents with precocious puberty in boys (pubic hair, acne, rapid growth); Elevated testosterone.
  • In adults: may cause gynecomastia; excess estrogen from androgen aromatization
  • Painless, firm testicular mass; often unilateral.
  • Histologic Features
  • Polygonal cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm.
  • Reinke crystals (rod-shaped intracytoplasmic inclusions)
  • No lymphocytic infiltrate or germ cell elements.
  • Pathogenesis
  • Arises from Leydig (interstitial) cells of the testis.
  • Not associated with GCNIS or i(12p) abnormalities.
  • Prognosis: Mostly benign
  • Surgical excision is typically curative.
  • Step 1 Buzzwords
  • “Precocious puberty in a boy with testicular mass.”
  • “Gynecomastia in an adult man with testicular mass.”
  • “Golden-brown tumor with Reinke crystals.”
  • “Normal AFP and hCG levels.”
Slide 46: Seminoma
  • LO: Describe the most important risk factors, genetic associations, and molecular basis for the development of testicular tumors and outline the clinicopathologic features for the different morphologic patterns seen.
  • A germ cell tumor presents as a soft, well-demarcated, gray-white, pale, fleshy tumor that bulges from the cut surface of the affected testis
  • Large tumors may contain foci of coagulative necrosis, usually without hemorrhage
  • It is composed of large, uniform cells with distinct cell borders, clear glycogen-rich cytoplasm, round nuclei, and conspicuous nucleoli
  • The cells often are arrayed in small lobules with intervening fibrous septa.
  • A lymphocytic infiltrate is usually present.
  • In approximately 15% of cases, syncytiotrophoblasts are present; these cells are the source of the minimally elevated serum human choriogonadotropin (hCG) that is seen in 10% to 15% of patients with stage I disease, increasing to 30% to 50% in disseminated disease.
  • Their presence has no bearing on prognosis, and the levels of hCG are usually much lower than in choriocarcinoma
  • Kumar, Vinay, MBBS, MD, FRCPath, Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 16, 582-601
Slide 47: Yolk sac tumor
  • LO: Describe the most important risk factors, genetic associations, and molecular basis for the development of testicular tumors and outline the clinicopathologic features for the different morphologic patterns seen.
  • Most common primary testicular neoplasm in children younger than 3 years of age
  • Has a very good prognosis in this age
  • Postpubertal yolk sac tumor is rarely “pure” and more frequently occurs in combination with embryonal carcinoma or other germ cell components.
  • Tumors are composed of low cuboidal to columnar epithelial cells that form microcysts, lacelike (reticular) patterns, sheets, glands, and papillae.
  • A distinctive feature is the structures resembling primitive glomeruli, so-called Schiller-Duval bodies.
  • Have eosinophilic hyaline globules containing α 1 -antitrypsin and alphafetoprotein (AFP); IHC
  • Male Genital System and Lower Urinary Tract

Kumar, Vinay, MBBS, MD, FRCPath, Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 16, 582-601

Slide 48: LO: Describe the most important risk factors, genetic associations, and molecular basis for the development of testicular tumors and outline the clinicopathologic features for the different morphologic patterns seen.

| Tumor Type | Typical Age | Histologic Features | Tumor Markers | Genetic Associations |

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| Seminoma | 40–50 | Sheets of uniform polygonal cells with clear cytoplasm (Fried-egg cell); lymphocytes in the stroma | APF is normal; 10% of patients have elevated hCG (syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells) | GCNIS, i(12p), KIT mutations |

| Embryonal carcinoma | 20–30 | Poorly differentiated, pleomorphic cells in cords, sheets, or papillary formation; most contain some yolk sac and choriocarcinoma cells | AFP may be elevated | GCNIS, i(12p) |

| Spermatocytic tumor | 50–60 | Small, medium, and large polygonal cells; no inflammatory infiltrate | Negative | Gain of chromosome 9q; not associated with GCNIS or i(12p) |

| Yolk sac tumor | 3 | Microcystic/reticular pattern; Schiller-Duval bodies may be present | 90% of patients have elevated AFP | Prepubertal type not associated with GCNIS or i(12p); postpubertal type may be associated |

| Choriocarcinoma | 20–30 | Cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast without villus formation | 100% of patients have elevated hCG | GCNIS, i(12p) |

| Teratoma | All ages | Tissues from all three germ cell layers with varying degrees of differentiation | 20%–25% have elevated AFP | Prepubertal type not associated with GCNIS or i(12p); postpubertal type associated with i(12p) |

| Mixed tumor | 15–30 | Variable, depending on mixture; commonly teratoma and embryonal carcinoma | AFP and hCG are variably elevated, depending on mixture | GCNIS, i(12p) |

Slide 50: Condyloma Acuminata (Genital Warts):
  • LO: Explain the spectrum of squamous neoplasia affecting the penis, ranging from condyloma acuminata to invasive squamous cell carcinoma, describing the risk factors, pathogenesis, morphologic features, complications, and treatment strategies.
  • 1. Condyloma Acuminata (Genital Warts):
  • Etiology: Caused by low-risk HPV types (mainly HPV-6 and HPV-11).
  • Morphology: Exophytic, papillary lesions on the penile shaft or glans.
  • Histology: Koilocytosis (perinuclear clearing), acanthosis (thickening of the epidermis, specifically the stratum spinosum ), papillomatosis.
  • Pathogenesis: Viral infection leads to benign epithelial proliferation.
  • Complications: Rare progression to malignancy; mostly cosmetic and psychological impact.
  • Treatment: Topical agents (imiquimod, podophyllin), cryotherapy, surgical excision.
  • Numerous cauliflower-like lesions
  • characteristic koilocytes with enlarged, hyperchromatic, wrinkled nuclei and perinuclear halo
  • https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/penscrotumcondyloma.html
Slide 51: Penile Intraepithelial Neoplasia (PeIN)
  • LO: Explain the spectrum of squamous neoplasia affecting the penis, ranging from condyloma acuminata to invasive squamous cell carcinoma, describing the risk factors, pathogenesis, morphologic features, complications, and treatment strategies.
  • 2. Penile Intraepithelial Neoplasia (PeIN)
  • Etiology: Associated with high-risk HPV types (especially HPV-16 and HPV-18).
  • Morphology: Solitary plaque, often on the shaft or glans.
  • Histology: Full-thickness epithelial atypia, nuclear pleomorphism, mitoses (arrows), intact basement membrane.
  • Pathogenesis: Dysplastic transformation of squamous epithelium without stromal invasion.
  • Complications: ~10% progress to invasive squamous cell carcinoma.
  • Treatment: Topical chemotherapy (5-FU), laser ablation, surgical excision.
  • Male Genital System and Lower Urinary Tract

Slide 52: Penile Invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)
  • 3. Invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)
  • Etiology: Strongly linked to HPV-16/18, poor hygiene, smoking, chronic inflammation, and lack of circumcision.
  • Morphology: Ulcerated, indurated, crusted lesion on the glans or prepuce.
  • Histology: Keratinizing squamous cells invading the stroma; nuclear atypia, mitotic figures.
  • Pathogenesis: Progression from PeIN with basement membrane breach and stromal infiltration.
  • Complications:
  • Local tissue destruction.
  • Lymphatic spread to inguinal and pelvic nodes.
  • Poor prognosis with nodal metastasis.
  • Treatment:
  • Early-stage: Partial penectomy, Mohs surgery.
  • Advanced: Total penectomy, lymphadenectomy, radiation, chemotherapy.
  • Special Variant: Verrucous Carcinoma
  • Etiology: Not HPV-related.
  • Morphology: Papillary, exophytic growth with pushing margins.
  • Histology: Minimal atypia, locally invasive but non-metastasizing.
  • Treatment: Surgical excision; radiation avoided due to risk of anaplastic transformation.

Slide 5: Question 1:
  • A 28-year-old man experiences orchitis after trauma to the scrotum. Which histologic structure was most likely disrupted, allowing immune recognition of sperm antigens?
  • A. Desmosomes between Sertoli cells B. Tight junctions between Sertoli cells C. Basement membrane of seminiferous tubules D. Gap junctions between Leydig cells E. Smooth muscle of myoid cells
Slide 6: Question 1: Answer and Explanation
  • A 28-year-old man experiences orchitis after trauma to the scrotum. Which histologic structure was most likely disrupted, allowing immune recognition of sperm antigens?
  • A. Desmosomes between Sertoli cells B. Tight junctions between Sertoli cells C. Basement membrane of seminiferous tubules D. Gap junctions between Leydig cells E. Smooth muscle of myoid cells
  • A. Desmosomes between Sertoli cells: provide mechanical strength, not selective permeability. Not responsible for immune isolation.
  • B. Tight junctions between Sertoli cells: These form the blood-testis barrier. Prevent immune cells from accessing developing sperm. Disruption allows immune recognition of sperm antigens, leading to autoimmune orchitis.
  • C. Basement membrane of seminiferous tubules: Supports the tubule structure and separates it from interstitial tissue.
  • D. Gap junctions between Leydig cells: Involved in cell communication and hormone regulation.
  • E. Smooth muscle of myoid cells: Helps in sperm transport. Not part of the blood-testis barrier.
Slide 7: Microscopic Structure of the Testis
  • Describe the microscopic structure of the testis.
  • Correlate the structure, location, and function of germ cells (spermatogonia, spermatocytes, spermatids, spermatozoa), Sertoli cells, and Leydig cells.
  • Seminiferous Tubules: Functional units of the testes (sperm production)
  • Cells:
  • Sertoli: secrete anti-Mullerian hormone in fetal testis (8-10) w--regression of the paramesonephric (Müllerian) duct; support developing sperm cells and spermatogenesis regulation; Androgen-binding hormone secretion—concentrates testosterone; phagocytosis of excess cytoplasm during spermatogenesis; form the testicular-blood barrier (prevents autoimmunity against sperm)
  • Germ cells: spermatogenesis
  • Leydig cells: in the interstitium between seminiferous tubules; production and secretion of testosterone; abundant SER (steroidogenic cells).
  • Myoid cells: contractile cells surrounding the seminiferous tubules; facilitate sperm movement into the epididymis
  • Supportive blood vessels, nerves, and connective tissues
  • Tunica albuginea; testicular capsule (Right Pointing Arrow). Numerous seminiferous tubules filling the capsule (Upward Pointing Arrows)
  • https://histologyprimer.abpath.org/Modules/Mod_TheMaleReproductiveSystem
Slide 8: Microscopic Structure of the Testis-Sertoli Cells and Spermatogonia
  • Describe the microscopic structure of the testis.
  • Correlate the structure, location, and function of germ cells (spermatogonia, spermatocytes, spermatids, spermatozoa), Sertoli cells, and Leydig cells.
  • Sertoli or Sustentacular Cells (Downward Arrows); clearer nucleoplasm & a prominent nucleolus. The myoid cells (Left Pointing Arrows); smooth muscle like cells.
  • https://histologyprimer.abpath.org/Modules/Mod_TheMaleReproductiveSystem
  • Spermatogonia (1) that develop into primary spermatocytes (2), followed by early spermatids (3) and late spermatids (4). Leydig cells are present in the interstitium between the seminiferous tubules (5).
  • Image attribution: "Michigan - Website Histology and Virtual Microscopy" at AnatomyTOOL.org by Michael Hortsch, UMich MedSchool, Kent Christensen, UMich MedSchool, J. Matthew Velkey, UMich MedSchool et al, license: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike.

Slide 10: Question 2:
  • A 20-year-old man’s biopsy shows abundant primary spermatocytes, but few or no secondary spermatocytes or spermatids. Which step is defective?
  • A. Mitosis of spermatogonia B. Meiosis I C. Meiosis II D. Spermiogenesis E. Fertilization
Slide 11: Question 2: Answer and Explanation
  • A 20-year-old man’s biopsy shows abundant primary spermatocytes, but few or no secondary spermatocytes or spermatids. Which step is defective?
  • A. Mitosis of spermatogonia B. Meiosis I C. Meiosis II D. Spermiogenesis E. Fertilization
  • A. Mitosis of spermatogonia: Produces primary spermatocytes. Not defective here, since primary spermatocytes are abundant
  • B. Meiosis I: Converts primary spermatocytes → secondary spermatocytes. If this step is defective, you’ll see accumulation of primary spermatocytes and absence of later stages
  • C. Meiosis II: Converts secondary spermatocytes → spermatids. If this were defective, you'd still see secondary spermatocytes, which are absent here
  • D. Spermiogenesis: Converts spermatids → spermatozoa. If defective, you'd see spermatids, which are also absent
  • E. Fertilization: Happens after spermatogenesis, in the female reproductive tract. Not relevant to this histologic finding
Slide 12: Cells Involved in Spermatogenesis
  • Describe the microscopic structure of the testis.
  • Correlate the structure, location, and function of germ cells (spermatogonia, spermatocytes, spermatids, spermatozoa), Sertoli cells, and Leydig cells.

| Cell Type | Location in Seminiferous Tubule | Ploidy | Histologic Appearance | Key Concepts |

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| Spermatogonia | Directly on basement membrane (basal compartment) | 2N, 2C | Small round cells with dark nuclei | Stem cells; undergo mitosis to form primary spermatocytes |

| Primary Spermatocytes | Just above spermatogonia (adluminal compartment) | 2N, 4C (DNA replicated) | Largest germ cells, coarse/clumped chromatin; most prominent cells seen in sections | Undergo Meiosis I. Most commonly observed meiotic cell because prophase I is long. |

| Secondary Spermatocytes | Between primary spermatocytes and spermatids | 1N, 2C | Smaller than primary spermatocytes; rarely seen | Undergo Meiosis II rapidly, so they are seldom identified on slides. |

| Spermatids | Closest to lumen | 1N, 1C | Smallest germ cells; round dense nuclei (early) or elongated nuclei (late) | Undergo spermiogenesis (no division; only morphological transformation). |

  • https://embryology.med.unsw.edu.au/embryology/index.php/Spermatozoa_Development
Slide 13: Spermatogenesis-Definition and Phases
  • LO: Explain the processes and regulation of spermatogenesis and spermiogenesis.
  • Spermatogenesis is the process of producing haploid sperm cells from diploid germ cells in the seminiferous tubules
  • Three main phases: Spermatocytogenesis, Spermatidogenesis, and Spermiogenesis
  • A final step, spermiation, involves the release of mature sperm
  • Spermatocytogenesis
  • Begins with spermatogonia (stem cells) located in the basal compartment of seminiferous tubules
  • Types of spermatogonia:
  • Type A dark (AD): stem cell maintenance
  • Type A pale (AP): differentiates into Type B
  • Type B: undergoes mitosis to form primary spermatocytes
  • Primary spermatocytes undergo meiosis I to form secondary spermatocytes.
  • Spermatidogenesis
  • Secondary spermatocytes undergo meiosis II to produce haploid spermatids
  • Aniebo Umoh, E. (2024). Spermatogenesis. IntechOpen. doi: 10.5772/intechopen.1007771

Notes:

Male: Germ cells are present at birth, but meiosis has not begun.

Female: Oogonia have already entered meiosis and become primary oocytes arrested in prophase I at birth.

Slide 14: Spermatogenesis: Spermiogenesis, maturation, and spermiation
  • LO: Explain the processes and regulation of spermatogenesis and spermiogenesis.
  • Spermiogenesis
  • Transformation of spermatids into mature spermatozoa.
  • Golgi phase: acrosome formation begins
  • Cap phase: acrosomal cap forms
  • Tail formation: development of flagellum
  • Maturation phase:
  • cytoplasm removal by Sertoli cells
  • Key organelles involved: Golgi apparatus, mitochondria, nucleus, centrioles
  • Spermiation
  • Final release of mature spermatozoa into the lumen of seminiferous tubules.
  • Facilitated by Sertoli cells.
  • Aniebo Umoh, E. (2024). Spermatogenesis. IntechOpen. doi: 10.5772/intechopen.1007771
  • Structure of Sperm - Sperm cells are divided into a head, containing DNA; a midpiece, containing mitochondria; and a tail, providing motility. The acrosome is oval and flattened

Notes:

The acrosome is a Golgi-derived, cap-like organelle covering the anterior portion of the sperm head.

It contains hydrolytic enzymes, including acrosin and hyaluronidase, that facilitate fertilization. During the acrosome reaction, these enzymes are released after sperm binding to the zona pellucida, helping the sperm penetrate the egg's protective layers.

Slide 15: Spermatogenesis: Regulation and Clinical Relevance
  • LO: Explain the processes and regulation of spermatogenesis and spermiogenesis.
  • Regulation of Spermatogenesis
  • FSH stimulates Sertoli cells
  • LH stimulates Leydig cells to produce testosterone
  • Testosterone is essential for all stages.
  • Calcium signaling also plays a role in regulation.
  • Influenced by temperature, toxins, medications, and genetic factors.
  • Clinical Relevance
  • Disruption in spermatogenesis can lead to:
  • Infertility
  • Genetic disorders (e.g., Klinefelter syndrome, Down syndrome)
  • Spontaneous abortion
  • Aniebo Umoh, E. (2024). Spermatogenesis. IntechOpen. doi: 10.5772/intechopen.1007771
Slide 16: Question 3:
  • A histologic section from the epididymis shows pseudostratified columnar epithelium with long apical processes. These structures are most accurately described as which of the following?
  • A. Cilia that sweep sperm along the tubule B. Stereocilia that absorb fluid and aid maturation C. Microvilli that increase surface area for diffusion D. Flagella that provide motility for spermatozoa E. Secretory vesicles for seminal plasma proteins
Slide 17: Question 3: Answer and Explanation
  • A histologic section from the epididymis shows pseudostratified columnar epithelium with long apical processes. These structures are most accurately described as which of the following?
  • A. Cilia that sweep sperm along the tubule B. Stereocilia that absorb fluid and aid maturation C. Microvilli that increase surface area for diffusion D. Flagella that provide motility for spermatozoa E. Secretory vesicles for seminal plasma proteins
  • A. Cilia that sweep sperm along the tubule: True cilia are motile and found in places like the respiratory tract or fallopian tubes. Epididymal stereocilia do not beat or move sperm.
  • B. Stereocilia that absorb fluid and aid maturation: These are long, non-motile microvilli; help absorb fluid and support sperm maturation.
  • C. Microvilli that increase surface area for diffusion: Stereocilia are modified microvilli, but the question asks for the most accurate description, which is B.
  • D. Flagella that provide motility for spermatozoa: Flagella are part of the sperm cell itself, not the epithelium.
  • E. Secretory vesicles for seminal plasma proteins: These are found in seminal vesicles, not the epididymis.
Slide 18: Histology of Epididymis
  • LO: Correlate the microscopic organization and function of the rete testis, ductuli efferentes, epididymis, and ductus deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate gland, and bulbourethral glands.
  • Location: Posterior side of each testis.
  • Connection: Receives sperm from the rete testis via efferent ductules.
  • Function: Site of sperm maturation, fluid absorption, and storage.
  • Regions of the Epididymis:
  • Head (Caput); Connected to the upper testis; Receives immature, non-motile sperm
  • Body (Corpus): Highly convoluted tubule; Site of sperm maturation and motility development
  • Tail (Cauda): Connects to the vas deferens; Stores fully mature, motile sperm
  • Histology of the Epididymis: Pseudostratified columnar:
  • Principal Cells: Have stereocilia (long, non-motile microvilli); Absorb excess fluid; Secrete glycerophosphocholine (supports sperm motility)
  • Basal cells: Stem cells for epithelial renewal
  • Clear (halo) cells: May assist in fluid reabsorption
  • Numerous sperm in the lumen. The Principal cells demonstrate apical, giant microvilli known as stereocilia. Basal cells (Upward Pointing Arrow) are present at the base of the epithelium. A thin layer of smooth muscle cells (Left Pointing Arrow) aids in the forward movement of sperm
  • https://histologyprimer.abpath.org/Modules/Mod_TheMaleReproductiveSystem

Slide 20: Cilia-Structural Details
  • EPITHELIUM | CELL BIOLOGY
  • Kierszenbaum, Abraham L., M.D., Ph.D., Histology and Cell Biology: An Introduction to Pathology, 1, 1-65
  • Cilia and ciliogenesis

  • A cilium has:
  • Nine pairs of peripheral microtubules surrounding two central microtubules; this 9 + 2 arrangement is called an axoneme.
  • Dynein proteins are the molecular motor proteins of this system, driving the beat of the cilia.
Slide 21: Stereocilia
  • EPITHELIUM | CELL BIOLOGY
  • Kierszenbaum, Abraham L., M.D., Ph.D., Histology and Cell Biology: An Introduction to Pathology, 1, 1-65
  • Microvilli and stereocilia (stereovilli)

Slide 22: Microvilli, Cilia, Stereocilia

| Feature | Microvilli | Cilia (Motile) | Cilia (Primary/Non-motile) | Stereocilia |

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| Core structure | Actin filaments (bundled) | Microtubules (9+2 axoneme) | Microtubules (9+0 axoneme) | Actin filaments (bundled) |

| Motor protein | None | Dynein (ATPase) | None | None |

| Size | Short (~1 μm) | Long (~5–10 μm) | Variable | Very long (up to 120 μm); tallest actin-based projections |

| Number per cell | Thousands (brush border) | ~200 per ciliated cell | One per cell | Dozens, arranged in staircase pattern |

| Motility | Non-motile | Motile (rhythmic beating) | Non-motile | Non-motile |

| Key cross-linkers | Villin, fimbrin, espin | N/A | N/A | Fimbrin, espin, fascin (no villin) |

| Function | Increase absorptive surface area | Mucociliary clearance; move fluid | Sensory/signaling (Hedgehog, flow sensing) | Mechanotransduction (hearing/balance); absorption (epididymis) |

| Key locations | Small intestine, proximal tubule | Respiratory epithelium, fallopian tubes, ependyma | Nearly all cell types | Inner ear hair cells, epididymis |

| Associated disease | Microvillus inclusion disease (MYO5B mutation → congenital diarrhea) | Primary ciliary dyskinesia / Kartagener syndrome (dynein arm defects → sinusitis, bronchiectasis, situs inversus) | Polycystic kidney disease (PKD1/PKD2); ciliopathies | Sensorineural hearing loss (mutations in espin, stereocilin, myosin VIIa → Usher syndrome) |

| Basal body | No (anchored to terminal web) | Yes (derived from centriole) | Yes (derived from mother centriole) | No (anchored to cuticular plate) |

  • A 70-year-old man reports nocturia and difficulty starting urination. Digital rectal exam reveals an enlarged, smooth prostate. Which mechanism best explains his symptoms? A. Increased estrogen only B. Increased apoptosis of stromal cells C. Dihydrotestosterone-induced proliferation in the transition zone D. Viral infection of prostatic epithelium E. Neoplastic transformation of basal cells

  • A 66-year-old man presents with difficulty urinating and an elevated serum PSA. Biopsy of the prostate reveals glands lined by simple columnar epithelium with prominent nucleoli and loss of basal cells. Which of the following best explains this finding?
  • A. Benign prostatic hyperplasia B. Acute bacterial prostatitis C. Prostate adenocarcinoma D. Chronic prostatitis E. Seminal vesiculitis
Slide 27: Question 4: Answer and Explanation
  • A 70-year-old man undergoes biopsy for urinary obstruction. Histology shows proliferation of both glandular and stromal tissue in the transitional zone. Which diagnosis is most consistent?
  • A. Acute prostatitis B. Chronic prostatitis C. Benign prostatic hyperplasia D. Prostate adenocarcinoma E. Seminal vesiculitis

| Option | Explanation |

| --- | --- |

| A. Acute prostatitis | Acute neutrophilic inflammation, fever, dysuria, tender prostate; does not cause nodular glandular and stromal hyperplasia. |

| B. Chronic prostatitis | Chronic inflammatory infiltrates and pelvic discomfort; lacks proliferation of both glands and stroma. |

| C. Benign prostatic hyperplasia | Hyperplasia of both glandular and stromal tissue in the transitional (periurethral) zone, causing urinary obstruction in older men. |

| D. Prostate adenocarcinoma | Usually arises in the peripheral zone and shows malignant glands rather than benign stromal-glandular hyperplasia. |

| E. Seminal vesiculitis | Inflammation of seminal vesicles; unrelated to transitional-zone prostatic enlargement. |

Slide 28: Question 5: Answer and Explanation
  • A 70-year-old man reports nocturia and difficulty starting urination. Digital rectal exam reveals an enlarged, smooth prostate. Which mechanism best explains his symptoms? A. Increased estrogen only B. Increased apoptosis of stromal cells C. Dihydrotestosterone-induced proliferation in the transition zone D. Viral infection of prostatic epithelium E. Neoplastic transformation of basal cells
  • C. Dihydrotestosterone-induced proliferation in the transition zone: BPH is driven by dihydrotestosterone (DHT), a potent androgen derived from testosterone via 5α-reductase. DHT stimulates proliferation of epithelial and stromal cells, especially in the transition zone of the prostate. This leads to urethral compression, causing urinary symptoms like hesitancy, weak stream, and nocturia
  • A. Increased estrogen only: Estrogen play a modulatory role, but it is not the primary driver of BPH.
  • B. Increased apoptosis of stromal cells: BPH involves proliferation, not apoptosis. Apoptosis would reduce prostate size
  • D. Viral infection of prostatic epithelium: No evidence supports viral infection as a cause of BPH. More relevant in prostatitis
  • E. Neoplastic transformation of basal cells: Prostate adenocarcinoma is a malignancy of prostatic glandular (secretory/luminal-type) epithelium and is characterized histologically by the absence of the basal cell layer. Prostate cancer typically involves the peripheral zone and presents with a hard, nodular prostate, not smooth enlargement.
Slide 29: BPH: Overview-Pathogenesis
  • LO: Explain the molecular and hormonal origins of prostatic nodular hyperplasia, the area of the gland affected, the natural history of the disease, various treatment strategies, and anticipated outcomes of treatment.
  • Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH):
  • Most common benign prostatic disease in men >50 years.
  • Prevalence increases with age; affects up to 90% of men by age 80.
  • Pathogenesis
  • Androgen-dependent proliferation of stromal and glandular elements.
  • Dihydrotestosterone (DHT) is the key mediator:
  • Synthesized from testosterone via 5α-reductase type 2.
  • Binds androgen receptors to promote growth and survival of prostate cells.
  • Estrogens may enhance DHT effects, especially as testosterone declines with age.
  • Hormonal Influence: Does not occur in:
  • Males castrated before puberty.
  • Males with genetic defects in androgen signaling.
  • DHT increases stromal cell proliferation and reduces epithelial cell apoptosis.
  • Kumar, Vinay, MBBS, MD, FRCPath, Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 16, 582-601
Slide 30: BPH: Morphology and C/P
  • LO: Explain the molecular and hormonal origins of prostatic nodular hyperplasia, the area of the gland affected, the natural history of the disease, various treatment strategies, and anticipated outcomes of treatment.
  • Morphology
  • Prostate weight increases 3–5× (up to 100 g or more).
  • BPH primarily affects the transition zone, leading to:
  • Urethral compression → urinary obstruction.
  • Nodules may be solid or cystic, depending on cellular content.
  • Clinical Consequences
  • Urinary symptoms include:
  • Nocturia
  • Hesitancy
  • Weak stream
  • Incomplete emptying
  • Kumar, Vinay, MBBS, MD, FRCPath, Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 16, 582-601
Slide 31: Question 6: Answer and Explanation
  • A 34-year-old man presents with dysuria, fever, and tender prostate. Urine cultures are positive for E. coli. Which of the following is contraindicated in this patient? A. Digital rectal exam B. Urine culture C. Antibiotic therapy D. PSA measurement E. Abdominal ultrasound
  • A. Digital rectal exam: In acute prostatitis, the prostate is inflamed and extremely tender. A digital rectal exam (DRE) can cause severe pain, and more importantly, risk of bacteremia or sepsis due to pressure on the infected gland.
  • B. Urine culture: Essential for identifying the causative organism and guiding antibiotic therapy.
  • C. Antibiotic therapy: Mainstay of treatment. Typically includes fluoroquinolones or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
  • D. PSA measurement: may be elevated due to inflammation, but it's not useful in acute settings.
  • E. Abdominal ultrasound: May be used to assess for urinary retention or abscess formation. Safe and not contraindicated.
Slide 32: Prostatitis
  • LO: Describe the pathophysiologic basis for inflammatory conditions affecting the prostate, including the causative organisms.
  • Types of Prostatitis
  • 1. Acute Bacterial Prostatitis
  • Sudden onset: fever, chills, dysuria, perineal pain, urinary obstruction
  • Caused by common uropathogens (e.g., E. coli)
  • Digital rectal exam is contraindicated due to risk of bacteremia
  • Diagnosis: urine culture, clinical features
  • Treated with antibiotics
  • 2. Chronic Bacterial Prostatitis
  • Recurrent UTIs with asymptomatic intervals
  • Symptoms: low back pain, dysuria, suprapubic/perineal discomfort
  • Diagnosis: leukocytes in expressed prostatic secretions, positive cultures
  • Treated with antibiotics
  • 3. Chronic Abacterial Prostatitis (Pelvic Pain Syndrome); Most common form
  • Similar symptoms to chronic bacterial prostatitis
  • No history of recurrent UTIs
  • Cultures are negative, but secretions show >10 leukocytes/HPF
  • Etiology unknown; diagnosis of exclusion
  • Treatment is empirical, based on symptoms
  • 4. Granulomatous Prostatitis
  • May mimic prostate cancer due to induration
  • Most common cause in the U.S.: BCG therapy for bladder cancer
  • Other causes: fungal infections (in immunocompromised), nonspecific foreign-body reactions
Slide 33: Prostatitis-Cont
  • LO: Describe the pathophysiologic basis for inflammatory conditions affecting the prostate, including the causative organisms.
  • Diagnosis Considerations
  • Biopsy is not routine due to nonspecific findings and risk of sepsis
  • Reserved for cases like granulomatous prostatitis or to rule out cancer
Slide 34: Question 7: Answer and Explanation
  • A 66-year-old man presents with difficulty urinating and an elevated serum PSA. Biopsy of the prostate reveals glands lined by simple columnar epithelium with prominent nucleoli and loss of basal cells. Which of the following best explains this finding?
  • A. Benign prostatic hyperplasia B. Acute bacterial prostatitis C. Prostate adenocarcinoma D. Chronic prostatitis E. Seminal vesiculitis

| Option | Explanation |

| --- | --- |

| A. BPH | Preserves the basal cell layer and does not show prominent nucleoli. |

| B. Acute bacterial prostatitis | Characterized by acute inflammation with neutrophils rather than malignant gland formation. |

| C. Prostate adenocarcinoma | Malignant glands lined by a single layer of cells with prominent nucleoli and loss of basal cells, often associated with elevated PSA. |

| D. Chronic prostatitis | Chronic inflammatory infiltrates may elevate PSA but do not cause malignant glandular architecture. |

| E. Seminal vesiculitis | Inflammation of seminal vesicles; does not explain prostatic biopsy findings. |

Slide 35: PCA: Epidemiology and Pathogenesis
  • Explain the epidemiology of prostate cancer with respect to age and family history.
  • Outline the cellular phenotype of the typical prostate adenocarcinoma cell and describe its molecular and immunohistochemical characteristics.
  • Epidemiology & Clinical Significance
  • Most common cancer in men and second leading cause of cancer death (after lung cancer).
  • Incidence increases with age:
  • ~20% in men in their 50s
  • ~70% in men aged 70–80
  • Most cases are asymptomatic, nonpalpable, and detected via needle biopsy following elevated PSA.
  • Pathogenesis
  • Androgens (especially DHT) are central to tumor growth and progression.
  • Tumors may initially respond to androgen deprivation, but often develop resistance via:
  • Androgen receptor (AR) gene amplification or mutation
  • Activation of alternative signaling pathways
  • Hereditary factors:
  • First-degree relatives → 2× increased risk
  • Germline mutations (e.g., BRCA2, MYC, mismatch repair genes) linked to aggressive disease
  • Environmental factors:
  • Western diet (charred meats, animal fats), estrogens, oxidants may contribute
  • Genetic alterations:
  • TMPRSS2–ETS fusion: common driver mutation
  • MYC amplification, PTEN deletion, TP53 loss, RB deletion
  • Epigenetic silencing of GSTP1, RB, MLH1, MSH2, APC
Slide 36: PCA: Morphology
  • LO: Define the histopathological diagnostic criteria for the diagnosis of PCA
  • Morphology & Histology:
  • 70% arise in the peripheral zone, often posteriorly → may be palpable on DRE
  • Gross appearance: firm, solid, gritty, pale, lacking normal spongy texture (circle)
  • Histologic features:
  • Small, crowded glands with single-layer epithelium
  • No basal cell layer (vs. BPH)
  • Enlarged nuclei with prominent nucleoli
  • HGPIN (high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia) seen in ~80% of cases
Slide 37: PCA: Gleason Grading System
  • LO: Define the histopathological diagnostic criteria for the diagnosis of PCA
  • Morphology & Histology:
  • Gleason grading system: Based on glandular architecture, not cytologic atypia.
  • Grades 1–5:
  • Grade 1: Well-differentiated, uniform glands
  • Grade 5: Undifferentiated sheets, cords, or nests of cells
  • Gleason Score = Primary grade + Secondary grade
  • Most treatable cancers: Score 6–7
  • Advanced/aggressive cancers: Score 8–10
  • Gleason scores are now grouped into Grade Groups 1–5, each with distinct prognostic implications.
  • Used alongside pathologic staging to guide treatment decisions.
  • Low-grade prostate adenocarcinoma (Gleason score 1 + 1 = 2) consisting of back-to-back uniform-sized malignant glands lined by a single layer of epithelial cells.
  • A focus of Gleason grade 4 prostatic adenocarcinoma displays large cribriform glands with multiple cellular bridges crossing the central lumina.
  • Grade group 5 adenocarcinoma (Gleason score 5 + 5 = 10) composed of sheets of malignant cells with no identifiable gland formation.
Slide 38: PCA: Diagnosis, Management, and Prognosis
  • LO: Compare and contrast the significance of “histological” prostatic adenocarcinoma versus a “clinically significant” adenocarcinoma.
  • Diagnosis
  • PSA testing: Widely used but has limited sensitivity and specificity
  • Elevated in BPH, prostatitis, and after instrumentation
  • MRI can help detect nonpalpable cancers
  • Serial PSA levels helpful in monitoring recurrence or progression
  • Bone metastases:
  • Common in late-stage disease
  • Typically osteoblastic (bone-forming), seen on radionuclide bone scans
  • Management & Prognosis
  • Surgery, radiation, ± hormonal therapy
  • 90% of treated patients have 15-year survival
  • Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT): Effective short-term, but androgen-independent clones often emerge
  • Achieved via LHRH agonists
  • Initially stimulates LH → then suppresses it → ↓ testosterone
  • Prognosis depends on:
  • Pathologic stage
  • Surgical margin status
  • Gleason grade
Slide 39: Histologic (Incidental) vs Clinically Significant Prostate Adenocarcinoma
  • LO: Compare and contrast the significance of “histological” prostatic adenocarcinoma versus a “clinically significant” adenocarcinoma.

| Feature | Histological PCA | Clinically Significant PCA |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Detection | Incidental (biopsy, PSA) | Symptomatic or palpable |

| Symptoms | None | Dysuria, obstruction, metastases |

| Gleason Score | Often ≤6 | Often ≥7 |

| Management | May be monitored | Requires treatment |

| Risk | Low progression | High morbidity/mortality |

Slide 44: Question 8: Answer and Explanation
  • LO: Describe the underlying abnormality causing Peyronie disease, the clinical consequences, and its treatment.
  • A 52-year-old man presents with painful erections and difficulty with intercourse. Physical exam reveals abnormal curvature during erection.
  • Which is the most likely underlying abnormality? A. Fibrous tissue deposition within the tunica albuginea B. Congenital malformation of the urethral opening C. Incomplete fusion of urethral folds D. HPV-induced dysplasia of penile epithelium E. Defective testicular descent
  • A. Fibrous tissue deposition within the tunica albuginea: This describes Peyronie disease, an acquired condition in middle-aged or older men. Characterized by: Fibrous plaque formation in the tunica albuginea (the fibrous sheath surrounding the corpora cavernosa). Leads to asymmetric erection, abnormal curvature, painful erections, and difficulty with intercourse.
  • B. Congenital malformation of the urethral opening: Refers to epispadias or hypospadias (abnormally located urethral meatus); diagnosed in infancy or childhood, not adulthood. Affect urination and cosmetic appearance
  • C. Incomplete fusion of urethral folds---hypospadias (urethral opening located on the ventral side of the penis).
  • D. HPV-induced dysplasia of penile epithelium can cause penile intraepithelial neoplasia or squamous cell carcinoma. Presents with lesions, ulcers, or masses, not curvature or fibrous plaques. Dysplasia affects the epithelium, not the tunica albuginea.
  • E. Defective testicular descent: cryptorchidism; one or both testes fail to descend into the scrotum--infertility and increased risk of testicular cancer.
Slide 45: Peyronie disease:
  • LO: Describe the underlying abnormality causing Peyronie disease, the clinical consequences, and its treatment.
  • An acquired condition in middle-aged or older men.
  • Characterized by fibrous plaque formation in the tunica albuginea (the fibrous sheath surrounding the corpora cavernosa). Leads to asymmetric erection, abnormal curvature, painful erections, and difficulty with intercourse.
  • Clinical Consequences
  • Penile curvature, especially during erection
  • Painful erections
  • Erectile dysfunction
  • Difficulty with intercourse
  • Psychological distress, including anxiety and depression
  • Diagnosis
  • Based on clinical history and physical exam
  • Palpable plaque on the shaft of the penis
  • Imaging (e.g., penile ultrasound) may be used to assess plaque size and calcification
  • Treatment Options
  • Treatment depends on severity, duration, and impact on function:
  • Non-surgical options:
  • Oral medications: Pentoxifylline (anti-fibrotic)
  • Intralesional injections: Collagenase Clostridium histolyticum (FDA-approved)
  • Verapamil or interferon (off-label)
  • Shockwave therapy: (limited evidence)
  • Surgical options (for severe or refractory cases)
Slide 46: Question 9: Answer and Explanation
  • A newborn boy is noted to have the urethral opening on the ventral surface of the penis, near the scrotum. Physical examination also reveals an inguinal hernia. Which of the following best describes the embryologic defect that led to this anomaly?
  • A. Failure of urethral folds to fuse B. Failure of genital tubercle elongation C. Abnormal descent of the gubernaculum D. Persistence of the paramesonephric ducts E. Defective positioning of the genital tubercle on the dorsal surface
  • A. Failure of urethral folds to fuse: Hypospadias results from incomplete fusion of the urethral folds during embryologic development--urethral opening being located on the ventral surface of the penis, anywhere from the glans to the perineum. Often associated with inguinal hernias and cryptorchidism due to concurrent developmental anomalies.
  • B. Failure of genital tubercle elongation--micropenis or ambiguous genitalia, not hypospadias. The genital tubercle forms the glans and shaft, but its elongation does not affect urethral fold fusion.
  • C. Abnormal descent of the gubernaculum--cryptorchidism (undescended testes), not hypospadias.
  • D. Persistence of the paramesonephric ducts: These form the female reproductive tract (uterus, fallopian tubes). Persistence in males may lead to Müllerian duct remnants, not hypospadias.
  • E. Defective positioning of the genital tubercle on the dorsal surface--epispadias, where the urethral opening is on the dorsal surface. This is not the defect seen in hypospadias, which is ventral.
Slide 47: LO: Discuss the morphology, consequences, and management of phimosis, hypospadias, and epispadias.
  • Hypospadias
  • Urethral opening on the ventral surface of the penis; may be glanular, penile, or perineal.
  • Incomplete fusion of urethral folds
  • Associated anomalies: Inguinal hernia, cryptorchidism
  • Abnormal urine stream, difficulty with urination and sexual function; Fertility issues if severe
  • Complications: Constricted urethral orifice may lead to Urinary tract obstruction and increased risk of urinary tract infections (UTIs)
  • Surgical correction, typically performed between 6–18 months of age
  • Avoid circumcision before repair (foreskin may be used in reconstruction)
  • Epispadias
  • Urethral opening on the dorsal surface of the penis
  • Defective positioning of the genital tubercle
  • Often associated with: Bladder exstrophy (anterior wall of the bladder and the lower abdominal wall fail to close, leaving the posterior bladder wall exposed to the outside).
  • May cause urinary incontinence
  • Complex surgical repair
  • Phimosis
  • Inability to retract the foreskin over the glans
  • Congenital or acquired (e.g., inflammation, scarring): Balanitis: inflammation of the glans; Balanoposthitis: inflammation of the glans and prepuce, due to poor hygiene in uncircumcised males or accumulation of smegma (desquamated cells, sweat, debris)
  • Results in hygiene issues: Increased risk of infection
  • Painful erections
  • Topical steroids
  • Circumcision if severe or recurrent
Slide 48: Question 10: Answer and Explanation
  • LO: Compare and contrast the pathogenesis and clinical consequences of disorders related to the tunica vaginalis.
  • A 30-year-old man presents with scrotal swelling. The scrotum transilluminates. Which is the most likely diagnosis? A. Hematocele B. Hydrocele C. Chylocele D. Varicocele E. Testicular tumor
  • B. Hydrocele: Fluid collection around the testicle. Transilluminates brightly. The most common cause of painless scrotal swelling in adults
  • A. Hematocele: Blood in the scrotal sac (usually after trauma or surgery). Does not transilluminate (opaque)
  • C. Chylocele: Lymphatic fluid in the scrotum (rare, often due to filariasis). May transilluminate, but very uncommon
  • D. Varicocele: Dilated veins in the pampiniform plexus. Feels like a "bag of worms“. Does not transilluminate
  • E. Testicular tumor: Solid mass. Does not transilluminate. Usually painless, firm swelling
Slide 49: Question 11: Answer and Explanation
  • A 15-year-old boy has sudden onset of severe testicular pain. Exam shows swollen tender testis with absent cremasteric reflex. Pathology: hemorrhagic infarction. Which mechanism best explains this condition? A. Venous outflow obstruction with continued arterial inflow B. Arterial occlusion by thrombosis C. Epididymal infection by Chlamydia trachomatis D. Failure of gubernaculum attachment E. Hemorrhage into tunica vaginalis
  • Twisting of the spermatic cord → obstructs venous outflow first.
  • Arterial inflow continues for a short time, leading to congestion, edema, and eventually hemorrhagic infarction due to compromised perfusion. Arterial occlusion by thrombosis
  • B. Arterial occlusion is not the initiating event in torsion. Venous obstruction occurs first.
  • C. Epididymal infection by Chlamydia trachomatis causes epididymitis---gradual onset, pain, and positive Prehn sign (pain relief with elevation).
  • D. Failure of gubernaculum attachment is a predisposing factor for torsion but not the mechanism of infarction.
  • E. Hemorrhage into the tunica vaginalis is a result, not a cause, of torsion-related ischemia.
Slide 50: Testicular Torsion:
  • LO: Describe the clinical features and pathologic findings in the testis that occur due to torsion of the spermatic cord
  • Twisting of the spermatic cord
  • Typically results in obstruction of testicular venous drainage while the thick-walled and more resilient arteries remain patent
  • If untreated---engorgement and infarction
  • Two types of testicular torsion:
  • Neonatal torsion ( in utero or shortly after birth); no associated anatomic defect
  • Adult torsion results from a bilateral anatomic defect in the anchoring of the testis in the scrotal sac that leads to its increased mobility; it typically occurs in adolescence and manifests with the sudden onset of testicular pain.
  • A urologic emergency
  • Manual untwisting within 6 hours of onset---testis remains viable.
  • Contralateral orchiopexy is performed to prevent recurrence in the unaffected testis.
  • Male Genital System and Lower Urinary Tract

Kumar, Vinay, MBBS, MD, FRCPath, Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 16, 582-601

Testicular torsion. The dark discoloration is the result of hemorrhage and infarction that occurs when twisting of the spermatic cord cuts off venous drainage. (From Klatt EC: Robbins and Cotran Atlas of Pathology, ed 4, Fig. 12.18, Philadelphia, ...
