Slide 56: Question 12: Answer and Explanation
  • A 28-year-old man presents with a painless enlargement of his left testis. He has a history of left-sided cryptorchidism that was corrected by orchiopexy at age 7. Physical examination reveals a firm, non-transilluminating testicular mass. Ultrasound confirms a solid intratesticular lesion.
  • Which of the following best describes the significance of this patient’s history?
  • A. Cryptorchidism increases the risk of germ cell tumors only in the undescended testis B. Cryptorchidism increases the risk of germ cell tumors in both the previously undescended and contralateral descended testis C. Early orchiopexy (before 1 year of age) eliminates the risk of infertility and malignancy D. Cryptorchidism predisposes primarily to Leydig cell tumors E. Cryptorchidism increases risk of seminoma only, not other germ cell tumors

| | Explanation |

| --- | --- |

| A. | Incorrect. Risk is increased in both testes, not only the undescended one. |

| B. | Correct. Cryptorchidism increases risk of germ cell tumors in the previously undescended testis and the contralateral testis. |

| C. | Early orchiopexy reduces risk but does not eliminate infertility or malignancy risk. |

| D. | Cryptorchidism is linked primarily to germ cell tumors, not Leydig cell tumors. |

| E. | Risk is increased for multiple germ cell tumors, although seminoma is classically associated. |

Notes:

Cryptorchidism (undescended testis) is a well-established risk factor for testicular germ cell tumors in both:

The previously undescended testis, even after orchiopexy.

The contralateral normally descended testis.

Slide 57: Cryptorchidism
  • LO:
  • Describe the complications observed for failure of the testes to descend (cryptorchidism).
  • Describe the most important risk factors, genetic associations, and molecular basis for the development of testicular tumors and outline the clinicopathologic features for the different morphologic patterns seen.
  • Cryptorchidism is a complete or partial failure of the intraabdominal testes to descend into the scrotal sac
  • It is associated with testicular dysfunction and an increased risk of testicular cancer
  • Cryptorchidism is found in approximately 1% of 1-year-old boys
  • Normally, the testes descend from the abdominal cavity into the pelvis by the third month of gestation and then through the inguinal canals into the scrotum during the last 2 months of intrauterine life.
  • The diagnosis of cryptorchidism is only established with certainty after 1 year of age particularly in premature infants
  • Undescended testes become atrophic, bilateral cryptorchidism results in sterility.
  • Even unilateral cryptorchidism may be associated with atrophy of the contralateral descended gonad.
  • Patients with unilateral cryptorchidism are also at increased risk for the development of cancer in the contralateral, normally descended testis ( intrinsic abnormality, rather than simple failure of descent)
  • Cryptorchid testes are small and firm.
  • The histologic changes include thickening of the basement membrane, loss of spermatogonia, increased interstitial stroma, and relative prominence of Leydig cells.
  • Germ cell neoplasia in situ may be present in cryptorchid testes; precursor of subsequent germ cell tumors.
  • Current recommendations are for surgical repositioning (orchiopexy), to be performed at 6 to 12 months of age.
Slide 58: Question 13: Answer and Explanation
  • A 7-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician because of early development of pubic hair, acne, and rapid growth. Physical exam shows asymmetry of the scrotum with a firm, non-tender mass in the left testis. Serum studies show elevated testosterone but normal α-fetoprotein (AFP) and human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG). Histology of the excised mass shows polygonal cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm containing rod-shaped intracytoplasmic inclusions.
  • Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
  • A. Seminoma B. Embryonal carcinoma C. Leydig cell tumor D. Yolk sac tumor E. Choriocarcinoma

| Option | Explanation |

| --- | --- |

| A. Seminoma | Usually presents in adults; not associated with testosterone excess or Reinke crystals. |

| B. Embryonal carcinoma | Aggressive germ cell tumor; often AFP and/or hCG abnormalities. |

| C. Leydig cell tumor | Testosterone-producing tumor causing precocious puberty; histology shows Reinke crystals. |

| D. Yolk sac tumor | Associated with elevated AFP and Schiller-Duval bodies. |

| E. Choriocarcinoma | Produces hCG, often causing gynecomastia rather than androgen excess. |

Slide 59: Leydig Cell Tumor
  • LO: Describe the most important risk factors, genetic associations, and molecular basis for the development of testicular tumors and outline the clinicopathologic features for the different morphologic patterns seen.
  • Leydig Cell Tumor
  • Most common sex cord-stromal tumor in children.
  • Can occur at any age (children and adults)
  • Presents with precocious puberty in boys (pubic hair, acne, rapid growth); Elevated testosterone.
  • In adults: may cause gynecomastia; excess estrogen from androgen aromatization
  • Painless, firm testicular mass; often unilateral.
  • Histologic Features
  • Polygonal cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm.
  • Reinke crystals (rod-shaped intracytoplasmic inclusions)
  • No lymphocytic infiltrate or germ cell elements.
  • Pathogenesis
  • Arises from Leydig (interstitial) cells of the testis.
  • Not associated with GCNIS or i(12p) abnormalities.
  • Prognosis: Mostly benign
  • Surgical excision is typically curative.
  • Step 1 Buzzwords
  • “Precocious puberty in a boy with testicular mass.”
  • “Gynecomastia in an adult man with testicular mass.”
  • “Golden-brown tumor with Reinke crystals.”
  • “Normal AFP and hCG levels.”

Notes:

Germ Cell Neoplasia In Situ: Abnormal germ cells remain confined within seminiferous tubules before developing into invasive cancer. Most seminomas and many nonseminomatous germ cell tumors arise from GCNIS.

i(12p) = classic cytogenetic marker of testicular germ cell tumors. In i(12p), the short arm (p arm) of chromosome 12 is duplicated.

Slide 60: Question 14: Answer and Explanation
  • A 42-year-old man presents with a painless enlargement of his left testicle. Physical examination reveals a firm, non-transilluminating mass. Ultrasound shows a well-circumscribed, homogeneous intratesticular lesion. Serum tumor markers reveal normal alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and mildly elevated human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG). The testis is surgically removed. Gross examination shows a pale, fleshy, homogeneous mass without hemorrhage or necrosis. Histology reveals large polygonal cells with clear cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, and prominent nucleoli arranged in lobules separated by fibrous septa with lymphocytic infiltrates.
  • Which of the following best describes the most likely diagnosis?
  • A. Embryonal carcinoma B. Yolk sac tumor C. Choriocarcinoma D. Seminoma E. Teratoma

| Option | Explanation |

| --- | --- |

| A. Embryonal carcinoma | Usually hemorrhagic and necrotic with pleomorphic cells. |

| B. Yolk sac tumor | Most common in children; AFP elevated. |

| C. Choriocarcinoma | Markedly elevated hCG; hemorrhagic tumor composed of trophoblasts. |

| D. Seminoma | Homogeneous fleshy mass with large clear cells, distinct borders, fibrous septa, and lymphocytes; AFP normal. |

| E. Teratoma | Contains tissues from multiple germ layers. |

Slide 61: Seminoma
  • LO: Describe the most important risk factors, genetic associations, and molecular basis for the development of testicular tumors and outline the clinicopathologic features for the different morphologic patterns seen.
  • A germ cell tumor presents as a soft, well-demarcated, gray-white, pale, fleshy tumor that bulges from the cut surface of the affected testis
  • Large tumors may contain foci of coagulative necrosis, usually without hemorrhage
  • It is composed of large, uniform cells with distinct cell borders, clear glycogen-rich cytoplasm, round nuclei, and conspicuous nucleoli
  • The cells often are arrayed in small lobules with intervening fibrous septa.
  • A lymphocytic infiltrate is usually present.
  • In approximately 15% of cases, syncytiotrophoblasts are present; these cells are the source of the minimally elevated serum human choriogonadotropin (hCG) that is seen in 10% to 15% of patients with stage I disease, increasing to 30% to 50% in disseminated disease.
  • Their presence has no bearing on prognosis, and the levels of hCG are usually much lower than in choriocarcinoma
  • Kumar, Vinay, MBBS, MD, FRCPath, Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 16, 582-601

Notes:

A huge syncytiotrophoblastic giant cell with hundreds of nuclei is seen in this image. It is surrounded by typical seminoma cells and lymphoid infiltrate. Syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells are positive for beta-hCG immunostain.

Slide 62: Question 15: Answer and Explanation
  • A 2-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because his parents noticed a painless enlargement of the right scrotum. Physical exam shows a firm, non-transilluminating testicular mass. Serum studies reveal markedly elevated alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) levels. Histologic examination of the excised mass shows structures resembling primitive glomeruli (Schiller-Duval bodies).
  • Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
  • A. Seminoma B. Embryonal carcinoma C. Yolk sac tumor D. Choriocarcinoma E. Teratoma

| Option | Explanation |

| --- | --- |

| A. Seminoma | Occurs mainly in adults and does not elevate AFP. |

| B. Embryonal carcinoma | Usually occurs in young adults with aggressive histology. |

| C. Yolk sac tumor | Most common testicular tumor in young children; associated with elevated AFP and Schiller-Duval bodies. |

| D. Choriocarcinoma | Associated with elevated hCG rather than AFP. |

| E. Teratoma | Contains differentiated tissues from multiple germ layers. |

Slide 63: Yolk sac tumor
  • LO: Describe the most important risk factors, genetic associations, and molecular basis for the development of testicular tumors and outline the clinicopathologic features for the different morphologic patterns seen.
  • Most common primary testicular neoplasm in children younger than 3 years of age
  • Has a very good prognosis in this age
  • Postpubertal yolk sac tumor is rarely “pure” and more frequently occurs in combination with embryonal carcinoma or other germ cell components.
  • Tumors are composed of low cuboidal to columnar epithelial cells that form microcysts, lacelike (reticular) patterns, sheets, glands, and papillae.
  • A distinctive feature is the structures resembling primitive glomeruli, so-called Schiller-Duval bodies.
  • Have eosinophilic hyaline globules containing α 1 -antitrypsin and alphafetoprotein (AFP); IHC
  • Male Genital System and Lower Urinary Tract

Kumar, Vinay, MBBS, MD, FRCPath, Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 16, 582-601

Yolk sac tumor demonstrating areas of loosely textured, microcystic tissue and papillary structures resembling a developing glomerulus (Schiller-Duval bodies). Histological section shows microcystic yolk sac tumor with Schiller-Duval bodies resemb...

Copyright © 2023 Copyright © 2023 Elsevier Inc. All rights are reserved, including those for text and data mining, AI training, and similar technologies.

Notes:

Papillary structures are called Schiller-Duval bodies. It consists of a fibrovascular core with a single central thin-walled vessel in a hyalinized stroma surrounded by a one or more layers of cuboidal or columnar tumor cells with clear cytoplasm. The papillary structure is contained within a cystic space lined by flattened cells. Schiller-Duval body is a hallmark of yolk sac tumor but is not required for diagnosis and may not be seen in every case.

Slide 64: Question 16: Answer and Explanation
  • A 25-year-old man presents with a painless enlargement of his right testis. Physical exam reveals a firm, non-transilluminating scrotal mass. Serum studies show elevated α-fetoprotein (AFP) and β-human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG). Gross pathology shows a variegated mass with hemorrhage and necrosis. Histology demonstrates sheets of primitive cells forming gland-like structures, admixed with areas of yolk sac tumor and syncytiotrophoblasts.
  • Which of the following is the most accurate classification of this tumor?
  • A. Seminoma B. Pure embryonal carcinoma C. Yolk sac tumor D. Mixed germ cell tumor E. Leydig cell tumor

| Option | Explanation |

| --- | --- |

| A. Seminoma | Pure seminomas do not contain multiple germ cell components. |

| B. Pure embryonal carcinoma | Histology shows embryonal carcinoma plus additional tumor types. |

| C. Yolk sac tumor | Cannot explain syncytiotrophoblast and embryonal carcinoma components. |

| D. Mixed germ cell tumor | Presence of multiple germ cell tumor elements (embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, syncytiotrophoblasts). |

| E. Leydig cell tumor | Sex cord-stromal tumor, not a mixed germ cell neoplasm. |

Slide 65: LO: Describe the most important risk factors, genetic associations, and molecular basis for the development of testicular tumors and outline the clinicopathologic features for the different morphologic patterns seen.

| Tumor Type | Typical Age | Histologic Features | Tumor Markers | Genetic Associations |

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| Seminoma | 40–50 | Sheets of uniform polygonal cells with clear cytoplasm (Fried-egg cell); lymphocytes in the stroma | APF is normal; 10% of patients have elevated hCG (syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells) | GCNIS, i(12p), KIT mutations |

| Embryonal carcinoma | 20–30 | Poorly differentiated, pleomorphic cells in cords, sheets, or papillary formation; most contain some yolk sac and choriocarcinoma cells | AFP may be elevated | GCNIS, i(12p) |

| Spermatocytic tumor | 50–60 | Small, medium, and large polygonal cells; no inflammatory infiltrate | Negative | Gain of chromosome 9q; not associated with GCNIS or i(12p) |

| Yolk sac tumor | 3 | Microcystic/reticular pattern; Schiller-Duval bodies may be present | 90% of patients have elevated AFP | Prepubertal type not associated with GCNIS or i(12p); postpubertal type may be associated |

| Choriocarcinoma | 20–30 | Cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast without villus formation | 100% of patients have elevated hCG | GCNIS, i(12p) |

| Teratoma | All ages | Tissues from all three germ cell layers with varying degrees of differentiation | 20%–25% have elevated AFP | Prepubertal type not associated with GCNIS or i(12p); postpubertal type associated with i(12p) |

| Mixed tumor | 15–30 | Variable, depending on mixture; commonly teratoma and embryonal carcinoma | AFP and hCG are variably elevated, depending on mixture | GCNIS, i(12p) |

Notes:

Germ cell tumors make tumor markers (AFP, hCG). Sex cord-stromal (Leydig cell) tumors make hormones (testosterone, estrogen); Sertoli cell

Is usually hormonally silent.

Slide 66: Question 17:
  • A 55-year-old uncircumcised man presents with an ulcerated lesion on the glans penis. Biopsy shows keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma. Which of the following is the strongest risk factor? A. Infection with HPV-16 B. Testicular torsion C. Peyronie disease D. Cryptorchidism E. Circumcision in infancy
Slide 67: Question 17: Answer and Explanation
  • A 55-year-old uncircumcised man presents with an ulcerated lesion on the glans penis. Biopsy shows keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma. Which of the following is the strongest risk factor? A. Infection with HPV-16 B. Testicular torsion C. Peyronie disease D. Cryptorchidism E. Circumcision in infancy
  • Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the most common penile malignancy
  • Strongest risk factor for penile SCC is infection with high-risk HPV types, especially HPV-16 and HPV-18. These viruses are oncogenic and contribute to malignant transformation through disruption of tumor suppressor pathways (e.g., p53 and Rb).
  • B. Testicular torsion: A urological emergency involving the spermatic cord; not related to penile cancer.
  • C. Peyronie disease: A fibrotic condition of the penile shaft; not associated with malignancy.
  • D. Cryptorchidism: Increases risk for testicular cancer, not penile SCC.
  • E. Circumcision in infancy: Protective against penile cancer due to improved hygiene and reduced HPV transmission.
Slide 68: Condyloma Acuminata (Genital Warts):
  • LO: Explain the spectrum of squamous neoplasia affecting the penis, ranging from condyloma acuminata to invasive squamous cell carcinoma, describing the risk factors, pathogenesis, morphologic features, complications, and treatment strategies.
  • 1. Condyloma Acuminata (Genital Warts):
  • Etiology: Caused by low-risk HPV types (mainly HPV-6 and HPV-11).
  • Morphology: Exophytic, papillary lesions on the penile shaft or glans.
  • Histology: Koilocytosis (perinuclear clearing), acanthosis (thickening of the epidermis, specifically the stratum spinosum ), papillomatosis.
  • Pathogenesis: Viral infection leads to benign epithelial proliferation.
  • Complications: Rare progression to malignancy; mostly cosmetic and psychological impact.
  • Treatment: Topical agents (imiquimod, podophyllin), cryotherapy, surgical excision.
  • Numerous cauliflower-like lesions
  • characteristic koilocytes with enlarged, hyperchromatic, wrinkled nuclei and perinuclear halo
  • https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/penscrotumcondyloma.html
Slide 69: Penile Intraepithelial Neoplasia (PeIN)
  • LO: Explain the spectrum of squamous neoplasia affecting the penis, ranging from condyloma acuminata to invasive squamous cell carcinoma, describing the risk factors, pathogenesis, morphologic features, complications, and treatment strategies.
  • 2. Penile Intraepithelial Neoplasia (PeIN)
  • Etiology: Associated with high-risk HPV types (especially HPV-16 and HPV-18).
  • Morphology: Solitary plaque, often on the shaft or glans.
  • Histology: Full-thickness epithelial atypia, nuclear pleomorphism, mitoses (arrows), intact basement membrane.
  • Pathogenesis: Dysplastic transformation of squamous epithelium without stromal invasion.
  • Complications: ~10% progress to invasive squamous cell carcinoma.
  • Treatment: Topical chemotherapy (5-FU), laser ablation, surgical excision.
  • Male Genital System and Lower Urinary Tract

Kumar, Vinay, MBBS, MD, FRCPath, Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, 16, 582-601

Slide 70: Penile Invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)
  • 3. Invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)
  • Etiology: Strongly linked to HPV-16/18, poor hygiene, smoking, chronic inflammation, and lack of circumcision.
  • Morphology: Ulcerated, indurated, crusted lesion on the glans or prepuce.
  • Histology: Keratinizing squamous cells invading the stroma; nuclear atypia, mitotic figures.
  • Pathogenesis: Progression from PeIN with basement membrane breach and stromal infiltration.
  • Complications:
  • Local tissue destruction.
  • Lymphatic spread to inguinal and pelvic nodes.
  • Poor prognosis with nodal metastasis.
  • Treatment:
  • Early-stage: Partial penectomy, Mohs surgery.
  • Advanced: Total penectomy, lymphadenectomy, radiation, chemotherapy.
  • Special Variant: Verrucous Carcinoma
  • Etiology: Not HPV-related.
  • Morphology: Papillary, exophytic growth with pushing margins.
  • Histology: Minimal atypia, locally invasive but non-metastasizing.
  • Treatment: Surgical excision; radiation avoided due to risk of anaplastic transformation.

Slide 5
  • Part 1: Anatomy and Histology
Slide 6
  • Tunica albuginea → septa → lobules → seminiferous tubules
  • Sertoli cells line the tubule; tight junctions form the blood-testis barrier (immune privilege)
  • Leydig cells in the interstitium, outside the barrier, beside capillaries
  • ≈90% of testicular volume is tubule: small testes = impaired spermatogenesis
  • Normal volume 15–25 mL by orchidometer: a bedside fertility measurement
  • Testis Architecture

Notes:

Build the two-compartment concept: inside the barrier (germ cells, Sertoli) vs outside (Leydig, vessels).

The tunica albuginea is the capsule; it sends in septa; the septa carve out ~250 lobules; each lobule packs 1–4 seminiferous tubules where Sertoli cells shepherd germ cells through spermatogenesis, while Leydig cells in the interstitium between tubules make testosterone. [1][3][6]

Slide 7
  • The Duct Pathway: SEVEn UP
  • Seminiferous tubules → Epididymis → Vas deferens → Ejaculatory duct → Urethra → Penis
  • Tubule → rete testis → efferent ductules → epididymis (head, body, tail)
  • Vas joins the seminal vesicle duct → ejaculatory duct → prostatic urethra
  • Sperm are stored in the cauda (tail) epididymis

Notes:

Say the mnemonic aloud. Retained quiz item.

The seminiferous tubules empty into the rete testis, which channels sperm through ~12 efferent ductules that reabsorb >90% of testicular fluid; the ductules merge into the single epididymal duct, where sperm mature (caput → corpus) and are then stored quiescent in the cauda until ejaculation — all while the sperm themselves remain passive passengers.

Slide 8
  • What Is Semen? Composition by Source
  • PSA’s day job: a serine protease that liquefies the seminal coagulum: a fertility protein we co-opted as a tumor marker
  • Low-volume, acidic, fructose-negative ejaculate → ejaculatory duct obstruction or absent vas

| Source | Share | Key constituents |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Seminal vesicles | 65–75% | Fructose, alkaline buffer, semenogelin (coagulum) |

| Prostate | 20–30% | PSA, zinc, citrate, acid phosphatase |

| Testis / epididymis | ≈5% | Spermatozoa |

| Bulbourethral glands | Trace | Pre-ejaculate lubrication |

Notes:

The fructose point returns in the azoospermia workup.

Slide 9
  • Peripheral zone: ≈70% of gland, posterior, palpable on DRE
  • → 70–80% of prostate cancer
  • Transition zone: periurethral → the exclusive site of BPH
  • Central zone: around ejaculatory ducts, rarely diseased
  • Anterior fibromuscular stroma: non-glandular
  • So: a huge prostate ≠ cancer; a normal DRE ≠ no cancer; TURP neither treats nor prevents cancer
  • Prostate Zonal Anatomy — The Most Portable Fact Today
Slide 10
  • Paired corpora cavernosa (erectile) + corpus spongiosum (surrounds urethra, stays compliant, forms glans)
  • Tunica albuginea — bilayered, inelastic.
  • Remember it: it returns in Peyronie disease, penile fracture, and the veno-occlusive mechanism
  • Arterial: internal pudendal → cavernosal → helicine arterioles → sinusoids
  • Venous: sinusoids → subtunical venous plexus → deep dorsal vein
  • Buck’s fascia contained hematoma to the shaft
  • Colles fascia extension → perineal “butterfly” →concern for urethral injury
  • Fascial planes
  • Scarpa's (abdomen) → dartos (penis/scrotum) → Colles’ (perineum) form one uninterrupted space, which is why extravasated blood or urine spreads across all three regions once Buck's fascia is breached
  • Penile Anatomy

Notes:

Flag the tunica three-appearances arc explicitly.

Helicine arteries are the terminal, coiled branches of the deep (cavernosal) artery that open directly into the sinusoidal (lacunar) spaces of the corpus cavernosum — they are the final arterial gateway controlling penile erection. The name "helicine" reflects their tortuous, corkscrew-like course in the flaccid state, which straightens and dilates during erection

The extent of bruising localizes the plane of injury. Confined to the shaft = Buck's fascia intact (isolated tunical/corporal injury). Butterfly perineal + scrotal + suprapubic spread = Buck's fascia breached, which should raise concern for anterior (bulbar) urethral injury and prompt retrograde urethrography before catheterization

Slide 11
  • Scrotal Layers, Paired With Their Pathology
  • Tunica vaginalis (from processus vaginalis) → hydrocele; patent processus → communicating hydrocele + indirect hernia
  • Cremaster (internal oblique) → cremasteric reflex: stroke medial thigh
  • Femoral branch carries afferents up
  • Genital branch caries motor efferent back to cremaster → elevation of ipsilateral testis
  • Reflex arc mediated by the genitofemoral nerve (L1–L2)
  • Dartos + skin → thermoregulation; the plane of Fournier gangrene
  • Reflex is absent in torsion: the single most useful acute-scrotum exam finding
  • Presence of reflex does not exclude torsion

Notes:

Tunica vaginalis / processus vaginalis → hydrocele & hernia. The tunica vaginalis is the peritoneal remnant left after the processus vaginalis (which the descending testis drags into the scrotum) normally obliterates; fluid trapped in a closed remnant is a simple (non-communicating) hydrocele, whereas a persistently patent processus allows peritoneal fluid down to give a communicating hydrocele and, if wide enough for bowel, an indirect inguinal hernia.

Cremaster (from internal oblique) → cremasteric reflex. Stroking the medial thigh sends afferents up the femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve, and the genital branch carries the motor efferent back to the cremaster, elevating the ipsilateral testis — a reflex arc mediated by the genitofemoral nerve (L1–L2).

Dartos + skin → thermoregulation and the Fournier plane. The dartos is the scrotal smooth-muscle layer that contracts in cold to wrinkle the skin and reduce heat-losing surface area for testicular thermoregulation, and — as part of the continuous dartos–Colles'–Scarpa's superficial fascial space — it is the anatomical plane along which Fournier gangrene spreads.

Absent reflex in torsion — the key acute-scrotum sign. In testicular torsion the cremasteric reflex is characteristically lost; it is the single most sensitive exam finding (absent in up to 100% of torsion cases, odds ratio ~47.6), though a present reflex does not fully exclude torsion.

Slide 12
  • Testicular arteries arise from the aorta
  • Right gonadal vein → IVC; left gonadal vein → left renal vein at 90° over a longer column → left-sided varicocele
  • Testis lymphatics → retroperitoneal para-aortic nodes: never inguinal
  • Penis and scrotal skin → inguinal nodes
  • Hence:
  • Testis cancer surgery is inguinal, never trans-scrotal
  • Penile cancer prognosis lives in the groin
  • Venous and Lymphatic Drainage — Two Asymmetries That Matter

Notes:

Testis = retroperitoneum by birth → drains para-aortic → operate through the groin, never the scrotum.

Penis/scrotal skin = surface structure → drains to the groin → the groin nodes are where the prognosis is decided.

Slide 13
  • Spermatogonia (D) at the basement membrane
  • Primary (B) → secondary spermatocytes → spermatids toward the lumen (E)
  • Spermatozoa in the lumen (C)
  • Sertoli cells (F) span basement membrane to lumen
  • Leydig cells in the interstitium between tubules
  • Histology 1 of 2: Seminiferous Tubule

Notes:

A-Basement membrane

True secondary spermatocytes are rarely caught on a section because meiosis II is so fast, so many "E" cells in any real slide are early spermatids

Slide 14
  • Epididymis: pseudostratified columnar epithelium with stereocilia; lumen packed with sperm
  • Prostate: tuboalveolar acini with papillary infoldings; corpora amylacea (calcified secretions) in older men
  • Seminal vesicle mimics prostate but has no corpora amylacea
  • Basal cell layer loss is a histologic criterion of prostate cancer
  • Histology 2 of 2: Epididymis and Prostate

Notes:

Corpora amylacea is the discriminator — a retained quiz item hinges on it.

Slide 15
  • Part 2: Spermatogenesis
Slide 16
  • The Three-Month Clock
  • Spermatogenesis: 64–74 days
  • Epididymal transit and maturation: 10–14 days
  • Total ≈ 3 months — today’s semen analysis reports events from 3 months ago
  • A febrile illness, hot tub, or new drug 2 months ago shows up today
  • Every intervention: varicocelectomy, stopping testosterone, weight loss — needs ≥3 months before the repeat semen analysis means anything

Notes:

This clock governs the entire infertility segment.

Slide 17
  • Stages of Spermatogenesis
  • Spermatogonia: type A dark (reserve) · A pale (renewing) · B (committed)
  • Meiosis I: primary spermatocyte → two secondary spermatocytes
  • Meiosis II: → spermatids (haploid)
  • Spermiogenesis (remodeling, no division): Golgi → acrosome; protamines replace histones; flagellum + mitochondrial midpiece; cytoplasm shed as residual body (Sertoli phagocytoses it)
  • Spermiation: released into the lumen — immotile and infertile
  • Motility is gained in the epididymis; capacitation and the acrosome reaction occur in the female tract — classic distractor

Notes:

Spermatogonia (mitotic pool, on the basement membrane). Type A-dark = reserve stem cells (rarely divide, the emergency backup), type A-pale = renewing/active stem cells (routine self-renewal + differentiation), and type B = committed cells that divide into primary spermatocytes and enter meiosis.

Meiosis I. One diploid primary spermatocyte → two haploid secondary spermatocytes; the long pachytene prophase (~3 weeks) is why primary spermatocytes are the most conspicuous germ cell on biopsy. [1][4]

Meiosis II. Each secondary spermatocyte divides quickly (<10 h, so rarely seen) into spermatids — haploid (1N).

Spermiogenesis (remodeling, NO cell division). Round spermatid → spermatozoon: the Golgi forms the acrosomal cap; protamines replace histones for extreme nuclear condensation and transcriptional silencing; a flagellum and mitochondrial midpiece are built; and excess cytoplasm is shed as a residual body that Sertoli cells phagocytose.

Spermiation. The spermatozoon is released into the tubular lumen but is still immotile and infertile at this point.

The classic distractors — the "where" questions. Motility is acquired later, during transit/storage in the epididymis; capacitation and the acrosome reaction occur in the female reproductive tract (capacitation begins in the uterus, hyperactivation/acrosome reaction in the oviduct/ampulla), NOT in the testis

the testis builds the sperm (through spermiogenesis), the epididymis makes it move, and the female tract makes it fertile (capacitation + acrosome reaction).

Slide 18
  • The Sertoli Cell — Most Testable Cell of the Day
  • Forms the blood-testis barrier → immune privilege for antigenically novel post-meiotic cells
  • Explains antisperm antibodies after vasectomy or trauma, and the severity of mumps orchitis
  • Responds to FSH
  • Secretes androgen-binding protein, inhibin B (FSH feedback + spermatogenesis marker), AMH (fetal)
  • Number fixed after puberty → sets the ceiling on sperm output
  • Contrast: Leydig = LH → testosterone, androstenedione, DHEA (DHT is made peripherally, not by Leydig cells)

Notes:

Blood-testis barrier → immune privilege. Adjacent Sertoli cells form tight junctions that create the blood-testis barrier, sequestering antigenically "novel" post-meiotic germ cells (which arise after puberty, long after central immune tolerance is set) from the immune system.

Explains antisperm antibodies and mumps orchitis severity. Because those germ-cell antigens are hidden, any breach — vasectomy, trauma, torsion, or infection — exposes them and triggers antisperm antibodies; the same principle underlies the immune-mediated inflammatory damage of mumps orchitis.

Responds to FSH. Sertoli cells carry the FSH receptor, making them the primary target of FSH within the tubule.

Secretory products. FSH stimulation drives androgen-binding protein (concentrates intratubular testosterone), inhibin B (negative FSH feedback and a clinical marker of spermatogenesis), and AMH (fetal — drives Müllerian regression; falls at puberty).

Fixed number after puberty → sets the sperm-output ceiling. Each Sertoli cell supports a finite number of germ cells, so the post-pubertal Sertoli population caps maximum sperm production.

Contrast — Leydig cells (interstitium, LH-driven). LH → Leydig cells → testosterone, plus weaker androgens androstenedione and DHEA; note DHT is generated peripherally by 5α-reductase, not synthesized by Leydig cells

Sertoli = FSH → barrier, ABP, inhibin B, AMH, and the sperm-output ceiling; Leydig = LH → testosterone (DHT made peripherally)

Slide 19
  • Thermoregulation: Why the Testis Lives Outside
  • Operates 2–4 °C below core temperature
  • Pampiniform plexus countercurrent exchange cools arterial inflow
  • Cremaster and dartos adjust position and surface area
  • One mechanism, four diseases: cryptorchidism, varicocele, obesity, occupational heat all impair spermatogenesis through the same thermal pathway

Notes:

Operates 2–4 °C below core temperature because spermatogenesis (and DNA/enzyme integrity in meiosis) is heat-sensitive and fails at core body temperature.

Pampiniform plexus countercurrent exchange — the venous plexus wraps the testicular artery so cool venous return draws heat out of warm arterial inflow before it reaches the testis.

Cremaster and dartos adjust testicular position (closer/farther from the body) and scrotal surface area to fine-tune heat loss.

One mechanism, four diseases — cryptorchidism, varicocele, obesity, and occupational heat exposure all raise testicular temperature and impair spermatogenesis through this same thermal pathway.

Slide 20
  • Poll 1: The Febrile Illness
  • A 29-year-old man had a high fever 6 weeks ago. His semen analysis today is abnormal.
  • Which germ-cell stage was most likely affected at the time of the fever?
  • A. Spermatozoa in the epididymis
  • B. Cells in late spermiogenesis
  • C. Meiotic spermatocytes / early stages
  • D. Only mature stored sperm

Notes:

Answer: C — work backward through the ≈74-day timeline. Reveal after polling; reinforce that capacitation happens in the female tract.

Mature stored sperm in the epididymis (A, D) and cells in late spermiogenesis (B) would already have been ejaculated or cleared within the first 2–3 weeks after the fever, so they would not account for an abnormality persisting at 6 weeks

Slide 21
  • Part 3: Hormonal Regulation
Slide 22
  • The Hypothalamic–Pituitary–Gonadal Axis
  • GnRH is pulsatile — and pulsatility is obligatory
  • Continuous GnRH exposure downregulates the receptor and shuts the axis off (hold that thought until leuprolide)
  • LH → Leydig → testosterone (rate-limiting step: StAR cholesterol transport)
  • FSH → Sertoli → androgen-binding protein + inhibin B
  • Feedback: testosterone and estradiol centrally; inhibin B selectively suppresses FSH

Notes:

Plant the leuprolide flag now, collect it in pharmacology. Spoken endocrine handoff.

GnRH is pulsatile, and pulsatility is obligatory — hypothalamic GnRH must be secreted in discrete pulses (~every 60–120 min) to sustain gonadotropin output.

Continuous GnRH exposure shuts the axis off — sustained (non-pulsatile) stimulation downregulates and desensitizes the pituitary GnRH receptor, collapsing LH/FSH release (the basis of leuprolide and other GnRH agonists causing chemical castration).

LH → Leydig → testosterone — LH drives Leydig-cell steroidogenesis, whose rate-limiting step is StAR-mediated cholesterol transport into the mitochondrion.

FSH → Sertoli → ABP + inhibin B — FSH stimulates Sertoli cells to secrete androgen-binding protein (concentrates intratubular testosterone) and inhibin B.

Feedback — testosterone and estradiol exert central negative feedback (hypothalamus + pituitary), while inhibin B selectively suppresses FSH at the pituitary

Slide 23
  • Intratesticular Testosterone — The Concept Behind Case B
  • Intratesticular testosterone ≈ 50–100× serum concentration — spermatogenesis requires the gradient
  • Exogenous testosterone: serum T up → LH suppressed → intratesticular T collapses → spermatogenesis stops
  • Testosterone is a male contraceptive
  • Never start testosterone in a man who wants near-term fertility
  • Every azoospermic young man gets asked directly about testosterone, “men’s clinic” injections, and anabolic steroids
Slide 24
  • Testosterone Transport: Why “Normal Total T” Can Mislead
  • ≈44–65% bound to SHBG (tight, unavailable) · ≈33–50% to albumin (loose) · 2–3% free
  • Bioavailable = free + albumin-bound
  • SHBG falls: obesity, insulin resistance, T2DM, hypothyroidism
  • SHBG rises: aging, hyperthyroidism, cirrhosis, estrogens, anticonvulsants
  • The obese 45-year-old with a “normal” total T can still be biochemically hypogonadal
  • → order free or bioavailable T only when SHBG is distorted

Notes:

Free testosterone measured by most labs is unreliable because the common direct analog immunoassay is inaccurate — it systematically misestimates free T and is not recommended; either calculated free T (from total T, SHBG, albumin) or equilibrium dialysis should be used instead.

The problem — the widely available direct analog radioimmunoassay for free T does not correlate well with the reference equilibrium-dialysis method, giving falsely low and unreliable values, especially when SHBG is abnormal.

Preferred alternatives — equilibrium dialysis (gold standard) or calculated free T using total T, SHBG, and albumin give far more accurate bioavailable/free estimates in the obese or SHBG-distorted patient.

Slide 25
  • One Hormone, Three Signals
  • Testosterone → (5-alpha-reductase) → DHT
  • Type 2: prostate, seminal vesicles, genital skin
  • Type 1: skin, liver
  • DHT binds the androgen receptor with higher affinity, dissociates slowly, cannot be aromatized
  • Testosterone → (aromatase, mostly adipose) → estradiol
  • Estradiol in men drives bone density, epiphyseal closure, libido, and central feedback
  • Obesity → more aromatization → low-T, high-E2, low-LH pattern

Notes:

Testosterone → DHT via 5-alpha-reductase — peripheral conversion amplifies androgen signaling in target tissues.

Type 2 5-alpha-reductase — dominant in prostate, seminal vesicles, and genital skin (the isoenzyme blocked by finasteride/dutasteride for BPH).

Type 1 5-alpha-reductase — predominant in skin (sebaceous glands) and liver.

DHT is the more potent androgen — binds the androgen receptor with higher affinity, dissociates slowly, and cannot be aromatized, making it a pure, amplified androgen signal.

Testosterone → estradiol via aromatase (mostly adipose tissue) — a substantial fraction of male estradiol derives from peripheral aromatization of testosterone.

Estradiol in men — drives bone mineral density, epiphyseal plate closure, libido, and central negative feedback on the HPG axis.

Obesity → increased aromatization — expanded adipose mass converts more testosterone to estradiol, producing the classic low-testosterone, high-estradiol, low/inappropriately-normal-LH pattern of obesity-related hypogonadism.

Slide 26
  • Testosterone vs DHT: Division of Labor
  • 5-alpha-reductase deficiency proves the split: normal internal ducts, undervirilized at birth, virilize at puberty — and no BPH, no balding. Nature ran the finasteride trial first.

| Testosterone | DHT |

| --- | --- |

| Wolffian ducts: epididymis, vas, seminal vesicles | External genitalia: penis, scrotum, urethra |

| Spermatogenesis | Prostate growth — and BPH |

| Muscle mass, bone, erythropoiesis | Male-pattern balding, sebaceous activity |

| Libido, voice deepening, growth spurt | |

Notes:

Testosterone and DHT are the same androgen signal split into two jobs: testosterone builds the internal machinery (Wolffian ducts, sperm, muscle, bone, libido), while its more potent metabolite DHT builds the external and cosmetic male features (genitalia, prostate, hairline).

That's why blocking the conversion with a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor shrinks the prostate and slows balding without stopping spermatogenesis — men born without the enzyme never develop BPH or male-pattern baldness.

Slide 27
  • The Aging Arc
  • After age 30–40, total testosterone falls ≈ 1% per year
  • SHBG rises with age → free T falls faster than total T
  • Gradual age-related decline is not the same entity as classical hypogonadism
  • The distinction drives appropriate prescribing

Notes:

Bridge from physiology to the TRT segment.

Slide 28
  • Primary vs Secondary Hypogonadism: The LH Fork
  • The LH is the entire diagnostic fork. Get it before you write for testosterone.

| | Primary (testicular) | Secondary (central) |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Testosterone | Low | Low |

| LH / FSH | High | Low or inappropriately normal |

| Causes | Klinefelter 47,XXY · mumps orchitis · chemo/RT · torsion · cryptorchidism | Kallmann (+anosmia) · pituitary adenoma · hyperprolactinemia · opioids · glucocorticoids · exogenous androgens · obesity · hemochromatosis |

| Fertility outlook | Poor; microTESE may still retrieve | Often fully treatable with gonadotropins |

Notes:

Testosterone is low in both, so the gonadotropins tell you where the lesion is — if the pituitary is shouting (high LH/FSH) the testis is broken and can't answer; if it's silent despite low testosterone (low or "normal" LH/FSH) the brain is broken, and that's the treatable one.

Slide 29
  • Part 4: Erection, Emission, Ejaculation
Slide 30
  • Neural Control: Point and Shoot
  • Three erection types: reflexogenic (sacral arc, survives suprasacral cord injury) · psychogenic (T11–L2) · nocturnal (REM, testosterone-dependent)

| Function | Pathway | Roots |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Point — erection | Parasympathetic · pelvic splanchnic / cavernous nerves | S2–S4 |

| Emission | Sympathetic · hypogastric nerves | T10–L2 |

| Shoot — ejaculation | Somatic · pudendal → bulbospongiosus + ischiocavernosus | S2–S4 |

Notes:

Preserved morning erections argue for a psychogenic contribution — developed on slide 31.

Slide 31
  • Localizing the Lesion by Erection Type
  • Reflexogenic erections preserved, psychogenic lost → suprasacral spinal cord lesion
  • Nocturnal and morning erections preserved → the machinery works → strong argument for a psychogenic contribution
  • Nocturnal erections lost + gradual decline → organic (vascular, neural, hormonal)
  • Nocturnal erections are testosterone-dependent — one reason hypogonadal men lose them

Notes:

Sleep/morning erections test the intact neurovascular-hormonal machinery, so their preservation with lost psychogenic erections localizes to a suprasacral cord lesion (intact S2–S4 reflex arc, blocked cerebral input), whereas their gradual loss signals organic (vascular/neural/hormonal) disease—and because nocturnal erections are the most testosterone-dependent, hypogonadal men lose them first

Slide 32
  • Stimulation → NANC nerves (nNOS) + endothelium (eNOS) release NO
  • NO → soluble guanylate cyclase → GTP → cGMP → protein kinase G → Ca²⁺ falls
  • Cavernosal smooth muscle relaxes → helicine arterioles dilate → sinusoids fill
  • Sinusoids expand against the tunica albuginea → subtunical venules compressed
  • = veno-occlusive mechanism → rigidity
  • The NO–cGMP Cascade (Build)

Notes:

Highest reading-order risk in the deck — verify animation order matches reading order before submission.

Slide 33
  • Detumescence — and Why Some Men Fail PDE-5 Inhibitors
  • PDE-5 hydrolyzes cGMP to 5′-GMP. (Say it slowly — the entire drug class follows from this line.)
  • Sympathetic norepinephrine at alpha-1 + RhoA/Rho-kinase restores tone
  • A scarred tunica (Peyronie) or fibrotic cavernosal muscle (diabetes, aging, post-priapism) cannot compress the venules → venous leak
  • Venous leak fails PDE-5 inhibitors at any dose — the drug amplifies a signal the anatomy can no longer contain

Notes:

Second appearance of the tunica albuginea.

Slide 34
  • Emission and the Bladder Neck
  • Sympathetic T10–L2 → coordinated contraction of vas, seminal vesicles, prostate
  • → while the bladder neck closes simultaneously under alpha-1 tone
  • Alpha-1a-selective blockers (tamsulosin, silodosin) impair both → retrograde or absent ejaculation
  • Orgasm preserved, fluid absent — the #1 uncounseled reason men quietly stop tamsulosin

Notes:

Sympathetic T10–L2 fibers drive emission—coordinated contraction of the vas, seminal vesicles, and prostate—while simultaneously closing the bladder neck via alpha-1 tone to direct semen forward

So alpha-1a-selective blockers (tamsulosin, silodosin) abolish both, producing retrograde or absent ejaculation.

Slide 35
  • Ejaculation ≠ Orgasm
  • Ejaculation: rhythmic pudendal-driven contraction of bulbospongiosus + ischiocavernosus
  • Central serotonergic tone sets the ejaculatory threshold (5-HT2C inhibitory, 5-HT1A facilitatory) — hold for SSRIs
  • Orgasm is a cortical event, dissociable from ejaculation:
  • After radical prostatectomy: orgasm without emission
  • On alpha-blockers: orgasm with retrograde flow
  • Patients conflate the three — physicians must not
Slide 36
  • Priapism: Two Diseases, One Word

| | Ischemic (low-flow) | Non-ischemic (high-flow) |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Mechanism | Failed detumescence → compartment syndrome | Arterial–lacunar fistula |

| Exam | Painful, rigid | Painless, partial |

| Causes | Sickle cell · intracavernosal injection · trazodone · antipsychotics · cocaine | Perineal / straddle trauma |

| Cavernosal gas | Hypoxic, hypercarbic, acidotic | Arterial |

| Action | Emergency: aspirate, irrigate, phenylephrine, shunt — fibrosis by 24–48 h | Not emergent — observe or embolize |

Slide 37
  • Part 5: Penis and Foreskin
Slide 38
  • Physiologic phimosis is normal in young boys
  • (separation by ≈3–5 years of age) — do not forcibly retract
  • Pathologic: lichen sclerosus (BXO), recurrent balanitis, diabetes → topical steroid ± circumcision
  • Paraphimosis = the emergency: trapped retracted foreskin → venous congestion → edema → arterial compromise
  • Frequently iatrogenic — replace the foreskin after every catheter and every exam. The most preventable urologic emergency
  • Manual reduction; occasionally dorsal slit
  • Phimosis and Paraphimosis
Slide 39
  • Fibrotic plaque of the tunica albuginea (appearance #2 of 3)
  • Repetitive microtrauma → subtunical bleeding → aberrant TGF-β wound healing, disordered collagen
  • Two phases: acute/active (pain, evolving curvature, 6–18 mo) → chronic/stable
  • Associations: Dupuytren contracture, plantar fibromatosis, diabetes, post-prostatectomy
  • Presents: plaque, curvature, shortening, pain, ± ED (often venous leak)
  • Peyronie Disease 1 of 2: Mechanism

Notes:

Distinguish from congenital curvature (no plaque, dates from puberty) and fracture (acute).

Slide 40
  • Peyronie Disease 2 of 2: Treatment — Stable Phase Only
  • Intralesional collagenase clostridium histolyticum + modeling — the only FDA-approved injectable
  • Intralesional verapamil or interferon — alternatives
  • Plication — good erections, adequate length, moderate curvature
  • Plaque incision/excision + graft — severe curvature (higher ED risk)
  • Penile prosthesis when refractory ED coexists
  • Nothing gets injected (board answer) or operated during the active phase

Notes:

Treatment ladder maps to curvature severity and erectile function.

Slide 41
  • Rupture of the tunica albuginea of the corpus cavernosum during erection
  • Tunica thins from ≈2 mm to 0.25–0.5 mm when erect — why fracture is an erect-state injury
  • Pop → immediate detumescence → pain → eggplant deformity (Buck fascia contains the hematoma)
  • Urethral injury in 10–20%: blood at meatus, hematuria, cannot void → retrograde urethrogram
  • Emergency: prompt exploration and repair — delay → ED and curvature
  • Penile Fracture
Slide 42
  • Poll 2: The Audible Snap
  • A 30-year-old hears a snap during intercourse → immediate detumescence, pain, swelling, ecchymosis, deviation.
  • Rupture of which structure?
  • A. Corpus spongiosum
  • B. Tunica albuginea of the corpus cavernosum
  • C. Suspensory ligament
  • D. Bulbourethral gland

  • Part 6: Scrotum and Testis
Slide 45
  • Case A Revisited: The Acute Scrotum
  • 17-year-old · sudden severe left scrotal pain during lacrosse · 3 hours · nausea · prior self-resolving episode
  • Differential: torsion · epididymitis/orchitis · torsed appendix testis · testicular rupture · incarcerated hernia · Fournier gangrene
  • The prior self-resolving episode suggests intermittent torsion
  • What one exam finding do you check first?

Notes:

Let them answer: cremasteric reflex. Advance to the table.

Slide 46
  • Torsion vs Epididymitis: Five Discriminators
  • Scrotal warmth and erythema occur in both — warmth alone excludes nothing

| | Torsion | Epididymitis |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Onset | Abrupt (minutes) | Gradual (days) |

| Peak age | 12–18 y (and neonatal) | Post-pubertal; >35 y |

| Cremasteric reflex | Absent | Present |

| Testis lie | High-riding, transverse | Normal |

| Prehn sign / UA | Negative · UA normal | Positive · often pyuria |

Slide 47
  • Bell-clapper deformity — high tunica insertion, freely hanging testis, bilateral in most
  • Neonatal = extravaginal · adolescent = intravaginal
  • Salvage: >90% at <6 h · ≈50% at 12 h · <10% beyond 24 h
  • Doppler supports but never overrides clinical suspicion — do not delay exploration for imaging
  • Manual detorsion (“open the book,” lateral) temporizes only
  • Bilateral orchiopexy — the defect is bilateral
  • Testicular Torsion
Slide 48
  • Blunt trauma → tear of the tunica albuginea with extrusion of seminiferous tubules
  • Ultrasound: heterogeneous parenchyma, contour loss, tunical discontinuity, hematocele
  • Explore within 72 h → salvage >80–90%; delay → orchiectomy
  • A large hematocele is not always observed
  • Same trauma spectrum: hematoma, hematocele, dislocation
  • Testicular Rupture

Notes:

The American Urological Association recommends scrotal ultrasonography for most blunt scrotal injuries with findings suggestive of testicular rupture, because clinical exam is limited by swelling and pain—and, critically, the hematocele is not the diagnostic anchor for rupture.

The most specific sonographic findings are loss of testicular contour and heterogeneous parenchymal echotexture, and these—not the size or presence of a hematocele—are what should prompt surgical repair.

Prompt exploration is indicated for sonographic rupture, equivocal imaging, a large hematoma, or clear physical findings, yielding salvage rates of 80–90%.

Surgeons should then perform exploration with debridement and tunical closure, or orchiectomy when non-salvageable

Slide 49
  • Mechanism: retrograde ascent along the vas from urethra/bladder
  • Age pattern in one line: sexually active younger men vs coliform pattern with obstruction/instrumentation — organisms and treatment: Microbiology session
  • Mumps orchitis: post-pubertal; pressure necrosis inside the noncompliant tunica → tubular atrophy (blood-testis barrier callback)
  • Chronic granulomatous epididymitis → think TB
  • Fournier gangrene: perineal necrotizing fasciitis · diabetes/immunosuppression · pain out of proportion, crepitus · emergent debridement
  • Epididymitis, Orchitis, Fournier Gangrene
Slide 50
  • Dilated pampiniform plexus — ≈15% of men, ≈40% of men with primary infertility
  • Left-sided predominance: left gonadal vein → left renal vein at 90°, longer column, ± nutcracker compression
  • Grades: I Valsalva-only · II palpable · III visible · “bag of worms,” decompresses supine
  • Red flag: isolated right-sided, or fails to decompress supine → image the retroperitoneum
  • Infertility mechanism: hyperthermia, oxidative stress/DNA fragmentation, metabolite reflux
  • Most common surgically correctable cause of male infertility — do not repair subclinical (US-only) varicoceles
  • Varicocele

Notes:

Renal vein anatomy callback

Slide 51
  • Hydrocele = fluid in the tunica vaginalis → transilluminates
  • Communicating (patent processus, pediatric, fluctuates, hernia association) — most resolve by 12–24 months
  • Non-communicating (adult) — may be reactive to infection, trauma, or tumor
  • Safety rule: every new adult hydrocele gets an ultrasound — it can conceal a tumor
  • Spermatocele / epididymal cyst: superior-posterior, separate from the testis, transilluminate, benign — excise only for pain
  • The discriminating finding is separability. A mass you cannot separate from the testis is a tumor until proven otherwise.
  • Hydrocele, Spermatocele, Epididymal Cyst
Slide 52
  • Cryptorchidism
  • Two-phase descent: transabdominal (INSL3, gubernaculum) → inguinoscrotal (androgen, genitofemoral/CGRP)
  • ≈3% term, ≈30% preterm · spontaneous descent by 6 months or not at all
  • Infertility: germ cell degeneration begins ≈6 months (thermal)
  • Malignancy: RR ≈3–8× — and the contralateral descended testis is also at risk → this is a dysgenesis syndrome, not just position
  • Orchiopexy 6–18 months: improves fertility, makes the testis examinable, reduces but does not eliminate cancer risk
  • Distinguish retractile vs undescended vs ascending
  • Bilateral non-palpable ± hypospadias = DSD workup: karyotype, 17-OHP, electrolytes

Notes:

The contralateral-risk fact is the conceptual core — make it explicit.

Slide 53
  • Poll 3: Four Hours In
  • A 16-year-old has 4 hours of severe scrotal pain, an absent cremasteric reflex, and a high-riding testis. Ultrasound is available in 90 minutes.
  • What do you do?
  • A. Order the ultrasound and analgesia
  • B. Trial of antibiotics for epididymitis

Answer C. Reveal discussion: the 90-minute wait spends half the remaining salvage window.

Slide 54
  • Part 7: Testicular Tumors
Slide 55
  • The Painless Mass in a Young Man
  • Most common solid malignancy in men 15–35 — and highly curable, so delay is the enemy
  • Risks: cryptorchidism · prior contralateral tumor · family history · GCNIS · infertility
  • Presentation: painless, firm, non-transilluminating intratesticular mass
  • Ultrasound is highly sensitive — and every new adult hydrocele already bought one

Notes:

Case framing: 24-year-old with a firm painless mass

Testicular dysgenesis syndrome ties cryptorchidism, hypospadias, poor spermatogenesis, and GCT together as downstream effects of disrupted fetal androgen signaling — one in-utero mechanism, several phenotypes

Slide 56
  • Classification in One Slide
  • Germ cell ≈95%
  • Seminoma: “fried-egg” cells + lymphocytes · radio/chemosensitive · never makes AFP
  • Non-seminomatous: embryonal · yolk sac (AFP) · choriocarcinoma (hCG, hematogenous — hemoptysis) · teratoma (chemoresistant → resect)
  • Sex cord–stromal ≈5%: Leydig (androgen/estrogen secretion → precocious puberty or gynecomastia) · Sertoli
  • Lymphoma — the most common testicular tumor over 60
Slide 57
  • Tumor Markers — and the Rule That Gets Tested
  • Draw markers BEFORE orchiectomy
  • Draw markers AFTER orchiectomy even if normal pre-surgery
  • Post-orchiectomy decay to nadir is timed to hCG and AFP half-lives → defines the S category and IGCCCG risk
  • A marker falling slower than its expected half-life = residual / metastatic disease
  • LDH is prognostic at diagnosis, not a decay tracker — persistently elevated in ~30% of disease-free patients

| Marker | Association |

| --- | --- |

| AFP | Yolk sac, embryonal. Elevated AFP excludes pure seminoma — manage as NSGCT regardless of histology report |

| β-hCG | Choriocarcinoma, embryonal — and up to ≈15% of seminomas (modest elevation acceptable) |

| LDH | Nonspecific; reflects tumor burden |

Notes:

Quiz item 10.

β-hCG

~24–36 h (≤3 days)

Fastest; normalizes within ~1 week of orchiectomy

AFP

~5–7 days

Slower; may still be falling at a 2-week recheck

LDH

~1–3 weeks (variable)

No formal half-life assigned; too slow/nonspecific to track

Slide 58
  • Management Principles
  • Radical inguinal orchiectomy with high cord ligation
  • Never trans-scrotal — violating scrotal lymphatics redirects drainage from retroperitoneal to inguinal nodes (slide 12 payoff)
  • Offer sperm banking before orchiectomy, chemotherapy, radiation, or RPLND — a recurring real-world failure
  • Predictable spread: right → interaortocaval · left → left para-aortic → chest
  • Contrast: prostate cancer → osteoblastic bone metastases (Batson plexus, ↑alk phos)

Notes:

The lymphatic logic is the anatomy slide cashing out.

Slide 59
  • Part 8: Prostate
Slide 60
  • BPH: True Hyperplasia of the Transition Zone
  • Hyperplasia (cell number), not hypertrophy — stromal + epithelial, transition zone only
  • DHT-dependent: no BPH in 5-AR deficiency or pre-pubertal castration → the mechanistic license for 5-ARIs
  • Static component = adenoma bulk → treat with 5-ARI
  • Dynamic component = alpha-1a smooth-muscle tone (stroma, capsule, bladder neck) → treat with alpha-blocker
  • Size correlates poorly with symptoms — a 30 gram gland with high tone can obstruct more than a 90 gram one

Notes:

BPH obstructs in two ways — the physical bulk of the gland and the muscular squeeze around the urethra — so 5-ARIs shrink the bulk while alpha-blockers relax the squeeze.

Slide 61
  • LUTS and the Bladder’s Response
  • Storage symptoms = secondary detrusor change → can persist after obstruction is relieved
  • Bladder arc: hypertrophy → trabeculation → diverticula → decompensation (rising PVR)
  • Endpoints: retention · UTI · stones · hematuria · bilateral hydronephrosis / post-renal azotemia
  • Mimics to exclude: anticholinergics/sympathomimetics · diabetes · neurogenic bladder · stricture · cancer

| Storage (irritative) | Voiding (obstructive) |

| --- | --- |

| Frequency · urgency · nocturia · urge incontinence | Weak stream · hesitancy · intermittency · straining · incomplete emptying · terminal dribbling |

Workup line: IPSS, UA, PSA, PVR, uroflow.

Slide 62
  • BPH Management Ladder
  • Watchful waiting + behavioral (evening fluids, caffeine, timed voiding)
  • Medical: alpha-blocker (days) · 5-ARI (months, larger glands) · combination · tadalafil 5 mg daily
  • MIST: water-vapor thermal therapy · prostatic urethral lift · Aquablation · temporary nitinol device · prostatic artery embolization
  • The current shift favors ejaculation-preserving options
  • Surgical: TURP · HoLEP · simple prostatectomy for the largest glands
  • Sequencing per the 2026 AUA LUTS/BPH guideline (linked on the resource slide)

| Category | Name | Key features |

| --- | --- | --- |

| I | Acute bacterial | Fever, rigors, exquisitely tender boggy prostate · abscess/sepsis risk · no vigorous massage |

| IV | Asymptomatic inflammatory | Incidental on biopsy or semen analysis |

Category III framing prevents years of futile antibiotics.

Slide 64
  • Prostate Cancer in Five Points
  • Peripheral zone adenocarcinoma, usually multifocal · risks: age, African ancestry, family history, BRCA2, Lynch
  • PSA is organ-specific, not cancer-specific — raised by BPH, prostatitis, instrumentation, retention, ejaculation · halved by 5-ARIs → double the value
  • Pathway: risk assessment → mpMRI (PI-RADS) → targeted + systematic biopsy → Gleason / Grade Group 1–5 drives management
  • Spectrum: active surveillance → prostatectomy → radiation ± ADT → systemic therapy · mets are osteoblastic bone
  • Screening is shared decision-making — mortality benefit vs overdiagnosis; ≈55–69 window; earlier for high-risk groups

Slide 31’s localization logic applied.

Slide 67
  • ED Is a Cardiovascular Sentinel
  • Cavernosal arteries ≈ 1–2 mm · coronaries ≈ 3–4 mm
  • The same endothelial dysfunction is symptomatic in the smaller vessel first
  • ED commonly precedes a cardiac event by 3 years
  • A 50-year-old with new ED has handed you a screening opportunity: lipids, A1c, blood pressure, smoking
  • Do not just write for sildenafil
Slide 68
  • ED Treatment Ladder
  • Lifestyle + risk-factor modification (exercise improves erections with an effect size rivaling medication)
  • PDE-5 inhibitor — first line (details in pharmacology, next part)
  • Intracavernosal injection (alprostadil / bimix / trimix) or intraurethral alprostadil
  • Vacuum erection device (constriction ring ≤30 min)
  • Penile prosthesis — highest satisfaction of any ED therapy. The correct answer for refractory disease, not an act of desperation

Notes:

Injection/device detail on reference slide R6.

Slide 69
  • Premature Ejaculation — and the SSRI Two-Way Street
  • Most common male sexual dysfunction · defined by short latency (≈1 min lifelong), inability to delay, and distress
  • Mechanism: central serotonergic threshold (slide 35) + genetics + hypersensitivity + psychological factors
  • Treat comorbid ED first — rushing to beat a failing erection mimics PE
  • Behavioral (stop-start, squeeze) · topical lidocaine-prilocaine (condom protects the partner) · SSRIs off-label (paroxetine strongest) · clomipramine
  • The same serotonergic effect that treats PE is the adverse effect in patients on SSRIs for depression: delayed ejaculation, reduced libido — one mechanism, two framings (erections typically intact)

Notes:

The bidirectionality is the teaching point; it covers the SSRI objective.

Slide 70
  • Male Infertility: Framework and Reference Limits
  • ≈15% of couples · male factor in ≈50% · evaluate both partners in parallel from day one
  • Three compartments:
  • Pre-testicular (often reversible): central hypogonadism, hyperprolactinemia, exogenous T / anabolics, opioids, obesity
  • Testicular: Klinefelter · Y-microdeletions (AZFa/b/c) · cryptorchidism · varicocele · mumps · gonadotoxins
  • Post-testicular: vasectomy · CBAVD (CFTR — test patient AND partner) · ejaculatory duct obstruction · retrograde ejaculation
  • WHO 6th ed lower reference limits: volume 1.4 mL · conc 16 M/mL · total 39 M · motility 42% · progressive 30% · morphology 4%
  • These are population reference limits from recent fathers — not fertile/infertile thresholds.
  • Two samples, ≥1 month apart (AUA/ASRM), 2–7 days abstinence
  • Exception: azoospermia is confirmed 1–2 weeks later with pellet analysis (centrifuge the specimen, examine the concentrate for rare sperm — finding any = cryptozoospermia, may permit ICSI without surgical retrieval)

Notes:

The reference-limit framing prevents the most common misread of a semen analysis.

Slide 71
  • Reading Azoospermia
  • Low-volume + acidic + fructose-negative → ejaculatory duct obstruction or CBAVD (slide 8 payoff)
  • Post-ejaculatory urinalysis → retrograde ejaculation
  • Karyotype + Y-microdeletions if <5 M/mL or azoospermic
  • Complete AZFa/AZFb deletion predicts failed retrieval — changes counseling before surgery
  • A semen analysis is a general health biomarker — infertile men carry higher cancer and comorbidity rates

| | Obstructive | Non-obstructive |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Testis volume | Normal | Small, soft |

| FSH | Normal | Elevated |

| Vas deferens | May be absent (CBAVD) | Present |

| Sperm retrieval | Essentially always present | microTESE — variable yield |

Notes:

The semen has no sperm either because the factory works but the pipes are blocked (obstructive: normal testis size, normal FSH) or

Because the factory itself has failed (non-obstructive: small soft testes, high FSH as the pituitary shouts at tubules that can't answer

Slide 72
  • Part 10: Pharmacology
Slide 73
  • PDE-5 Inhibitors: Mechanism and the Counseling Point
  • Inhibit PDE-5 → cGMP accumulates → amplify an existing NO signal — they do not create one
  • They require sexual stimulation. The most common “it didn’t work” is a counseling failure, not a drug failure
  • An adequate trial = maximal dose · correct timing · appropriate stomach · several attempts
  • Also treats: pulmonary arterial hypertension
  • Tadalafil 5 mg daily for LUTS ± ED — the one-drug answer to Case C
Slide 74
  • PDE-5 Agents, Contraindications, Rare Harms
  • Absolute: nitrates in any form (including amyl nitrite) and Riociguat — same pathway, profound hypotension
  • Separate 24 h (sildenafil/vardenafil), 48 h (tadalafil)
  • Alpha-blockers: additive hypotension — stabilize the alpha-blocker first ·
  • Practical cardiac screen: can he climb two flights of stairs
  • Rare, board-relevant: NAION · sudden sensorineural hearing loss

| Agent | Onset | Half-life | Distinguishing feature |

| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| Sildenafil | 30–60 min | ≈4 h | PDE-6 → blue-tinged vision · fatty meals delay absorption |

| Vardenafil | 30–60 min | ≈4 h | QT prolongation |

| Tadalafil | ≈2 h | ≈17.5 h | 36-h window · daily dosing · PDE-11 → back pain/myalgia · food-independent |

| Avanafil | ≈15 min | ≈5 h | Most selective, fastest onset |

Notes:

Non-Arteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy

Slide 75
  • BPH Drugs Mapped to Static and Dynamic

| Class | Agents | What to counsel |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Alpha-1 blockers (dynamic) | Doxazosin, terazosin (non-selective) · tamsulosin, silodosin (α-1a) · alfuzosin | Onset in days · orthostasis (non-selective) · retrograde/absent ejaculation (selective) · ask about cataract surgery — floppy iris |

| 5-ARIs (static) | Finasteride (type 2) · dutasteride (1+2) | Gland shrinks 20–25% over 6 mo · PSA halves — double the value · sexual AEs · teratogenic (Cat X): no handling of broken tablets in pregnancy |

| Combination | α-blocker + 5-ARI | Best for progression in larger glands |

| Storage add-ons | Antimuscarinics · mirabegron | Check post-void residual first |

Slide 76
  • Androgen Therapy — and the Fertility-Sparing Alternatives
  • Indication: consistent symptoms + two morning total T <300 ng/dL · get the LH (the fork), hematocrit, PSA if age-appropriate — and have the fertility conversation
  • Adverse effects (all predictable): erythrocytosis · azoospermia + testicular atrophy · gynecomastia · acne · worsened OSA
  • TRAVERSE (2023): CV non-inferior in at-risk hypogonadal men (MACE 7.0% vs 7.3%) — but more AF, PE, and AKI
  • Fertility-sparing instead of T:
  • clomiphene/enclomiphene (SERM → ↑endogenous LH/FSH)
  • hCG (LH analog, preserves intratesticular T)
  • Anabolic steroid users: axis recovery takes months to years, sometimes incomplete — screen non-judgmentally
  • FDA relabeled the class in early 2025:
  • Boxed warning for cardiovascular risk removed
  • TRAVERSE results added to all labels
  • New warning for increased blood pressure, limitation-of-use for age-related hypogonadism retained.

Notes:

Formulation table incl. transdermal transference on reference slide R3.

Slide 77
  • ADT for Prostate Cancer — The GnRH Pulsatility Payoff
  • GnRH agonists (leuprolide, goserelin): continuous stimulation downregulates the receptor → castration ·
  • Initial testosterone flare → cover with an antiandrogen in high-burden disease
  • GnRH antagonists (degarelix; oral relugolix): no flare, faster castration
  • AR antagonists:
  • bicalutamide · flutamide (hepatotoxic)
  • 2nd-gen: enzalutamide (seizure signal), apalutamide, darolutamide (least CNS)
  • Abiraterone + prednisone: CYP17A1 blockade; prednisone prevents mineralocorticoid excess (HTN, hypokalemia)
  • Systemic ADT toll — bone, metabolic, cognitive — on reference slide R4

Notes:

Slide 22’s planted flag collected.

Slide 78
  • Three Cases — Revisited
  • Case A. 17-year-old male. Sudden severe left scrotal pain 3 hours ago during lacrosse. Nausea. One prior episode that resolved on its own.
  • Case B. 34-year-old male. 18 months of infertility. “Working out hard.” Taking a supplement from a men’s clinic. Semen analysis: azoospermia.
  • Case C. 68-year-old male. Nocturia ×3, weak stream, PSA 6.2. Mentions at the end of the visit that erections have declined over 2 years.
Slide 79
  • Cases Resolved
  • A — Torsion. Absent cremasteric reflex, high transverse lie, negative Prehn, prior intermittent episodes → emergent exploration + bilateral orchiopexy. No waiting for ultrasound if delayed
  • B — Exogenous testosterone. “Supplement” = androgen → LH suppressed → intratesticular T collapsed. Check LH/FSH/T/prolactin · stop the androgen · consider hCG + SERM · repeat SA ≥3 months
  • C — Transition-zone BPH + sentinel ED + independent PSA workup. IPSS, PVR, repeat PSA, MRI pathway · daily tadalafil treats LUTS and ED with one drug (no nitrates) · lipids, A1c, BP

Notes:

Tie each resolution to the slide where its concept was taught.

Slide 80
  • Ten Things to Remember
  • BPH is transition zone; prostate cancer is peripheral zone
  • Spermatogenesis takes 3 months — every fertility intervention runs on that clock
  • Intratesticular testosterone drives spermatogenesis; exogenous T is a contraceptive
  • LH separates primary from secondary hypogonadism — get it before prescribing
  • Testosterone builds the body; DHT builds the prostate and the hairline
  • Point (parasympathetic S2–4) and Shoot (sympathetic T10–L2; pudendal expels)
  • PDE-5 inhibitors amplify a signal — never with nitrates
  • Torsion is clinical. Six hours. Do not wait for imaging (if delayed)
  • Testis drains retroperitoneal → inguinal orchiectomy · penis drains inguinal · bank sperm first
  • 10. Replace the foreskin after the catheter — and new ED is a cardiovascular workup
Slide 81
  • Resources
  • AUA Medical Student Curriculum (free account) — modules mapping to today: Acute Scrotum · BPH · Erectile Dysfunction · Male Infertility · Prostate Cancer/PSA · Urologic Emergencies
  • AUA Male GU Exam video module — testicular and digital rectal examination
  • StatPearls (free): Physiology of the Male Reproductive System · Physiology, Erection · Physiology, Testosterone
  • AUA Guidelines: LUTS/BPH (2026) · Erectile Dysfunction — skim the algorithms
  • Note: testicular cancer, penile cancer, cryptorchidism, Peyronie disease, prostatitis, and PE have no AUA student module — the reference slides that follow are your primary resource for those, but some of these topics available on ScholarRX

Notes:

Descriptive link text goes on the Canvas page; do not read URLs aloud.

Slide 83
  • Reference Slides — Posted and Examinable
Slide 84
  • Reference R1 — Penile Cancer: Risk and Precursors
  • Squamous cell carcinoma in ≈95%. Uncommon in the US; substantially more common in parts of Africa, South America, and Asia.
  • Risk factors: phimosis and chronic inflammation, lichen sclerosus (BXO), smoking, HPV 16/18 (≈half of cases), absence of neonatal circumcision.
  • Premalignant lesions: penile intraepithelial neoplasia (PeIN); erythroplasia of Queyrat (glans); Bowen disease (shaft); verrucous carcinoma (locally destructive, rarely metastasizes).
  • Typical story: a non-healing glans or foreskin lesion with a long delay from embarrassment. Any non-healing penile lesion gets a biopsy.
Slide 85
  • Reference R2 — Penile Cancer: Spread and Treatment
  • Penile lymphatics drain to inguinal nodes — the exact opposite of the testis. Inguinal node status is the dominant prognostic factor.
  • Palpable nodes may be reactive or metastatic; imaging and sentinel/superficial dissection stage intermediate- and high-risk disease.
  • Treatment is organ-sparing where feasible: topical therapy or laser for PeIN, glansectomy or partial penectomy with margins for invasive disease, total penectomy for extensive tumors.
  • Chemoradiation and systemic therapy for advanced nodal or metastatic disease.

Notes:

Pairs with lecture slide 12’s drainage contrast.

Slide 86
  • Reference R3 — Testosterone Formulations
  • IM cypionate/enanthate: inexpensive, peak-trough swings, highest erythrocytosis rates.
  • IM undecanoate: long-acting; REMS program for pulmonary oil microembolism (POME) risk.
  • Subcutaneous auto-injector: steadier levels, self-administered.
  • Transdermal gel/solution: physiologic profile; counsel on skin-to-skin transference to women and children — wash hands, cover the site.
  • Patch (skin irritation), pellets (surgical insertion, months-long), oral undecanoate (lymphatic absorption), buccal, intranasal.
  • Monitor on any formulation: symptoms, trough or mid-interval T, hematocrit, PSA if age-appropriate.
Slide 87
  • Reference R4 — Systemic Consequences of ADT
  • Hot flashes; loss of libido and erectile function; gynecomastia; fatigue; mood and cognitive effects.
  • Body composition: sarcopenia with increased fat mass; insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome; anemia.
  • Bone: accelerated loss → baseline DEXA, calcium + vitamin D, and an antiresorptive (bisphosphonate or denosumab) for those at fracture risk.
  • QT prolongation with some agents; cardiovascular risk-factor management throughout.
  • Treat ADT like any systemic endocrine therapy: it needs its own survivorship plan.
Slide 88
  • Reference R5 — Drugs That Cause Male Sexual Dysfunction
  • Thiazides, spironolactone, beta-blockers: ED, decreased libido, gynecomastia (spironolactone).
  • SSRIs/SNRIs, TCAs: delayed or absent ejaculation, reduced libido, ED.
  • Antipsychotics: hyperprolactinemia → secondary hypogonadism.
  • Opioids: central suppression — opioid-induced androgen deficiency.
  • 5-ARIs, antiandrogens, GnRH agents: ED, libido loss, ejaculatory dysfunction.
  • Alpha-1a blockers: retrograde/absent ejaculation
  • Cimetidine, ketoconazole: antiandrogen effects.
  • Anabolic steroids / exogenous T: azoospermia, atrophy
  • Alkylating chemo, pelvic RT: often permanent gonadotoxicity
  • Alcohol, tobacco
Slide 89
  • Reference R6 — Injections, Devices, Prosthesis
  • Intracavernosal alprostadil (PGE1): works via cAMP — a parallel pathway — so it works when PDE-5 inhibitors fail.
  • Bimix/trimix: papaverine (non-selective PDE inhibitor) + phentolamine (alpha-blocker) ± alprostadil.
  • Mandatory counseling for any injection: seek care for an erection lasting more than 4 hours.
  • Intraurethral alprostadil (MUSE) and topical formulations — less effective, needle-free.
  • Vacuum erection device: constriction ring ≤ 30 minutes.
  • Penile prosthesis (inflatable or malleable): highest satisfaction rates of any ED therapy — definitive treatment for refractory disease.
Slide 90
  • Reference R7 — The Supplement Problem
  • The FDA repeatedly finds over-the-counter “male enhancement” products adulterated with undeclared sildenafil or tadalafil analogs.
  • A patient on nitrates taking one of these is exposed to the full interaction — without knowing he took a PDE-5 inhibitor.
  • Ask about supplements with the same seriousness as prescriptions, especially in men with ED and cardiac disease.
  • Same vigilance for “testosterone boosters” and men’s-clinic injections — Case B’s lesson.
Slide 91
  • Reference R8 — Capacitation and the Acrosome Reaction
  • Ejaculated sperm are mature but not yet fertilization-competent.
  • Capacitation (female tract, hours): cholesterol efflux destabilizes the membrane; bicarbonate and calcium influx activate soluble adenylate cyclase → PKA signaling; tyrosine phosphorylation; hyperactivated motility.
  • Acrosome reaction (at the zona pellucida): exocytosis of acrosomal enzymes (acrosin, hyaluronidase) enabling zona penetration; membrane fusion follows at the equatorial segment.
  • Board distractor: neither event happens in the epididymis.
Slide 92
  • Reference R9 — Experiments of Nature
  • 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency (46,XY): normal Wolffian (internal) ducts; undervirilized external genitalia at birth; marked virilization at puberty from the testosterone surge; no BPH, no male-pattern balding in adulthood. The physiologic proof-of-concept for finasteride.
  • Complete androgen insensitivity (46,XY): defective androgen receptor; testes present (often inguinal); AMH intact → no uterus; external phenotype female; presents with primary amenorrhea or inguinal masses.
  • Together they dissect the axis: 5-AR deficiency separates testosterone’s jobs from DHT’s (what survives is testosterone; what fails is DHT), and CAIS shows both hormones act through one shared androgen receptor — the final common pathway.
Slide 93
  • Reference R10 — Worked Semen Analysis
  • 34-year-old, 18 months infertility. SA #1: volume 0.8 mL · pH 6.6 · azoospermia · fructose negative. SA #2 confirms.
  • Step 1 — volume and pH: low-volume, acidic, fructose-negative → the seminal vesicle contribution is missing → ejaculatory duct obstruction or CBAVD.
  • Step 2 — exam: are the vasa palpable? Absent → CBAVD → CFTR testing for patient and partner.
  • Step 3 — labs: normal testis volume + normal FSH fits obstruction (contrast: small testes + high FSH = non-obstructive).
  • Step 4 — plan: surgical sperm retrieval + ICSI; genetic counseling.
  • The pattern recognition, not the numbers, is the skill.
Slide 94
  • Reference R11 — CPPS and UPOINT
  • Category III (CP/CPPS) is a phenotype-driven syndrome, frequently non-infectious — which is why serial antibiotics fail.
  • Urinary — LUTS → alpha-blocker, behavioral
  • Psychosocial — depression, catastrophizing → CBT, treatment of mood disease
  • Organ-specific — prostatic tenderness → anti-inflammatories, phytotherapy
  • Infection — documented → one targeted antibiotic course only
  • Neurologic/systemic — IBS, fibromyalgia overlap → neuromodulators
  • Tenderness — pelvic-floor myalgia → pelvic-floor physical therapy (often the highest-yield single intervention)
  • Multimodal beats monotherapy; set expectations for management, not cure.
Slide 95
  • Reference R12 — Circumcision: The Evidence in Brief
  • Protective associations:
  • Reduced UTI in infancy
  • Reduced HIV and some STI acquisition (strongest data from high-prevalence settings)
  • Reduced penile cancer (largely via phimosis/chronic inflammation)
  • Reduced HPV transmission.
  • Risks: bleeding, infection, meatal stenosis, rare glans injury; anesthesia considerations.
  • AAP position: benefits outweigh risks but are not large enough to recommend universally → parental shared decision-making.
  • Medical indications in adults: pathologic phimosis, recurrent balanitis, BXO.
