Canvas course 70351, file 23774873 (pdf, 4.3 MB); session ANAT-PERINEUM-LEC (Week 2, 8/24/2026: Anatomy Lecture: Basic Reproductive Anatomy (Perineum Male/Female)). Text extracted verbatim on 2026-09-26 for REPRO-PLAN P1.2 (43 pages; 5 image-only or title/disclosure pages omitted).

Page 2

Learning Objectives

•

Differentiate the subdivisions of the perineum (urogenital and anal regions) based on their

boundaries and spatial orientation.

•

Describe the attachment of the perineal membrane.

•

Compare the blood supply, venous drainage, and lymphatic drainage of the anal canal with particular

attention to the differences superior and inferior to the pectinate line.

•

Describe the anatomy of female external genitalia (mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, vestibule,

clitoris, urethra, bulbs of the vestibule, greater vestibular (Bartholin's) glands, vagina).

•

Describe the anatomy of male external genitalia (penis, testicles, epididymis, and course of the male

urethra).

•

Explain the innervation, blood supply, and venous drainage of the external genitalia, emphasizing the

role of the pudendal nerves and vessels.

•

Trace the lymphatic drainage of pelvic and perineal organs in males and females, including the

clinical applications of affected lymph nodes in various invasive cancers and infections of internal

pelvic structures.

•

Describe the autonomic innervation of the pelvic & perineal regions and the effects of sympathetic

vs. parasympathetic input on pelvic organs.

Page 3

Perineum

The urogenital triangle is the anterior triangular region of the diamond-shaped perineum.

In anatomical position, it is oriented in a horizontal plane & contains the urethra and external genitalia.

The anal triangle is the posterior triangular region

In anatomical position, It is oriented in a plane that is almost vertical and contains the anal canal, anus,

external anal sphincter, inferior rectal nerve (branch of pudendal nerve), and the fat-filled ischiorectal fossa.

Page 4

Urogenital Triangle: Perineal Membrane

Perineal membrane: thin fibromuscular horizontal layer with fibers running parallel to

pelvic diaphragm (i.e., levator ani), divides urogenital triangle into a deep (superior to

membrane) & superficial (inferior to membrane) pouch

Page 5

Perineum Overview

Page 6

Perineum Overview

Page 8

Ischioanal (Ischiorectal) Fossa

•

Fossa filled with fat, poorly vascularized.

•

Allows for expansion of the anal canal during defecation & accommodates the fetus during childbirth.

•

Infections from one of the fossae can spread to the other & into the urogenital triangle.

  • Contents: Fat, pudendal nerves and vessels giving the inferior rectal nerve & vessels
Page 9

Male Surface Anatomy

Proliferation of mesoderm around the cloacal membrane

causes the overlying ectoderm to form three elevated

structures. Stimulated by testosterone

Page 10

Female Surface Anatomy

Page 11

Female & Male Superficial Pouch

Male: Bulb & crura (attached) of the penis give rise to erectile sinuses of the penis – corpus

spongiosum & corpora cavernosa (free), respectively.

Female: Bulb of the vestibule & crura (attached) give rise to erectile sinuses of clitoris – glans clitoris

& corpora cavernosa (free) respectively.

Page 12

Female & Male Superficial Pouch: Erectile Tissue

Root/attached components: sit/attach to the perineal membrane & are the bulb and crus.

Free components: corpora cavernosa - body of the clitoris (F) & body of the penis (M), and corpus

spongiosum –glans clitoris (F) and glans penis (M).

Page 14

Superficial pouch contains external genitalia & associated skeletal muscles: bulbospongiosus,

ischiocavernosus, & superficial transverse perineal muscles. Because of their action during

urination/erection, these muscles are generally more developed in males.

  • Sup. transverse perineal muscles: provide a firm base for the penis during erection
  • Bulbospongiosus: aids in emptying of urine/semen.
  • Ishiocavernosus: force blood from crura to corpora cavernosa, increasing turgidity of penis.
Page 15

Superficial pouch contains external genitalia & associated skeletal muscles, including

bulbospongiosus, ischiocavernosus, & superficial transverse perineal muscles. Muscles cover

erectile tissue.

  • Sup. transverse perineal muscle: support pelvic floor, fix perineal body
  • Bulbospongiosus: “sphincter” of vagina aids in erection, compresses greater vestibular gland.
  • Ishiocavernosus: forces blood from crura to corpora cavernosa, maintains erection of clitoris.
Page 16

Male Urethra

Page 17

Male & Female Deep Pouch

•Fat of the ischioanal fossae

  • Dorsal vessels of penis/clitoris from

the internal pudendal a.

  • Dorsal nerve of penis/clitoris from

the pudendal nerve

  • Deep transverse perineal m
  • Sphincter urethrae
  • Membranous urethra
  • Bulbourethral glands
  • openings for urethra & vagina
  • Urethrovaginal sphincter
Page 18

Nerves of the Perineum

Page 19

Arteries of the Perineum

•Inferior rectal a. to the anal canal inferior to the pectinate line, anal sphincter & peri-anal skin

•Perineal a. to superficial perineal muscles

•Posterior labial a. to skin of posterior labia

•A. of bulb of vestibule to bulb of vestibular bulbs and

greater vestibular glands

•Deep a of clitoris to crura of clitoris

•Dorsal a of clitoris to glans of clitoris

  • Posterior scrotal a to skin of posterior scrotum
  • A. of bulb of penis to supply bulb, penile urethra, corpus

spongiosum, bulbourethral glands

  • deep a of penis - travels through the center of each corpus

cavernosum; gives off straight and helicine aa, which open

directly into the sinusoids of the corpora.

  • dorsal a of penis to corpora
  • superficial external pudendal a to anterior scrotum
Page 20

Innervation of Pelvis & Perineum

Sensory & motor innervation of skin, skeletal muscle

  • Somatic division of PNS: sacral plexus (L4-S4)̶

Nerve to obturator internus (L5-S1)̶

Nerve to piriformis (S1-S2)̶

Nerve to levator ani (S4, S5)̶

Nerve to coccygeus (S4, S5 )̶

Pudendal nerve (S2-S4) (perineum)

Motor innervation of viscera

•

Autonomic division of PNS: inferior hypogastric plexus̶

Sympathetic innervation

•

Lumbar & sacral splanchnics: effects – vasoconstriction,

contraction of internal urethral (male) & anal sphincters,

stimulate glandular secretion, ejaculation (male)̶

Parasympathetic innervation

•

Pelvic splanchnics (S2-S4): effects – vasodilation,

contraction of the detrusor, engorgement of erectile tissue.

Page 21

Autonomic Regulation of Sexual Function

Erection: parasympathetic (S2-4 via pelvic splanchnic nn)

•Emission: sympathetic (L1-2)

Smooth muscle contraction of the ductus deferens to move sperm into the urethra. Contractions of

seminal vesicles, prostate, and bulbourethral glands secrete seminal fluid into the urethra.

•Ejaculation:

•Sympathetic (L1-2): rhythmic contraction of smooth muscle in the ductus deferens & urethra; closure of

internal urethral sphincter. Somatic (S2-4, pudendal n): contraction of bulbospongiosus &

ischiocavernosus muscles compress the bases of the penile erectile tissue.

Point = Parasympathetic = Erection

Shoot = Sympathetic = Ejaculation

Page 22

Pudendal Nerve Block

Pudendal nerve:

Passes out of the pelvis via the greater sciatic foramen &

around the sacrospinous ligament into the lesser sciatic

foramen, where it enters the pudendal (Alcock's)

canal; provides somatic innervation (S2-S4) to the skin &

skeletal muscles of the perineum & gives rise to inferior

rectal (anal), perineal, labial, & dorsal clitoral nerve

branches.

To relieve perineal pain during childbirth, pudendal nerve

block anesthesia may be performed by injecting a local

anesthetic agent into the tissues surrounding the pudendal

nerve.

To abolish sensation from the anterior part of the perineum,

an ilioinguinal nerve block is performed.

Page 23

Male Urethral Rupture

Straddle injury: rupture of the spongy urethra below the perineal membrane. Urine extravasates to

the scrotum, penis, superficial perineum, and lower anterior abdominal wall.

Pelvic fractures: rupture of the membranous (intermediate part) of the urethra. Urine extravasates to

the deep perineal pouch.

Question 1:

A 23-year-old woman presents with mucopurulent vaginal discharge and post-coital bleeding.

On pelvic exam, her cervix appears erythematous with scattered petechiae. NAAT confirms

the presence of a protozoan.

Which organism is the most likely cause of her symptoms?

A. Chlamydia trachomatis

B. Neisseria gonorrhoeae

C. Trichomonas vaginalis

D. Herpes simplex virus type 2

E. Ureaplasma urealyticum

Page 6

LO: Correlate the histological structure of the cervix with its function.

•

Cervix is lined by columnar epithelium (endocervix) +

squamous epithelium (ectocervix).

•

Provides a barrier and mucus secretion to regulate

sperm entry and protect the upper genital tract.

•

The ectocervix, like the vagina (i.e., the part of the

cervix protruding into the vagina), is lined with

squamous epithelium

•

The epithelial lining of the endocervical canal is

columnar mucous-secreting glandular epithelium

•

This epithelium infolds to form the plicae palmatae

("palm folds"), also known as cervical crypts or

glands.

•

In the presence of high estrogen levels at ovulation,

the cells lining the crypts secrete abundant alkaline

secretions (grey arrows). This mucus lubricates the

vagina and nourishes spermatozoa.

•

Inflammation alters epithelial integrity → friability,

bleeding, ↑ susceptibility to ascending infection, and

progression to neoplasia (esp. HPV-related).

Functional Histology of the Cervix

Page 7

Cervicitis: Definition, Types, Etiology

LO: Discuss common pelvic infections, including those affecting the vulva, vagina, and cervix, and describe the pathogenesis of these diseases,

common organisms involved, and related complications.

Definition & Types:

•

Inflammation of the ectocervix. Acute = mostly infectious. Chronic = often noninfectious (chemical,

mechanical, autoimmune).

Infectious (most common):

•

Chlamydia trachomatis (most common, ~40%).

•

Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

•

Trichomonas vaginalis → classic “strawberry cervix” (punctate hemorrhages).

•

HSV-2 → vesicles/ulcers.

•

HPV (some types), Ureaplasma urealyticum.

•

Associated with bacterial vaginosis.

Noninfectious causes:

•

Chemical: soaps, detergents, spermicides, douches, contraceptive creams.

•

Mechanical: condoms, diaphragms, caps, tampons.

•

Systemic inflammatory diseases: lichen planus, Behçet syndrome.

Page 8

Cervicitis: C/P, Diagnosis, Treatment

Clinical Presentation:

•

asymptomatic.

•

Symptoms: mucopurulent discharge (leukorrhea), post-coital bleeding, dyspareunia,

pelvic/abdominal pain.

Exam findings:

•

Yellow mucoid discharge from os.

•

Swollen cervix with red punctate hemorrhages → “Strawberry cervix” (especially

Trichomonas).

•

HSV → vesicles/ulcers.

Complications:

•

linked with pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), infertility, ↑ HIV transmission risk.

Diagnosis

•

Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT) = gold standard (detects Chlamydia,

Gonorrhea, Trichomonas).

•

Samples: vaginal secretions or urine.

•

Important to rule out co-infections with BV, Candida, or normal flora.

Treatment

•

Empiric antibiotics (covering chlamydia + gonorrhea) for high-risk patients or when

pathogen not detected.

•

Specific therapy based on pathogen once identified.

•

Partner treatment (esp. trichomoniasis, gonorrhea, chlamydia).

Infection with Trichomonas vaginalis

may produce a “strawberry”

appearance of the cervix because of

focal round patches of dilated

capillaries on the surface.

Histological Structure–Function Correlation of the Vagina:

LO: Correlate the histological structure of the vagina with its functions.

  • Stratified squamous epithelium (non-keratinized):

protects against trauma & infection.

  • Glycogen-rich (during reproductive life) epithelial

cells: metabolized by Lactobacilli → lactic acid →

acidic pH (protective barrier).

  • Absence of glands: vaginal lubrication derived from

cervical and vestibular glands.

  • Mucosal immunity: supports balance of microbiota

and defense against pathogens.

Page 12

Vaginitis: Etiology, Pathogenesis, Pathophysiology

LO: Discuss common pelvic infections, including those affecting the vulva, vagina, and cervix, and describe the

pathogenesis of these diseases, common organisms involved, and related complications.

Etiology:

•

Infectious causes: Bacterial vaginosis (BV): overgrowth of Gardnerella vaginalis &

anaerobes after ↓ Lactobacillus.

•

Vulvovaginal candidiasis (VVC): Candida albicans overgrowth triggered by antibiotics,

hormones, immunosuppression.

•

Trichomoniasis: Trichomonas vaginalis (protozoan STI).

•

Noninfectious causes: atrophic vaginitis (low estrogen), allergic/chemical irritation, foreign

body, desquamative inflammatory vaginitis, lichen planus.

Pathogenesis:

•

BV: Loss of protective H₂O₂-producing Lactobacillus → ↑ anaerobes (e.g., Gardnerella).

•

VVC: Candida shifts from commensal yeast → pathogenic hyphae.

•

Trichomoniasis: direct protozoal infection.

•

Common mechanism: oxidative stress → ROS, cytokine release (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6) →

epithelial injury & inflammation.

Pathophysiology & Clinical Features:

•

BV: Thin, gray-white, fishy discharge; ↑ pH > 4.5; clue cells on microscopy.

•

VVC: Thick, “cottage-cheese” discharge; erythema; yeast & pseudohyphae on KOH prep.

•

Trichomoniasis: Frothy yellow-green discharge, strawberry cervix, motile flagellates on

wet mount.

•

Atrophic vaginitis: Postmenopausal; dryness, burning, dyspareunia; thin mucosa, loss of

rugae, ↑ pH.

Two epithelial cells are seen; the one on

the left is 'coated' with gram variable

bacilli (Gardnerella vaginalis) making the

cell appear purplish. These are usually

seen with some frequency in a patient

experiencing bacterial vaginosis.

Page 13

Vaginitis: Complications, Diagnosis, Treatment

LO: Discuss common pelvic infections, including those affecting the vulva, vagina, and cervix, and describe the pathogenesis of these diseases,

common organisms involved, and related complications.

Complications:

  • ↑ Risk of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), adverse pregnancy outcomes (preterm labor, low birth weight).
  • Trichomoniasis increases susceptibility to HIV and other STIs.
  • Chronic/recurrent infections affect quality of life.

Diagnosis

  • BV: Amsel’s criteria (discharge, pH >4.5, clue cells, whiff test), Nugent score on Gram stain.
  • VVC: KOH prep (budding yeast, pseudohyphae); culture for non-albicans species.
  • Trichomoniasis: Wet mount (motile protozoa), NAAT.
  • Atrophic: Clinical exam, microscopy (↑ WBCs, parabasal cells, ↓ Lactobacilli).

Treatment

•

BV: Metronidazole or clindamycin (oral or topical).

•

VVC: Oral fluconazole (single dose) or topical azoles; longer regimens for complicated/recurrent cases.

•

Trichomoniasis: Metronidazole/tinidazole (single dose); treat partners.

•

Atrophic vaginitis: Topical vaginal estrogen; lubricants/moisturizers.

urethra that help moisten its orifice

B. Serous acini that secrete antimicrobial peptides into the vaginal canal; unlike nearby sebaceous glands that

produce lipids

C. Apocrine glands involved in scent signaling; unlike adjacent glands that secrete enzymes into the bladder

D. Squamous-lined crypts that produce keratin; unlike neighboring ciliated ducts that propel secretions

Bartholin’s Glands:

LO: Correlate the histological structure of greater vestibular (Bartholin’s)

glands and paraurethral glands with their functions.

•

Location of the swelling: The mass is described as being at the

posterolateral vestibule near the labia minora.

•

This is the classic location of the Bartholin glands, which are

situated at the 5 and 7 o’clock positions of the vaginal introitus.

•

The mucinous glands seen here make up the Bartholin's gland in

the wall of the vagina.

•

This small gland is about 1 cm in size and the secretions drain

via a duct lined by cuboidal to transitional epithelium.

•

Function and duct obstruction: Bartholin glands secrete mucus

for vaginal lubrication, especially during sexual arousal.

•

Their ducts open into the vestibule, and duct obstruction can

lead to cyst formation (transitional epithelium) or abscess,

which presents as painful, fluctuant swelling.

•

Clinical presentation: Unilateral pain and swelling with a

fluctuant mass is typical of a Bartholin gland abscess.

•

Paraurethral gland (Skene) glands: infections are less common

and usually present with urethral symptoms (e.g., dysuria,

purulent discharge from the urethra), not posterolateral

vestibular swelling.

3. Vulvar Condylomas (HPV-related)

LO: List the differential diagnosis for benign and neoplastic lesions of the vulvar epithelium as well as the clinical and pathologic features of each,

including lichen sclerosus, squamous cell hyperplasia, vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia, vulvar carcinoma, and extramammary Paget disease.

•

•

Etiology: Condyloma lata → syphilis (rare).

•

A) Numerous condylomas of the

vulva. (B) Histopathologic features of

condyloma acuminatum include

acanthosis, hyperkeratosis, and

human papillomavirus cytopathic

effect (koilocytic atypia) characterized

by atypical, enlarged, hyperchromatic

nuclei with perinuclear halos (arrow).

Page 24

VIN and Valvular SCC

LO: List the differential diagnosis for benign and neoplastic lesions of the vulvar epithelium as well as the clinical and pathologic features of each,

including lichen sclerosus, squamous cell hyperplasia, vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia, vulvar carcinoma, and extramammary Paget disease.

4. Vulvar Intraepithelial Neoplasia (VIN)

HPV-related (classic VIN):

Younger women (~60), high-risk HPV (16).

Precancerous lesion → basaloid/warty carcinoma.

HPV-negative (differentiated VIN, dVIN):

Older women (~75), associated with lichen sclerosus or squamous hyperplasia.

Precursor to keratinizing SCC.

5. Vulvar Squamous Cell Carcinoma

Epidemiology: ~3% of female genital cancers; >60 yrs.

Types:

HPV-positive: basaloid/warty, multifocal, poorly differentiated.

HPV-negative: keratinizing, unifocal, well-differentiated, arises in background of lichen sclerosus/dVIN.

Spread: Local invasion → lymph nodes → distant metastasis.

Page 25

5. Extramammary Paget Disease

•

Clinical: Red, scaly,

eczematoid plaque; mimics

dermatitis.

•

Pathology: Large pale-staining

malignant epithelial (Paget)

cells within epidermis, singly

and in clusters.

•

Notes: Rare intraepithelial

adenocarcinoma of vulva;

usually not associated with

underlying carcinoma (unlike

breast Paget).

•

Course: Indolent but may

persist for years; invasive

cases carry poor prognosis.

Large tumor cells with

pale-pink cytoplasm are

seen infiltrating the

epidermis. Chronic

inflammatory cells are

present in the underlying

dermis.

Cervical Histology:

LO: Correlate the histological structure of the cervix with its function.

•

The ectocervix, like vagina (i.e., the

part of the cervix protruding into the

vagina) is lined with squamous

epithelium

•

The epithelial lining of the

endocervical canal is columnar

mucous-secreting glandular

epithelium

•

Infolds of this epithelium form plicae

palmatae (“palm folds”); these are

known as cervical crypts or glands.

•

In the presence of high estrogen levels

at ovulation, the cells lining the crypts

secrete abundant alkaline secretions

(grey arrows). This mucus lubricates

the vagina and nourishes

spermatozoa.

The squamocolumnar junction SCJ and the Transformation Zone

LO: Correlate the histological structure of the cervix with its function.

Predict functional outcomes that result from altered structure and function of the uterine cervix

(e.g., cervical cancer).

1.

Fetal stage

•

The SCJ (where squamous epithelium of the ectocervix meets columnar

epithelium of the endocervix) is located relatively low on the cervix.

•

During development, the columnar epithelium extends outward.

2. Pre-pubertal stage

•

The cervix is smaller, and the SCJ moves inward (up in the canal) compared to the

fetal stage.

•

This is because of cervical growth and changes in the hormonal environment (low

estrogen state before puberty).

3. Post-adolescent (eversion and transformation zone)

•

With puberty and estrogen stimulation, the cervix enlarges, and columnar

epithelium everts outward onto the ectocervix.

•

This exposed columnar epithelium undergoes squamous metaplasia, forming the

transformation zone (high-risk site for HPV infection and cervical neoplasia). The

area between the original SCJ and the newly formed SCJ is known as the

transformation Zone (TZ).

4. Post-menopausal stage

•

Due to low estrogen, the cervix shrinks, and the SCJ recedes further upward into

the endocervical canal.

•

The transformation zone becomes smaller and less accessible.

Which of the following best describes the diagnosis and its associated features?

Page 35

Pathogenesis of Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia (CINs)

LO: Discuss the common human papillomavirus types that affect the cervix and discuss the pathogenesis of cervical dysplasia and neoplasia, and

cervical screening methods and prevention.

•

CINs are the precursor lesions of cervical carcinomas.

•

Arise from normal cervical epithelium; low-grade and high-grade CINs.

•

The most important factor in the pathogenesis is the High-risk HPV (hrHPV).

•

Other contributing factors (smoking, immune status)

•

Low oncogenic risk HPV (types 6 and 11) and high oncogenic risk (types 16 and 18; longer to clear) based on their genotypes

•

High-risk HPVs are the main pathogenic factors of squamous cell carcinomas of other tissues (e.g., oropharynx, tonsils, anus,

vagina, vulva, and penis).

•

Risk factors associated with HPV infections are early age at first intercourse, multiple sexual partners, and persistent infection

with high-risk strains of HPV.

•

The hrHPV infection into the cervical epithelium results in host genome alterations, leading to the silencing of various tumor-

suppressor factors on one hand and inducing aberrant functioning of various tumor-promoting factors on the other

•

The imbalance and instability caused by various hrHPV-derived oncogenic factors drive neoplastic progression

Page 36

Pathogenesis of Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia (CINs)-Cont

•

The major oncoproteins are E5, E6, and E7 encoded by the HPV genome

•

They disrupt the normal functioning of the major histocompatibility complex I (MHC class I), p53 and Rb, Notch1, Wnt,

MAPK, mTOR, and STAT-associated pathways, which are central players controlling normal cellular growth, differentiation,

and immune function

•

HPVs induce carcinogenesis through dysregulation of the activity of tumor suppressor proteins such as p53 and RB by the

viral E6 and E7 proteins, respectively---prevents the normal arrest of TZ cells in the G1 phase of the cell cycle.

•

The viral E6 upregulates telomerase and binds to p53, leading to its destruction.

•

E7 binds to the RB protein, leading to the release of the E2F transcription factors from the inhibitory effect of RB. This results

in progression through the cell cycle.

•

High-risk HPVs also integrate into the host cell genome. This integration results in increased expression of the viral E6 and E7

proteins, and host cell genomic instability----acquisition of prooncogenic mutations.

•

Low-risk HPVs do not integrate into the host genome.

•

The mechanism for low-grade dysplasia is accumulation of viral particles (DNA), producing the classic koilocyte

  • Although CIN II/III has a higher risk for progression to invasive cervical carcinoma, not all women experience this; in fact, only

about 20% progress.

  • VIN (vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia) is similar in appearance to CIN but affects the vagina and affects an older population. It

may represent a field effect from viral infection of the cervix.

Page 37

Spectrum from normal to high-grade SIL

There is no perfect correlation (e.g., a person

with LSIL (Low-grade squamous intraepithelial

lesion) on Pap smear can have CIN II/III on

biopsy, and the reverse is true), but in general,

there is good correlation.

Slide 5: Question 1:
  • A 23-year-old woman presents with mucopurulent vaginal discharge and post-coital bleeding. On pelvic exam, her cervix appears erythematous with scattered petechiae. NAAT confirms the presence of a protozoan.
  • Which organism is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
  • A. Chlamydia trachomatis B. Neisseria gonorrhoeae C. Trichomonas vaginalis D. Herpes simplex virus type 2 E. Ureaplasma urealyticum
Slide 6: Question 1: Answer and Explanation
  • A 23-year-old woman presents with mucopurulent vaginal discharge and post-coital bleeding. On pelvic exam, her cervix appears erythematous with scattered petechiae. NAAT confirms the presence of a protozoan.
  • Which organism is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
  • A. Chlamydia trachomatis B. Neisseria gonorrhoeae C. Trichomonas vaginalis D. Herpes simplex virus type 2 E. Ureaplasma urealyticum
  • Trichomonas vaginalis is a flagellated protozoan that causes vaginitis.
  • Classic findings include: Frothy, greenish discharge; strawberry cervix (punctate hemorrhages); post-coital bleeding; nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT is the most sensitive test for diagnosis. Motile trophozoites may be seen on wet mount (less sensitive, 44-68%).
  • A. Chlamydia trachomatis: Obligate intracellular bacterium (not a protozoan); Often asymptomatic; may cause mucopurulent discharge and cervical inflammation; Cervix may show friability but not petechiae; NAAT is used for diagnosis, but it detects bacterial DNA, not protozoa
  • B. Neisseria gonorrhoeae: Gram-negative diplococcus (bacterium); Purulent discharge, dysuria, cervical petechiae are not typical
  • D. Herpes simplex virus type 2: DNA virus; Painful genital ulcers, systemic symptoms; Cervical Ulcerations, vesicles
  • E. Ureaplasma urealyticum: Bacterium (lacks cell wall); Often asymptomatic; may be associated with urethritis or cervicitis
Slide 7: Functional Histology of the Cervix
  • LO: Correlate the histological structure of the cervix with its function.
  • Cervix is lined by columnar epithelium (endocervix) + squamous epithelium (ectocervix).
  • Provides a barrier and mucus secretion to regulate sperm entry and protect the upper genital tract.
  • The ectocervix, like the vagina (i.e., the part of the cervix protruding into the vagina), is lined with squamous epithelium
  • The epithelial lining of the endocervical canal is columnar mucous-secreting glandular epithelium
  • This epithelium infolds to form the plicae palmatae ("palm folds"), also known as cervical crypts or glands.
  • In the presence of high estrogen levels at ovulation, the cells lining the crypts secrete abundant alkaline secretions (grey arrows). This mucus lubricates the vagina and nourishes spermatozoa.
  • Inflammation alters epithelial integrity → friability, bleeding, ↑ susceptibility to ascending infection, and progression to neoplasia (esp. HPV-related).
Slide 8: Cervicitis: Definition, Types, Etiology
  • LO: Discuss common pelvic infections, including those affecting the vulva, vagina, and cervix, and describe the pathogenesis of these diseases, common organisms involved, and related complications.
  • Definition & Types:
  • Inflammation of the ectocervix. Acute = mostly infectious. Chronic = often noninfectious (chemical, mechanical, autoimmune).
  • Infectious (most common):
  • Chlamydia trachomatis (most common, ~40%).
  • Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
  • Trichomonas vaginalis → classic “strawberry cervix” (punctate hemorrhages).
  • HSV-2 → vesicles/ulcers.
  • HPV (some types), Ureaplasma urealyticum.
  • Associated with bacterial vaginosis.
  • Noninfectious causes:
  • Chemical: soaps, detergents, spermicides, douches, contraceptive creams.
  • Mechanical: condoms, diaphragms, caps, tampons.
  • Systemic inflammatory diseases: lichen planus, Behçet syndrome.
Slide 9: Cervicitis: C/P, Diagnosis, Treatment
  • Clinical Presentation:
  • asymptomatic.
  • Symptoms: mucopurulent discharge (leukorrhea), post-coital bleeding, dyspareunia, pelvic/abdominal pain.
  • Exam findings:
  • Yellow mucoid discharge from os.
  • Swollen cervix with red punctate hemorrhages → “Strawberry cervix” (especially Trichomonas).
  • HSV → vesicles/ulcers.
  • Complications:
  • linked with pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), infertility, ↑ HIV transmission risk.
  • Diagnosis
  • Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT) = gold standard (detects Chlamydia, Gonorrhea, Trichomonas).
  • Samples: vaginal secretions or urine.
  • Important to rule out co-infections with BV, Candida, or normal flora.
  • Treatment
  • Empiric antibiotics (covering chlamydia + gonorrhea) for high-risk patients or when pathogen not detected.
  • Specific therapy based on pathogen once identified.
  • Partner treatment (esp. trichomoniasis, gonorrhea, chlamydia).
  • Infection with Trichomonas vaginalis may produce a “strawberry” appearance of the cervix because of focal round patches of dilated capillaries on the surface.
Slide 10: Question 2:
  • A 62-year-old woman with urinary incontinence develops intense vulvar pruritus after using antiseptic wipes. The exam reveals well-defined erythematous, weeping, and crusting papules/plaques on the vulva. No fever.
  • What is the most likely cause?
  • A. Allergic/contact irritant dermatitis B. Candida vulvitis C. HSV-2 infection D. Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection of vulvovaginal glands E. HPV 16 infection
Slide 11: Question 2: Answer and Explanation
  • A 62-year-old woman with urinary incontinence develops intense vulvar pruritus after using antiseptic wipes. The exam reveals well-defined erythematous, weeping, and crusting papules/plaques on the vulva. No fever. What is the most likely cause?
  • A. Allergic/contact irritant dermatitis B. Candida vulvitis C. HSV-2 infection D. Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection of vulvovaginal glands E. HPV 16 infection
  • A. Allergic/contact irritant dermatitis: Common in older women due to thinner vulvar epithelium and reduced estrogen. Triggered by irritants (e.g., antiseptic wipes); Presents with erythema, pruritus, weeping plaques, and no systemic symptoms.
  • B. Candida vulvitis: causes intense pruritus, white discharge, and satellite lesions. More common in diabetics or immunocompromised. Lesions are usually white and curdy, not weeping plaques.
  • C. HSV-2 infection: painful vesicles or ulcers, often with fever or systemic symptoms. Lesions are not typically described as weeping plaques.
  • D. Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection of vulvovaginal glands: Can cause Bartholin gland abscesses not diffuse vulvar plaques; presents with purulent discharge, not crusting plaques.
  • E. HPV 16 infection----VIN and vulvar carcinoma. Lesions are white, thickened, or exophytic, not acute erythematous plaques. No pruritus or acute inflammation.
Slide 12: Question 3:
  • A 29-year-old woman presents with vaginal pruritus and thin, homogeneous discharge with a fishy odor. Vaginal pH is elevated (>4.5), and microscopy reveals clue cells.
  • Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of this condition?
  • A. Overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria disrupting normal lactobacilli flora B. Invasion of vaginal epithelium by Candida albicans hyphae C. Viral cytopathic effect leading to ulceration of mucosal surfaces D. Protozoal motility causing epithelial disruption and inflammation E. Estrogen deficiency leading to thinning of vaginal epithelium
Slide 13: Question 3: Answer and Explanation
  • A 29-year-old woman presents with vaginal pruritus and thin, homogeneous discharge with a fishy odor. Vaginal pH is elevated (>4.5), and microscopy reveals clue cells.
  • Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of this condition?
  • A. Overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria disrupting normal lactobacilli flora B. Invasion of vaginal epithelium by Candida albicans hyphae C. Viral cytopathic effect leading to ulceration of mucosal surfaces D. Protozoal motility causing epithelial disruption and inflammation E. Estrogen deficiency leading to thinning of vaginal epithelium
  • A. Overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria disrupting normal lactobacilli flora: describes the pathogenesis of bacterial vaginosis (BV) which is caused by a shift in vaginal flora, with loss of protective lactobacilli and overgrowth of anaerobes like Gardnerella vaginalis.
  • B. Candida albicans hyphae: Describes vaginal candidiasis, not BV.
  • C. Viral cytopathic effect: Refers to HSV infection, which causes ulcers.
  • D. Protozoal motility: Refers to Trichomonas vaginalis, which causes frothy discharge and strawberry cervix.
  • E. Estrogen deficiency: Refers to atrophic vaginitis, common in postmenopausal women.
Slide 14: Histological Structure–Function Correlation of the Vagina:
  • LO: Correlate the histological structure of the vagina with its functions.
  • Stratified squamous epithelium (non-keratinized): protects against trauma & infection.
  • Glycogen-rich (during reproductive life) epithelial cells: metabolized by Lactobacilli → lactic acid → acidic pH (protective barrier).
  • Absence of glands: vaginal lubrication derived from cervical and vestibular glands.
  • Mucosal immunity: supports balance of microbiota and defense against pathogens.
Slide 15: Vaginitis: Etiology, Pathogenesis, Pathophysiology
  • LO: Discuss common pelvic infections, including those affecting the vulva, vagina, and cervix, and describe the pathogenesis of these diseases, common organisms involved, and related complications.
  • Etiology:
  • Infectious causes: Bacterial vaginosis (BV): overgrowth of Gardnerella vaginalis & anaerobes after ↓ Lactobacillus.
  • Vulvovaginal candidiasis (VVC): Candida albicans overgrowth triggered by antibiotics, hormones, immunosuppression.
  • Trichomoniasis: Trichomonas vaginalis (protozoan STI).
  • Noninfectious causes: atrophic vaginitis (low estrogen), allergic/chemical irritation, foreign body, desquamative inflammatory vaginitis, lichen planus.
  • Pathogenesis:
  • BV: Loss of protective H₂O₂-producing Lactobacillus → ↑ anaerobes (e.g., Gardnerella).
  • VVC: Candida shifts from commensal yeast → pathogenic hyphae.
  • Trichomoniasis: direct protozoal infection.
  • Common mechanism: oxidative stress → ROS, cytokine release (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6) → epithelial injury & inflammation.
  • Pathophysiology & Clinical Features:
  • BV: Thin, gray-white, fishy discharge; ↑ pH > 4.5; clue cells on microscopy.
  • VVC: Thick, “cottage-cheese” discharge; erythema; yeast & pseudohyphae on KOH prep.
  • Trichomoniasis: Frothy yellow-green discharge, strawberry cervix, motile flagellates on wet mount.
  • Atrophic vaginitis: Postmenopausal; dryness, burning, dyspareunia; thin mucosa, loss of rugae, ↑ pH.
  • Two epithelial cells are seen; the one on the left is 'coated' with gram variable bacilli (Gardnerella vaginalis) making the cell appear purplish. These are usually seen with some frequency in a patient experiencing bacterial vaginosis.
Slide 16: Vaginitis: Complications, Diagnosis, Treatment
  • LO: Discuss common pelvic infections, including those affecting the vulva, vagina, and cervix, and describe the pathogenesis of these diseases, common organisms involved, and related complications.
  • Complications:
  • ↑ Risk of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), adverse pregnancy outcomes (preterm labor, low birth weight).
  • Trichomoniasis increases susceptibility to HIV and other STIs.
  • Chronic/recurrent infections affect quality of life.
  • Diagnosis
  • BV: Amsel’s criteria ( 3 of 4 are required: discharge, pH >4.5, clue cells, whiff test), Nugent score on Gram stain.
  • VVC: KOH prep (budding yeast, pseudohyphae); culture for non-albicans species.
  • Trichomoniasis: Wet mount (motile protozoa), NAAT.
  • Atrophic: Clinical exam, microscopy (↑ WBCs, parabasal cells, ↓ Lactobacilli).
  • Treatment
  • BV: Metronidazole or clindamycin (oral or topical).
  • VVC: Oral fluconazole (single dose) or topical azoles; longer regimens for complicated/recurrent cases.
  • Trichomoniasis: Metronidazole/tinidazole (single dose); treat partners.
  • Atrophic vaginitis: Topical vaginal estrogen; lubricants/moisturizers.

Notes:

The Amsel criteria are a set of clinical findings used to diagnose bacterial vaginosis (BV) at the bedside. A definitive clinical diagnosis requires the presence of at least three of the following four criteria:

The 4 Diagnostic Components

Discharge: Thin, white, gray, or yellow homogeneous vaginal discharge that smoothly coats the vaginal walls.

pH Level: An elevated vaginal fluid pH greater than 4.5 (normal vaginal pH is usually ≤ 4.5).

Whiff Test: Release of a strong, fishy amine odor immediately after adding a 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) solution to the vaginal discharge sample.

Clue Cells: Demonstration of "clue cells" (vaginal epithelial cells heavily studded and coated with adherent bacteria) making up more than 20% of the epithelial cells visible under wet-mount microscopy.

Nugent Score (Gram stain): Quantitative assessment of vaginal flora based on Lactobacillus, Gardnerella/Bacteroides, and Mobiluncus morphotypes. Score 0–3 = normal, 4–6 = intermediate, 7–10 = bacterial vaginosis.

Amsel criteria = clinical diagnosis

Nugent score = Gram stain-based microbiologic diagnosis

Clue cells = hallmark microscopic finding of BV

  • A 27-year-old woman presents with severe unilateral vulvar pain and swelling. The exam reveals a tender, fluctuant mass at the posterolateral vestibule near the labia minora. You explain that obstruction of the affected gland’s duct can lead to abscess formation.
  • Which of the following best correlates the histologic structure and function of the affected gland ?

Serous acini that secrete antimicrobial peptides into the vaginal canal; unlike nearby sebaceous glands that produce lipids C. Apocrine glands involved in scent signaling; unlike adjacent glands that secrete enzymes into the bladder D. Squamous-lined crypts that produce keratin; unlike neighboring ciliated ducts that propel secretions E. Slide 18: Question 4: Answer and Explanation
  • A 27-year-old woman presents with severe unilateral vulvar pain and swelling. The exam reveals a tender, fluctuant mass at the posterolateral vestibule near the labia minora. You explain that obstruction of the affected gland’s duct can lead to abscess formation.
  • Which of the following best correlates the histologic structure and function of the affected gland?
  • A. Mucus-secreting tubuloalveolar glands that lubricate the vaginal opening; similar to smaller glands near the urethra that help moisten its orifice B. Serous acini that secrete antimicrobial peptides into the vaginal canal; unlike nearby sebaceous glands that produce lipids C. Apocrine glands involved in scent signaling; unlike adjacent glands that secrete enzymes into the bladder D. Squamous-lined crypts that produce keratin; unlike neighboring ciliated ducts that propel secretions E. Endocrine cords that release hormones into the lamina propria; unlike surrounding glands that regulate pH
  • A. Greater vestibular (Bartholin’s) glands are mucus-secreting compound tubuloalveolar glands located at the posterolateral vestibule. Their function is to lubricate the vaginal introitus. The paraurethral (Skene) glands, located near the urethral opening, are also mucus-secreting and help moisten and protect the urethral orifice.
  • B: Serous acini... : Bartholin’s glands are mucus-secreting, not serous. Paraurethral glands are not sebaceous
  • C: Apocrine glands...: are associated with sweat and scent signaling, not lubrication. Paraurethral glands do not secrete enzymes into the bladder; they secrete mucus near the urethral opening.
  • D: Squamous-lined crypts...: Bartholin’s glands are glandular, not crypts lined by squamous epithelium. Paraurethral glands do not have ciliated ducts; they secrete mucus, not propel secretions.
  • E: Endocrine cords...: Neither gland is endocrine — they do not release hormones. Paraurethral glands do not regulate pH; their role is lubrication, not chemical balance.
Slide 19: Bartholin’s Glands:
  • LO: Correlate the histological structure of greater vestibular (Bartholin’s) glands and paraurethral glands with their functions.
  • Location of the swelling: The mass is described as being at the posterolateral vestibule near the labia minora.
  • Paired mucus-secreting glands located in the posterior vestibule at the 4 and 8 o'clock positions. Their ducts open into the vulvar vestibule and may be depicted near the 5 and 7 o'clock positions.
  • The mucinous glands seen here make up the Bartholin's gland in the wall of the vagina.
  • This small gland is about 1 cm in size and the secretions drain via a duct lined by cuboidal to transitional epithelium.
  • Function and duct obstruction: Bartholin glands secrete mucus for vaginal lubrication, especially during sexual arousal.
  • Their ducts open into the vestibule, and duct obstruction can lead to cyst formation or abscess, which presents as painful, fluctuant swelling.
  • Clinical presentation: Unilateral pain and swelling with a fluctuant mass is typical of a Bartholin gland abscess.
  • Paraurethral (Skene) glands; Female Prostate: infections are less common and usually present with urethral symptoms (e.g., dysuria, purulent discharge from the urethra), not posterolateral vestibular swelling.

  • A 45-year-old woman presents with thickened, leathery vulvar skin and intense pruritus. Biopsy shows hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and elongation of rete ridges.
  • Which condition is most consistent with these findings?
  • A. Lichen sclerosus B. Squamous cell hyperplasia C. Vulvar carcinoma D. Paget disease E. HSV infection
Slide 22: Question 5: Answer and Explanation
  • A 68-year-old woman presents with chronic vulvar itching and pain during intercourse. On exam, there are white, thin plaques with areas of skin fragility and scarring. Biopsy reveals thinning of the epidermis, loss of rete ridges, homogenization of the dermal collagen, and a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate.
  • Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
  • A. Lichen sclerosus B. Squamous cell hyperplasia C. Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia D. Vulvar carcinoma E. Extramammary Paget disease
  • A. Lichen sclerosus: a chronic inflammatory dermatosis, most common in postmenopausal women. Clinical and histological features are characteristic. Risk of progression to differentiated VIN and keratinizing squamous cell CA
  • B. Squamous cell hyperplasia: thickened, leathery skin due to chronic irritation (lichen simplex chronicus); Histology: Hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, elongation of rete ridges; No dermal homogenization or band-like infiltrate; seen in younger women with chronic scratching.
  • C. Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN): a precancerous lesion associated with HPV (especially type 16); Histology: Atypical squamous cells confined to the epithelium; present as multifocal pigmented or erythematous lesions; no dermal collagen changes or lymphocytic infiltrate
  • D. Vulvar carcinoma: a mass or ulcerated lesion; pain or bleeding; Invasive squamous cells
  • E. Extramammary Paget disease: red, eczematous, or velvety plaques; Large pale-staining Paget cells within the epidermis.
Slide 23: Question 6: Answer and Explanation
  • A 45-year-old woman presents with thickened, leathery vulvar skin and intense pruritus. Biopsy shows hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and elongation of rete ridges.
  • Which condition is most consistent with these findings?
  • A. Lichen sclerosus B. Squamous cell hyperplasia C. Vulvar carcinoma D. Paget disease E. HSV infection
  • B. Squamous cell hyperplasia or Lichen simplex Chronicus: Chronic irritation or scratching; Hyperkeratosis (thickened stratum corneum); Acanthosis (epidermal thickening); Elongated rete ridges; Thickened, leathery skin due to chronic rubbing or scratching. Management: Remove irritants, topical corticosteroids
  • A. Lichen sclerosus: Postmenopausal women; White, thin plaques; skin fragility; scarring; Thinned epidermis, Loss of rete ridges, Homogenization of dermal collagen, Band-like lymphocytic infiltrate.
  • C. Vulvar carcinoma: Ulcerated or exophytic mass, pain or bleeding; Invasive squamous cells breaching the basement membrane.
  • D. Paget disease: Red, eczematous, velvety plaques; often misdiagnosed as dermatitis. Large pale-staining Paget cells within the epidermis.
  • E. HSV infection: Painful vesicles or ulcers, often recurrent. Histology: Multinucleated giant cells, viral cytopathic changes.
Slide 24: 1. Lichen Sclerosus:
  • LO: List the differential diagnosis for benign and neoplastic lesions of the vulvar epithelium as well as the clinical and pathologic features of each, including lichen sclerosus, squamous cell hyperplasia, vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia, vulvar carcinoma, and extramammary Paget disease.
  • Smooth, white plaques (leukoplakia), atrophy, labial stiffening, narrowing of vaginal orifice.
  • Pathology: Epidermal thinning, loss of rete ridges, dermal fibrosis, bandlike lymphocytic infiltrate.
  • Common in postmenopausal women & prepubertal girls.
  • Autoimmune association.
  • Risk: Slight ↑ risk of squamous cell carcinoma, but not premalignant itself.
  • Hyperkeratosis of the epidermis (A), epidermal atrophy with loss of rete ridges (B), homogenization of the collagen below the dermal-epidural junction (C), and lichenoid T-lymphocyte infiltrate(D).
Slide 25: 2. Squamous Cell Hyperplasia (Lichen Simplex Chronicus)
  • LO: List the differential diagnosis for benign and neoplastic lesions of the vulvar epithelium as well as the clinical and pathologic features of each, including lichen sclerosus, squamous cell hyperplasia, vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia, vulvar carcinoma, and extramammary Paget disease.
  • Leukoplakia due to chronic irritation/pruritus.
  • Pathology: Epidermal thickening (acanthosis), elongated rete ridges, hyperkeratosis.
  • Notes: Nonspecific; no cytologic atypia.
  • Must biopsy to exclude VIN or carcinoma.
  • Squamous Cell Hyperplasia
  • Lichen Sclerosus

Notes:

A leukoplakia is:

A white patch on a mucosal surface that cannot be scraped off and cannot be explained by another specific disease.

Slide 29: Question 7: Answer and Explanation
  • A 21-year-old woman has multiple exophytic, verrucous papules on the labia minora. Biopsy shows papillary exophytic stroma covered by thickened squamous epithelium with koilocytosis. Which statement is most accurate?
  • A. Caused by high-risk HPV 16/18 with frequent malignant progression B. Often multifocal; lesions commonly regress without therapy C. Caused by low-risk HPV 6/11 and do not progress to cancer D. Associated with basal atypia and TP53 mutation (dVIN) E. Best prevented only by bivalent vaccine
  • Clinicopathological features align with Condyloma acuminatum (genital warts); Caused by low-risk HPV types 6 and 11; Papillary architecture, Acanthosis, Koilocytosis (perinuclear clearing in squamous cells due to HPV effect); multiple and exophytic lesions; regress spontaneously or persist; Do not progress to cancer
  • A. Caused by high-risk HPV 16/18 with frequent malignant progression: HPV 16/18 are high-risk types associated with VIN, cervical dysplasia, and carcinoma; They cause flat or pigmented lesions, not verrucous papules; atypia, not koilocytosis
  • B. Often multifocal; lesions commonly regress without therapy: too vague and not the most accurate statement.
  • D. Associated with basal atypia and TP53 mutation: dVIN (differentiated vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia) is not HPV-related. Occurs in older women, often with lichen sclerosus; basal atypia, keratinization, and TP53 mutations; Not associated with koilocytosis or verrucous papules
  • E. Best prevented only by bivalent vaccine: The bivalent vaccine (Cervarix) targets HPV 16 and 18 (high-risk types); does not protect against HPV 6/11, which cause condyloma acuminatum; Quadrivalent (Gardasil) and nonavalent (Gardasil 9) vaccines cover HPV 6/11 and are better for wart prevention
Slide 30: Question 8: Answer and Explanation
  • A 73-year-old woman with long-standing lichen sclerosus has a solitary leukoplakic vulvar plaque. Biopsy shows basal atypia with parakeratosis and irregular rete ridges; tumor shows aberrant p53 and absent/focal p16. Which is the most likely pathway?
  • A. HPV-associated HSIL → warty/basaloid SCC B. HPV-independent dVIN → keratinizing SCC C. Paget disease with CK7+/GATA3+ cells D. Condyloma acuminatum with Ki-67 in upper third E. HPV 6/11–associated VIN
  • B. HPV-independent dVIN → keratinizing SCCdVIN = differentiated vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia; Non-HPV-related → keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma; Associated with Lichen sclerosus; Older age group; Basal atypia, parakeratosis, irregular rete ridges; Aberrant p53 (mutation), Absent or focal p16 (not HPV-driven); presents as leukoplakia, solitary lesion
  • A. HPV-associated HSIL → warty/basaloid SCCHSIL = high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion; HPV types: 16, 18; Full-thickness atypia, mitoses, koilocytosis; Diffuse p16 positivity; Wild-type p53
  • C. Paget disease with CK7+/GATA3+ cells: Intraepithelial adenocarcinoma; Large pale cells in epidermis; CK7+, GATA3+, CEA+; Red, eczematous plaques, often misdiagnosed as dermatitis
  • D. Condyloma acuminatum with Ki-67 in upper third: HPV 6/11 (low-risk); Papillary architecture, koilocytosis; Ki-67: Proliferation marker in upper third of epithelium; Condylomas are verrucous, not leukoplakic
  • E. HPV 6/11–associated VIN: Low-risk HPVs are associated with Condyloma, not VIN with atypia. VIN is associated with high-risk HPV. HPV 6/11 lesions are benign and do not show basal atypia or p53 mutation
Slide 31: Question 9: Answer and Explanation
  • A 68-year-old woman presents with a persistent red, scaly vulvar plaque that has not responded to topical corticosteroids. Biopsy reveals intraepidermal atypical cells. Immunostaining is positive for CK7 and CEA, and negative for S100 and HMB-45.
  • Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
  • A. Vulvar melanoma B. Squamous cell carcinoma C. Extramammary Paget disease D. Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN) E. Chronic contact dermatitis
  • C. Extramammary Paget disease: an intraepithelial adenocarcinoma arising in apocrine gland-rich areas (e.g., vulva, perineum).Histology: Large pale Paget cells with prominent nuclei within the epidermis. CK7+, CEA+, EMA+, PAS+S100–, HMB-45– → excludes melanoma. Red, scaly, eczematous plaque that mimics dermatitis but persists despite treatment. Management: Wide local excision with margin control (e.g., Mohs surgery).
  • A. Vulvar melanoma: present as pigmented or amelanotic vulvar lesions. Atypical melanocytes; S100+, HMB-45+, Melan-A+
  • B. Squamous cell carcinoma: a mass, ulcer, or leukoplakic plaque. Invasive squamous cells breaching the basement membrane. p63+, CK5/6+
  • D. Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN): a precursor to HPV-associated vulvar carcinoma. Full-thickness atypia, mitoses, koilocytosis. p16+ (HPV-driven), p53 wild-type (in HSIL)
  • E. Chronic contact dermatitis: Red, itchy, scaly plaques; often bilateral. Spongiosis, acanthosis, lymphocytic infiltrate.
Slide 32: 3. Vulvar Condylomas (HPV-related)
  • LO: List the differential diagnosis for benign and neoplastic lesions of the vulvar epithelium as well as the clinical and pathologic features of each, including lichen sclerosus, squamous cell hyperplasia, vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia, vulvar carcinoma, and extramammary Paget disease.
  • Warty, exophytic papules; red-pink to hyperpigmented.
  • Etiology: Condyloma lata → syphilis (rare).
  • Condyloma acuminata → low-risk HPV (6, 11).
  • Pathology: Papillary squamous proliferation with koilocytosis (perinuclear halos, wrinkled nuclei).
  • Notes: Benign, do not progress to cancer, but signal HPV exposure.
  • A) Numerous condylomas of the vulva. (B) Histopathologic features of condyloma acuminatum include acanthosis, hyperkeratosis, and human papillomavirus cytopathic effect (koilocytic atypia) characterized by atypical, enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei with perinuclear halos (arrow).

Notes:

Condyloma acuminata

Think "A = Acuminata = HPV = Above the surface"

Raised, pointed, cauliflower-like growths

Condyloma lata

Think "L = Lata = Large and Level"

Broad, flat, moist plaques

Characteristic of secondary syphilis

High-Yield Board Pearls

Condyloma acuminata

HPV 6 and 11

Koilocytes

Usually benign

Often described as papillary or cauliflower-like

Condyloma lata

Secondary syphilis

Broad, flat, moist lesions

Accompanied by other signs of secondary syphilis:

Diffuse rash (including palms and soles)

Generalized lymphadenopathy

Mucous patches

Condyloma acuminata = raised cauliflower-like HPV warts; condyloma lata = broad, flat, moist lesions of secondary syphilis.

Slide 33: VIN and Valvular SCC
  • LO: List the differential diagnosis for benign and neoplastic lesions of the vulvar epithelium as well as the clinical and pathologic features of each, including lichen sclerosus, squamous cell hyperplasia, vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia, vulvar carcinoma, and extramammary Paget disease.
  • 4. Vulvar Intraepithelial Neoplasia (VIN)
  • HPV-related (classic VIN):
  • Younger women (~60), high-risk HPV (16).
  • Precancerous lesion → basaloid/warty carcinoma.
  • HPV-negative (differentiated VIN, dVIN):
  • Older women (~75), associated with lichen sclerosus or squamous hyperplasia.
  • Precursor to keratinizing SCC.
  • 5. Vulvar Squamous Cell Carcinoma
  • Epidemiology: ~3% of female genital cancers; >60 yrs.
  • Types:
  • HPV-positive: basaloid/warty, multifocal, poorly differentiated.
  • HPV-negative: keratinizing, unifocal, well-differentiated, arises in background of lichen sclerosus/dVIN.
  • Spread: Local invasion → lymph nodes → distant metastasis.
Slide 34: 5. Extramammary Paget Disease
  • Clinical: Red, scaly, eczematoid plaque; mimics dermatitis.
  • Pathology: Large , pale-staining malignant epithelial (Paget) cells within the epidermis, single and in clusters.
  • Notes: Rare intraepithelial adenocarcinoma of vulva; usually not associated with underlying carcinoma (unlike breast Paget).
  • Course: Indolent but may persist for years; invasive cases carry poor prognosis.
  • Large tumor cells with pale-pink cytoplasm are seen infiltrating the epidermis. Chronic inflammatory cells are present in the underlying dermis.

Slide 36: Question 10: Answer and Explanation
  • A 3-year-old girl presents with vaginal bleeding and a grape-like mass protruding from the vagina. Histology shows small round blue cells in a cambium layer beneath the epithelium.
  • Which diagnosis is most likely?
  • A. Clear cell carcinoma B. Endodermal sinus tumor C. Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma D. Teratoma E. Neuroblastoma
  • C. Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (sarcoma botryoides): a subtype of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma. Classic presentation: Young children, especially girls under 5; grape-like polypoid mass protruding from the vagina; Vaginal bleeding; Histology: Small round blue cells; Cambium layer: Dense subepithelial cellular zone; Origin: Mesenchymal tumor of skeletal muscle lineage; Management: Multimodal (surgery, chemo, sometimes radiation)
  • A. Clear cell carcinoma: Typically occurs in: Adolescents or young women with in-utero exposure to diethylstilbestrol (DES); Histology: Clear cytoplasm; Hobnail cells; Glandular or tubulocystic architecture
  • B. Endodermal sinus tumor (yolk sac tumor): Typically occurs in: Adolescents and young adults; vaginal bleeding possible, but more common in ovary or testis; Schiller-Duval bodies; AFP-positive
  • D. Teratoma: Typically occurs in: Ovary or testis; Mixed tissues from all three germ layers (e.g., hair, cartilage, neural tissue)
  • E. Neuroblastoma: Typically occurs in: Adrenal gland or sympathetic chain; Small round blue cells, Homer-Wright rosettes
Slide 37: Sarcoma Botryoides or Embryonal Rhabdomyosarcoma
  • LO: Describe the clinicopathologic features of vaginal embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (sarcoma botryoides).
  • Children < 4yo
  • Polypoid, grape-like soft tissue protruding from vagina
  • Micro: Cambium layer: dense layer of malignant cells just beneath the vaginal epithelium.
  • Cells: Rhabdomyoblasts (primitive skeletal muscle cells) with eosinophilic cytoplasm, sometimes with “strap” or “tadpole”shapes.
  • Immunohistochemistry: Desmin (+), Myogenin (+), MyoD1 (+)
  • https://mynotes4usmle.tumblr.com/post/43609759641/sarcoma-botryoides-or-embryonal-rhabdomyosarcoma
  • Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma with primitive round cells and occasional strap cells (arrow) with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and cross-striations (inset).

Slide 41: Question 11: Answer and Explanation
  • A 19-year-old nulligravid woman has a normal pelvic exam. Where is the squamocolumnar junction (SCJ) most likely located in a healthy adolescent or young adult?
  • Deep within endocervical canal above external os
  • Within endocervical canal
  • On the ectocervix
  • At the internal os
  • Not visible
  • A. Deep within endocervical canal above external os: typical of postmenopausal women, not adolescents. In young women, estrogen causes eversion of the endocervical epithelium.
  • B. Within endocervical canal: true for menopausal women, but the question is about a young adult.
  • C. On the ectocervix, due to eversion after puberty: estrogen causes the endocervical columnar epithelium to evert onto the ectocervix, moving the SCJ outward. This exposes the transformation zone, where HPV infection and dysplasia are most likely.
  • D. At the internal os: The SCJ may shift during pregnancy, but not to the internal os. The question is about a non-pregnant adolescent.
  • E. Not visible: The SCJ is visible on the ectocervix in adolescents and young adults. It becomes less visible postmenopause due to regression into the canal.
Slide 42: Question 12: Answer and Explanation
  • A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman undergoes routine cervical screening. On speculum exam, the squamocolumnar junction is not visible. Cytology reveals atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US).
  • Which of the following best explains the location of the transformation zone in this patient?
  • A. On the ectocervix due to estrogen-induced eversion B. Within the endocervical canal due to age-related regression C. At the internal os due to pregnancy-related changes D. Deep in the cervical stroma due to chronic inflammation E. Not present in postmenopausal women
  • A. On the ectocervix due to estrogen-induced eversion: This is true for adolescents and reproductive-age women, not postmenopausal women.
  • B. Within the endocervical canal due to age-related regression: In postmenopausal women, low estrogen causes the SCJ to regress into the canal, making it harder to visualize. This is why colposcopy or endocervical sampling may be needed.
  • C. At the internal os due to pregnancy-related changes: The patient is not pregnant, and the SCJ does not migrate to the internal os.
  • D. Deep in the cervical stroma due to chronic inflammation: Chronic inflammation may alter cervical architecture, but it does not determine SCJ location.
  • E. Not present in postmenopausal women: The SCJ is always present, but its location changes. It may be inaccessible, but it does not disappear.
Slide 43: Question 13: Answer and Explanation
  • A 44-year-old presents with postcoital bleeding. Workup reveals HSIL and a lesion in the TZ. Which functional concept links the TZ’s histology to her risk?
  • A. Mature glycogenated squamous cells are resistant to HPV B. Immature metaplastic squamous cells in the TZ are susceptible to HPV oncogenesis C. Columnar epithelium of ectocervix is most resistant to integration D. The SCJ location is fixed after puberty E. HPV replicates only in basal cells, not maturing cells
  • B: Postcoital bleeding and HSIL (high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion) suggest a significant cervical pathology, often associated with HPV infection. The transformation zone (TZ) is the area between the original squamocolumnar junction and the new squamocolumnar junction, where columnar epithelium is replaced by squamous epithelium through metaplasia. The immature metaplastic squamous cells in the TZ are proliferative and not fully differentiated, making them more vulnerable to HPV infection and oncogenesis.
  • A. Mature glycogenated squamous cells are resistant to HPV→ mature cells are not the primary site of oncogenesis; HPV infects basal cells in immature epithelium.
  • C. Columnar epithelium of ectocervix is most resistant to integration→ The ectocervix is lined by squamous epithelium, not columnar.
  • D. The SCJ location is fixed after puberty→ The squamocolumnar junction (SCJ) shifts with hormonal changes, pregnancy, and age.
  • E. HPV replicates only in basal cells, not maturing cells→ True in terms of viral replication, but this doesn’t explain the oncogenic susceptibility of the TZ.
Slide 44: Cervical Histology:

| LO: Correlate the histological structure of the cervix with its function. |

| --- |

  • The ectocervix, like vagina (i.e., the part of the cervix protruding into the vagina) is lined with squamous epithelium
  • The epithelial lining of the endocervical canal is columnar mucous-secreting glandular epithelium
  • Infolds of this epithelium form plicae palmatae (“palm folds”); these are known as cervical crypts or glands.
  • In the presence of high estrogen levels at ovulation, the cells lining the crypts secrete abundant alkaline secretions (grey arrows). This mucus lubricates the vagina and nourishes spermatozoa.
Slide 45: The squamocolumnar junction SCJ and the Transformation Zone

| LO: Correlate the histological structure of the cervix with its function. |

| --- |

| Predict functional outcomes that result from altered structure and function of the uterine cervix (e.g., cervical cancer). |

  • Fetal stage
  • The SCJ (where squamous epithelium of the ectocervix meets columnar epithelium of the endocervix) is located relatively low on the cervix.
  • During development, the columnar epithelium extends outward.
  • 2. Pre-pubertal stage
  • The cervix is smaller, and the SCJ moves inward (up in the canal) compared to the fetal stage.
  • This is because of cervical growth and changes in the hormonal environment (low estrogen state before puberty).
  • 3. Post-adolescent (eversion and transformation zone)
  • With puberty and estrogen stimulation, the cervix enlarges, and columnar epithelium everts outward onto the ectocervix.
  • This exposed columnar epithelium undergoes squamous metaplasia, forming the transformation zone (high-risk site for HPV infection and cervical neoplasia). The area between the original SCJ and the newly formed SCJ is known as the transformation Zone (TZ).
  • 4. Post-menopausal stage
  • Due to low estrogen, the cervix shrinks, and the SCJ recedes further upward into the endocervical canal.
  • The transformation zone becomes smaller and less accessible.

Notes:

These metaplastic changes occur throughout the reproductive period and until menopause.

The immature squamous cells in the TZ are the most susceptible to Human Papilloma Virus (HPV) oncogenesis, and these are the cells of origin of cervical carcinomas.

Moderate dysplasia involving the lower two-thirds of the epithelium; variable regression or progression D. Mild dysplasia confined to the basal third of the epithelium; typically managed with observation E. Invasion of basement membrane by atypical cells; requires staging and oncologic treatment
Slide 47: Question 15:
  • A 49-year-old woman presents with abnormal vaginal bleeding. She has not had a Pap smear in over 10 years. Pelvic examination reveals a friable, exophytic cervical mass. Biopsy shows nests of malignant cells invading the cervical stroma, with keratin pearls and intercellular bridges.
  • Which of the following best describes the diagnosis and its associated features?
  • A. CIN III; full-thickness dysplasia without stromal invasion B. Adenocarcinoma in situ; arises from glandular epithelium C. Invasive squamous cell carcinoma; associated with high-risk HPV types D. CIN I; koilocytosis and mild nuclear atypia E. High-grade glandular dysplasia; precursor to squamous carcinoma
Slide 48: Question 14: Answer and Explanation
  • A 32-year-old woman presents for routine cervical cancer screening. Her Pap smear reveals cells with enlarged nuclei, irregular nuclear contours, and increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. Colposcopic biopsy confirms CIN II. She is counseled on management options.
  • Which of the following best describes the morphologic and clinical features of CIN II?
  • A. Koilocytosis with minimal nuclear atypia; spontaneous regression is common B. Full-thickness epithelial dysplasia; high risk of progression to invasive carcinoma C. Moderate dysplasia involving the lower two-thirds of the epithelium; variable regression or progression D. Mild dysplasia confined to the basal third of the epithelium; typically managed with observation E. Invasion of basement membrane by atypical cells; requires staging and oncologic treatment
  • C. Moderate dysplasia involving the lower two-thirds of the epithelium; variable regression or progression: CIN II (Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia grade II) is characterized by moderate dysplasia. dysplastic cells extend into the lower two-thirds of the epithelium. Clinical outcomes are variable: some cases regress, others progress to CIN III or invasive carcinoma. Management may include observation or excisional procedures, depending on age, fertility desires, and risk factors.
  • A. Koilocytosis with minimal nuclear atypia; spontaneous regression is common: Describes CIN I, not CIN II. Koilocytosis is a hallmark of HPV effect, seen in low-grade lesions. CIN I often regresses spontaneously, especially in younger women.
  • B. Full-thickness epithelial dysplasia; high risk of progression to invasive carcinoma: Describes CIN III, involves severe dysplasia or carcinoma in situ, with high risk of progression. Requires definitive treatment (e.g., LEEP, conization).
  • D. Mild dysplasia confined to the basal third of the epithelium; typically managed with observation: Also describes CIN I. Involves only the lower third of the epithelium. Managed with repeat cytology or HPV testing, especially in younger patients.
  • E. Invasion of basement membrane by atypical cells; requires staging and oncologic treatment: Describes invasive cervical carcinoma, not CIN. Requires oncologic staging and treatment (e.g., surgery, radiation, chemotherapy).

Notes:

Bethesda = cytology terminology (Pap smears). LAST = histology terminology (biopsies). Both use LSIL and HSIL to categorize HPV-associated squamous lesions.

current LAST/Bethesda two-tier terminology collapses CIN2 and CIN3 into HSIL, with CIN1 = LSIL; p16 immunostaining is used to resolve morphologic CIN2. Because CIN2 is more heterogeneous and less reproducible than CIN3, guidelines recommend qualifying HSIL as "CIN2" vs "CIN3," and observation is an acceptable option for CIN2 in patients concerned about fertility.

Slide 49: Question 15: Answer and Explanation
  • A 49-year-old woman presents with abnormal vaginal bleeding. She has not had a Pap smear in over 10 years. Pelvic examination reveals a friable, exophytic cervical mass. Biopsy shows nests of malignant cells invading the cervical stroma, with keratin pearls and intercellular bridges.
  • Which of the following best describes the diagnosis and its associated features?
  • A. CIN III; full-thickness dysplasia without stromal invasion B. Adenocarcinoma in situ; arises from glandular epithelium C. Invasive squamous cell carcinoma; associated with high-risk HPV types D. CIN I; koilocytosis and mild nuclear atypia E. High-grade glandular dysplasia; precursor to squamous carcinoma
  • C. Invasive squamous cell carcinoma; associated with high-risk HPV types: The presence of stromal invasion, keratin pearls, and intercellular bridges confirms invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Most cases are linked to high-risk HPV types, especially HPV 16 and 18. This is the most common type of cervical cancer, especially in women with inadequate screening.
  • A. CIN III; full-thickness dysplasia without stromal invasion: CIN III is carcinoma in situ, with no invasion of the basement membrane. The biopsy in this case shows invasion, ruling out CIN III.
  • B. Adenocarcinoma in situ; arises from glandular epithelium: Adenocarcinoma in situ involves glandular cells, not squamous cells. The histologic features described (keratin pearls, intercellular bridges) are squamous, not glandular.
  • D. CIN I; koilocytosis and mild nuclear atypia: CIN I is a low-grade lesion with minimal atypia and no invasion.
  • E. High-grade glandular dysplasia; precursor to squamous carcinoma: Glandular dysplasia is a precursor to adenocarcinoma, not squamous carcinoma. The histology clearly indicates a squamous origin.
Slide 50: Pathogenesis of Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia (CINs)

| LO: Discuss the common human papillomavirus types that affect the cervix and discuss the pathogenesis of cervical dysplasia and neoplasia, and cervical screening methods and prevention. |

| --- |

  • CINs are the precursor lesions of cervical carcinomas.
  • Arise from normal cervical epithelium; low-grade and high-grade CINs.
  • The most important factor in the pathogenesis is the High-risk HPV (hrHPV).
  • Other contributing factors (smoking, immune status)
  • Low oncogenic risk HPV (types 6 and 11) and high oncogenic risk (types 16 and 18; longer to clear) based on their genotypes
  • High-risk HPVs are the main pathogenic factors of squamous cell carcinomas of other tissues (e.g., oropharynx, tonsils, anus, vagina, vulva, and penis).
  • Risk factors associated with HPV infections are early age at first intercourse, multiple sexual partners, and persistent infection with high-risk strains of HPV.
  • The hrHPV infection into the cervical epithelium results in host genome alterations, leading to the silencing of various tumor-suppressor factors on one hand and inducing aberrant functioning of various tumor-promoting factors on the other
  • The imbalance and instability caused by various hrHPV-derived oncogenic factors drive neoplastic progression
Slide 51: Pathogenesis of Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia (CINs)-Cont
  • The major oncoproteins are E5, E6, and E7 encoded by the HPV genome
  • They disrupt the normal functioning of the major histocompatibility complex I (MHC class I), p53 and Rb, Notch1, Wnt, MAPK, mTOR, and STAT-associated pathways, which are central players controlling normal cellular growth, differentiation, and immune function
  • HPVs induce carcinogenesis through dysregulation of the activity of tumor suppressor proteins such as p53 and RB by the viral E6 and E7 proteins, respectively---prevents the normal arrest of TZ cells in the G1 phase of the cell cycle.
  • The viral E6 upregulates telomerase and binds to p53, leading to its destruction.
  • E7 binds to the RB protein, leading to the release of the E2F transcription factors from the inhibitory effect of RB. This results in progression through the cell cycle.
  • High-risk HPVs also integrate into the host cell genome. This integration results in increased expression of the viral E6 and E7 proteins, and host cell genomic instability----acquisition of prooncogenic mutations.
  • Low-risk HPVs do not integrate into the host genome.
  • The mechanism for low-grade dysplasia is accumulation of viral particles (DNA), producing the classic koilocyte
  • Although CIN II/III has a higher risk for progression to invasive cervical carcinoma, not all women experience this; in fact, only about 20% progress.
  • VIN (vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia) is similar in appearance to CIN but affects the vagina and affects an older population. It may represent a field effect from viral infection of the cervix.
Slide 52: Spectrum from normal to high-grade SIL
  • There is no perfect correlation (e.g., a person with LSIL (Low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion) on Pap smear can have CIN II/III on biopsy, and the reverse is true), but in general, there is good correlation.

Session Objectives

  • Explain how viruses function as obligate intracellular parasites, utilizing and

manipulating host cellular machinery to support their replication and

persistence.

  • Compare the key biological features of retroviruses and DNA viruses, including

their mechanisms of persistence, latency, and genome integration within host

cells.

  • Describe the clinical presentation, transmission routes, tissue tropism, and

disease outcomes of viral infections, and evaluate the strategies retroviruses and

DNA viruses use to evade and subvert host immune responses.

  • Analyze how viral genome structure and replication strategies influence viral

pathogenesis, latency, oncogenesis, diagnosis, prevention, and therapeutic

interventions.

  • Three stages of HIV infection
