PREGNANCY DATING AND ULTRASONOGRAPHY

Accurate gestational age estimation is critical to quality care

because it enables more precise timing of interventions (e.g.,

aspirin for preeclampsia prevention, steroids for fetal lung

maturity), screening tests, and delivery. Up to 40% of people estimate their last menstrual period

incorrectly; therefore, ultrasonography is recommended if uncertainty

exists and for patients with irregular

menstrual cycles, irregular bleeding, and discrepancy between uterine

size and gestational age.1,38 Ultrasonography before 24 weeks decreases

missed multiple gestations and post-

term inductions.39 Although routine

third-trimester ultrasonography may

increase detection of IUGR, it does not

improve outcomes.40 If malpresentation

is suspected on physical examination,

confirmation with ultrasonography is

recommended.4

Screening

ALLOIMMUNIZATION

For patients who are RhD-negative and

carrying a fetus who is RhD-positive,

the alloimmunization risk is 1.5% to 2%

in the setting of spontaneous abortion

and 4% to 5% with dilation and curettage. The risk is decreased by 80% to 90%

with anti-D immune globulin.41 Testing for the ABO blood group and RhD

antibodies should be performed early

in pregnancy. A 300-mcg dose of anti-D

immune globulin is recommended for

RhD-negative pregnant patients at 28

weeks and again within 72 hours of

delivery if the infant is RhD-positive.41

ANEMIA

Iron deficiency anemia increases the

risk of preterm delivery, IUGR, and

perinatal depression. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force found insufficient evidence to assess the benefits and

harms of screening for anemia in pregnancy.42 Screening is recommended by

the American College of Obstetricians

and Gynecologists early in pregnancy,

with iron treatment if deficient.43 Intravenous iron should be considered for

with non–iron deficiency anemia, or if iron repletion is ineffective within six weeks, should be referred to a hematologist

for further evaluation. Iron supplementation in the first trimester decreases the prevalence of iron deficiency.43

INHERITED CONDITIONS

Pregnant patients should be counseled and offered aneuploidy

(extra or missing chromosomes) screening in early pregnancy,

regardless of age.44 In the United States, 1 in 150 infants has

a chromosomal condition, the most

common being trisomy 21 (Down

syndrome).44 Table 4 compares screening tests for Down syndrome.1,45,46 If a

screening test is positive, amniocentesis

at 15 weeks or more or chorionic villous

sampling between 11 and 13 weeks is

recommended. Both procedures have

similar rates of fetal loss.47 At 35 years

of age, the risk of Down syndrome

(1 in 294 births) is similar to that of fetal

loss from amniocentesis.47 Serum and

nuchal translucency testing can screen

for other trisomies, including 13 and

18, the protocols for which have lower

sensitivities and higher specificities

compared with screening protocols for

trisomy 21 because they are rarer.47

Additional genetic screening should

be based on maternal and paternal

personal and family histories. Race is

a social construct, necessitating a shift

in genetic risk stratification from race-

based to ancestry-based. Sickle cell disease affects up to 100,000 people in the

United States, but its inheritance pattern (1: 10) is based on people with African ancestry, which includes much of

the world.48 Cystic fibrosis is inherited

mainly by people of European ancestry (1: 25), but ignoring the possibility

of European ancestry in certain racial

and ethnic groups results in an underestimation of its prevalence: African

(1: 61), Hispanic (1: 40), and Mediterranean (1: 29).49

NEURAL TUBE DEFECTS

In the United States, neural tube

defects affect approximately 2,600

infants per year, with the highest prevalence in Hispanic

populations.35,50 All pregnant patients should be counseled

and offered screening with maternal serum alpha fetoprotein.35 Folic acid, 400 to 800 mcg daily, started at least one

month before conception and continued until the end of the

first trimester, decreases the incidence of neural tube defects

by nearly 78%.35 Patients taking folic acid antagonists (e.g.,

carbamazepine, methotrexate, trimethoprim) or who have a

history of carrying a fetus with a neural tube defect should

take 4 mg of folic acid daily, starting at least three months

before conception.35

American Family Physician  143

THYROID DISORDERS

There is no evidence that screening

for thyroid disorders improves pregnancy outcomes. Thyroid-stimulating

hormone levels should be measured

if there is a history of thyroid disease

or symptoms of disease. If the level is

abnormal, a free thyroxine test helps

determine the etiology.51 Hypothyroidism complicates 1 to 3 per 1,000 pregnancies and increases the risk of fetal

loss, preeclampsia, IUGR, and stillbirth. Hyperthyroidism occurs in 2 per

1,000 pregnancies and is associated

with miscarriage, preeclampsia, IUGR,

preterm delivery, thyroid storm, and

congestive heart failure.51 The effect

of subclinical hypothyroidism on a

child’s neurocognitive development is

not well understood, and the effectiveness of treatment with levothyroxine

is unproven.51

CERVICAL CANCER

Intervals for cervical cancer screening are based on patient age, cytology

history, and history of the presence

of high-risk human papillomavirus

(HPV). Routine screening for people at average risk of cervical cancer should begin at 21 years of age.

Screening can be performed with

either cytology alone every three

years, HPV screening alone every five

years, or cytology plus HPV screening

every five years starting at 25 years

of age. Screening is not indicated for

people 65 years and older with negative screening in the previous 10 years,

and no history of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or higher

in the past 25 years.52 Colposcopy is

indicated when the risk of cervical

intraepithelial neoplasia grade 3 is

greater than 4%. Surveillance of high-

grade lesions should be performed

every 12 to 24 weeks.52,53 Although

colposcopy and cervical biopsy can be

safely performed during pregnancy,

endocervical sampling should be

deferred until postpartum.53

Infectious Disease

BACTERIURIA

Asymptomatic bacteriuria complicates up to 15% of pregnancies in the United States, 30% of which progress to pyelonephritis if untreated.54 All pregnant patients should be

screened for bacteriuria at the first prenatal visit.54 A culture

from a midstream or clean-catch sample with greater than

100,000 colony-forming units per mL of a single pathogen is

considered positive and treated to decrease the risk of pyelonephritis and subsequent preterm delivery.54

SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED INFECTIONS

Sexually transmitted infections can affect prenatal outcomes.55-57 Table 5 lists routine screening and treatment for

sexually transmitted infections in pregnancy.55,56

RUBELLA

Rubella immunity screening during the first prenatal visit

is recommended. Postpartum vaccination should also be

offered if the patient is not immune to prevent congenital

rubella syndrome in subsequent pregnancies.1,58 The presence

of rubella immunoglobulin G should be interpreted with caution in patients recently migrating from areas where rubella

is endemic because this may indicate a recent infection.58

Rubella is a live vaccine and should not be administered

during pregnancy but is safe during lactation after delivery.59,60

VARICELLA

Maternal varicella can result in congenital varicella syndrome (i.e., IUGR

and limb, ophthalmologic, and neurologic abnormalities) and neonatal

varicella; infection can occur from

approximately five days before to two

days after birth. A negative history of

varicella infection or vaccination warrants serologic testing, and if immunoglobulin G is negative, varicella

exposure should be avoided. Postpartum vaccination should be offered.61

TDAP

Although tetanus toxoid, reduced diphtheria toxoid, and acellular pertussis

(Tdap) vaccination is recommended for

anyone in close contact with the infant,

only antenatal maternal vaccination

ensures increased protection against

neonatal pertussis.62 Pregnant patients

should receive a Tdap vaccine beginning at 27 weeks to maximize time for

passive immunity to the fetus through the placental transfer

of maternal antibodies; vaccination is recommended in each

subsequent pregnancy.62

INFLUENZA AND COVID-19

Influenza and COVID-19 infection in pregnancy increase

the risk of intensive care unit admission, preterm delivery,

stillbirth, and maternal death.63,64 COVID-19 infection

almost doubles the risk of developing preeclampsia64; therefore, initiating low-dose aspirin (81 mg daily) starting at 12

weeks should be considered.5 Pregnant patients and their

household contacts should be vaccinated for influenza and

COVID-19.63,64

GROUP B STREPTOCOCCUS

In the United States, group B Streptococcus (GBS) is the leading cause of infection in the first three months of life; 25% of

all pregnant patients are GBS carriers.65,66 Screening with a

vaginal-rectal swab for culture between 36 and 37 weeks is recommended.67 Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis decreases

neonatal mortality. Antibiotics are recommended when there

is GBS bacteriuria with the current pregnancy, a history of

a previous infant affected by GBS (e.g., septicemia, meningitis, pneumonia, death), or unknown GBS status and risk factors (e.g., preterm labor, rupture of membranes more than 18

hours before delivery, GBS in previous pregnancy).67 Patients

Social Determinants of Health

Social determinants of health represent up to 80% of the factors that directly affect a person’s health.68 Physicians who

provide prenatal care play a critical role in mitigating the burden that social determinants of health play on maternal-child

health without compromising the quality of care delivered.69

An increased burden from social determinants of health

increases the risk of depression, anxiety, intimate partner

violence, substance use, and food insecurity70,71; therefore,

universal screening is recommended early in pregnancy.

DEPRESSION AND ANXIETY-RELATED DISORDERS

After the COVID-19 pandemic, rates of perinatal depression and anxiety have increased. People who are non-White,

24 years or younger, or who have 12 years or less of education, lower socioeconomic status, or a history of intimate

partner violence or sexual trauma are at higher risk.11,72,73 If

untreated, depression and anxiety-related disorders increase

the risk of preeclampsia, preterm delivery, IUGR, substance

use, maternal suicide, infanticide, psychosis, and homicide.11

INTIMATE PARTNER VIOLENCE

Intimate partner–related homicide is the leading cause of

death in the United States in pregnancy. Screening is recommended at the first prenatal visit and once per trimester.13

Intimate partner violence increases the risk of miscarriage,

placental abruption, premature rupture of membranes,

IUGR, and preterm delivery.13 Family physicians should be

aware of the signs of intimate partner violence (e.g., frequent

sexually transmitted infections, repeated requests for pregnancy tests when pregnancy is not desired, fear of asking a

and the increased risk of child abuse after delivery.13

SUBSTANCE USE

Substance use during pregnancy increases the risk of IUGR,

preterm delivery, stillbirth, fetal malformations, and maternal death.74 The use of prescription opioids complicates 7%

of pregnancies in the United States; of these, 20% of patients

report misuse.75 Opioid use in pregnancy increased by 131%

from 2010 to 2017 in the United States, and the incidence

of babies born with withdrawal symptoms in that time

increased by 82%.76 Fetal alcohol exposure is the leading

cause of preventable neurodevelopmental disorders in the

United States.14 However, 14% of pregnant patients report

current drinking, and 5% report binge drinking in the past

30 days.77 Exposure to cigarette smoking in utero increases

the risk of sudden intrauterine and infant death.15

FOOD INSECURITY

Maternal food insecurity increases the risk of poor outcomes

(e.g., IUGR, preterm delivery, gestational diabetes, hypertension, depression, anxiety). However, few patients disclose

this due to concerns about social stigma; therefore, a universal approach to screening is encouraged. The Hunger Vital

Sign tool may be used.12

Complications of Pregnancy

GESTATIONAL DIABETES

Gestational diabetes complicates up to 14% of U.S. pregnancies, with up to 67% of patients developing type 2 diabetes

later in life.78 Racial and ethnic minorities are at the highest

risk.79 Gestational diabetes is associated with hypertension,

macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, and cesarean deliveries.80

Screening for undiagnosed type 2 diabetes at the initial

prenatal visit is recommended for people at increased risk80

(Table 65,80). Universal screening for gestational diabetes

should occur between 24 and 28 weeks with a one-hour

(50-g) glucose tolerance test and, if results are abnormal,

should be followed by a confirmatory, fasting, three-hour

(100-g) test.80

HYPERTENSION

Blood pressure should be monitored at each prenatal visit,

and education should be provided on preeclampsia warning signs.5 Patients at increased risk of preeclampsia should

be screened for thrombocytopenia, transaminitis, and

renal insufficiency, including proteinuria, during the first

or second trimester and started on prophylactic daily low-

dose aspirin (81 mg) between 12 and 16 weeks5 (Table 65,80).

Screening for proteinuria in isolation has little predictive

value for detecting preeclampsia.5 Chronic hypertension

(hypertension before 20 weeks) is treated to less than

140/90 mm Hg.81

PRETERM DELIVERY

Preterm delivery (between 20 and 37 weeks) is a significant

cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality, complicating

10.5% of U.S. pregnancies.2 Modifiable risk factors include

prepregnancy BMI (less than 18.5 kg per m2 and greater than

25 kg per m2), substance use, and short interval between

pregnancies (i.e., less than 18 months).82 Several options are

available for the prevention of preterm labor in a singleton

pregnancy.82 Patients with a previous preterm delivery before

34 weeks should have a cervical length assessment starting

at 16 weeks through 24 weeks.82 These patients should be

treated with progesterone supplementation (vaginal or intramuscular). In the asymptomatic patient with a short cervix

and without a history of spontaneous birth before 34 weeks,

POST-TERM DELIVERY

Stillbirth complicates 3 per 1,000 post-term (42 weeks or

greater) pregnancies.20 Antenatal testing should be initiated

at 41 weeks; if the results are not reassuring, induction of

labor is recommended.20,21

Cultural Considerations

Maternity care improves outcomes; however, vulnerable

populations (i.e., racial, ethnic, and religious minorities) are

less likely to engage in care if it is not culturally centered,

which acknowledges the effect of culture on health conditions (e.g., depression) and enhances patient-physician

trust.83 Addressing cultural needs (e.g., doula, community

health workers, interpreters) throughout pregnancy helps

mitigate barriers and improves outcomes.

Carlough1; Kirkham, et al.17; and Kirkham, et al.84

Early pregnancy quick guide.docx TBL-EARLY-PREG · Week 6

Canvas course 70351, file 24017951 (docx, 0.03 MB); session TBL-EARLY-PREG (Week 6, 9/22/2026: TBL 3: Early Pregnancy). Text extracted verbatim on 2026-09-26 for REPRO-PLAN P1.2 (104 paragraphs, 1 tables).

Early Pregnancy Quick Guide M2 TBL

For every patient presenting in early pregnancy:

Is she pregnant?

  • Positive urine pregnancy test o serum β-hCG

How pregnant is she?

  • Determine gestational age using the first day of the last menstrual period (LMP) +/- ultrasound when dates are uncertain

Where is the pregnancy?

  • Confirm with ultrasound and if unable to confirm, consider a possible ectopic pregnancy.

Is the pregnancy viable?

  • Assess symptoms, trend serum β-hCG levels and use ultrasound to confirm

Does she need urgent evaluation?

Look for:

  • Severe abdominal pain
  • Heavy vaginal bleeding
  • Syncope
  • Shoulder pain
  • Hemodynamic instability

What can be done to improve outcomes for both parent and child?

Consider opportunities for:

  • Preconception counseling and early prenatal care
  • Lifestyle management opportunities (including nutrition, exercise and smoking cessation)
  • Folic acid and iron supplementation
  • Vaccination
  • Social and behavioral support
  • Chronic disease optimization (preferably before pregnancy)

Pregnancy Dating

Gestational age is calculated from the first day of the last menstrual period (LMP).

Gestational age ≠ fetal age

Example:

  • LMP was 8 weeks ago
  • Gestational age = 8 weeks
  • Fertilization occurred approximately 6 weeks ago

Dating Matters Because It:

  • Determines estimated due date (EDD) and expected ultrasound findings
  • Guides prenatal care and testing

Estimated Due Date (Nägele's Rule)

EDD = LMP + 1 year − 3 months + 7 days

β-hCG Physiology

The syncytiotrophoblast produces human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) after implantation.

hCG is important because hCG maintains the corpus luteum, which produces progesterone needed to maintain the endometrium and support the pregnancy.

What Is hCG Used For Clinically?

  • Confirms pregnancy and helps determine viability
  • Helps evaluate possible ectopic pregnancy
  • Guides interpretation of ultrasound findings

Key Concept

Trends are usually more useful than a single value.

In a normal early pregnancy, β-hCG generally rises over time.

Normal Ultrasound Milestones

(Transvaginal Ultrasound)

| Gestational Age | Expected Finding |

| --- | --- |

| 5 weeks | Gestational sac |

| 5-6 weeks | Yolk sac |

| 6 weeks | Fetal pole |

| 6-7 weeks | Cardiac activity |

Easy Way to Remember: Sac → Yolk Sac → Fetal Pole → Heartbeat

If expected findings are absent, consider:

  • Incorrect dating
  • Early pregnancy loss
  • Ectopic pregnancy

Major Causes of First-Trimester Bleeding

Normal Early Pregnancy: Implantation bleeding can cause mild spotting

Pregnancy Loss: Bleeding with cramping may signal a nonviable pregnancy

Ectopic Pregnancy: Positive pregnancy test, pain ± bleeding, pregnancy outside the uterine cavity

The Diagnosis You Cannot Miss:

Ectopic Pregnancy

In any pregnant patient with pelvic pain + vaginal bleeding + unconfirmed intrauterine pregnancy

Look out for emergency warning signs

  • Syncope
  • Shoulder pain
  • Severe abdominal pain
  • Hemodynamic instability

Pregnancy, Lifelong Health and Chronic Disease

Pregnancy is more than a nine-month event. It is a unique opportunity to improve the health of both the pregnant individual and their future child.

Many adverse pregnancy outcomes are influenced by pre-pregnancy and early pregnancy factors, including hypertension or being at risk of developing hypertension/hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, diabetes or being at risk of developing gestational diabetes, obesity, smoking, inadequate nutrition, lack of folic acid supplementation, and delayed prenatal care.

Optimizing health before and during pregnancy may reduce the risk of:

  • Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
  • Gestational diabetes
  • Preterm birth
  • Fetal growth abnormalities
  • Some congenital anomalies

Healthy pregnancies are associated with improved lifelong outcomes for both parent and child. Pregnancy may also provide an opportunity to identify and possibly prevent chronic health conditions that affect long-term well-being for both the individual and the entire community.

Key Take-Home Message

Preventing adverse pregnancy outcomes is not only about improving pregnancy and birth outcomes. It is an investment in the lifelong health of the parent, the child, and the community.

Clinical Framework for TBL Cases

For every case, ask:

Is she pregnant?

How far along is the pregnancy?

Is the pregnancy intrauterine?

Is the pregnancy viable?

Does she need urgent evaluation?

How can identifying and addressing risks during pregnancy improve the long-term health of the parent, child, and community?

Proliferative Endometrium

Proliferative phase endometrium is characterized by round glands with pseudostratified cells and numerous mitotic figures

in both glands and stroma.

Pathologies

1. Adenomyosis: Endometrial tissue (gland and stroma) invading the

myometrium

•

This ectopic tissue induces reactive hypertrophy of surrounding

smooth muscle

•

Results in a globular, enlarged uterus with a thickened uterine wall

•

The stromal component of adenomyosis is thought to be the major

driver of reactive myometrial hypertrophy and hyperplasia through

local inflammatory, estrogenic, and growth-factor signaling.

Endometrial Stromal Cells

Myometrium

Endometrial Glands

•

Uterus appears enlarged and boggy

•

Wall may be diffusely thickened

•

Hemorrhagic cystic spaces representing

ectopic endometrial tissue

•

Well-differentiated SCC of the cervix

•

Infiltrating networks of bands of neoplastic cells invading

stroma

•

Malignant cells demonstrate keratinization and keratin

pearls (whorls of epidermoid cells containing central nests

of keratin

•

The nuclei are large and hyperchromatic with coarse

chromatin.

2. Cervical SCC:

Large squamous carcinoma (bottom of

the picture) has obliterated the cervix

and invaded the lower uterine segment

with areas of hemorrhage and necrosis

Sheets of malignant

squamous cells

Keratin Pearls

Page 7

3. Endometrial Polyp

Endometrial Polyp

simple cystic hyperplasia with dilated glands in loose stroma

•

Endometrial polyps are abnormal growths of

the endometrium

•

either sessile (a non-mobile polyp with a

broad base with no stalk)

or pedunculated (projecting into the uterine

cavity and attached by a stalk).

•

Histologically, they resemble the stratum

basalis of the endometrium

(i.e., cystically dilated glands with small

muscular arteries)

•

The endometrial polyp stroma is

more collagenous than the normal

endometrial stroma (more cellular)

•

diagnosed in the presence of 2 of the

following 3:

•Thick-walled vessels

•Collagenous stroma

•Epithelium on at least 3 sides

•

Endometrial polyps usually present with

abnormal uterine bleeding.

•

Although malignant transformation is rare,

Endometrial carcinoma can arise in

endometrial polyps

Page 8

4. Non-atypical Endometrial Hyperplasia:

•

Closely packed tubular, irregular or branching glands

•

lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium resembling

proliferative phase endometrium.

•

There is no cytologic atypia.

Compare To

Atypical Endometrial Hyperplasia:

Atypical Endometrial Hyperplasia/Endometrioid

Intraepithelial Neoplasia (AEH/EIN): The glands are

arranged back-to-back with little intervening stroma

(gland-to-stroma ratio >1). The glandular profiles

are round and tubular or have complex, stellate or

irregular shapes with branching and outpouchings.

Cytologic atypia is characterized by large round or

elongated nuclei with high N:C ratio, loss of nuclear

polarity with irregular distribution of nuclei, and

inconspicuous nucleoli. Some cases show distinct

nucleoli. Mitotic activity is variably increased.

https://www.webpathology.com/search-result?query=endometrial%20hyperplasia

Grade 1 Endometroid Endometrial Carcinoma:

predominantly confluent (back-to-back) glandular to

papilliform growth with no intervening stroma (DDX

hyperplasia), cytologically resembling proliferative-type

endometrium. Glands invade the myometrium

Myometrium invaded

by malignant glands

Back to back endometrial

glands without intervening

stroma

  • Carcinoma occupies most of the endometrial cavity with areas of hemorrhage
  • The cervix is unaffected

6. Leiomyoma (Fibroid)

Gross:

  • Sharply circumscribed, firm gray-white masses with a

characteristic whorled cut surface

  • Embedded within the myometrium (intramural), lie beneath

the endometrium (submucosal) or the serosa (subserosal;

may extend out on attenuated stalks (pedunculated)

Microscopic:

  • Bundles of intersecting uniform smooth

muscle cells (elongated nuclei and

eosinophilic cytoplasm)

  • Similar in appearance to typical myometrium
  • Foci of fibrosis (collagen bundles),

calcification, and degenerative softening may

be present

Leiomyosarcoma is a cellular tumor composed of

fascicles of spindle cells exhibiting smooth muscle

differentiation with moderate to severe

pleomorphism. Usually coagulative tumor cell

necrosis is present and abnormal mitoses exceed

I. Rete Testis

•

Rete testis is an anastomosing network of delicate

channels located in the testicular hilum.

•

It is lined by flattened squamous or low cuboidal

epithelium. Epithelium-covered strands and columns

seen in the photomicrograph are called chordae retis

which connect the opposing walls of the channels.

•

Rete receives the luminal contents of seminiferous

tubules and empties them into the efferent ductules.

Menopause.pptx MENOPAUSE · Week 5

Canvas course 70351, file 24117199 (pptx, 3.9 MB); session MENOPAUSE (Week 5, 9/14/2026: Menopause Physiology/Pharmacology). Text extracted verbatim on 2026-09-26 for REPRO-PLAN P1.2 (48 slides; 44 with text kept; 1 image-only slides and 3 title/boilerplate slides omitted).

Slide 2: Objectives
  • Define the stages of the reproductive life cycle
  • Explain the pathophysiology of common menopausal symptoms (vasomotor, genitourinary, sleep, mood, cognition, and sexual dysfunction)
  • Explain the health effects of estrogen deficiency on bone health, cardiovascular health, cognition, and GU health
  • Describe pathophysiology of osteoporosis
  • Describe bleeding pattern changes during perimenopause & menopause
  • Characterize the evidence-based medicine labwork in menopause diagnosis/care
  • Explain preventative health items in menopause: osteoporosis prevention & monitoring, cardiovascular risk reduction, cancer screening and immunizations.
  • Describe how to evaluate postmenopausal bleeding
  • Describe menopause mimics and other conditions to rule out
  • Explore the impact of the Women’s Health Initiative study on menopause education & training and subsequent care of menopausal women
  • Describe disparities in the care of menopausal symptoms
  • Explore how the impact of wellness/influencers intersects with evidenced based medicine
Slide 4: Stages of the Reproductive Cycle
  • Prepubertal – the time period between birth and when puberty ends & menses start, fertility is not yet started
  • Ages 0 going up to about 9-14 yrs of age
  • About 1 million follicles are present at birth
  • Fertile – the time period in which a pregnancy could occur and is from the start of the first menses to 1 year after the last menses
  • About 10-14 yrs of age going up to about 45-56 yrs of age
  • 250,000-400,000 follicles remain at puberty
  • Postmenopausal – 1 year after the last menses until death, fertility has ended during this time period
  • About 45-56 yrs age until death
  • Medium age in the US is 51
Slide 5: Physiology of Menopause
  • Depletion of Ovarian Follicles
  • Reduces Granulosa Cell Activity
  • Lowers Estradiol, Inhibin, & AMH
  • Disruption of HPO axis
  • Impair normal endometrial
  • development
  • Increasing FSH & LH
  • Irregular Cycles &
  • Ultimately Cessation of Menses
Slide 6: Menopause Hormone Changes
  • Ovarian reserve also drops and can be measured by Anti-Mullerian Hormone (AMH) which will be low
  • Estradiol falls
  • Follicle Stimulating Hormone (FSH) increases
  • https://gpexams.com/menopause/
Slide 7: Staging of Menopause
  • STRAW +10 staging system with Menopause designated as 0
  • https://www.herstasis.com/menopause-primer/
Slide 8: Causes of Menopause
  • Natural
  • Surgical (removal of ovaries)
  • Chemotherapy or Radiation Therapy related to cancer treatments
  • Chronic illnesses like HIV-AIDs
  • Anti-estrogenic agents
  • Remember Primary Ovarian Insufficiency
  • Note:
  • MHT = Hormone Therapy started after natural menopause
  • HRT = Hormone Replacement Therapy started when menopause comes early for whatever reason
Slide 9: Perimenopause
  • Can occur 10 years before an individual is considered postmenopausal
  • Hormones fluctuate in irregular patterns causing symptoms
  • Menses can be variable
  • Usually follicular phase is shortened which leads to frequent menses then longer cycles
  • Cycles are anovulatory
  • Vasomotor - hot flashes, night sweats
  • Genitourinary - vaginal dryness, itching, painful intercourse, urinary incontinence, nocturia, frequent UTIs
  • Emotional lability - anxiety, depression
  • Low libido
  • Sleep disturbances - fatigue
  • Cognitive decline - brain fog, memory impairment
Slide 10: Estrogen Receptors are Everywhere!
  • Symptoms
  • are
  • Everywhere!
Slide 11: Symptoms of Menopause
  • Menses have stopped for 12 months
  • Vasomotor Symptoms (VMS) - hot flashes, night sweats
  • 80% of women worldwide
  • Can last 7-8 years
  • Genitourinary Symptoms of Menopause (GSM) - vaginal dryness, itching, painful intercourse, urinary incontinence, nocturia, freq UTIs
  • 50% of women worldwide
  • Progressive if left untreated
  • Emotional lability - anxiety, depression
  • 70% of women
  • Low libido
  • Sleep disturbances - fatigue
Slide 12: Vasomotor Symptoms of Menopause (VMS)
  • Upper temp limit decreases so small increases in core temp trigger mechanisms to dissipate heat (ie vasodilation & sweating)
  • Lower temp limit increases so small drops in core temp trigger mechanisms to preserve heat (ie shiver & chills)
  • Rapid decreases in estrogen
  • WITHDRAWAL
  • Increased norepinephrine stimulation
  • Increased serotonin activation
  • Increased central opioid peptide activity
  • Narrows the thermoneutral zone (range of core temps) in the thermoregulatory center (hypothalamus)
Slide 13: VMS cont
  • Hot flashes can be unpredictable & occur day & night
  • Typically last 3-4 minutes
  • Begin with a sensation of hot flushing that spreads across the upper body followed by chills
  • Persist for 1-6 yrs most commonly, but can go 15 yrs in 10-15%
  • Factors that worsen symp
  • EtOH, Tobacco,
  • Obesity, Sedentary,
  • Emotional Stress, Mood Disorder
  • Black, Lower SES, Lower Edu
  • Women with greater VMS burden have
  • More adverse lipid profiles, greater insulin resistance, elevated risk of HTN & DM, great atherosclerosis (carotids, aorta, cerebral small vessels), increased risk of dementia, OSA
  • Migraines can be triggered by estrogen fluctuations so they can worsen in early menopause & resolve later in menopause
  • When symptoms can affect sleep (ie insomnia), there is an assoc with negative CVD outcomes
  • MHT leads to 70-80 % improvement in VMS, relief starts within 2-4 wks
Slide 14: Genitourinary Symptoms of Menopause (GSM)
  • Declining estrogen levels cause thinning of the vaginal mucosa & reduced elasticity via decreased muscle & increased fatty deposits leading to Dryness, Burning, Itching, & Irritation of the vagina
  • Urinary frequency, urgency, dysuria, & nocturia can occur as there are estrogen receptors in the bladder & urethra
  • Vaginal & Urethral atrophy can occur as well
  • Declining estrogen levels lead to less glycogen & lactic acid increasing the vaginal pH (4.5 -> 7.0) promoting bacterial colonization of the vagina
  • Increases risk & frequency of UTIs
  • MHT (vaginal estrogen) confers relative risk reduction of 42% in UTIs
  • Urinary incontinence & pelvic structure prolapse due to muscle weakness & reduction in ligamentous laxity affecting pelvic floor muscles
  • These symptoms can affect sleep
  • Vaginal estrogen is 1st line & may be needed even with systemic MHT
  • Vaginal estrogen has little systemic absorption & can be used in women in which system MHT is contraindicated
Slide 15: Sexual Dysfunction
  • Estrogen decline leads to
  • Reduced sexual desire
  • Diminished sexual function
  • GSM causing pain with intercourse
  • MHT is not contraception so if there is a pregnancy risk, can use COC or estrogen MHT + Mirena IUD
Slide 16
  • https://www.everydayhealth.com/womens-health/genitourinary-syndrome-of-menopause/
Slide 17: Breast changes
  • Volume loss due to decreasing levels of estrogen which affects ductal structures and decreasing levels of progesterone which affects lobular structures
  • Ultimately replacement of dense breast tissue with soft adipose tissue
Slide 18: Mood disorders
  • Anger or irritability, Anxiety or tension, Depression, Reduced Self Esteem or confidence, Impaired Concentration
  • Estrogen receptors are also present in the brain regions involved in mood & cognitive regulation
  • Estrogen also modulates serotonin & noradrenaline secretion
  • These symptoms can affect sleep
  • MHT is just as effective as antidepressants in perimenopause, but not in postmenopause
Slide 19: Sleep disturbance
  • Difficulty falling asleep
  • Early morning awakening
  • Repeated nighttime awakening
  • Hot flashes?
  • Night sweats?
  • Nocturia?
Slide 20: Cognitive Decline
  • Temporary decline during perimenopause, but improves in postmenopausal years
  • In women who undergo early surgical menopause, HRT does seem to have a protective effect when started immediately
Slide 21: Cardiovascular Complications
  • Alterations in autonomic regulation
  • Relative high proportion of androgens leads to truncal obesity which is an independent CV risk (decreased estrogen + insulin resistance)
  • Estrogen is cardioprotective as it increases HDL & decreases LDL so a drop in estrogen reverses this
  • Impaired arterial endothelial function & renin-angiotensin system activation
  • CAD rates 2-3x higher than same aged premenopausal women
  • Oral MHT can increase risk of VTE – thought to be related to 1st pass effect & activation of coagulation system increasing liver biosynthesis of procoagulant factors – however transdermal does not appear to
Slide 22: Bone changes
  • Osteoporosis increases – thinning of the bones
  • This process can start years before menopause
  • Estrogen decline increases osteoclastic activity compared to osteoblastic activity (so bone is broken down faster than it is rebuilt)
  • Increases risk of fracture
  • Joint pain & stiffness
  • Women with longer reproductive life spans have reduced risk of total knee replacements
  • https://stock.adobe.com/search?k=osteoporosis+infographic
Slide 23: Skin changes
  • Thinning of skin & loss of elasticity due to decreased collagen
  • Thinning hair/hair loss could be due to decreased collagen, less oil from sebaceous glands, reduction in estrogen without similar reduction in testosterone or DHT
Slide 24: Gastrointestinal changes
  • Oral estrogen, but not transdermal estrogen, increases risk of symptomatic gallstones
  • Remember the 4 Fs?
Slide 26: Physical Exam in Menopause
  • High BP due to arterial constriction
  • Weight gain (avg 5 lbs/2kg)
  • Height reduction (related to BMD loss)
  • Fatty deposition of breast tissue
  • Thinning hair
  • Vaginal dryness & urogenital atrophy
Slide 27: Evaluation of Menopause
  • Clinical diagnosis – based on history >> physical exam
  • Laboratory evaluation is unnecessary in most cases
  • FSH > 30
  • May transiently rise after pelvic surgery, wait 3 mon to test
  • Hormonal medications can alter values, wait 2 wks after discontinuation
  • Estradiol? < 20
  • Rises in perimenopause
  • Hormonal medications can alter values, wait 2 wks after discontinuation
  • AMH??
  • The variation of decline between individuals makes reliable values difficult to determine
Slide 28: Differential Diagnosis
  • Pregnancy
  • Thyroid disorders
  • PMOS (PCOS)
  • Depression, Anxiety, Eating disorders
  • Chronic Illnesses – IBD, CKD, Cancer
  • Poor nutrition or excessive exercise
  • Stress
  • UTIs
  • Sheehan Syndrome or Pituitary adenoma
  • Ovarian tumors
  • Premature Ovarian Insufficiency
Slide 29: Treatments for Menopause Symptoms
  • Hormone Therapy (MHT)
  • Estrogen is first line therapy
  • Must add progesterone if the individual still has a uterus OR endometriosis even s/p hysterectomy (reduces risk of endometrial cancer)
  • Testosterone is needed for treatment of low libido & other sexual dysfunction
  • SSRIs/SNRIs - Citalopram, Escitalopram, Paroxetine, Desvenlafaxine, Venlafaxine
  • Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERMs) - Ospemifene, Tamoxifen, Bazodoxifene, Raloxifene
  • Neurokinin 3 Receptor Antagonist - Fezolinetant
  • Gabapentin/Pregabalin
  • Clonidine
  • Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)
  • Hypnosis
  • Black cohosh
  • Soy/isoflavones
  • DHEA
  • Oxybutynin
  • Vaginal moisturizers/lubricants
  • Bisphosphonates – alendronate
  • Denosumab
  • Calcium + Vitamin D
Slide 30: Treatment Considerations
  • Consider what symptom(s) need treating & which treatment provides most benefit with least risk
  • Initiate hormone therapy near onset of symptoms, delayed initiation of therapy increases risk
  • Generally within 10 years of symptoms onset and ideally younger than 60
  • Risk/Benefit eval for continuing past 60 yrs of age
  • No universal recommendation for when to discontinue HT
  • Estrogen-only therapy may reduce risk of breast cancer in women w/o a uterus while Estrogen+Progesterone therapy may increase the risk of breast cancer in women with a uterus
  • Smoking with estrogen therapy increases risk
  • Nov 2025, FDA recommended removal of black box warning for estrogen therapy for CV disease, breast cancer, and dementia while maintaining warning for endometrial cancer with estrogen only therapy
  • Sequential MHT (daily estrogen + progesterone 12-14 days/mon) vs Continuous (combined) MHT
  • Produces predictable withdrawal bleeding with the former vs breakthrough bleeding with the latter (transdermal>oral)
Slide 31: Treatment Considerations cont
  • Bioidenticals have no evidence to suggest superiority & may be riskier as they are compounded in small batches and not regulated for safety or effectiveness
  • CBT & Hypnosis – evidence for short term efficacy for VMS & sleep
  • Supplements – effective compared to placebo, but not superior to HT & there are concerns for safety due to lack of standardization & regulatory oversight
Slide 32: Benefits/Harms of MHT
  • Data reviewed in 2022 from 20 RCTs & 3 large Cohort studies
Slide 33: Treatment Guidelines

| Society/ / Guideline | Yr/Latest Update | Main Indications | Key Recommendations | Warnings/ / Contraindications |

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| NAMS (The Menopause Society) | 2022–2024 | Moderate–severe VMS, GSM, prevention of bone loss and fractures | Initiation <60 years or <10 years since menopause → best benefit–risk ratio ('timing hypothesis’) / MHT is most effective treatment for VMS & GSM / Prefer transdermal route in women at increased VTE risk / Progestogen required if uterus present / Continuation >65 years may be acceptable in selected women | Periodic benefit–risk / re-assessment / Avoid oral estrogen in active/recent VTE, stroke, or breast cancer |

Slide 36: Notable treatments that don’t work for Menopause
  • Exercise
  • Yoga
  • Cooling solutions
  • Cannabinoids
  • Acupunction
  • Primrose Oil
  • Ginseng
  • Relaxation Therapy
Slide 37: Preventative Care Recommendations in Menopause
  • Stop smoking, especially if considering MHT/HRT
  • Exercise can reduce CV risk (150 min/wk)
  • Weight bearing exercise can reduce Osteoporosis risk (2-3 days/wk)
  • Heart healthy diet (Mediterranean diet low in saturated fats, DASH)
  • Contraception is recommended until menopause (MHT is not contraception)
  • Screening tests like Bone Mineral Density, Mammography, Colon Cancer Screening, Cervical Cancer Screening
  • Clinician should survey perimenopause/menopause symptoms as not all women will report symptoms
Slide 38: Menopause Symptom Survey
  • https://menopausealliance.au/menopause/menopause-symptoms-checklist2/
Slide 39: Women’s Health Initiative - Background
  • 1992-2005, recruitment of 161,000 postmenopausal women between 1993-1998 with an age range of 50-79
  • Mean age was 63-64 yrs old
  • 40 centers across the US
  • 68,000 in RCTs & 93,676 in observational study
  • HT included conjugated equine estrogen (0.625 mg/day) +/- medroxyprogesteone acetate (2.5 mg/day) & measured as it’s end point
  • Coronary Heart Disease
  • Breast Cancer
  • Stroke
  • Pulmonary Embolism
  • Endometrial Cancer
  • Colorectal Cancer
  • Hip Fracture
  • Death from other causes
Slide 40: Women’s Health Initiative - Outcomes
  • Trial stopped early in 2002 because risks were higher than benefits in combined therapy group vs placebo
  • 29% higher CHD risk
  • 41% higher CVA risk
  • 2+ higher risk of PE
  • 26% higher breast cancer risk
  • 37% fewer colorectal cancers
  • 34% fewer hip fractures
  • Trial stopped in 2004 for estrogen only arm vs placebo
  • No significant CHD reduction
  • 39% higher CVA risk
  • 39% fewer hip fractures
  • Lower incidence of breast cancer (no defined stat given) & was later found to have significantly lower incidence and mortality
  • No significant total mortality difference
  • Lots of confounding factors
  • Age, time since menopause, duration of treatment, baseline CV risk, & hormone types & route of administration
Slide 41: Women’s Health Initiative - Review
  • Average age of women was 63, older than the start of menopause
  • 1/5 to 1/4 were 70-79 yrs old which possibly contributed to increase in CV risk
  • Only oral MHT was tested & only 1 estrogen & 1 progesterone
  • Transdermal estrogen has been shown to be safer
  • Multiple doses of each hormone are available & multiple types
  • Current research suggests this matters particularly for VTE risk
  • The basis for WHI was to see if HT could prevent disease & did not really test if MHT was effective at treatment of symptoms
  • Don’t use MHT to reduce CV risk or as 1st line for Osteoporosis treatment
  • Timing matters, starting earlier at onset may not increase risks as high
  • Dose, route, and type of hormone also matters
Slide 42: Combating Misinformation
  • Wellness influencers
  • Credentials, Evidence, Regulation
  • Supplement industry
  • Evidence, Regulation
Slide 43: Postmenopausal Bleeding (PMB)
  • Uterine bleeding 12 months or more after their final menses (ie menopause)
  • 90% of patients diagnosed with endometrial cancer have PMB
  • 2026 updated ACOG guideline
  • Combination of both transvaginal US and endometrial tissue sampling is recommended as part of the initial eval in most patients with PMB
  • Transvaginal US w/o endometrial biopsy may be used during the initial eval of select patients with a single episode of PMB & US showing a fully visualized endometrium that is <4mm in thickness & no risk factors for endometrial cancer, educated on f/u for recurrent bleeding, & no barriers to f/u
  • Risk factors - HT, SERM, BMI>30, G0, AA, DM, or genetic (ie Lynch or Cowden syndromes or FH of endometrial cancer), etc
Slide 44: Guideline Rational for PMB workup
  • Incidence increased from 23.5/100,000 women in 2000 to 28.8 in 2022
  • Death rate increased from 4.1/100,000 women per year in 2019 to 5.3 in 2023
  • Incidence role disproportionately for non-Hispanic Black women at 2.7% per yr through 2022 compared to 0.7% increase for white women
  • Death rate in non-Hispanic Black women was 9.8/100,000 women per year compared to 4.8/100,000 women per year in non-Hispanic White
  • Technique requires cervical to fundal measurement & measurement could be affected by uterine orientation, adenomyosis, and leiomyomas (the latter assoc with higher incidence in Black women)
Slide 45: Differential Diagnosis for PMB
  • GU Atrophy
  • Polyps, either Endometrial or Cervical
  • Uterine leiomyomas
  • Endometrial Hyperplasia with or without atypia
  • Exogenous HT
  • Endometrial Cancer (DO NOT MISS!)
  • Cervical Cancer
  • Other Cancers of the Genital Tract
  • Infections – endometritis, cervicitis, vaginitis, cystitis
  • Medications – anticoagulants, HT, SERMs
  • GI causes or Urinary causes

Slide 2: Session Objectives
  • Differentiate the clinical indications, contraindications, and adverse effects of estrogen-only versus combined estrogen-progestin therapy.
  • Explain the main mechanisms, risks, and clinical utility of some non-hormonal pharmacological therapies utilized for menopausal vasomotor symptoms.
  • Select the most appropriate menopausal pharmacotherapy for a patient by analyzing comorbid conditions and individual risk stratification.
Slide 3: Session Roadmap: Menopausal Pharmacotherapy
  • Pharmacological Principles & Hormone Regimens
  • Evidence-Based Safety & Risk Stratification-The WHI Vs. E3N
  • Special Populations & Non-Hormonal Pharmacology
  • Applications-Questions (lecture day)
Slide 7: Legend:
  • From: 25 Estrogens, Progestogens, and Androgens
  • Lippincott ® Illustrated Reviews: Pharmacology, 8e, 2023
  • Transcriptional regulation by intracellular steroid hormone receptors.
Slide 8: Estrogen
  • Binds intracellular estrogen receptors ERα and ERβ.
  • The hormone–receptor complex binds DNA response elements and alters transcription.
  • Stabilizes hypothalamic thermoregulation.
  • Stimulates endometrial proliferation.
  • Reduces osteoclast-mediated bone resorption.
Slide 9: Progestogen
  • Progestogen includes endogenous progesterone and synthetic progestins such as medroxyprogesterone acetate.
  • Binds intracellular progesterone receptors.
  • Opposes estrogen-induced endometrial proliferation.
  • Promotes secretory endometrial differentiation.
Slide 10: Characteristic Estrogen only Estrogen plus progestogen

| Characteristic | Estrogen only | Estrogen plus progestogen |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Appropriate patient | Prior hysterectomy | Intact uterus |

| Primary indication | Moderate-to-severe VMS when systemic HT is appropriate | Same, with endometrial protection |

| Major benefit | Most effective VMS treatment without unnecessary progestogen exposure | VMS relief while preventing endometrial hyperplasia |

| Principal unique risk | Endometrial hyperplasia and cancer if used with an intact uterus | Additional bleeding, breast tenderness, bloating, and possible mood effects |

Slide 11: Endometrial protection
  • Continuous combined: estrogen and progestogen daily
  • Cyclic: estrogen daily with progestogen for approximately 12–14 days each month
  • Conjugated estrogen plus bazedoxifene: bazedoxifene acts as the endometrial antagonist
  • Levonorgestrel intrauterine system may provide endometrial protection in selected patients, depending on product and clinical context
  • Cyclic regimens usually produce scheduled withdrawal bleeding. Continuous regimens may cause initial unscheduled bleeding followed by amenorrhea.
Slide 12: Estrogen routes
  • Oral estradiol or conjugated equine estrogen
  • Transdermal estradiol patch, gel, or spray
  • Vaginal estrogen for GSM, not VMS
Slide 13: Local (Vaginal) Estrogen & Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause (GSM)
  • Clinical Indication:
  • Specifically indicated for GSM: vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, urinary urgency, and recurrent UTIs
  • Pharmacokinetics & Systemic Exposure:
  • Low-dose vaginal formulations (creams, inserts/tablets, low-dose rings) maintain serum estradiol within the postmenopausal basal range (4-14pg/mL)
  • Negligible systemic absorption; no observed increased risk of VTE, stroke, CHD, or breast cancer recurrence
  • Endometrial Safety:
  • Opposing progestogen therapy is NOT required for low-dose local vaginal estrogen.
  • Clinical Utility:
  • Can be continued long-term and used safely even when systemic MHT is contraindicated or discontinued
Slide 14: Transdermal therapy
  • It may be preferred when systemic HT remains appropriate in patients with:
  • Hypertriglyceridemia
  • Gallbladder disease
  • Migraine
  • Moderate cardiometabolic or VTE risk
Slide 15: Oral and transdermal estrogen

| Oral estrogen | Transdermal estradiol |

| --- | --- |

| Undergoes hepatic first-pass metabolism | Largely bypasses hepatic first-pass exposure |

| Increases hepatic clotting-factor production | Less hepatic effect on coagulation proteins |

| Increases triglycerides | Less effect on triglycerides |

| Increases SHBG, TBG and CBG | Smaller effect on binding proteins |

| Greater gallbladder effect | Lower observed gallbladder risk |

| Higher observed VTE risk | Lower VTE risk in observational studies |

  • Transdermal estrogen as risk-free. The route evidence comes mainly from observational studies.
Slide 16: Modern MHT Dosing Strategy: "Start Low, Titrate Up”
  • Shift in Clinical Practice: Historical Approach: Fixed "standard" starting doses (e.g., CEE 0.625mg/day or oral estradiol 1mg/day).
  • Current Guideline Approach: Initiate therapy at lower doses (e.g., transdermal estradiol 0.025mg/day or oral estradiol 0.5 mg/day) and titrate upward based on symptom response
Slide 17: Modern MHT Dosing Strategy: "Start Low, Titrate Up”- (Continued)
  • Clinical Advantages of Low-Dose Initiation:
  • Effectively eliminates or reduces vasomotor symptoms in the majority of patients.
  • Lower adverse effect profile: Significantly reduces rates of breast tenderness, fluid retention, and unscheduled vaginal bleeding.
  • Improved safety markers: Exerts fewer effects on hepatic coagulation factors and inflammatory markers.
  • Duration & Tapering:
  • Re-evaluate periodically; when discontinuing, taper gradually (e.g., reducing by 1 pill/patch increment per week) to minimize rebound hot flashes
Slide 18: Contraindications to systemic hormone therapy
  • Systemic HT should generally be avoided with:
  • Current or previous breast cancer
  • Known coronary heart disease
  • Previous stroke or TIA
  • Previous VTE or a major thrombophilia
  • Active liver disease
  • Unexplained vaginal bleeding until evaluated
  • High-risk endometrial cancer
  • Pregnancy
Slide 19: Contraindications to systemic hormone therapy-
  • A different route does not automatically overcome a major contraindication.
  • Low-dose vaginal estrogen has low, formulation-dependent systemic absorption. It should be distinguished from systemic therapy, but decisions in patients with estrogen-dependent cancer require individualized discussion.
Slide 20: Adverse effects and monitoring
  • Common estrogen effects
  • Breast tenderness
  • Nausea
  • Headache
  • Fluid retention
  • Vaginal bleeding
Slide 21: Adverse effects and monitoring-
  • Progestogen-related effects
  • Breakthrough or withdrawal bleeding
  • Breast tenderness
  • Bloating
  • Mood symptoms
Slide 22: Risks
  • VTE and pulmonary embolism
  • Ischemic stroke
  • Gallbladder disease
  • Endometrial hyperplasia or cancer with unopposed systemic estrogen
  • Regimen- and duration-dependent breast-cancer risk
  • New or persistent bleeding after initial treatment adjustment requires evaluation rather than automatic attribution to hormone therapy
Slide 23: What the WHI actually tested

| WHI hormone trial | Population | Tested regimen |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Combined trial | Intact uterus | Oral CEE 0.625 mg + MPA 2.5 mg daily |

| Estrogen-alone trial | Prior hysterectomy | Oral CEE 0.625 mg daily |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Coronary events | +2.5 | −5.5 |

| Invasive breast cancer | +3 | −2.5 |

| Stroke | +2.5 | −0.5 |

| Pulmonary embolism | +3 | +1.5 |

| All-cause mortality | −5 | −5.5 |

Slide 25: Risks and Benefits of MHT
Slide 26: Breast cancer and formulation evidence WHI randomized trial

| Regimen | Breast-cancer incidence | Breast-cancer deaths |

| --- | --- | --- |

| CEE alone after hysterectomy | 30 vs 37 with placebo: approximately 7 fewer cases | 3 vs 5 with placebo: approximately 2 fewer deaths |

| CEE + MPA with an intact uterus | 45 vs 36 with placebo: approximately 9 additional cases | 5 vs 4 with placebo: approximately 1 additional death, but this difference was not statistically significant |

Slide 27: E3N observational cohort
  • Estrogen plus micronized progesterone:
  • Estrogen plus dydrogesterone
  • Estrogen plus other progestogens
  • Progestogen type may matter but cannot establish that micronized progesterone carries no breast-cancer risk.
Slide 28: Custom-Compounded Bioidentical Hormone Therapy (cBHT)
  • Defining Terms:
  • FDA-Approved Bioidenticals: Structurally identical to endogenous human hormones (17beta-estradiol, micronized progesterone) available in regulated commercial products
  • Custom-Compounded (cBHT): Non-FDA-approved multi-hormone mixtures (creams, pellets, sublinguals) adjusted via salivary testing
  • Safety & Quality Concerns:
  • Lack of regulatory oversight for purity, potency, and batch consistency (tested potencies range from 67.5% to 268%of labeled strength)
  • Unpredictable bioavailability and variable progestogen absorption, predisposing patients to unintended endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma
  • Professional Guidelines:
  • The Menopause Society, Endocrine Society, and ACOG strongly advise against cBHT when FDA-approved options are available
Slide 29: Individual risk stratification
  • Before systemic HT:
  • Confirm that symptoms warrant systemic treatment.
  • Determine uterine status.
  • Evaluate unexplained bleeding.
  • Review breast-cancer and cardiovascular history.
  • Measure blood pressure.
  • Assess smoking, diabetes and lipid profile.
  • Review VTE history and thrombophilia.
  • Assess liver disease.
  • Review current medications and interactions.
Slide 30: General principle:
  • For appropriate candidates, benefit–risk is generally most favorable before age 60 or within 10 years of menopause.
  • Age and timing do not override contraindications.
  • 10-year CVD risk below 5%: generally low
  • 5–10%: intermediate; consider transdermal therapy if HT remains appropriate
  • Above 10%: generally favor nonhormonal treatment
Slide 31: Special Populations: Primary Ovarian Insufficiency (POI) & Surgical Menopause
  • Clinical Definitions:
  • Primary Ovarian Insufficiency (POI): Loss of ovarian function before age 40.
  • Early/Surgical Menopause: Menopause or bilateral oophorectomy before age 45
  • Dosing & Therapeutic Goals:
  • Require higher replacement doses (e.g., transdermal estradiol 0.1mg/day or oral estradiol 2mg/day) to restore physiological premenopausal levels.
  • Terminology: Classically termed Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT) rather than MHT
  • Recommended Duration:
  • Continue therapy until at least the average age of natural menopause ( 50-51years).
  • Primary Indications:
  • Essential for primary prevention of premature bone loss, coronary heart disease, ischemic stroke, and cognitive impairment.
  • Crucial Distinction: WHI safety risks in older women (mean age 63) do NOT apply to POI
Slide 32: Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulators (SERMs)
  • Mechanism of Action:
  • Bind intracellular estrogen receptors, displaying tissue-selective agonism or antagonism depending on target organ expression.
  • High-Yield SERM Agents:
  • Raloxifene: Estrogen agonist in bone (increases bone mineral density, reduces vertebral fractures) and antagonist in breast & endometrium. Approved for postmenopausal osteoporosis and breast cancer risk reduction. (No increased risk of endometrial cancer).
  • Tamoxifen: Estrogen antagonist in breast, but partial agonist in endometrium and bone. Used in ER+ breast cancer. (Carries increased risk of endometrial hyperplasia/carcinoma and VTE).
  • Bazedoxifene (+ CEE): Estrogen antagonist in the uterus; protects the endometrium without requiring a progestogen.
  • Clomiphene: Hypothalamic estrogen receptor antagonist; blocks negative feedback to increase GnRH, LH, and FSH to induce ovulation.
  • Shared Adverse Effects:
  • Increased risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) and hot flashes (except bazedoxifene + CEE)
Slide 33: Menopause, MHT, & Bone Health
  • Bone Loss Trajectory:
  • Estrogen depletion accelerates RANKL-mediated osteoclast resorption, leading to a loss of 15–20% of bone density in the 5–7 years surrounding the menopausal transition.
  • Fracture Reduction Efficacy:
  • Systemic MHT reduces vertebral, hip, and total osteoporotic fractures by 30–50% during active treatment.
  • Guideline :
  • Secondary Benefit: Bone preservation is a valuable secondary benefit when treating VMS.
  • Not First-Line Solely for Osteoporosis: MHT is not recommended as first-line primary therapy solely for isolated chronic osteoporosis prevention in asymptomatic women (bisphosphonates preferred).
  • Rebound Loss: Discontinuing MHT leads to rapid resumption of bone loss, returning to untreated baseline trajectory within a few years.
  • Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulators (SERMs):
  • Raloxifene: Estrogen agonist in bone (increases BMD, reduces vertebral fractures) and antagonist in breast/endometrium.
  • CEE + Bazedoxifene: Preserves bone density and protects the endometrium without requiring a progestogen
Slide 34: Androgen Therapy in Menopausal Pharmacology
  • Physiologic Context:
  • Endogenous testosterone levels decline gradually with age and sharply after bilateral oophorectomy.
  • Primary Clinical Indication:
  • Hypoactive Sexual Desire Disorder (HSDD) in postmenopausal women when MHT alone provides incomplete relief.
  • Regulatory Status & Prescribing:
  • No FDA-approved female testosterone product currently exists in the US (approved in UK/Australia).
  • Clinical practice utilizes off-label micro-dosing of transdermal male preparations or compounded products under specialist care.
  • Adverse Effects & Safety:
  • Potential Effects: Acne, hirsutism, fluid retention, and adverse lipid changes (decreased HDL, increased LDL).
Slide 36: SSRIs and SNRIs

| Therapy | Mechanism and utility | Important risks |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Paroxetine | Serotonin reuptake inhibition; low-dose paroxetine is FDA-approved for VMS | Sexual dysfunction, nausea, withdrawal; strong CYP2D6 inhibition |

| Escitalopram or citalopram | Serotonin reuptake inhibition | Sexual dysfunction, nausea, QT concerns with higher citalopram doses |

| Venlafaxine or desvenlafaxine | Serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibition | Nausea, BP elevation, withdrawal |

Notes:

Joffe trial, n=339

Slide 37: Gabapentin
  • Binds the auxiliary subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels.
  • The precise mechanism for VMS relief remains uncertain.
  • Useful for predominantly nocturnal VMS, insomnia, or concurrent neuropathic pain.
  • Risks: sedation, dizziness and ataxia.
  • Requires renal dose adjustment.
  • It is not a GABA-receptor agonist.
Slide 38: Oxybutynin
  • Competitive muscarinic-receptor antagonist.
  • Can reduce VMS and may benefit concurrent overactive bladder.
  • Risks: dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention and cognitive adverse effects.
  • Avoid or minimize in older adults with high anticholinergic burden.
Slide 39: Clonidine
  • Central α2-adrenergic agonist.
  • Modest efficacy with hypotension, dry mouth, sedation and rebound hypertension.
  • Generally not recommended routinely for VMS.
Slide 40: Neurokinin-receptor antagonists

| Drug | Pharmacology | Major safety considerations |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Fezolinetant | NK3-receptor antagonist | Hepatotoxicity warning, CYP1A2 interactions, cirrhosis and severe renal impairment |

| Elinzanetant | Dual NK1/NK3 antagonist | Sedation, hepatic-enzyme elevation, CYP3A4 interactions, pregnancy contraindication and seizure warning |

Slide 41: Comorbidity-based treatment selection

| Clinical situation | Most appropriate direction |

| --- | --- |

| Healthy patient with prior hysterectomy | Estrogen alone |

| Intact uterus and appropriate HT candidate | Estrogen plus endometrial protection |

| Previous breast cancer | Nonhormonal treatment |

| Tamoxifen treatment | Venlafaxine, gabapentin, or appropriate neurokinin antagonist; avoid paroxetine/fluoxetine |

| Previous VTE, stroke, or CHD | Generally avoid systemic HT |

| Hypertriglyceridemia or gallbladder risk | Transdermal rather than oral estrogen if HT remains appropriate |

| Uncontrolled hypertension | Control BP before systemic HT; use SNRIs cautiously |

| Liver disease | Avoid systemic HT; assess restrictions for neurokinin antagonists |

| Severe renal impairment | Renally adjust gabapentin; avoid fezolinetant |

| High anticholinergic burden | Avoid oxybutynin |

| Nocturnal VMS with neuropathic pain | Gabapentin may be useful |

Question 1

A 30-year-old woman presents with 2 years of unexplained infertility.

Evaluation of her partner reveals normal sperm concentration, morphology,

and motility. During assisted reproductive testing, sperm successfully reach

and surround the secondary oocyte but are unable to bind effectively to the

zona pellucida or undergo the acrosome reaction. Further studies

demonstrate failure of the biochemical changes that normally occur as sperm

transit through the female reproductive tract. Which of the following

processes is most likely defective in this patient?

A. Completion of meiosis II by the secondary oocyte

B. Capacitation of spermatozoa

C. Cortical granule exocytosis

D. Formation of the male pronucleus

E. Fusion of the male and female pronuclei

Page 6

Fertilization

Moore and Persaud, The Developing Human 9th ed

Page 7

Capacitation is the step in the maturation of sperm that is required to fertilize an oocyte.

This step is a biochemical event; the sperm move normally and look mature prior to capacitation.

In vivo, capacitation occurs after ejaculation, when the sperms leave the vagina and enter the female

reproductive system. The uterus aids in the steps of capacitation by lipoproteins, proteolytic enzymes,

and glycosidase enzymes.

Source : Figure in Drake, Vogl, Mitchell, Tibbitts, & Richardson (2015). Gray’s Atlas of anatomy (2nd ed., p. 242). Elsevier.

Page 8

Question 1

A 32-year-old woman presents with 2 years of unexplained infertility.

Evaluation of her partner reveals normal sperm concentration, morphology,

and motility. During assisted reproductive testing, sperm successfully reach

and surround the secondary oocyte but are unable to bind effectively to the

zona pellucida or undergo the acrosome reaction. Further studies

demonstrate failure of the biochemical changes that normally occur as sperm

transit through the female reproductive tract. Which of the following

processes is most likely defective in this patient?

A. Completion of meiosis II by the secondary oocyte

B. Capacitation of spermatozoa

C. Cortical granule exocytosis

D. Formation of the male pronucleus

E. Fusion of the male and female pronuclei

B

Page 9

Explanation

Capacitation is a functional maturation process that occurs within the female

reproductive tract.

During this process, sperm undergo membrane and metabolic changes that enable

binding to the zona pellucida and initiation of the acrosome reaction.

Without capacitation, sperm may exhibit normal count, morphology, motility, and

transport through the reproductive tract, but they cannot penetrate the zona

pellucida and fertilize the oocyte.

Takeaway:

Capacitation → Acrosome reaction → Zona penetration → Cortical reaction

→ Completion of meiosis II → Pronuclear fusion.

Failure of capacitation is a classic cause of infertility despite otherwise normal

semen analysis.

following multiple cycles of in vitro fertilization. Genetic testing demonstrates

Page 13

Question 2

A 34-year-old woman undergoes evaluation for recurrent implantation failure

following multiple cycles of in vitro fertilization. Genetic testing demonstrates

a normal embryo karyotype, and embryo development progresses

appropriately to the blastocyst stage. Endometrial biopsy reveals inadequate

invasion of maternal endometrial tissue by trophoblastic cells, preventing

establishment of normal maternal-fetal exchange. Which of the following

embryonic cell populations is primarily responsible for invasion of the

endometrium and establishment of implantation?

A. Cytotrophoblast

B. Epiblast

C. Syncytiotrophoblast

D. Hypoblast

E. Extraembryonic mesoderm

C

Page 14

Explanation

Following implantation, the trophoblast differentiates into two layers:

  • Cytotrophoblast: the inner cellular layer that retains mitotic activity and gives rise to new

trophoblastic cells.

  • Syncytiotrophoblast: the outer multinucleated layer that invades the endometrium, erodes

maternal capillaries, and establishes the early uteroplacental circulation.

  • The syncytiotrophoblast also secretes human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), which

maintains the corpus luteum during early pregnancy. Failure of syncytiotrophoblast

invasion can lead to implantation failure, early pregnancy loss, and abnormal placentation.

Takeaway:

  • Syncytiotrophoblast = implantation + invasion + hCG production.
  • A useful association is:

Cytotrophoblast → proliferates

Syncytiotrophoblast → invades and secretes hCG

Page 17

Placenta

Parts:

  • Maternal → Decidua basalis.
  • Fetal → chorionic villi (chorion

frondosum)

Dudek, RW Board Review Series: Embryology 4th ed

https://www.preventaccreta.org/accreta

Page 18

Placental abnormalities

  • Placenta previa occurs when the placenta

attaches in the lower part of the uterus, covering

the internal os.

  • Placental abruption occurs when a normally

implanted placenta prematurely separates from

the uterus before delivery of the fetus. It is

associated with maternal hypertension.

  • Placental accreta occurs when there is

abnormal adherence of the chorionic villi to the

uterine wall with partial or complete absence of

the decidua basalis.

  • Placental percreta occurs when the chorionic

villi penetrate the myometrium to reach the

perimetrium

Page 19

Question 3

A 38-year-old woman, gravida 4 para 3, presents in labor at 39 weeks'

gestation. Her obstetric history is significant for two prior cesarean deliveries.

Following an uncomplicated vaginal delivery, the placenta fails to separate

spontaneously. Attempts at manual extraction result in massive postpartum

hemorrhage requiring emergent surgical intervention. Histologic examination

demonstrates chorionic villi abnormally attached directly to the myometrium.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

A. Placenta accreta

B. Placental abruption

C. Placenta previa

D. Velamentous placenta

E. Membranous placenta

A

Page 20

Explanation

Placenta accreta occurs when there is defective formation of the decidua basalis,

allowing chorionic villi to attach directly to the myometrium. This abnormal

adherence prevents normal placental separation after delivery and can result in life-

threatening postpartum hemorrhage. Risk factors include: previous cesarean

delivery, placenta previa, prior uterine surgery, multiparity.

  • Placenta previa: placenta overlies or is near the internal cervical os and presents

with painless third-trimester vaginal bleeding before delivery.

  • Placental abruption: premature separation of a normally implanted placenta and

presents with painful vaginal bleeding, uterine tenderness, and fetal distress.

  • Velamentous placenta: umbilical vessels travel within the membranes before

reaching the placenta and is associated with vasa previa and fetal hemorrhage.

  • Membranous placenta (placenta membranacea): rare condition in which villi

persist over a large portion of the chorion and does not characteristically cause

failure of placental separation after delivery.

Page 22

Question 4

A 28-year-old primigravid woman at 29 weeks' gestation presents with a 2-

week history of worsening headaches, lower-extremity edema, and visual

disturbances. Her blood pressure is 170/110 mm Hg, and urinalysis

demonstrates 4+ proteinuria. Fetal ultrasonography reveals growth

restriction. Following delivery, placental histopathology demonstrates

inadequate remodeling of the maternal spiral arteries. Failure of which of

the following developmental processes most likely contributed to this

patient's condition?

A. Formation of the bilaminar embryonic disc

B. Migration of neural crest cells into the pharyngeal arches

C. Trophoblastic invasion of maternal vessels

D. Gastrulation and formation of the trilaminar embryonic disc

E. Development of the allantois and urachus

Page 23

Normal placentation: Trophoblast invasion → Spiral artery remodeling → Low-

resistance uteroplacental circulation

Preeclampsia: Defective trophoblast invasion → High-resistance spiral arteries →

Placental ischemia → Hypertension and proteinuria. Therefore, defective

trophoblastic invasion of maternal vessels is the embryologic process most directly

responsible for this condition.

Osmosis.org

Page 24

Question 4

A 28-year-old primigravid woman at 29 weeks' gestation presents with a 2-

week history of worsening headaches, lower-extremity edema, and visual

disturbances. Her blood pressure is 170/110 mm Hg, and urinalysis

demonstrates 4+ proteinuria. Fetal ultrasonography reveals growth

restriction. Following delivery, placental histopathology demonstrates

inadequate remodeling of the maternal spiral arteries. Failure of which of

the following developmental processes most likely contributed to this

patient's condition?

A. Formation of the bilaminar embryonic disc

B. Migration of neural crest cells into the pharyngeal arches

C. Trophoblastic invasion of maternal vessels

D. Gastrulation and formation of the trilaminar embryonic disc

E. Development of the allantois and urachus

C

Page 25

Explanation

  • Preeclampsia is caused by abnormal placentation,

specifically inadequate invasion of the maternal

spiral arteries by trophoblasts.

  • During normal development, trophoblastic cells

invade and remodel the spiral arteries, converting

them from small, high-resistance vessels into large,

low-resistance vessels. Failure of this trophoblastic

invasion results in poor placental perfusion and the

release of factors that cause widespread maternal

endothelial dysfunction, leading to hypertension,

proteinuria, and end-organ injury characteristic

of preeclampsia.

Page 27

The Reproductive Systems

  • The components include gonads, ducts &

external genitalia from mesoderm and endoderm.

  • The genotype is determined at fertilization (XX,

XY).

  • Week 7 embryo begins phenotypic sexual

differentiation.

  • The presence of the Y chromosome determines

sexual dimorphism. The germ cells have an

inductive influence on the differentiation of

the gonad.

  • Week 12 external genitalia recognizable
  • Week 20 phenotypic differentiation complete.

At gastrulation, the primordial germ cells migrate to

the yolk sac. During week 6, they migrate to the

genital ridge.

Langman’s Medical Embryology 14th ed fig 16-19

Page 30

Question 5

A newborn phenotypic female is evaluated for primary gonadal failure.

Genetic testing reveals a 46,XX karyotype. Pelvic ultrasonography

demonstrates small, poorly developed ovaries with a marked deficiency of

germ cells. The physician explains that normal ovarian development

depends on the migration of primordial germ cells during early

embryogenesis. Failure of this migration can result in gonadal dysgenesis

and infertility. Primordial germ cells normally migrate to the developing

gonadal ridges from which of the following structures?

A. Cloaca

B. Mesonephric duct

C. Paramesonephric duct

D. Yolk Sac

E. Genital ridge

D

Page 31

Explanation

Primordial germ cells (PGCs) are the

precursors of spermatozoa and oocytes.

They originate in the wall of the yolk sac near

the allantois and subsequently migrate through

the dorsal mesentery to the developing gonadal

ridges during weeks 4 to 6 of development.

Once they reach the gonads, they differentiate

into oogonia or spermatogonia. Failure of this

migration results in a marked reduction or

absence of germ cells within the gonads,

leading to gonadal dysgenesis and infertility.

Dudek, RW Board Review Series: Embryology 4th ed

A newborn is evaluated for ambiguous genitalia. Karyotype analysis

demonstrates 46,XY chromosomes. Pelvic ultrasonography reveals the

product would most directly disrupt which of the following

A. Descent of the testes into the scrotum

B. Regression of the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts

C. Conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT)

D. Fusion of the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts

E. Differentiation of Sertoli cells within the primitive sex cords

Question 6

Page 34

•

Female development is the default pathway: it occurs in the absence of SRY gene expression

and without requiring estrogen.

•

Male development requires active hormonal signaling: SRY → testes → testosterone + AMH.

•

Remove the testes (or block testosterone/AMH) and female structures develop regardless of

karyotype.

A newborn is evaluated for ambiguous genitalia. Karyotype analysis

demonstrates 46,XY chromosomes. Pelvic ultrasonography reveals the

absence of a uterus and fallopian tubes. Genetic testing identifies a

mutation in the SRY gene that prevents expression of its protein

product during embryogenesis. Failure of expression of the SRY gene

product would most directly disrupt which of the following

developmental processes?

A. Descent of the testes into the scrotum

B. Regression of the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts

C. Conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT)

D. Fusion of the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts

E. Differentiation of Sertoli cells within the primitive sex cords

Question 6

E

Page 38

Explanation

  • The SRY (Sex-determining Region of the Y chromosome) gene is the testis-

determining gene located on the short arm of the Y chromosome. Its protein

product functions as a transcription factor that initiates differentiation of the

indifferent gonad into a testis.

  • The earliest major effect of SRY expression is the development of Sertoli cells

from the primitive sex cords. Sertoli cells subsequently secrete anti-Müllerian

hormone (AMH), causing regression of the Müllerian ducts.

A developmental sequence to remember is:

  • SRY expression → Testis formation → Leydig cell differentiation →

Testosterone production → Wolffian duct development.

  • SRY expression → Sertoli cell differentiation → AMH secretion → Müllerian

duct regression

Persistent Müllerian Duct Syndrome

Caused by deficiency of anti-Müllerian hormone

(AMH) or defects in the AMH receptor.

Normally, Sertoli cells secrete AMH, causing

regression of the paramesonephric (Müllerian)

ducts.

The Müllerian ducts give rise to: fallopian tubes,

uterus, cervix, upper vagina

Because testosterone production is normal, testes

develop normally, and Wolffian derivatives are

present. However, failure of Müllerian regression

results in persistence of female internal

reproductive structures.

A 17-year-old adolescent is evaluated for primary amenorrhea. Physical

Karyotype analysis reveals 46,XY. Which of the following is the most

likely diagnosis?

A. Müllerian agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome)

B. Androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS)

D. Cryptorchidism

Sex Differentiation

Reproductive Embryology | NRE Step-1 | High Yield Notes | Multipotent Medverse Academy

Page 60

Takeaway

AIS = 46,XY + testes + AMH present + androgen receptor defect

  • AMH → no uterus, no fallopian tubes, blind-ending vagina
  • Androgen insensitivity → female external genitalia
  • Testosterone aromatization → normal breast development
  • Lack of androgen action → sparse pubic and axillary hair
  • This combination of primary amenorrhea + normal breasts + sparse pubic hair +

blind-ending vagina + absent uterus + 46,XY is the classic presentation of

Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (CAIS)

Page 61

Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome

  • AIS is caused by a mutation in the androgen receptor,

resulting in complete resistance to testosterone and

dihydrotestosterone (DHT). Although the testes

develop normally under the influence of the SRY

gene, the body's tissues cannot respond to androgens.

  • Sertoli cells produce anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH),

causing regression of the Müllerian ducts and

resulting in the absence of the uterus and fallopian

tubes.

  • Testosterone is aromatized to estrogen, leading to

normal breast development.

Reproductive Embryology | NRE Step-1 | High Yield Notes | Multipotent Medverse Academy

Page 65

Sex Differentiation

Reproductive Embryology | NRE Step-1 | High Yield Notes | Multipotent Medverse Academy

Key Diagnostic Clue

46,XY + female/ambiguous genitalia at birth + virilization at puberty

Page 66

Explanation

  • During fetal development, testosterone must be converted to dihydrotestosterone

(DHT) by the enzyme 5α-reductase. DHT is required for the development of the

penis, scrotum, and prostate

  • When DHT is deficient, external genitalia appear female or ambiguous at birth.

However, at puberty, rising testosterone levels can produce significant

masculinization.

5-alpha-reductase Deficiency | Concise Medical Knowledge

"Virilizes Later" = 5α-Reductase

Deficiency

  • DHT is needed for fetal external genitalia
  • Testosterone drives pubertal virilization

"Androgens Can't Act" = AIS

  • Testosterone present
  • Receptors absent
  • No virilization despite normal/high

testosterone levels

Descent of testis

Gubernaculum: is a fibrous band extend from the caudal part of testis.

It plays a role in the descent of the testis.

Gray’s anatomy for students / Richard L. Drake, A. Wayne Vogl, & Adam W. M. Mitchell—2nd Ed.

Processus vaginalis: is a diverticulum or out pouching of the peritoneum.

Inguinal canal is formed in relation to the relocation of the gonads

during the fetal development.

The Developing Human (Clinically oriented Embryology) 9th Ed.

Page 71

Explanation

  • This infant has cryptorchidism (undescended testis). Normally,

the testes descend into the scrotum during late fetal

development. Failure of descent results in an undescended

testis, most commonly located in the inguinal canal or

abdomen.

  • In 1 % of newborns, one or both testes fail to descend into the

scrotum. Undescended testes fail to produce mature sperm.

The most important long-term complication of untreated

cryptorchidism is an increased risk of testicular germ cell

tumors, particularly seminoma.

  • Cryptorchidism is also associated with:

✓Infertility or subfertility

✓Testicular atrophy

✓Increased risk of testicular torsion

✓Inguinal hernia

Question 13

During an anatomy lab session, a medical student learns that in females, a

certain embryonic structure persists as the ovarian ligament and the round

ligament of the uterus. These ligaments play an essential role in maintaining

the anatomical position of the ovaries and uterus within the pelvis. Which

structure gives rise to both of these ligaments in female development?

A. Paramesonephric ducts

B. Urogenital sinus

C. Genital tubercle

D. Gubernaculum

E. Labioscrotal swellings

D

Page 76

Explanation

•

The gubernaculum is a fibrous cord that connects

the developing gonad to the labioscrotal swelling.

In females, the gubernaculum persists and

becomes:

•

Ovarian ligament: connects the ovary to the

uterus.

•

Round ligament of the uterus: extends from the

uterus, passes through the inguinal canal, and

attaches to the labia majora.

•

The developing uterus interrupts the

gubernaculum, resulting in these two separate

ligamentous structures.
