C

Page 81

Explanation

  • Hypospadias: Ventral urethral opening, due to

incomplete fusion of urethral folds

  • Epispadias: Dorsal urethral opening & associated

with bladder exstrophy

•

This infant has hypospadias, a congenital anomaly in which the urethral

opening is located on the ventral surface of the penis due to incomplete

fusion of the urethral folds. A key management principle is that circumcision

should be avoided because the foreskin is frequently used as graft material

during surgical reconstruction of the urethra. Therefore, preservation of the

foreskin is essential until evaluation by a pediatric urologist.

Slide 2: APPLICATIONS
Slide 3: CASE 1(1)
  • A 15 year old boy is seen by a primary care physician for short stature and delayed sexual development. His PMH is remarkable only for asthma in early childhood, which has been well controlled. He uses no medications.
  • He is an average student in the 9th grade and smallest in his class. His older classmates harass him about his size. His parents are concerned because he is becoming withdrawn and a “loner”.
  • Pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. H5 was born 8.5 lbs and 20 inches long. Head circumference was 35 cm. Immunizations are current.
  • Adapted from: Case Based Pediatrics for Medical Students and Residents, Department of Pediatrics, University of Hawaii John A. Burns School of Medicine, Sherrel L. Hammar, MD. March 2002
Slide 4: CASE 1 (2)
  • FH: Mother 48 yo, in good health. Ht is 167 cm (50th %ile) and underwent menarche at age 13. Father 51 yo, in good health, Ht 184 cm (75th %ile). He was shaving regularly by age 15. One older male sibling in good health began puberty at age 11. No FH of smoking, alcoholism, mental illness, drug abuse, or learning disabilities.
  • Exam: VS T 37.1, P 110, R 32, BP 100/60, HT 158 cm (3rd %tile) Wt. 42 kg (10th %tile). He is pale and anxious but cooperative. HEENT, Chest, Heart, and pulse exams normal. No abdominal tenderness or mass. Genitalia: normal circumcised phallus, Tanner pubic hair stage 1, genital stage 2. Testes firm, 2.5 cm in length and 4 ml in volume. Scrotum reddened and stippled. Otherwise physical exam is normal.
  • Lab: CBC, Hb 13, WBC 9.5, normal differential, platelets 350,000, UA normal.
  • Adapted from: Case Based Pediatrics for Medical Students and Residents, Department of Pediatrics, University of Hawaii John A. Burns School of Medicine, Sherrel L. Hammar, MD. March 2002
Slide 5: CASE 1 (3)
  • QUESTION
  • If you could only request one test, what would it be? You may list the tests you want and put an asterisk by the one you think will be most helpful.
Slide 6: CASE 1 (4)
  • QUESTION
  • Bone age (left hand and wrist) is 12.0 years. LH and FSH are decreased but normal for SMR stage 1-2. Given this information, what is the most likely diagnosis?
Slide 7: CASE 2 (1)
  • A 6-year girl is brought for evaluation of breast enlargement. She weighs 25 kg (90th percentile) and is 128 cm (>95th percentile). She has enlarged breasts, sexual maturity rating 2-3, with pigmentation of the areola and hyperpigmented macules.
  • A pelvic ultrasound reveals a left ovarian cyst 3.7 x 3.4 cm. The uterus is enlarged with a length of 4.6 cm (normal < 3 cm) with a prominent endometrium.
  • Bone age is consistent with age 8 years. Estradiol is elevated at 113 pg/ml (normal <36 pg/ml), and LH 1.7 mIU/ml (normal <1 mIU/ml). DHEAS and FSH are normal. The patient complains of pain in her lower limb. Area radiographs are shown.
  • Adapted from: Moein Mobini; Rahim Vakili; Saba Vakili, International J Pediatr Volume 2, Issue 2.2, April 2014, pp 153-156
Slide 8: CASE 2 (2)
  • QUESTIONS
  • What is the most likely diagnosis?
  • Central nervous system tumor
  • Kisspeptin gain-of-function mutation
  • McCune-Albright Syndrome
  • Tuberous sclerosis
  • Turner Syndrome
Slide 9: CASE 2 (3)
  • QUESTIONS
  • Of the choices given for this case, which diagnosis/diagnoses may cause gonadotropin-dependent precocious puberty?
  • Central nervous system tumor
  • Kisspeptin gain-of-function mutation
  • McCune-Albright Syndrome
  • Tuberous sclerosis
  • Turner Syndrome
Slide 10: CASE 3 (1)
  • A 12-year-old boy is concerned about a lack of pubertal development during a recent annual physical exam. Although he is currently healthy, his medical history is notable for lack of midfacial fusion, including cleft lip and palate involving the nasal structure at birth, for which he underwent multiple surgeries. He was found to be anosmic postoperatively in early childhood.
  • His growth chart reveals he has been consistently along the 10th percentile for height. As he approached the usual age of the pubertal growth spurt (12 years), he continue to grow 5 cm annually.
  • His current height and weight are at the 25th and 10th percentiles for age, respectively. Vital signs and physical exam are normal, demonstrating good results from his facial surgeries. He has small, firm testes, 1 cc in volume bilaterally, and < 1 cm in length. His penis is prepubertal, and he has no sexual hair.
  • Adapted from: Medscape Pediatrics, authors PA Lee and CP Houk
Slide 11: CASE 3 (2)
  • QUESTIONS
  • What is the best approach to the care of this patient at this time?
  • Acknowledge his concerns, reexamine in 6 months
  • Obtain bone age films, ask additional family history
  • Refer to Endocrinology for further workup
  • Send a karyotype to rule out Klinefelter syndrome
Slide 12: CASE 3 (3)

  • Laboratory testing was notable for luteinizing hormone (LH), follicle stimulating hormone (FSH), and testosterone levels below detectable limits. CBC and complete metabolic panel were normal.

  • Transvestite
  • Transgender

Slide 13: LEGAL TRANSITION CHALLENGES
Slide 14: Gender Transition: Individualized
  • Each Person desires different Outcomes
  • Medication + Surgery-Not required Parts of Transition
  • Legal Name Change: (Medications + Surgery not required)

  • Name/Driver's License/Birth Certificate
Slide 16: 4 States Not Recommended for Transgender People -2026
  • Texas
  • Florida
  • Idaho
  • Kansas
Slide 17: Comparison- Legal Policies
  • Texas
  • Birth Certificate: No gender change unless resolving a clerical error from birth
  • Medicaid coverage for Gender therapy: Banned (surgery, hormone therapy)
  • Drivers License: Gender change prohibited ID must match sex assigned at Birth
  • Illinois
  • Birth Certificate: Self Attestation

  • Drivers License: Self select: M F X (non-binary)

  • DSM 5 – Gender Dysphoria (previously Gender Identity Disorder)
  • World Heath Organization (WHO) Gender Incongruence ICD –F64.9
Slide 20: MEDICAL TRANSITION
Slide 21: TRANSGENDER HISTORY +EXAM
Slide 22: Sexual and Reproductive History:
  • TOP:
  • Right sized binder
  • 1. Ask about Nipple discharge
  • 2. Any Lumps or Bumps
  • 3. Binding History
  • Binding:
  • Right sized binder
  • Breathable fabric
  • Dry well after bathing-towel dry then blow dry on cool
  • Wrong Binder:
  • Can restrict blood flow
  • Can make it hard to breathe
  • Causes Rashes & Bruising, Broken Ribs- especially Yeast
  • Breathable fabric
  • Dry well after bathing-towel dry then blow dry on cool
  • Wrong Binder:
  • Can restrict blood flow
  • Can make it hard to breathe
  • Causes Rashes & Bruising, Broken Ribs- especially Yeast
  • BOTTOM:
  • Genital itching , burning, unusual discharge
  • Pelvic pain/Pelvic Pressure
  • Burning w/Urination/Leakage
  • Diarrhea /Constipation or Leakage of Stool
  • Bleeding Pattern history
  • Cervical Cancer Screening
  • HPV Vaccination discussion
  • STD Screening history
Slide 23: Sexual History: 1. Who do you have Sex with? 2. What parts (Anatomy) do they have? 3. Have you been intimate in a way that includes: Exchange of Genital body fluids? 4. Do you have Oral or Anal sex?
Slide 24: Sexual History: 5. Is there a possibility that any of your partners: Could get you Pregnant or you could get them Pregnant? 6. Pregnancy Plans or Contraception needed? 7. RADAR: Ask about Abuse Remember to ask routinely Ask directly about violence Document Assess your patient’s safety Review Resource options with your patient
Slide 25: PHYSICAL EXAM: 1. Delay exam-Develop Rapport 1st 2. Exam - Based on Organs present 3. Discuss: Purpose of the exam
Slide 26: PHYSICAL EXAM: Testosterone use: Beard growth Clitoromegaly Acne Androgenic alopecia Estrogen use: Breast tenderness Loss of muscle tone Urinary symptoms (prostate)
Slide 27: PHYSICAL EXAM: Testosterone use: Beard growth Clitoromegaly Acne Androgenic alopecia Estrogen use: Breast tenderness Loss of muscle tone Urinary symptoms (prostate)

  • Need the right sized Binder / Breathable Fabric

  • Can cause Breathing issues
  • Can cause Rashes(Yeast), Broken ribs, Bruising
  • Towel dry / Blow dry on cool
Slide 29: Correct Binding

  • Pelvic
  • Fam Hx Ovarian Cancer
  • As indicated
  • Anal
  • Vulva
  • Cervix
  • > Age 40
  • PMOS

  • Diabetes or Hypertension
  • Unexplained Bleeding
  • PMOS
  • Obesity
  • Over 40
  • Older Transgender Patients

  • Blind Pap- Label as Transgender
  • Can use Vaginal Estrogen
Slide 31: PUBERTY BLOCKERS
Slide 32: Gender Care for Adolescents
  • Menstrual suppression
  • Medical transition
  • Surgical Transition
Slide 34: Puberty blocking therapy is Permanent?
  • True
  • False
Slide 35: Tanner Stage 2
  • Females – Age 8 -11
  • Breast buds
  • Areola
  • Sparse Pubic hair
  • Males – Age 11
  • Testicles enlarge
  • Sparse Pubic hair
  • Scrotum enlarges
Slide 36: Gender Care for Adolescents
  • GNRH Agonists – Main puberty blocker
  • Inhibits LH & FSH secretion
  • Decreased gonadal sex steroids- Pre puberty
  • Decreased risk to bones – If using Cross Sex Hormones
  • Cross sex Hormones are usually started Age 13
Slide 37: When is it appropriate to start medical therapy for a transgender adolescent?
  • After reaching Tanner Stage 2 development
  • After establishing a diagnosis of Transgender identity
  • After an established diagnosis of Transgender identity and has reached Tanner Stage 2 development
Slide 38: True or False? Transgender Male adolescents can develop medical complications of their gynecologic organs and may also become pregnant.
  • True (breasts, uterus, ovaries)
  • False
Slide 39: MENSTRUAL SUPPRESSION
  • GOAL: Decrease Frequency + Volume of Menses
  • Complete Amenorrhea may be difficult
  • Hormone Therapy doesn’t affect Future Fertility
  • Hormone Therapy doesn’t increase Cancer risk
Slide 40: MEDICAL OPTIONS: MENSTRUAL SUPPRESSION
  • Combined OCPS: Daily up to 88% Amenorrhea
  • Transdermal: Weekly Adhesive problems
  • Vaginal Ring: Monthly High Amenorrhea rate
  • Oral Progestins: Daily
  • Depo Provera: 11-13 weeks Weight gain Affects Bones
  • Nexplanon: 3 – 5 yrs Only 22% Amenorrhea rate
  • Progestin IUD: 5-8 years Cost/Insertion Pain 60%
  • GNRH agonist: Daily to 3 mo High Amenorrhea rate
Slide 41: Testosterone Effects on the Menstrual Cycle
  • 1. Cycles will stop within a few months of starting Testosterone
  • 2. For Continued Bleeding – Use Progesterone
  • 3. Testosterone causes Vaginal Atrophy
  • Increased Risk: Bacterial vaginosis, Cystitis, Cervicitis, Dyspareunia
  • Use Topicals – Lubricants, Vaginal moisturizers, Topical Estrogen
Slide 42: Medications
  • Majority of Meds are Common
  • Specific Certification Not needed to Prescribe
  • Know the Risks & Side Effects
Slide 43: When should fertility preservation be discussed?
  • 3 months after starting Hormone therapy
  • 6 months after starting Hormone therapy
  • Before starting Hormone therapy
Slide 44: MEDICAL TRANSITION- Masculinizing Therapy
  • GOALS:
  • Facial Hair
  • Deeper Voice
  • Increasing Body Hair
  • Muscle Mass
  • SIDE EFFECTS: Hormone Therapy
  • Increased Libido
  • Change in Sweat/Odor
  • SubQ Fat Redistribution
  • Recessed Hairline/Baldness
  • Cessation of Menses
  • Vaginal Atrophy
  • Increased Clitoral Size
Slide 45: Medical Transition-Masculinizing
  • CONTRAINDICATIONS: 1.Unstable Coronary Artery Disease 2.Polycythemia (HCT > 55%) 3.Current Pregnancy
  • LAB STUDIES:
  • 1. Lipid panel: HDL + Triglycerides
  • 2. Hematocrit q 3 mo x 1 yr/ Then q 6 mo
  • 3. Testosterone level-q 3 mo x 1 yr Goal: 320-1000 ng/dl
Slide 49
  • Can achieve pregnancy : Stop Testosterone 1st
  • Partner Insemination/Donor Sperm
  • Carry pregnancy themselves or
  • IVF with embryo transfer to a Partner / Surrogate
  • Pregnancy: Can Trigger Dysphoria or Isolation
  • No Testosterone - Chest feeding planned
  • Transmasculine: Fertility and Pregnancy
Slide 50: Feminizing Therapy
  • SIDE EFFECTS:
  • Breast Growth
  • Decreased Erectile Function
  • Increased Body Fat
  • Decreased Testicular Size
Slide 51: Medical Transition –Feminizing Therapy
  • Transdermal Estrogen is the safest /Best dosing
  • Oral Estrogen – use 17-B Estradiol
  • Antiandrogens/Hormone Blockers: decrease Testosterone, less Estrogen needed - Spironolactone - monitor BP and Potassium - GNRH Agonists (expensive – Lupron) - Progesterone - (insufficient breast growth data)
  • Finasteride – less safe, questionable efficacy
Slide 52: Medical Transition-Feminizing
  • CONTRAINDICATIONS: Cardiovascular –possibly VTE
  • LAB STUDIES:
  • 1. Estradiol 2. Total Testosterone 3. Sex Hormone Binding Globulin
Slide 56: Medical Transition: Feminizing Therapy
  • RISKS:
  • Venous Thromboembolism
  • High Triglycerides
  • Gallstone development
  • Elevated Liver Enzymes
  • Try to decrease cardiovascular risks – Like Smoking
Slide 57: TRANSFEMININE: Fertility/Pregnancy/Contraception
  • If Gonads are retained - May need Assisted Reproduction
  • Fertility may return after stopping Hormone therapy
  • Long term Estrogen can cause Testicular damage
  • Do Sperm Banking before Starting Hormones
Slide 58: SURGICAL TRANSITION
Slide 59: SURGICAL TRANSITION
Slide 60: SURGICAL TRANSITION
  • Health Assessment Letter- Required by some Insurance plans
  • Sample Letter- University of San Francisco Center for Excellence for Transgender Health
Slide 62: Transgender Surgery Costs
Slide 63: Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy & Surgery
  • No need to stop Hormone therapy
  • Before or After Surgery
Slide 64: Bilateral Mastectomy or Top Surgery Observe scar line if surgery done. Chest & axillary exam (some Breast tissue will remain) Testosterone doesn’t increase Breast cancer risk.
Slide 65: Hysterectomy with/without Ovary removal
  • Necessary if Gender incongruence is present
  • Consider Vaginal hysterectomy
  • Ovarian removal depends on Fertility desire /Pt choice
  • Cardiovascular Health: No studies have found increased Cardiovascular risk in the Transmasculine
  • Bone Health: Testosterone can prevent Bone demineralization
Slide 66: Bottom Surgery - tissue is taken from a donor site (anterolateral thigh, radial forearm, latissimus dorsi) - tissue is shaped into a phallus - Later: Penile implant
Slide 67: Vaginoplasty
Slide 69: Surgical Transition – Aesthetic Procedures
Slide 70: PREVENTATIVE CARE
Slide 71: Preventive Care
  • Mental Health
  • Depression
  • Substance Abuse
  • Cancer
  • STD screening
  • Immunization –including HPV
  • 40% of Transgender pts – Attempt Suicide
  • Screen for Intimate Partner Violence
Slide 72: Cancer screening for a Transgender patient should be based on: A. Present Anatomy B. Gender identity C. Sex assigned at birth
Slide 73: Transmasculine Cancer Screening
  • Cancer Screening:
  • A Neovagina doesn’t need Cervical ca screen
  • Prostate Cancer screening:
  • Higher risk: Hormone therapy after Age 50
  • Breast Cancer screening
  • After Age 50 + 5 yrs- Feminizing hormones
Slide 74: Cancer Screening: Transmasculine
  • Breast cancer screening
  • Genetic counseling-Fam hx Breast/Ovarian ca
  • Cervical cancer screening
  • Self collection (>Age 30)
  • Primary HPV testing
  • Uterine Ca Screening:
  • Endometrium atrophic with Testosterone
  • Hx mastectomy vs Breast reduction
  • Not needed
Slide 75: The Aging Transgender Male
  • 1. Consider Sex assigned at Birth + Anatomy
  • 2. Length of Hormone use
  • 3. Type of Hormone regimen
  • 4. Switch to Transdermal Estrogen
  • 5. Lifelong Anticoagulation -VTE Hx
Slide 76: The Aging Transgender Female
  • BREAST CANCER RISKS:
  • Same guidelines as Cisgender
  • CAVEATS:
  • 1. Current Estrogen dosage
  • 2. When were Hormones started?
  • 3. Hx-Augmentation Mammoplasty?
Slide 77: The Aging Transgender Patient: Transgender Female
  • PROSTATE CANCER RISKS
  • The prostate is not removed with Gender Affirming surgery
  • General screening Age 55- 69
  • Digital Prostate exam
  • done through the neovaginal canal

Canvas course 70351, file 24312038 (pptx, 7.5 MB); session TBL-EARLY-PREG (Week 6, 9/22/2026: TBL 3: Early Pregnancy). Text extracted verbatim on 2026-09-26 for REPRO-PLAN P1.2 (12 slides; 11 with text kept; 0 image-only slides and 1 title/boilerplate slides omitted).

Slide 2
  • APPLICATIONS
Slide 3
  • CASE 1
  • Sources, date
  • A 25 year old G1P0 comes to see you after having a positive home pregnancy test. She notes that her last menstrual period was approximately 8 weeks ago. She notes that she gets a normal period every 5-7 weeks. She has been having some mild nausea and breast tenderness but otherwise feels well. She denies any pain or bleeding.
  • Her β-hCG is 2,400 mIU/mL. You get an ultrasound and it shows a gestational sac but no fetal pole.

Notes:

Is she pregnant?

How pregnant is she? What assumptions are being made if pregnancy dating relies only on the LMP?

Why did you get an ultrasound? She’s not having any sx that would signal this as an abnl pregnancy. Is her B-hcg level what you would expect?

What additional information would be most useful?

What is the most appropriate next step?

Slide 4
  • QUESTIONS
  • Is she pregnant?
  • How pregnant is she?
  • Why did you get an ultrasound?
  • What is the next best step?

Notes:

Q1: Yes

Q2: 5ish wks. Is her B-hcg level what you would expect? What assumptions are being made if pregnancy dating relies only on the LMP? (that this is an abnl pregnancy, etc.)

Q3: Why did you get an ultrasound? She’s not having any sx that would signal this as an abnl pregnancy so what is the purpose of the ultrasound? (given her LMP and her BHCG, she’s not as pregnant as we would expect, etc.)

Q4: What is the most appropriate next step? What additional information would be most useful?

Slide 5
  • CASE 2
  • Sources, date
  • A 30 year old G3P0020 comes to see you for an appointment. LMP was 6 weeks ago so she took a pregnancy test and it was positive. She has also been having some left abdominal pain but no vaginal bleeding. Her β-hCG level is 1,500 mIU/mL. She has a transvaginal ultrasound that demonstrates no intrauterine pregnancy. You get a repeat β-hCG 48 hours later and it is now 1,850 mIU/mL.
Slide 6
  • QUESTION
  • Is the pt pregnant?
  • How pregnant?
  • What additional information do you need?
  • What is the differential diagnosis?
  • What is the next best step?

Notes:

Q1: Is the pt pregnant?

Q2: How pregnant? Based on LMP? (8wks) Based on BHCG? (5-6 wks) so Is it normal? (probably not)

Q3: What additional information would be helpful? [Are her periods normal and how long is her menstrual cycle? (28-30 days) Has she had any sti infections in the past? Chlamydia in college) Has she ever been pregnant before? (Yes – 1 SAB, 1 ectopic s/p methotrexate and her current pregnancy) Is she stable? What are her vitals? (Pain is mild, she is not hypotensive, abdominal exam does not demonstrate guarding, normal pulse)].

Q4: What is on the DDx?

Q5: Next best step? Serial b-hcg vs f/u ultrasound? At what point do you move from observation to tx?

Teaching Tip: the object of this question is NOT to recognize an ectopic pregnancy but rather to manage diagnostic uncertainty while avoiding harm from both missed ectopic pregnancy and premature treatment of a potentially viable intrauterine pregnancy.

Slide 7
  • CASE 3
  • Sources, date
  • 34-year-old G4P1021 presents to clinic with vaginal bleeding and clots with cramping for the past 24 hrs. LMP was 10 wks ago. She was seen 2 weeks ago and at that visit had an ultrasound that confirmed an intrauterine pregnancy with a CRL consistent with 8 weeks and a fetal heart rate of 160.
  • Today is a febrile, has a BP of 118/72 and pulse of 84.
  • β-hCG:
  • 2 weeks ago: 38,000 mIU/mL
  • Today: 24,500 mIU/mL
  • Ultrasound today: Intrauterine gestational sac present, embryo measures 8 weeks 2 days, no cardiac activity identified.
Slide 8
  • QUESTIONS
  • Is the pt pregnant?
  • How pregnant?
  • What other information do you need?
  • What is the probable diagnosis?
  • What do you tell the patient and her partner when they say “But we saw a heartbeat 2 wks ago.”

Notes:

Is the pt pregnant

How pregnant?

What pieces of information are most important in determining whether this pregnancy is viable? Another bhcg? Ultrasound?

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Discussion Points

Students frequently struggle with:

Distinguishing bleeding from pregnancy loss

Understanding that fetal cardiac activity may later cease

Communicating certainty and uncertainty compassionately

Slide 9
  • CASE 4
  • A 21-year-old G1P0 presents to the emergency department for severe nausea and vaginal spotting. LMP was 11 weeks ago. She had a positive pregnancy test 7 wks ago.
  • Over the past month she has had progressively worsening nausea and vomiting so much so she is having problems holding down even water, much less food. She has also had some intermittent vaginal bleeding but is not having any cramping.
  • Today she is afebrile, BP 148/92 and a pulse of 110. You do a bimanual exam and feel like her uterus is larger than you would expect for what you would expect based on her LMP.
  • You get a β-hCG and it is 250,000 IU and an ultrasound demonstrates “heterogeneous intrauterine material with multiple cystic spaces.” No fetus is identified within the uterine cavity.
Slide 10
  • QUESTIONS
  • Is the pt pregnant?
  • How pregnant?
  • What aspect of this pt’s presentation to your clinic is the most concerning?
  • What’s the diagnosis?
  • Why are the hCG levels so high?
  • What part of embryology has gone awry?
  • You must ALWAYS follow the hCG to zero in gestational trophoblastic disease

Notes:

Is she pregnant? Yes

How pregnant?

What aspect of this is the most concerning? BP? Spotting? N/V?

What’s the diagnosis? Gestational trophoblastic disease

Why are the hCG levels so high? Excess trophoblastic proliferation

What part of embryology has gone awry?

Why do you have to follow the hcg to 0 even after she’s had a d&c?

Slide 11
  • CASE 5
  • 29-year-old G2P1102 presents for early prenatal care. First pregnancy was complicated by gestational diabetes, 2nd pregnancy was complicated by gestational diabetes, preeclampsia and preterm delivery.
  • She comes in today for pregestational counseling.

Notes:

Tell me what you’re looking for

Slide 12
  • QUESTIONS
  • How can the patient best prepare for another pregnancy?
  • What impact does pregnancy have on the patient’s future health?
  • What impact does the pregnancy have on the health of the child with whom they were pregnant?

Notes:

What recommendations do you have?

What impact do her pregnancies have on her future health?

What impact does the pregnancy of a child’s mother have on their future health?

Page 2

Objectives

  • Identify risk factors for molar pregnancy
  • Identify risk factors for gestational trophoblastic disease
  • Describe initial workup and management for patients with molar pregnancy
  • Describe initial workup and management for patients with gestational

trophoblastic disease

  • Discuss pathology and pathophysiology of molar pregnancy
  • Discuss pathology and pathophysiology of gestational trophoblastic disease
Page 3

Case Presentation

A 16-year-old G1P0 presents to the hospital with vaginal bleeding and

passage of tissue from the vagina. Her LMP was about 14 weeks ago. She

has been experiencing nausea and vomiting. She has not yet established

prenatal care.

She has no prior medical or surgical history. Family history is unremarkable.

On examination, her heart rate is 115. Her fundus is palpable on

examination to the level of the umbilicus. Pelvic exam is pertinent for

vesicular tissue in the vaginal fornix along with a scant amount of vaginal

bleeding. Nursing is unable to obtain fetal heart tones.

Laboratory testing reveals hCG level of 478,000.

Molar pregnancy: Risk Factors

  • Extremes of age (<15 yo or >45 yo)
  • Risk is 5–10 times greater for > 45 yo
  • History of prior molar pregnancy
  • Second molar pregnancy: risk 1–2% (vs 0.1%)
  • Third molar pregnancy: risk 15–20%
  • Risk is much higher after a complete mole
  • Nulliparity
  • Familial recurrent hydatidiform mole syndrome (FRHM)
  • Autosomal recessive NLRP7 mutation
  • Incidence: 1-2/1000 pregnancies in western countries
  • (2-3 times higher in Asia, Brazil, India)

Case Presentation

A 45-year-old G3P1011 presents to the hospital with vaginal bleeding. Her

LMP was about 6 weeks ago. She has been experiencing nausea. She has

not yet established prenatal care.

She has no prior medical or surgical history. Family history is unremarkable.

She has a history of one prior spontaneous abortion and one prior full term

vaginal delivery

On examination, her heart rate is 105. Pelvic exam is pertinent for a

moderate amount of vaginal bleeding.

Laboratory testing reveals hCG level of 45,000.

Molar Pregnancy: Treatment 101

  • Medical management (e.g., misoprostol, mifepristone) ineffective, risks

hemorrhage, and progression to GTN requiring chemotherapy

  • Simple hysterectomy is alternative if fertility is not desired (especially if age >40yo)
  • RhoGam if needed
  • Contraception – what kind? Why is this critical?
  • Follow hCG levels to zero and trend for ~6 months given risk of progression to

invasive disease / choriocarcinoma

  • Managed by an OB/GYN

Beta hCG and TSH

  • Because of the super elevated level of beta

Page 24

Beta hCG and TSH

  • Elevated circulating levels of hCG seen in complete molar

pregnancy can increase T4 secretion, which, in turn,

suppresses TSH.

  • hCG and TSH receptors exhibit similar homology of

approximately 70% for the transmembrane domain and

45% for the extracellular domains of the receptors.

  • Hyperthyroidism is known to be associated with GTDs

because of this cross-reactivity and significantly higher and

sustained β-hCG levels compared to normal pregnancy.

Page 25

Gestational Trophoblastic Disease: Epidemiology

  • 80% of molar pregnancies do not progress to invasive disease
  • Most go on to have normal subsequent pregnancies without cancer
  • 20% progress to invasive disease:
  • Locally invasive
  • Metastatic
  • Molar Pregnancy
  • Baseline incidence = 0.001%
  • Risk of recurrence after 1 mole= 1%
  • Risk of recurrence after 2 subsequent moles = 23%
Page 26

Malignant Gestational Trophoblastic Disease

  • Managed by a gynecologic oncologist
  • Three types of malignant histology:
  • Persistent / invasive moles (75%)
  • Choriocarcinoma (25%)
  • Placental Site Trophoblastic Tumor (<1%, extremely rare)
  • Epithelioid trophoblastic tumor (ETT) (<1%, even rarer)
Page 27

Who Gets Invasive Disease?

  • Of those who have malignant GTD…
  • 50% had an antecedent molar pregnancy
  • 25% had an antecedent normal pregnancy
  • 25% had an antecedent abortion or ectopic

pregnancy

Invasive Mole

  • Most commonly arises after a molar pregnancy
  • Presentation:
  • Plateauing or rising hCG after a molar pregnancy;
  • May present as abnormal uterine bleeding
  • Can spontaneously regress
  • Rarely metastasize
  • Incidence 1/15,000 pregnancies

and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. Eighth Edition. Philadelphia, PA: Saunders ElSevier; 2010.

Treatment: chemotherapy (methotrexate)

Fertility can be spared

Where else have you seen methotrexate used?

Page 29

Methotrexate

  • How does methotrexate work?
  • Folate antimetabolite that inhibits DNA synthesis,

repair, and cellular replication.

  • Binds to and inhibits dihydrofolate reductase
  • Inhibits formation of purine and thymidylic acid

synthesis

  • Interfers with DNA synthesis, repair, and cellular

replication.

  • Methotrexate is cell cycle specific for the S phase of

the cycle.

  • Actively proliferative tissues are more susceptible to

the effects of methotrexate.

https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/325549

Page 30

Choriocarcinoma

  • Hematogenous spread, vascular invasion
  • Lungs, Vagina, Pelvis
  • Brain, Liver, Intestines
  • A rare metastatic cancer that can be cured
  • Elevated beta hCG (tumor marker)
  • Arises after a normal pregnancy, abortion, or ectopic

pregnancy

  • Presentation: late post-partum bleeding
  • If arises from gestational pathway (this one!)
  • Chemo-sensitive
  • Ovarian germ cell pathway
  • Chemo-resistant
  • Treated with multi-agent chemotherapy; fertility spared

Ellenson LH & Pirog EC. The Female Genital Tract. In Kumar V, Abbas AK, Fausto N, et al. In Robbins

and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. Eighth Edition. Philadelphia, PA: Saunders ElSevier; 2010.

Page 31

Side-note: Non-Gestational Choriocarcinoma

  • Extremely rare
  • Germ cell tumor (ovaries and testes)
  • Can’t distinguish gestational vs non-gestational on IHC or tumor markers-

need tumoral genetics

  • Ovarian: poor prognosis. Do not respond to chemo.
  • You can also technically have a gestational choriocarcinoma of the ovary

(metastasis or ovarian pregnancy)

Page 32

Placental-Site Trophoblastic Tumor

(PSTT)

  • Rare (<2%) of GTN
  • Neoplasm of intermediate trophoblasts

(normally found at the implantation site)

  • Presentation:
  • Uterine mass
  • Abnormal uterine bleeding or amenorrhea
  • Moderately elevated hCG
  • 85% have local disease (excellent prognosis)

Ellenson LH & Pirog EC. The Female Genital Tract. In Kumar V, Abbas AK, Fausto N, et al. In Robbins

and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. Eighth Edition. Philadelphia, PA: Saunders ElSevier; 2010.

Page 33

Placental Site Trophoblastic Tumor (PSTT)

  • Not usually post-molar
  • Often diagnosed 18 mos after term pregnancy
  • Slow growing
  • Those with local disease are cured with

hysterectomy +/- lymphadenectomy

  • High risk disease may require adjuvant multi-

agent chemo

  • Metastases are rare, but treated with debulking

and multiagent chemo

  • Less sensitive to chemo
  • About 15% die of disease
Page 34

Epithelioid trophoblastic tumor (ETT)

  • Extremely rare
  • Incidence: 0.1 per 100,000 deliveries
  • +hCG (<3000 mIU/ml)
  • Arise from chorionic-type intermediate trophoblast cells
  • Not usually post-molar (avg 6 yrs post preg)

Pathologic Features:

  • Nodular growth, deep invasion
  • Mild nuclear atypia
  • “geographic necrosis”
  • Treated with surgery (hysterectomy) +/- multiagent chemotherapy
  • Metastasis in 25%
  • Less sensitive to chemo
  • Half die of disease

Slide 2: Objectives
  • Learn relevant anatomy and embryology of adrenal glands
  • Understand pathophysiology of adrenal insufficiency and treatment
  • Define polyglandular autoimmune syndromes
  • Understand steroid synthesis pathways and pathology of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) 1
  • Describe the varying clinical features of CAH and how they relate to hormonal abnormalities.2
  • Understand hormonal causes of hypertension – Primary hyperaldosteronism and pheochromocytoma
  • Describe the genetic features, cellular origins, and presentation and treatment of pheochromocytoma.3
  • 4
Slide 3
  • The adrenal gland comprises 2 distinct tissues: the outer cortex and the inner medulla. It weighs about 5 gm.
Slide 4: Embryology
  • In the 5th week of development, an isolated cluster of cells emerges within the urogenital ridge, identified as the adrenal-gonadal primordial germ cells.
  • The Adrenal cortex and medulla have different embryologic origins.
  • By week 8 -
  • The adrenal cortex is derived from mesoderm.
  • The adrenal medulla derives from neural crest (ectoderm).
  • So it produces the neurotransmitters norepinephrine and epinephrine
  • The gland is not mature at birth,
  • and evolves over the first 4 years of life into its adult form
Slide 5
  • The names of these zones can also be recalled by remembering "GFR" for glomerulosa, fasciculata, and reticularis.
Slide 6: Adrenal cortex
  • The adrenal cortex is much larger than the smaller medulla, accounting only for approximately 15% of the gland. It is composed of 3 distinct zones:
  • Zona Glomerulosa -- Aldosterone synthesis under ACTH, regulated by Renin
  • The zona glomerulosa (outer layer) synthesizes mineralocorticoids, the most important of which is aldosterone. This hormone plays an important role in electrolyte balance and blood pressure regulation.
  • Zona Fasciculata --under ACTH control
  • The zona fasciculata (middle layer) produces glucocorticoids, the predominant hormone being cortisol. This hormone regulates blood sugar via gluconeogenesis, modulates the immune system, and regulates the metabolism of fat, protein, and carbohydrates. Cortisol secretion is regulated by the adrenocorticotropic hormone, which is released from the pituitary gland.
  • Zona Reticularis—under ACTH control
  • The zona reticularis (inner zone) produces androgens and plays a role in the development of secondary sexual characteristics. The primary androgen produced in the zona reticularis is dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), which is the most abundant hormone in the body. It serves as a precursor for synthesizing many other hormones the adrenal gland produces, such as progesterone, estrogen, cortisol, and testosterone.
Slide 8: Adrenal medulla
  • The adrenal medulla synthesizes catecholamines.
  • Once norepinephrine has been created, it is then methylated via phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT), which is only present in the adrenal medulla to epinephrine. In the adrenal gland, norepinephrine and dopamine act mainly as precursor molecules to adrenaline, but in neurons and the central nervous system, they have their own unique roles as important neurotransmitters.
  • Adrenal medulla
  • Protein-rich foods, including meats, poultry, fish, dairy products, and certain nuts and seeds.
Slide 10: Adrenal medulla
Slide 11: spinal cord's lateral horn from the T5–T8 spinal cord segments.
  • 2. Some fibers of the greater splanchnic nerve circumvent the celiac ganglion and directly enter the adrenal gland to synapse at the chromaffin cells' membranes. This is why the adrenal medulla acts as a neuroendocrine junction between the 2 physiological segments. The chromaffin cells release their neurohormones directly into the bloodstream to produce a widespread sympathetic response
  • Spinal cord's lateral horn from the T5–T8 spinal cord segments.
Slide 12
  • The venous drainage from the adrenal glands is dependent on the side of the gland. The left adrenal gland is anatomically further away from the inferior vena cava; therefore, the left adrenal vein drains into the left renal vein. The right adrenal vein is much closer to the inferior vena cava and drains directly into this large vessel.
Slide 13: Adrenal ( Adrenocortical) insufficiency- Addison's disease
  • 32 year man presents with weight loss of 15 pds, skin darkening in spite of staying out of sun, poor appetite, dizziness and fatigue. Non smoker.
  • Labs- Glucose – normal , Na normal , K mild high 5.5, Renal function normal.
  • 8 am cortisol 4 mcg/dl ( low) and ACTH is 500( high)
  • TSH 6 mild high , with low FT4 and + Thyroperoxidase ab
Slide 14: Causes
Slide 15
  • Primary adrenal insufficency - Hyperpigmentation of skin (elbows and palmarcreases) and tongue – pigmented fungiform papillae
Slide 17
  • Causes of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison’s Disease)
  • 1. Autoimmune Adrenocortical Insufficiency – positive 21 hydroxylase antibodies
  • Most common cause;
  • Adrenal glands are small and atrophic
  • Frequently accompanied by other immune disorders as described above (APS-2)
  • Adrenal Hemorrhage – observed in patients that have been taking anti-coagulant therapy or are predisposed to thrombosis
  • Infections – Tuberculosis is a common cause in countries outside the US; systemic fungal infection (and treatment with antifungal agents that inhibit adrenal cytochrome P450 steroidogenic enzymes); HIV/AIDS,
  • Metastatic adrenal disease – adrenal glands are common sites of metastasis for lung, GI, breast, and renal neoplasia; non-Hodgkin and Hodgkin lymphoma
  • Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) – autosomal recessive genetic defect in one of the adrenal enzymes involved in synthesizing adrenal steroid hormones from cholesterol
Slide 18
  • Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome (APS), Type II (also known as Polyglandular Autoimmune Syndrome, or PGAS) – heterogeneous group of diseases of the immune system which may lead to inflammatory damage of various endocrine glands
  • About 1 in 7 people have Type II APS; In addition to type 1 diabetes, they develop thyroid disease, malfunctioning adrenal glands and sometimes other immune disorders.
  • Type II APS is characterized by AI (100% frequency), hypothyroidism/hyperthyroidism (69%), and type 1 (52%) diabetes. Usually occurs in adults; peak incidence is age 30, and occurs more often in women
  • Monitor for premature menopause
Slide 20
  • What is a cosyntropin stimulation test? Evaluate adrenal corticosteroid insuff
  • Rationale: Cosyntropin, (ACTH 1-24), consists of the first 24 amino acids of the N-terminal portion of the intact native ACTH molecule (ACTH 1-36).
Slide 21: Treatment
  • PRIMARY ADRENAL INSUFF:
  • Corticosteroids – Hydrocortisone 10-15 mg am and 5-10 mg late afternoon, Prednisone 5 mg daily , dexamethasone
  • AND
  • Mineralocorticoid – Fludrocortisone 0.1 to 0.2 mg daily as entire cortex is destroyed
  • Sick day advice- doubling of steroids when ill or during emergency
  • Caution: starting Thyroid hormone therapy prior to replacement of glucocorticoids can precipitate acute adrenal insufficiency and crisis.
Slide 22: Addison's crisis
  • Acute adrenal crisis is precipitated by
  • Missed steroid doses/ abrupt steroid withdrawal
  • Infections/ MI/ surgery etc
  • Symptoms: Hypotension, Tachycardia, vomiting/ abdominal pain/electrolyte changes( low Na/ High K, low glucose)
  • Treatment: Immediate..
  • IV Fluids- Normal saline till BP is normal
  • IV high dose steroids
Slide 23: Secondary Adrenal insufficiency
  • Commonest cause -
  • Abrupt withdrawal of exogenous steroids (injections, pills etc)
  • Pituitary adenoma/ lesions or post surgical/ post radiation
  • Hypophysitis – inflammation, cancer immunotherapy, post partum etc
  • Labs – ACTH and cortisol are both low
  • SECONDARY ADRENAL INSUFF: Only corticosteroid replacement is needed
Slide 24: Do not abruptly stop long term steroids
  • Withdrawal of Glucocorticoids. The abrupt withdrawal from prolonged use of glucocorticoid drugs like prednisone is the most common cause of AI overall.
  • Glucocorticoid drugs act like endogenous cortisol to suppress the HPA axis (lower CRH and ACTH secretion). Over time, the low ACTH levels lead to adrenal atrophy and insufficiency (secondary AI), so the gland cannot make cortisol. As long as patients take the glucocorticoid drug, they will appear normal or have signs of hypercortisolism (Cushing syndrome) like moon facies and mood swings. But, if the drug is abruptly stopped, the suppressed ACTH secretion and insufficient adrenal gland cannot produce enough cortisol to maintain body functions, and signs of hypocortisolism can occur, including nausea, vomiting, hypotension, and hypoglycemia.
  • Steroids are anti-inflammatory.
  • Creams
  • Injections
  • Pills
Slide 25: Cushing syndrome
  • 42 yr woman with DM2 , HTN, complains that she is unable to lose weight in spite of dieting. She has a h/o irregular menses, and is seeing a therapist for depression. She also had an ankle fracture few years ago.
  • Exam – 150/100, Skin – facial acne, purple striae in abdomen, central abdominal obesity with some fat padding of neck.
  • Labs- Na/renal function normal , Mild low potassium, A1c 10,
  • 11 pm salivary cortisol high
  • 1 pm low dose dexamethasone suppression test – 2.5 and 4 mcg/dl ( high)
  • 24 h Urine Free Cortisol – 100 mcg/dl ( high)
  • Bone density is low
Slide 26: What is the difference between Cushing Syndrome and Cushing Disease?
  • Cushing syndrome is a constellation of symptoms and physical features due to chronic glucocorticoid excess -from any source - pituitary, adrenal, ectopic or exogenous.
  • Cushing disease – term is used when cortisol excess is due to excess ACTH secretion from a pituitary source.
Slide 27
  • Clinical features of Cushing Syndrome? THE MECHANISMS BEHIND THE CLINICAL FEATURES
  • Central obesity/ Buffalo hump (90% prevalence)--redistribution of fat
  • skin changes-
  • Atrophy of epidermis and connective tissue leads to skin thinning, easy bruising , purple striae > 1 cm due to bleeding dermal vessels,
  • reduced fibroblast activity
  • Acne due to excess Cortisol or hyperandrogenism.
  • High cortisol reduces immunity - recurrent infections
  • High risk of blood clots, MI
  • Hypertension (85%) esp diastolic due to increased Na/ H20 retention
  • Proximal muscle weakness (65%) due to loss of muscle mass and body protein
  • Glucose intolerance or diabetes mellitus (75%) due to insulin resistance
  • Menstrual irregularities, decreased libido or impotence (70-85%) due to high androgens and cortisol.
  • Depression or psychosis (85%)
  • Low bone mass (85%) and Osteoporosis due to excess calcium loss in urine, increased osteoclast / reduced osteoblast action, poor calcium absorption etc
  • Hirsutism – excess hair growth (75%) due to hypersecretion of adrenal androgens
  • Reduced linear growth in kids
Slide 30: Causes of Cushing syndrome
  • ACTH-dependent = Pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease 80%) or nonpituitary neoplasm (ectopic ACTH- small cell cancer lung etc)
  • ACTH-independent = Iatrogenic (glucocorticoid use), Adrenal neoplasm (adenoma, carcinoma), or nodular adrenal hyperplasia
  • Pseudo- Cushing- Clinically similar to Cushing syndrome , but tests are nonconclusive. It seen in people with chronic alcoholism, depression etc.
Slide 32: Testing - 3
  • There are 3 tests that are used for diagnosis. If one test is abnormal, it is recommended to confirm with another test and also to repeat the test 1. Low dose 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test Rationale is that Dexamethasone should suppress plasma cortisol in healthy subjects to less than 1.8 ug/dL following an overnight 1 mg test. Dexamethasone provides negative feedback to the HPA axis, thus blocking production of natural corticoids as the binding of dexamethasone to glucocorticoid receptors in hypothalamus –this inhibits corticotropin-releasing hormone, which blocks ACTH secretion. 2. 24-hr urinary cortisol – A 24 hour urine free cortisol level reflects the cortisol secretion throughout an entire day. . 3. Late night salivary cortisol test – This is one of the most sensitive diagnostic tests for Cushing’s syndrome. Elevated cortisol between 11:00 p.m. and midnight appears to be the earliest detectable abnormality in many patients
Slide 33
  • ACTH-Independent (Adrenals) = ACTH level <5 pg/mL
  • ACTH-Dependent (ACTH Tumors) = ACTH level > 10 pg/mL . ACTH secreting tumors are not responsive to negative feedback.
  • Surgical therapy offered first line.
  • Step 1
  • Step 2
Slide 34: Treatment
  • Exogenous (iatrogenic) disease is treated by lowering the glucocorticoid dose or removing the drug, if possible. The drug should be tapered off, not stopped abruptly, to avoid acute adrenal insufficiency.
  • Pituitary adenomas can be surgically resected.
  • Adrenal adenomas and bilateral adrenal hyperplasia are treated with adrenalectomy, sometimes along with drugs that inhibit the synthesis of cortisol; such medicines include metyrapone, ketoconazole, and mitotane.
  • Ectopic cancers are located and treated surgically or with chemotherapy, depending on the cancer. Cortisol-reducing drugs can be used in cancer for unresectable metastatic disease.
Slide 35: Aldosterone excess- Primary hyperaldosteronism
  • Aldosterone producing adenoma
  • or bilateral hyperplasia
  • Labs- High aldosterone and Low renin
  • Difficult to control HTN , hypokalemia
  • Treatment -
  • Medical :Spironolactone, eplerenone
  • ( aldosterone receptor antagonist)
  • Improve myocardial remodeling
  • Surgical removal after localization
  • Aldosterone is secreted from the zona glomerulosa under the primary control of angiotensin II, potassium, and corticotropin (ACTH).
  • The secretion of aldosterone is restricted to the zona glomerulosa because of zonal-specific expression of aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2)
  • Aldosterone causes the renal tubules to increase the reabsorption of sodium and water into the blood, while at the same time causing the excretion of potassium (to maintain electrolyte balance). This increases the volume of extracellular fluid in the body, which also increases blood pressure.
Slide 36: Adrenal cancer - rare
  • Usually present with symptoms of excess adrenal androgen precursors- virilization, voice changes, weight loss etc
  • CT/ PET scan etc
  • If adrenal biopsy needed – Rule out pheochromocytoma first (make sure catecholamines are negative)
  • Treatment- Chemotherapy, radiation
Slide 37: Adrenal medulla - Pheochromocytoma
  • A pheochromocytoma is a rare neuroendocrine tumor of adrenal medulla.
  • The tachycardia is caused by β1-adrenergic stimulation.
  • α1-Adrenergic–mediated vasoconstriction can cause patients to appear pale (pallor).
  • The sweating/ flushing - is in response to the increased thermogenesis and vasoconstriction.
  • Symptoms – Paroxysmal HTN, Tachycardia, sweating, tachycardia, flushing
  • 90% Intra adrenal, 10 % bilateral, 10% metastatic , 10 % extra –adrenal
  • Labs
  • 24 hour urine catecholamines and metabolites – normetanephrine and metanephrines are increased
  • Plasma free metanephrines – sensitive test – usually used for screening
Slide 38
  • Genetics
  • About 30% to 40% of pheochromocytomas arise from an inherited gene mutation, and another 20% come from a somatic mutation that occurs after birth. Most of these mutations are random, but some happen as part of an inherited syndrome.
  • The most common distinct inherited syndromes are the multiple endocrine neoplasia 2 (MEN2) syndrome with RET gene mutations, neurofibromatosis type 1 with NF1 mutations, and the Von Hippel-Lindau disease with VHL mutations. Because of these, genetic testing is an important part of the evaluation of people with pheochromocytoma.
Slide 39
  • Cellular Origins
  • These epithelial tumors arise from neuroendocrine cells, which are hormone-secreting cells with glandular and neural features. During normal fetal development, neural crest cells migrate to the adrenal medulla and sympathetic chain ganglia near the vertebral column. The adrenal chromaffin cells are derived from a neural crest and normally secrete catecholamines to support BP. Pheochromocytomas arise from these chromaffin cells.
  • Histology
  • This neoplasm is composed largely of polygonal/spindle cells arranged in nests within a rich vascular network The nuclei of the cells are oval to round and frequently contain prominent nucleoli. The cytoplasm is red-purple.
Slide 40
  • An alpha-adrenergic blocker like phenoxy benzamine , Doxazocin ( selective) followed by beta blocker or calcium channel blockers is given for at least seven days preoperatively to normalize blood pressure and expand the contracted intravascular space.
  • A minimally invasive approach to the adrenal gland is the procedure of choice
Slide 42: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) is a group of autosomal recessive genetic disorders that affect the adrenal glands, leading to deficiencies in the production of cortisol
Slide 43: CAH
  • Publication of Luigi De Crecchio’s classic, Sopra un Caso di Apparenze Virili in una Donna (A Case Report of Masculine Appearance in a Woman) in Il Morgagni. The paper is generally regarded as the first detailed report of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH), describing the autopsy and life of Giuseppe Marzo, who lived as a man but had internal female anatomy and enlarged adrenals, and died in an apparent Addisonian crisis at the age of 44 years.
  • ENDOCRINOLOGY VOL 156, Issue 4 , April 2015
Slide 44
  • Biology of Reproduction, Volume 101, Issue 3, September 2019
  • Y chromosome
  • Fetal testes- Testosterone
  • Anti Mullerian Factor – regression of Mullerian duct
Slide 45: In tandem...
  • Endocrine reviews Aug 2019 Vol40, issue 4
Slide 47: CAH
  • ACTH stimulation is needed for adrenal steroidogenesis.
  • Some of the intermediate precursors like 11-deoxycortisol and androstenedione are active hormones as well. They normally circulate at much lower levels. But in CAH, because of enzymatic blocks, the levels of these precursors can go up in the blood, causing hormonal effects.
Slide 48: 21 hydroxylase deficiency
  • Genetic Basis:
  • The CYP21A2 gene is located on the short arm of chromosome 6. The most common mechanisms leading to defects in this gene are large deletions and gene conversion, which are exchanges of genetic material between CYP21A2 and its pseudogene, CYP21A1P.
  • Inheritance Pattern:
  • Because it's autosomal recessive, parents who are heterozygous (one normal and one mutated CYP21A2 copy) can be carriers and may not exhibit symptoms themselves. When two carriers have a child, there's a 25% chance of the child inheriting two mutated copies and being affected, a 50% chance of inheriting one normal and one mutated copy and being a carrier, and a 25% chance of inheriting two normal copies and being unaffected.
  • Clinical Significance:
  • The amount of functional 21-hydroxylase enzyme determines the severity of the disorder. In salt-wasting CAH, the deficiency of aldosterone leads to sodium loss and dehydration, while in simple virilizing CAH, cortisol deficiency leads to androgen excess.
  • Diagnosis:
  • Very high 17-OHP levels in the blood are a key diagnostic tool, with high levels indicating a potential diagnosis of 21-hydroxylase deficiency. However, comprehensive CYP21A2 genotyping remains the gold standard for confirmation.
Slide 49
  • Endocrine reviews Aug 2019, Vol 40 issue 4
Slide 50: 21 hydroxylase deficiency
  • Newborn screening programs that test for 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels, which are elevated in CAH
  • Incidence of 21 hydroxylase def - Commonest
  • Classic (salt wasting) 1 in 15,000
  • Non classic/ Simple virilizing 1 in 1000
  • The "salt-wasting" form of the disorder (most severe) is most often associated with large deletions or mutations that result in no enzyme activity. Seventy-five percent of patients with classic 21OHD have this form.
  • Twenty-five percent of patients with classic 21OHD have the "simple-virilizing" form (less severe) with low but detectable enzyme activity (1 to 2 percent) that supports some aldosterone production. This form most commonly results from point mutations leading to nonconservative amino acid substitutions such as Ile172Asp. A mutation in intron 2 that variably impairs splicing (g.A/C656G) manifests with a range of classic 21OHD phenotypes.
  • Individuals with the nonclassic form (least severe) retain 5 to 20 percent of normal enzymatic activity
  • Nonclassic 21OHD may present as early pubarche or sexual precocity in school-age children, hirsutism and menstrual irregularity in young women, or there may be no symptoms.
Slide 51: 21 hydroxylase def
Slide 52
  • September 23, 2020
  • N Engl J Med 2020;383:1248-1261
Slide 53: Clinical presentation
  • 46,XX infants with classic 21OHD are typically born with atypical genitalia characterized by clitoral enlargement , labial fusion, and formation of a urogenital sinus
  • Males – 46,XY infants with classic CAH have normal-appearing genitalia at birth but may have subtle findings such as hyperpigmentation of the scrotum or an enlarged phallus.
  • Males with the salt-wasting form who are not identified by neonatal screening may present with failure to thrive, dehydration, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia and hyperkalemia typically at 7 to 14 days of life (Adrenal crisis)
  • Adults in both – present with early puberty, short stature, fertility issues. Adult male can have testicular adrenal rest tumors
Slide 54: CAH treatment
  • Glucocorticoid therapy – In adults with classic 21OHD, glucocorticoid therapy is required to treat cortisol deficiency, optimize reproductive function and, in females, minimize hyperandrogenic symptoms. Hydrocortisone therapy often achieves these goals and imparts lower risk of long-term complications than longer-acting glucocorticoids.
  • Mineralocorticoid therapy – Fludrocortisone therapy is needed to treat mineralocorticoid deficiency
  • As with any form of adrenal insufficiency, patients with classic 21OHD should be provided with sick-day rules for stress dosing, medical alert identification, and injectable hydrocortisone sodium succinate (or other injectable glucocorticoid) for emergencies . At each visit, we verify that patients always wear or carry a medical alert identifier and have an unexpired emergency glucocorticoid injection kit.
  • Glucocorticoid dose adjustment during acute stress – An increase in glucocorticoid dose is critical during acute physiologic stress including illness or surgery.
Slide 55
  • Crinicerfont – To suppress CRF and then ACTH.
  • Given with steroids
Slide 56: Other CAH
  • The hallmarks of 17OHD, include hypertension and hypokalemia due to the accumulation of cortisol precursors with mineralocorticoid activity upstream of the block, plus sexual infantilism due to inability to synthesize androgens and estrogens.
  • Clinical presentation — The classic presentation of severe 17OHD in phenotypic females (who can have 46,XX or 46,XY karyotype) includes :
  • Hypertension- early adulthood, severe.
  • Primary amenorrhea
  • Absence of secondary sexual characteristics
  • ( XY Males – out 1/3 vaginal pouch, XX female –rudeimentary uterus, cervix and upper part vagina)
  • CYP17A1 gene codes for both 17 a hydroxylase and 17,20 lyase

Slide 2: Objectives
  • Explain the histology and function of the islets of Langerhans.2
  • Explain insulin and glucagon synthesis and sites of production.3
  • Explain the physiologic actions of insulin and glucagon.4
  • Explain the regulation of insulin and glucagon release.
  • Identify insulin target tissues and relevant physiological effects of insulin secretion
  • Understand the etiology and risk factors for type 1 and type 2 diabetes
  • Describe the pathophysiology and symptoms of type 1 and type 2 diabetes
  • Describe the mechanistic basis for changes in vital signs and electrolytes in patients with DKA
  • Discuss the acute management of DKA and potential complications associated with treatment
  • Define normoglycemia and outline the diagnostic criteria for diabetes
  • Describe hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS)
  • Discuss the long-term management and treatment of type 1 and type 2 diabetes and it's complications
Slide 3: Pancreas
  • Exocrine 80%
  • Endocrine - Dysfunction causes disturbance in nutrient homeostasis
  • The pancreas has tiny glands called islets of Langerhans, which
  • secrete hormones.
  • Alpha cells- Glucagon
  • Beta cells- Insulin and its precursors
  • Delta cell- somatostatin
  • Epsilon cell- ghrelin ( predominantly Ghrelin is produced from stomach)
  • PP cells- pancreatic polypeptide
Slide 4
  • He identified nine different cell types: one in particular greatly fascinated him. It was a “small, irregularly polygonal structure. Its cytoplasm is brilliant and free of any granules. Its nucleus distinct, round and moderate size…these cells lie together generally in considerable numbers, diffusely scattered” throughout the pancreas.--Royal Canadian Institute for Science
Slide 6
  • Insulin release is stimulated by parasympathetic stimulation.
  • Glucagon release is stimulated by sympathetic activation.
Slide 7: Insulin is a peptide hormone
  • Preproinsulin is cleaved to form proinsulin, which is broken into insulin + C peptide in equimolar amounts
  • Secretion :Human pancreas makes about 30 units/day.
  • Basal=10 units, constantly made in tiny amount.
  • Why? Insulin is an anabolic hormone- necessary for life.
  • Prandial- rest is produced after meal ingestion. Glucose is the most potent stimulator.
Slide 8: Insulin – Anabolic hormone
  • The normal fasting glucose level is 60 to 100 mg/dL. Maintaining this normal level is important
  • After a glucose load, the level of blood glucose increases. The excess glucose signals the endocrine pancreas to secrete insulin, which promotes glucose storage in the liver and muscles. This stored glycogen is the primary short-term storage form of glucose.
  • When the liver is saturated with glycogen, any additional glucose taken up by hepatocytes is instead converted to fatty acids, which enter the blood as lipoproteins. These can provide free fatty acids for adipocytes. The adipocytes are stimulated by insulin to take up glucose and convert it to glycerol. In the adipocyte, this glycerol combines with the free fatty acid to make triglycerides, stored in the adipocyte for future energy use. So insulin leads to storage: liver glycogen and adipocyte triglycerides.
Slide 9: Insulin secretion
  • Glut 2 for glucose sensing at pancreas.
  • Glut 4 for glucose uptake in fat and muscle.
Slide 10
  • Hormone Transport and Receptor Binding
  • After synthesis in the islet cells as water-soluble peptide hormones, both insulin and glucagon travel unbound in the circulation to their target cells. Three primary actions occur next:
  • Insulin stimulates glucose uptake into cells.
  • Glucose Uptake. Insulin is a storage hormone that facilitates the conversion of glucose to glycogen, fat, and other storable substances. To do this, insulin binds to target cells by using the insulin receptor, a receptor tyrosine kinase
Slide 11: Glucose uptake
  • Autophosphorylation of tyrosine residues starts the signaling pathway, which ends with glucose transporter type 4 (GLUT4) moving to the cell membrane. This allows glucose to enter the cell by using facilitated diffusion down its concentration gradient. (Intracellular glucose levels are very low, since glucose is quickly metabolized). This pathway stimulates the formation of glycogen, lipids, and proteins in multiple cell types. Separately, another insulin-dependent pathway, the mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase pathway, promotes cell growth and DNA synthesis.
Slide 12: Glucagon is catabolic Glucagon stimulates glycogenolysis. Glucagon stimulates gluconeogenesis – production of glucose from non carbohydrates.
  • Glycogenolysis. Opposing the function of insulin, glucagon performs glycogenolysis—the breakdown of stored glycogen to provide glucose (and energy). This mainly occurs in the liver, where glucagon receptors are dense.
Slide 13: How do insulin and glucagon act together?
Slide 14: Diabetes Mellitus
  • Diabetes mellitus is a group of metabolic disorders of carbohydrate(fuel) metabolism in which glucose is both underutilized as an energy source and overproduced due to inappropriate gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, resulting in hyperglycemia
  • Dx in non pregnant adults

| OR |

Slide 15
  • Total: 38.4 million people have diabetes (11.6% of the U.S. population)
  • Diagnosed: 29.7 million people, including 29.4 million adults
  • Undiagnosed: 8.7 million people (22.8% of adults with diabetes are undiagnosed)

Slide 17: GLYCATION of Hb
  • Glycation of protein and lipids--- Advanced Glycation Endproducts.
  • AGE
  • Increase viscosity
  • Increase free radical damage to endothelium and vascular smooth muscle
Slide 18: Glycohemoglobin A1c
  • A1C reflects glucose bound to hemoglobin over the life span of the erythrocyte (∼120 days) and is thus a “weighted” average that is more heavily affected by recent blood glucose exposure.
  • A1C is an indirect measure of glucose exposure, and factors that affect hemoglobin concentrations or erythrocyte turnover can affect A1C (e.g., thalassemia or folate deficiency) . anemia, people treated with erythropoietin, or hemodialysis or HIV treatment

Slide 19: Monitoring
  • Using fingerstick blood glucose -
  • Using continuous glucose monitoring ( sensor)
  • CGM measures interstitial glucose which correlates well with plasma glucose
  • mean CGM glucose, correlates with A1C
  • TIME IN RANGE 70% ( SUGARS between 70-180) -- correlates with a1c of 7 approx
  • Time below range (<70 and <54 mg/dL and time above range (>180 mg/d])
  • are useful parameters
Slide 20
  • The Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT) , a prospective randomized controlled trial of intensive (mean A1C ∼7% [∼53 mmol/mol]) versus standard (mean A1C ∼9% [∼75 mmol/mol]) glycemic management in people with type 1 diabetes, showed definitively that better glycemic status is associated with 50–76% reductions in rates of development and progression of microvascular complications (retinopathy, neuropathy, and diabetic kidney disease)
Slide 21: Classification
  • 1. Type 1 diabetes (due to autoimmune β-cell destruction, usually leading to absolute insulin deficiency, including latent autoimmune diabetes in adults)
  • 2. Type 2 diabetes (due to a nonautoimmune progressive loss of adequate β-cell insulin secretion, frequently on the background of insulin resistance)
  • 3. Specific types of diabetes due to other causes, e.g., monogenic diabetes syndromes, diseases of the exocrine pancreas, and drug- or chemical-induced diabetes
  • 4. Gestational diabetes mellitus (diabetes diagnosed in the second or third trimester of pregnancy that was not clearly overt diabetes prior to gestation or other types of diabetes occurring throughout pregnancy, such as type 1 diabetes).
  • AABBCC approach: Age (e.g., for individuals <35 years old, consider type 1 diabetes); Autoimmunity (e.g., personal or family history of autoimmune disease or polyglandular autoimmune syndromes); Body habitus (e.g., BMI <25 kg/m); Background (e.g., family history of type 1 diabetes); Control (preferred term is “goal,” i.e., the inability to achieve glycemic goals on noninsulin therapies); and Comorbidities (e.g., treatment with immune checkpoint inhibitors for cancer can cause acute autoimmune type 1 diabetes)
  • Loss of pancreas tissue- pancreatitis, surgery etc – use insulin for therapy
Slide 23: Autoimmunity in type 1
  • Type 1 diabetes is immune- related in 95% of diabetes and is caused by autoimmune destruction of the pancreatic β-cells. Highest incidence in Scandinavians / Northern European descent.
  • Autoimmune markers include islet cell autoantibodies and autoantibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) (such as GAD65- seen in 75%), insulin, the tyrosine phosphatases islet antigen 2 (IA-2) and IA-2b, and zinc transporter 8 (ZnT8).
  • Cromosome 6 short arm- The disease has strong HLA associations, with linkage to the DQB1 and DRB1 haplotypes, and genetic screening has been used in some research studies to identify high-risk populations. Specific alleles in these genes can be either predisposing (e.g., DRB1*0301-DQB1*0201 [DR3-DQ2] and DRB1*0401-DQB1*0302 [DR4-DQ8])
  • Type 1 diabetes can be associated with polyglandular autoimmune syndromes-Hashimoto thyroiditis, Graves disease, celiac disease, Addison disease, vitiligo, autoimmune hepatitis, myasthenia gravis, and pernicious anemia
Slide 24: Genetics
  • Family members of type 1 diabetes have an increased lifetime risk of developing type 1
  • Offspring of mother - risk of 3%
  • Offspring a father - risk of 6%
  • Monozygotic twin studies show environmental factors Play a role - 50% genetic / 50% Environmental factors.
Slide 25
  • Diabetes 2005 Vol 54
Slide 26: CIADM
  • Introduction of immunotherapy, specifically checkpoint inhibitors, most commonly occurs with agents that block the programmed cell death protein 1/programmed cell death ligand 1 pathway for cancer treatment has led to unexpected adverse events, including immune system activation precipitating autoimmune disease.
  • Incidence 1%
  • Fulminant onset of type 1 diabetes can occur, with DKA and low or undetectable levels of C-peptide as a marker of endogenous β-cell function
Slide 27
  • Endocrine practice, Vol 30:issue 6
  • Diabetes care Vol 46: Issue 6
Slide 28: Hamen y León, Juan van der Madrid, 1596 - Madrid, 1631 See author's file Still Life with Sweetmeats and Glass Vessels
Slide 29
  • Type 2 diabetes accounts for 90–95% of all diabetes. This form encompasses individuals who generally have relative (rather than absolute) insulin deficiency and have insulin resistance (i.e., decreased biological responses to insulin like glucose uptake into skeletal muscle).
  • 60-80% of individuals with type 2 diabetes are obese (BMI >30)
  • Abdominal/visceral fat accumulation is tightly correlated with insulin resistance
  • Insulin resistance initially leads to a hyperinsulinemia state to compensate.
  • Lack of the ability for the pancreas to compensate (beta cell exhaustion)
  • leads to diagnosis of type 2 diabetes.
Slide 30: Leptin- Peripheral and central actions
  • Endocrine reviews Vol 42: Issue 1
Slide 31
  • Brain
  • Leptin from fat
  • Ghrelin from stomach/ duodenum
  • Satiety
  • Hunger
  • Ghrelin and leptin are two hormones that play opposing roles in regulating appetite and energy balance.
  • Ghrelin:
  • Function: Ghrelin is primarily known for stimulating appetite and increasing food intake.
  • Levels: Ghrelin levels tend to rise before a meal and decrease after eating.
  • Leptin:
  • Function: Leptin acts as a satiety signal, signaling the body that it has enough energy stored. It suppresses appetite and reduces food intake.
  • .
  • Ghrelin stimulates appetite, while leptin suppresses it.
  • Leptin levels are directly proportional to the amount of body fat.
  • Leptin Resistance: In some individuals, particularly those with obesity, the body can become resistant to leptin's effects, leading to continued hunger even with high leptin levels.
Slide 32: Metabolic syndrome
  • Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of medical conditions that increases the risk of heart disease, stroke, and type 2 diabetes.
  • It's diagnosed when a person has at least three of the following:
  • Conditions associated with Metabolic Syndrome:
  • High Blood Pressure: A reading of 130/85 mmHg or higher.
  • High Blood Sugar: Fasting glucose level of 100 mg/dL or higher.
  • Excess Abdominal Fat: Waist circumference of 40 inches or more for men and 35 inches or more for women.--Visceral fat linked to vascular disease
  • High Triglycerides: Fasting triglycerides level of 150 mg/dL or higher.
  • Low HDL (Good) Cholesterol: HDL cholesterol level less than 40 mg/dL in men or 50 mg/dL in women.
  • Acanthosis nigricans as an indicator for insulin resistance or diabetes
  • Characterized by velvety, papillomatous, hyperkeratotic, darkly pigmented skin lesions found in body folds such as the neck, axilla, and groin
  • High circulating insulin levels of insulin bind to the insulin like growth factor receptors in melanin containing skin cells which leads to skin hyperplasia with papillomatosis and hyperpigmentation.
Slide 33: Prevention of Type 2 DM- Diabetes prevention trial
  • In the DPP, weight loss was an important factor in reducing the risk of progression, with every kilogram of weight loss conferring a 16% reduction in risk of progression over 3.2 years
  • In the DPP, metformin was as effective as lifestyle modification in participants with BMI ≥35 kg/m2 and in younger participants aged 25–44 years . In individuals with a history of GDM in the DPP, metformin and intensive lifestyle modification led to an equivalent 50% reduction in diabetes risk . Both interventions remained highly effective during a 10-year follow-up period
  • Decreased vitamin B12 levels due to impaired absorption are a known consequence of long-term treatment with metformin . Periodic assessment of vitamin B12 level in those taking metformin chronically should be considered
  • Newer Therapies- GLP 1 agonists –
  • Semaglutide , Liraglutide etc
Slide 34: Symptoms
  • What are common symptoms for diabetes?
  • Polyuria – due to osmotic diuresis (glucose in blood attracts water; excess glucose is removed from blood by the kidneys and excreted via the urine, along with water and electrolytes) = hyperosmolar state (loss of water and high glucose/sodium)
  • Polydipsia – excessive thirst due to hyperosmolar state/ water loss
  • Polyphagia – increased hunger; due to lack of insulin and ability for glucose to enter cells. Body cannot convert glucose into usable source of energy.
  • Weight loss – despite normal or increased appetite; due to depletion of water, glycogen( glucose stores); skeletal muscle catabolism and conversion of amino acids to glucose via gluconeogenesis in the liver
  • Dizziness and weakness – due to dehydration, low BP, whole body potassium loss
  • High ketones contribute to nausea and vomiting (cause unknown), leading to decreased food and fluid intake, exacerbating hyperosmolar state. Ketones also result in sweet, fruity breath odor and increased respiratory compensation (Kussmaul respiration)
  • Hyperkalemia-induced cardiac arrhythmias...???
  • Blurry vision – due to exposure of lenses and retinas to hyperosmolar fluids,

Slide 40: DM Chronic Complications
Slide 42: Microvascular complications of diabetes mellitus—due to ischemia of vessels supplying endorgans
  • 1. Ophthalmology complications
  • Diabetic retinopathy-Type 1 diabetes for more than 5 years and all patients with type 2 diabetes should be referred to an ophthalmologist.
  • After 15 years 50% show some sign of retinopathy.
  • Non- proliferative / background retinopathy–The capillaries leak proteins,
  • lipids and red cells into the retina and when it occurs in the macula it is
  • called macular edema and compromises visual acuity.
  • Proliferative retinopathy - this involves a growth of new capillaries and fibrous tissue due to small vessel occlusion causing retinal hypoxia. This stimulates new vessel growth.
  • Cataracts -Glycosylation of lens proteins and excess of sorbitol from increased glucose accumulation leads to osmotic changes in the lens resulting in fibrosis and sclerosis ( cataract) formation.
  • Glaucoma – Increased intra ocular pressure, due to new vessel growth at angle of eye( drainage block) + increased fluid leak
Slide 44
  • Adults with type 1 diabetes should have an initial dilated and comprehensive eye examination by an ophthalmologist or optometrist within 5 years after the onset of diabetes.
  • People with type 2 diabetes should have an initial dilated and comprehensive eye examination by an ophthalmologist or optometrist at the time of the diabetes diagnosis.
  • To reduce the risk of vision loss
  • Panretinal laser photocoagulation therapy
  • Intravitreous injections of anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) --esp for macular edema
  • Macular focal/grid photocoagulation and intravitreal injections of corticosteroid
Slide 45: Renal complications
  • Diabetic nephropathy-Thickened capillary basement membranes of renal glomeruli results in glomerulosclerosis and renal insufficiency. This results in proteinuria.
  • Necrotizing papillitis - this occurs primarily in diabetic patients.
  • Presents with fever, pain and sloughing of the renal papillae.
  • Contrast induced diabetic renal failure- increase in serum
  • creatinine after exposure to IV contrast. This happens within a
  • week. Adequate hydration before a procedure is important
Slide 46

| Albumin Cr Ratio (mg/g) | <30 normal | 30 to 299- Mild increase | ≥300- Severe |

Slide 47: Neurology complications Peripheral Cranial Autonomic
Slide 48: Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy
  • The most common early symptoms are induced by the involvement of small fibers and include pain and dysesthesia (unpleasant sensations of burning and tingling).
  • The involvement of large fibers may cause balance issues, numbness, and loss of protective sensation (LOPS). LOPS indicates the presence of distal sensory polyneuropathy and is a risk factor for diabetic foot ulceration.
  • The following clinical tests may be used to assess small- and large-fiber function and protective sensation:
  • 1. Small-fiber function: pinprick and temperature sensation.
  • 2. Large-fiber function: lower-extremity reflexes, vibration perception. 128 MHz, and
  • 3. Protective sensation: 10-g monofilament.
  • The denervation of small muscles of the food results in clawed toes and displacement of fat pads
  • altering the biomechanics of the foot. This leads to calluses from repetitive injury and ulceration in high pressure
  • areas such as the metatarsal head. Finally this leads to bone loss and fractures and deformity called the
  • Charcot foot.
  • Gabapentin is a medication that inhibits the release of excitatory neurotransmitters
Slide 49
  • Cranial mononeuropathy: This can cause double vision, eye pain, or paralysis on one side of the face.
  • Focal neuropathies: These can cause pain in the thighs, lower back, or pelvis, or even mimic heart attack or appendicitis symptoms.
  • Entrapment neuropathies: These can cause numbness or weakness in the hands or feet.
  • Commonly affected nerves:
  • The oculomotor nerve (controls eye movement) is frequently affected in cranial mononeuropathy—Diplopia Other nerves that can be affected include the median nerve (causing finger weakness and numbness), and the peroneal nerve (causing foot drop).
Slide 50: Diabetic Autonomic Neuropathy
  • Individuals who have had type 1 diabetes for ≥5 years and all individuals with type 2 diabetes should be assessed annually for autonomic neuropathy
  • Major clinical manifestations of diabetic autonomic neuropathy include
  • resting tachycardia,
  • orthostatic hypotension,
  • gastroparesis, constipation, diarrhea, fecal incontinence,
  • erectile dysfunction,
  • neurogenic bladder, and
  • sudomotor dysfunction with either increased or decreased sweating.
Slide 51: Skin
  • Necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum-Oval plaques with the reddish
  • border and a glistening yellow surface due to thinning of dermis. Seen on
  • the anterior surfaces of legs. This happens due to degeneration of collagen
  • and granulomatous inflammation. More commonly associated with type 1
  • diabetes.
  • Bone and Joint complications
  • Dupytrne’s contractures -Fibrosis results in contracture of the Palmar
  • fascia producing flexion contractures of the fingers.
  • Carpal tunnel syndrome - when median nerve is compressed probably
  • due to glycosylation of collagen. Frozen shoulder due to adhesive capsulitis
  • in long standing diabetes.
  • Infections Picture source- wikipedia
Slide 52: Medical emergencies
  • DKA- Diabetic KetoAcidosis
  • HHS- Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State
  • Pathogenesis of DKA and HHS.
  • In HHS, compared with DKA, there is less severe insulin deficiency and, therefore, sufficient insulin to prevent ketogenesis but not enough to prevent hyperglycemia, due to increased hepatic glucose production and decreased glucose utilization by peripheral tissues. Hyperglycemia leads to an osmotic diuresis, leading to volume depletion
Slide 53: Precipitating factors
  • 25-30% of Type 1 DM present with DKA
  • Poor metabolic control or missed insulin doses – makes up the majority of cases; frequent among adolescents. Pump malfunction.
  • Infections - increased need for insulin.
  • Illness – stress hormones can increase hepatic glucose output and insulin resistance. Also, vomiting and dehydration can interrupt food intake, and patients sometimes omit insulin to avoid hypoglycemia. Occult MI
  • Medications – corticosteroids, atypical antipsychotics, and others
  • Pregnancy
  • Drugs and alcohol
Slide 55
  • Kussmaul’s breathing = hyperventilation characterized by constantly deep sighing respirations in a rapid manner. Generally noted in the last stages of severe acidosis/diabetic acidosis. Patients suffering from Kussmaul’s breathing become “air-hungry” and are seen desperately gasping for more air.
Slide 56: Diagnostic criteria
Slide 57: Clinical presentation
Slide 58: Diabetic ketoacidosis
  • 18 year girl presents with vomiting, epigastric pain. Vitals – HR 120, BP 100/60, Afebrile
  • Upon further history -polyuria and weight loss over 3 weeks. CT – negative for appendicitis or other acute conditions.
  • Labs
  • Glu 510, PH 7.2, HCO3 9, Na 130, K 5.5 , cr 1.8
  • Anion gap- HIGH 28
  • A1c 12%
  • Beta hydroxy butyrate 5.8 mmol/L – high
  • UA- +++ glucose, ++ ketones, pregnancy test negative, no infection
Slide 60: HHS
  • 70 yr woman with h/o type 2 DM, presents with cough ,confusion , lethargy, polyuria and dehydration over 4 days . She was given steroids for cough recently. Vitals show low BP 80/60, low grade fever and HR 120s
  • Labs-
  • Glucose 900, PH 7.3, Na corrected to glucose- 150, potassium normal,
  • Serum osmolality high, Mild renal failure,
  • urine glucose ++, ketones trace to negative , beta hydroxy butyrate negative, A1c 12%,
  • CXR- = Right lobe pneumonia
  • Effective Posm = [2 x Na (mEq/L)] + [glucose (mg/dL) ÷ 18]
  • Effective Posm = [2 x Na (mmol/L)] + glucose (mmol/L)
  • The Na concentration in these equations is the actual measured plasma Na concentration and not the corrected Na concentration.
Slide 61: MANAGEMENT
Slide 64
  • During DKA, much of it shifts out into the blood, causing hyperkalemia. This happens for three main reasons:
  • Insulin normally stimulates the Na+/K+-ATPase to pump potassium from the blood into cells, so a lack of insulin means this pump is inactive, raising the potassium level in the blood.
  • Hyperglycemia increases the serum osmolarity, pulling water out of all cells, and the potassium follows along (osmotic shift).
  • To buffer the decreased serum pH, the membrane H+/K+ exchanger brings extracellular H+ into the cell and pumps K+ out.
  • So, the total level of potassium is low in the patient’s body, but the initial level in the serum is high.
Slide 65: POTASSIUM
Slide 66
  • Type 1 Diabetic patient wants to start empagliflozin ( SGLT-2 inhibitor) as she had read good things about its cardiovascular benefits and her mother who is a 59-year-old Type 2 DM is taking it. You discourage its use in this patient due to risk of what complication?
  • a) Lactic acidosis
  • b) Ketoacidosis
  • c) Hypoglycemia
Slide 67: Euglycemic DKA
  • DKA with sugars under 250 – Acidosis+, PH is < 7.3 , dehydration
  • When –
  • Pregnancy – is a state of relative insulin deficiency despite normal or low blood glucose levels due to increased fetal consumption of glucose, and increase in stress hormones causing increased fat breakdown and ketone production, ultimately leading to EDKA.
  • SGLT2 inhibitors- Cause glycosuria and natriuresis causing dehydrationà increase stress hormones, lipolysis and ketogenesisà DKA with normal glucose
