Slide 2: Objectives
  • Understand anatomy , synthesis and regulation of Thyroid hormones
  • Able to identify relevant histopathology
  • Identify the various causes, pathophysiology and treatment of hyperthyroidism and hyperthyroid crisis
  • Understand the investigations associated with Thyroid disorders, nodules and thyroid cancer
  • Identify the pathophysiology and treatment of hypothyroidism , myxedema coma and understand pregnancy related changes.
  • Understand the presentations of primary hyperparathyroidism
Slide 3
  • Regulation of Thyroid Hormone
  • Thyrotropin-releasing hormone
  • (TRH) potently stimulates synthesis and release of thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) (or thyrotrophin) from anterior pituitary.
  • TSH induces thyroid hormone
  • production
  • Thyroid hormones provide
  • negative feedback
Slide 4
  • The thyroid arises from endoderm in the floor of the primitive mouth, just where the tongue forms. The follicular cell primordia arise in the midline, and the C cell primordia arise nearby from the fourth pharyngeal pouches. During fetal development, this endoderm descends from its original location to its final location in the neck. Initially, the thyroid is connected to the tongue via the thyroglossal duct. This duct atrophies, leaving only a small remnant, a tiny pit on the dorsum of the tongue called the foramen cecum.
  • Thyroglossal Duct Cyst. A portion of the thyroglossal duct may also persist as a midline neck mass
Slide 5
  • The inferior and superior thyroid arteries supply the thyroid gland.
  • The recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) is a branch of the vagus nerve that supplies all the intrinsic muscles of the larynx, except for the cricothyroid muscles. It plays an essential role in speech, swallowing, and breathing
Slide 6
  • Thyroid Gland Anatomy
  • Butterfly shaped gland (isthmus = body, two lobes attached)
  • Wraps around trachea just below
  • larynx
  • Largest endocrine gland
  • 20 grams, can become enlarged
  • Significant blood and nerve supply
Slide 7
  • Thyroid Gland Histology
  • Composed of numerous spherical follicles (variable size). Thyroid epithelial cells are arranged in follicles and produce thyroid hormones, which are stored in the lumen of the follicle (colloid)
  • Thyroid also contains parafollicular cells (C cells), which produce calcitonin
  • https://slideplayer.com/slide/10922862/
Slide 8
  • Iodine Metabolism
  • Iodine, which is required for thyroid hormone synthesis, enters the body in food or water and is reduced to iodide or iodate ion; Iodine supply can be limited in mountainous or inland (away from ocean) areas.
  • Thyroid gland is the principal organ that takes up iodide and stores it
  • Recommended daily intake: adults 150 µg, pregnancy 200 µg, intake <50 µg results in hypothyroidism
  • Hypothyoidism is rare in Western countries because table salt is supplemented with iodine
Slide 9
  • Thyroid Synthesis & Secretion
  • Under TSH stimulation-Thyroglobin (TG) synthesized and extruded to follicular lumen
  • Iodide transported into follicular cells (Trapping) and iodide oxidized by thyroid peroxidase (TPO) (Oxidation)
  • TPO covalently links iodine with tyrosine on TG to form MIT and DIT
  • Coupling of 2 DIT = T4 and 1 DIT + 1 MIT = T3
  • Iodinated TG stored until stimulated; endocytosis and cleavage from TG following stimulation by TSH
Slide 10
  • Endocrine Reviews, Volume 45, Issue 6, December 2024,
Slide 11: Amiodarone
  • Amiodarone is rich in iodine, which the thyroid gland uses to produce hormones. The large amount of iodine released when amiodarone is metabolized can disrupt thyroid hormone production and release.
  • Hyperthyroidism
  • Amiodarone induced direct toxic Thyroiditis
  • Amiodarone induced Hyperthyroidism due to reduced conversion of T3 from T4 and also due to iodine content
  • Amiodarone induced hypothyroidism—more common
Slide 12
  • T4 80%
  • T3 -20% made in thyroid
  • T3 and T4 (refers to number of iodide). T3 (10X higher affinity for TH receptor!). Thus, T4 provides a reservoir for the active T3 hormone
  • In the periphery T4 is converted to T3
Slide 13: Transport
  • In the blood, more than 99% of T3 and T4 are bound to proteins. The vast majority are bound to thyroid-binding globulin, or TBG. Hormones bound to TBG are not biologically active, and they cannot bind to their receptors.
  • The small percentage of these hormones that are left unbound are called free T3 and free T4. These are the biologically active forms that can readily bind thyroid hormone receptors.
  • Effects of Changes in TBG Levels.
  • TBG levels are increased during pregnancy and with oral contraceptive use because estrogen promotes TBG synthesis in the liver. In these patients, bound and total thyroid hormones are elevated, whereas free T3 and free T4 remain normal.
Slide 14
  • Receptors are intracellular and binding results in non-genomic (cAMP) and genomic effects
  • Non-Genomic: Stimulates Na+-K+ ATPase activity and mitochondrial enzymatic function. Rapid action
  • Genomic: Increases βAR (contractility and heart rate; breakdown of energy from storage) and αAR integrin (decreases peripheral resistance) = increased cardiac output and increased BP
  • Thyroid Functions- sequential and overlap
  • Barreto-Chaves, et al., Endocrine Connections, 9: R59-69, 2020

Notes:

Nongenomic actions of thyroid hormone and steroids are in contrast initiated at binding sites on the plasma membrane or in cytoplasm or organelles and do not primarily require formation of intranuclear receptor protein-hormone complexes. Importantly, hormonal actions that begin nongenomically outside the nucleus often culminate in changes in nuclear transcriptional events that are regulated by both traditional intranuclear receptors as well as other nuclear transcription factors. In the case of thyroid hormone, the extranuclear receptor can be the classical “nuclear” thyroid receptor (TR), a TR isoform, or integrin αvβ3. In the case of steroid hormones, the membrane receptor is usually, but not always, the classical “nuclear” steroid receptor. This concept defines the paradigm of overlapping nongenomic and genomic hormone mechanisms of action.

Slide 16
  • 34 yr woman presents with fatigue, anxiety, palpitations and 15 pd weight loss. Also has dry, slightly prominent eyes and itching and neck swelling. She is not pregnant and her basic blood counts, liver/ renal normal except for mildly high alkaline phosphatase
  • TSH < 0.01 suppressed and high T3 level 355 ng/dl and T4- 16 mcg/dl levels.
Slide 17
  • Primary hyperthyroidism is a disease state characterized by an overactive thyroid gland. The hallmark lab values to identify primary hyperthyroidism are low TSH and high T3 and T4, because the thyroid produces too much T3 and T4. These hormones feed back to the anterior pituitary and reduce TSH secretion.
Slide 18: Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
  • Graves’ disease (80%, autoimmune,
  • Toxic nodule/adenoma or toxic multinodular goiter (15%, autonomously secrete thyroid hormone)
  • Thyroiditis (2-4%, inflammation-induced release during early stage, autoimmune
  • TSH-secreting pituitary tumor (<1%)--secondary hyperthyroidism
  • Exogenous administration, and a few other rare conditions (extrathyroidal contribution, exposure to excess iodine).
Slide 19: Graves' disease- pathogenesis
  • Autoimmune
  • In Graves' disease, the main autoantigen is the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH, thyrotropin) receptor (TSHR)
  • Stimulating TRAb / TSI
  • They are specific for autoimmune thyroid disease
  • Once bound T cells are recruited
  • Adapted from: Latif R, Morshed SA, Zaidi M, Davies TF. The thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor: impact of thyroid-stimulating hormone and thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor antibodies on multimerization, cleavage, and signaling. Endocrinol Metab Clin North Am. 2009; 38:319.

Slide 20: Eye findings
  • Lid lag/ stare – delay in moving upper eyelid during downgaze due to Increased contraction of levator palpebrae muscle due to sympathetic overactivity
  • Graves’ ophthalmopathy – an autoimmune inflammatory disorder of the orbit and periorbital tissues, characterized by upper eyelid retraction ( mechanical), redness, conjunctivitis, and bulging eyes (exophthalmous). TSH R antigen is expressed in eye --Immune cells infiltrate orbital connective tissue. Fibroblasts in the eyes are also stimulated to differentiate into fat cells.
  • Smoking can aggravate the condition of Graves’ ophthalmopathy
Slide 21
  • UpToDate
Slide 22: Pretibial myxedema
Slide 23: Histology
  • Scalloping of colloid
  • In Graves' hyperthyroidism, histology shows thyroid follicles with tall, crowded epithelial cells and a "scalloped" appearance of the colloid. The colloid, which stores thyroid hormones, appears to have irregular indentations or "scalloping" due to increased follicular cell activity and hormone production.
  • wikimedia
Slide 24: Symptoms
  • Diffuse goiter may be present in Graves’ disease
  • Visible or palpable thyroid nodules may be present with toxic nodular or multinodular goiter.
  • Rapid heartbeat (80%),
  • Diffuse palpable goiter (70%),
  • Tremor (40%),
  • Exophthalmos (25%),
  • fatigue (70%),
  • weight loss (60%),
  • heat intolerance (55%), palpitations (50%),
  • Pretibial nonpitting myxedema
Slide 25: Hyperthyroidism
  • 1. Metabolism:
  • Increased Basal Metabolic Rate: Thyroid hormones increase the rate at which the body uses energy at rest, impacting oxygen consumption, respiration, and body temperature. --upregulate Na/ K ATPase and increase cellular oxygen consumption.
  • Carbohydrate Metabolism: They stimulate the breakdown of glycogen and glucose production.
  • Fat Metabolism: lipolysis
  • Protein Metabolism:-- protein breakdown (catabolism)
  • 2. Cardiovascular System:
  • Heart Rate and Contractility: Thyroid hormones increase the heart rate and the force of heart muscle contractions,
  • Cardiac Output: increased.
  • Beta1 -adrenergic Receptor Expression: Thyroid hormones increase the number of beta-adrenergic receptors in the heart, making it more sensitive to adrenaline and other sympathetic nervous system signals
  • Bone Cell Function: affect the function of chondrocytes, osteoblasts, and osteoclasts, which are cells involved in bone formation and remodeling.--Bone loss
  • Digestive System: Thyroid hormones influence the speed at which food moves through the digestive tract.
  • Reproductive System: through changes in prolactin / HPA axis – affect menstrual cycles, flow and fertility.
  • Skeletal Muscle: catabolic.
Slide 26: Investigations
  • To confirm diagnosis
  • Thyroid stimulating antibodies TSI - which is highly specific for diagnosis
  • To rule out other causes - radiology
Slide 27: Primary vs secondary hyperthyroidism

Slide 28: Radiological studies
  • THE THYROID GLAND AND IODINE
  • The cells in the thyroid gland take up and hold onto iodine. Iodine is an essential ingredient used by the thyroid cells to make thyroid hormones. Since thyroid cells use iodine, radioactive iodine can be used to both diagnose and treat thyroid problems.
  • WHAT IS RADIOACTIVE IODINE (RAI)?
  • Iodine can be made into two radioactive forms that are commonly used in patients with thyroid problems:
  • I-123 (does not damage thyroid cells)
  • I-131 (can be used to destroy thyroid cells)
Slide 29: Radio iodine scan and uptake
  • Definition: Radioactive Iodine Uptake, or RAIU, is a test of thyroid function. The test measures the amount of radioactive iodine (taken by mouth) that accumulates in the thyroid gland.
  • How the test is performed: RAIU is a type of nuclear test that measures how much radioactive iodine is taken up by the thyroid gland in a given time period.
  • Patient ingests radioactive iodine (I-123 or I-131) in liquid or capsule form. After 6 and 24 hours later, they return to have the radioactivity measured.
  • A gamma probe is placed over the thyroid gland in the neck to measure the amount of radioactivity in the thyroid gland. This amount of radioactivity is compared with the original dose of radioactivity and reported as a percent of the original dose.
Slide 30

| Pertinent clinical history |

| --- |

| Pregnancy/breastfeeding status |

| History of potentially interfering medications (eg. thyroid hormones, iodine containing medicines), amiodarone |

| Exposure to iodinated contrast |

| Ingestion of iodine rich foods (eg. kelp) |

Slide 31: Normal report At 6 hours: 3% to 16% At 24 hours: 8% to 25% Normal sized gland , normal uniform uptake

Slide 38: Treatment Graves
Slide 39: Treatment
  • Beta-blockers (beta adrenergic blocking agents like propranolol) decrease conversion of T4 to T3, which would slow heart rate and provide symptomatic relief.
  • Anti-Thyroid Medications - Thioamides (Methimazole, Propylthyiouracil (PTU)); these interfere with the action of thyroid peroxidase, thereby inhibiting thyroid hormone production; Methimazole is preferred due to more favorable side effect profile.
  • BOTH can cause blood count changes/ bone marrow suppression- Neutropenia, thrombocytopenia
  • Liver – acute liver failure
  • Pregnancy – PTU preferred drug in first trimester due to aplasia cutis in methimazole
  • Radioactive iodine (RAI) ablation -RAI treatment (I-131 oral administration-- beta or gamma radiation) destroys the thyrocytes and can take up 3-6 months to have full effect; can’t be used if pregnant or have active eye disease; may result in long-term hypothyroidism and replacement of hormones with Levothyroxine.
  • Thyroidectomy – in the case of large goiter, severe hyperthyroidism and intolerance to anti-thyroid drugs
Slide 40: BETA BLOCKERS- Main stay
  • β1-Adrenergic receptors have a stimulatory effect on cardiac myocytes, increasing contractility and heart rate. Thyroid hormones upregulate these receptors, leading to tachycardia and arrhythmias. For this reason, β-blockers are an important treatment for hyperthyroidism.
  • Examples – propranolol , atenolol etc
Slide 41
  • Mechanism. Thioamides inhibit the enzymatic incorporation of iodine into thyroxine, a key step in hormone synthesis.
  • PTU ( propyl thio uracil) and methimazole are actively transported into the thyroid, where they inhibit both the organification of iodine to tyrosine and the coupling of monoiodotyrosine (MIT) and diiodotyrosine (DIT) for synthesis of thyroid hormone; this works through inhibition of the enzyme thyroid peroxidase (TPO). In addition, PTU inhibits peripheral 5′-monodeiodinase, preventing T4 from converting to T3 in tissues.
Slide 42: Thyrotoxic crisis
  • 25 yr woman presents with anxiety, palpitations, diarrhea, confusion, weight loss of 20 pds over 2 months. HR 130, Atrial fibrillation , BP 140/100 and low grade fever 99.8 F
  • Labs – high WBC 14,000, with high PMN, mild high liver tests (alk phosphatase 180), negative pregnancy test
  • TSH< 0.01 suppressed, T3 500 ng/dl, T4 24 ng/dl –both high
  • Do not waste time investigating with scans etc
Slide 43: Treatment
  • IV fluids and IV antibiotics if needed .
  • Beta blockers to control rate – IV propranolol 20-40 mg Q4-6 hrs
  • Rhythm control / conversion if needed
  • Anti thyroid drug
  • Propylthiouracil ( PTU) – reduce T4 to T3 conversion peripherally 100 mg every tid or Methimazole 20-40 mg bid
  • Steroids – Reduce peripheral conversion of T4 to T4 ( active hormone)
  • SSKI iodine only after anti thyroid drug has been started
  • Avoid iodine dye ( CT scan) or amiodarone ( to control Atrial arrythmias)
  • Once stable, continue meds as outpatient
Slide 44
  • ↑ Estrogen = ↑ TBG = ↓ Free T4 = ↑ TSH (*stimulate more T4)
  • ↑ hCG = *↑ Free T4 = ↓ TSH
  • ↑ Iodine required (prenatal vitamin)
  • Overall, increased demand on thyroid gland
  • Hyper: Serum HCG shares the alpha subunit wit TSH.
  • hCG-mediated subclinical hyperthyroidism is transient and mild – thus, not usually treated;
  • Pregnancy
  • http://www.vivo.colostate.edu
Slide 45: Hypothyroidism
  • 22 yr woman presents with loss of hair/ eyebrow, constipation and dry skin .
  • Exam –Dry skin, bradycardia, pedel edema, Delayed ankle reflex seen
  • TSH – 50 HIGH and T4 is low , Thyroid peroxidase( TPO) antibodies high in 500s
Slide 46
  • Hypothyroidism may be classified as
  • 1) Primary –When Thyroid gland is affected
  • Hashimoto’s thyroiditis
  • After radioactive iodine therapy for Graves’ disease,
  • Post thyroidectomy for Graves’ disease/nodular goiter/thyroid cancer,
  • Transient – postpartum Thyroiditis
  • Excessive iodide intake, iodide deficiency
  • 2) Secondary (due to pituitary TSH deficiency)
Slide 47: Hashimoto's - Autoimmune
  • Hashimoto thyroiditis, also called chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis, is the most common type of thyroiditis as well as the most common cause of hypothyroidism in developed countries. It occurs in up to 2% of people in the United States.
  • Anti–thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO). These are present in most patients with Hashimoto thyroiditis.
Slide 48
  • + TPO ab
  • Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies. TPO is a crucial enzyme that converts iodide into iodine and allows it to be incorporated into thyroglobulin and subsequently production of T3 T4
Slide 49
  • Histology. Hashimoto thyroiditis is characterized by abundant lymphocytic infiltrate that may organize into lymphoid follicle-like structures with germinal centers
Slide 50: Symptoms
  • Fatigue, muscle weakness – slowing relaxation phase of deep tendon reflex due to reduced muscle and nerve metabolism
  • Cold intolerance/decreased sweating – due to decreased rate of metabolism
  • Weight gain, despite normal or increased appetite and intake – Decreased synthesis of beta-adrenergic receptors, resulting in decreased sensitivity to catecholamines and subsequent reduction of glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, and lipolysis (oxidation of glycogen, glucose and fat).
  • Impaired CV function – impaired ventricular contraction, bradycardia, and increased peripheral resistance, resulting in diminished cardiac output.
  • Dry skin and hair loss
  • Constipation – reduced gut motility
  • Menstrual irregularities – impairs conversion of estrogen precursors to estrogens, resulting in altered FSH and LH secretion, Anovulatory cycles and infertility
  • Depression
Slide 51: Hypothyroidism treatment
  • Thyroid hormone replacement
  • T4; Levothyroxine tablets once daily is usually given, which is converted in the periphery to the active hormone T3
  • Dose of T4 should be titrated to keep TSH low normal range (usual replacement dose is around 1.4 mcg/kg)
  • Takes up to 4 weeks for TSH level to normalize. So repeat labs after at least 4 weeks
  • Pregnancy – requirements are higher , need close monitoring and changes
  • Usually advise to take 2 extra pills per week
  • Hypo: Elevated TSH, +TPO = high risk of pregnancy complications. Pregnancy requires preemptive increase in Levo by ~30-50%. Need to prevent fetal hypothyroidism.
Slide 52: Myxedema coma
  • 68 yr man with h/o HTN, presents with weight gain, lethargy,
  • On exam , BP 90/60, Temp – 98, HR 50
  • Puffy eyelids, Skin is dry, pedel edema+, lungs – coarse crackles
  • Labs
  • Sodium low 131- dilutional hyponatremia,
  • TSH 100 , low free T4 1.0 , Thyroid peroxidase ab++
  • Treatment
  • Active warming, BP support- warm IV fluids, IV steroids first so you don’t precipitate adrenal insufficiency followed by IV levothyroxine.
Slide 53: Thyroiditis
  • Inflammation of the thyroid occurs for a variety of reasons.
  • PAINFUL – Viral/ subacute / De Quervains, Radiation
  • Painless- Hashimoto's, Postpartum, Riedel's or Fibrous Thyroiditis
Slide 54: Post partum Thyroiditis
  • Thyroiditis is inflammation of the thyroid gland leading to damage of thyroid follicular cells.
  • Course
  • When these cells are damaged, premade (stored) thyroid hormone leaks out into the bloodstream. This unregulated release of thyroid hormone may initially cause symptoms of hyperthyroidism (high serum levels of triiodothyronine [T3] and thyroxine [T4]). Eventually, however, the damage can become so severe that the thyroid no longer produces T3 and T4. Once this happens, patients present instead with hypothyroidism (low thyroid hormone levels).
Slide 55
  • The Child’s Bath
  • Date:
  • 1893
  • Artist:
  • Mary Cassatt (American, 1844–1926
Slide 56: Other Thyroiditis
  • Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (also called acute thyroiditis or de Quervain thyroiditis)
  • Presentation
  • This is the only type of thyroiditis to cause a painful goiter. Patients with subacute granulomatous thyroiditis usually present with a painful thyroid, neck, or jaw and symptoms of hyperthyroidism that generally resolve to the euthyroid state after several weeks.
  • Riedel Thyroiditis
  • Riedel thyroiditis, also called fibrosing thyroiditis, is a rare form of thyroiditis in which the thyroid gland, and sometimes other organs, become replaced by fibrous tissue.
  • Presentation
  • The rigid, fixed thyroid appears clinically as a hard, rock-like goiter, but there is no associated pain. Most patients are hypothyroid or euthyroid.
  • Riedel thyroiditis frequently causes local compressive symptoms. It can impinge on the trachea and interfere with breathing. A unique characteristic of this type of thyroiditis is that it can affect structures beyond the thyroid. Fibrosis can spread to the parathyroid glands to cause hypoparathyroidism, or to the recurrent laryngeal nerve to cause hoarseness.
Slide 58: Thyroid nodules
  • Causes
  • Obesity
  • Female sex
  • H/o radiation
  • Smoking
  • Family history
  • Iodine status
  • Aging
Slide 59: Thyroid ultrasound
  • All thyroid nodules should be examined with a thyroid ultrasound. An ultrasound can be used to determine the size, shape, and location of a nodule. An ultrasound is also used to identify suspicious nodules for biopsy. Calcifications, irregular borders, and invasion into surrounding tissue are strong indications for malignancy and prompt further evaluation, whereas cystic nodules are usually caused by benign disease, such as goiters.
Slide 60: Thyroid Ultrasound
  • Best: Cystic
  • Worst: Solid
Slide 61
  • PARTIAL CYST
  • CYST
  • SOILD HYPOECHOIC
  • SPONGIFORM nodule
Slide 62
  • Radioactive Iodine Uptake Scanning
  • Most often used for evaluating hyperthyroidism, the radioactive iodine uptake scan can also be done to assess the likelihood of malignancy in thyroid nodules. Hyperfunctioning “hot” nodules (those that take up the iodine isotope) are more often benign, whereas the lack of uptake in “cold” nodules raises the odds of malignancy.
Slide 63: Ultrasound guided thyroid nodule Fine Needle Aspiration - based on certain criteria
Slide 64
  • Thyroid genetic testing is a method used to analyze genes and DNA/RNA patterns within thyroid tissue samples, primarily from fine needle aspiration (FNA) biopsies, to aid in the diagnosis and management of thyroid nodules and cancers. These tests can help determine the risk of malignancy, guide surgical decisions, and inform treatment strategies.
Slide 65
  • Thyroid Adenomas
  • Thyroid adenomas are benign thyroid neoplasms that originate from follicular epithelial cells. Most adenomas are nonfunctional tumors , but some can produce thyroid hormone and lead to clinical hyperthyroidism.
Slide 66: Thyroid cancer

| Type | Incidence/ prognosis | Risk factors | Pathology | Monitoring |

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| Papillary | Most common/ excellent | Radiation, BRAF or RET mutation | Orphan Annie–eye nuclei, psammoma bodies | Thyroglobulin |

| Follicular | Rare/very good | Radiation, RAS mutation | Capsular invasion | Thyroglobulin |

| Medullary | Rare/good | Radiation, MEN2A and MEN2B | Amyloid stroma, stains with Congo red | Calcitonin |

| Anaplastic | Rare/poor | Radiation, older patients, RAS mutation, inactivation of p53 | Undifferentiated | None |

Slide 67
  • Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma
  • Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common form of thyroid cancer, constituting 70% to 85% of all thyroid cancer diagnoses. It usually spreads locally to the cervical lymph nodes AND HAS A GOOD PROGNOSIS
  • Risk Factors and Pathogenesis. Patients who experienced childhood radiation or who have a family history of thyroid cancer are at an increased risk for papillary carcinoma.
  • chromosomal recombination, leading to gain-of-function mutations in the BRAF or RET oncogenes.
Slide 68
  • Follicular carcinoma is the next most common form of thyroid cancer, accounting for 10% to 20% of all thyroid cancers. It is more common in females and older patients,. Compared with papillary cancer, follicular carcinoma grows faster and is more likely to spread hematogenously, sometimes metastasizing to bones or lungs.
  • Risk Factors and Pathogenesis. Follicular carcinoma is associated with RAS oncogene gain-of-function mutations.
Slide 69
  • Medullary Carcinoma
  • Medullary carcinoma makes up only 1% to 2% of all thyroid cancer diagnoses. Its prognosis is worse than the previously discussed types, and it often has metastasized to the liver, lungs, or bones at the time of diagnosis.
  • Risk Factors and Pathogenesis. About 25% of medullary cancers are genetically derived, usually associated with the RET oncogene mutations. This includes some patients with the genetic syndromes multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) types 2A and 2B, who are at high risk of developing medullary carcinoma.
  • MEN2A is characterized by medullary thyroid cancer, pheochromocytoma, and parathyroid adenomas.
  • MEN2B is characterized by medullary thyroid cancer, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas, and marfanoid features.
  • Medullary carcinoma is derived from parafollicular cells (C cells), and it secretes calcitonin. Calcitonin is a sensitive tumor marker
Slide 70: Treatment
  • Total or partial thyroidectomy for Thyroid nodules- if compressive symptoms, malignancy or suspected in FNA/ Genetic testing, rapid growth, PET scan + nodules( high risk of cancer)
  • Thyroid cancer- depends on size , histology etc
  • Thyroidectomy followed by Radioactive I 131 ablation of remnant cells, suppressive levothyroxine therapy, Monitoring of Thyroglobulin
Slide 71: PARATHYROID
  • 70 year old man is found to have a high calcium during annual physical.
  • Labs
  • Calcium 11.2 mg/dl( normal 8-10.4 mg/dl)
  • PTH parathyroid hormone 120 ( normal -35-70pg/ml)
  • Normal renal function
  • 24 urine calcium with creatinine is high - 400 mg/dl
  • DIAGNOSIS =High Calcium+ High PTH----> Primary Hyperparathyroidism
Slide 73
  • Development
  • The parathyroid glands arise from the endoderm of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches. The third pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the inferior parathyroids, and the fourth pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the superior parathyroids.
  • An abnormal migration may lead to ectopic placement of the gland (eg, inferior parathyroid glands in the anterior mediastinum with the thymus).
  • DiGeorge syndrome (also referred to as 22q11) occurs by a similar process and leads to congenital thymic aplasia and absent parathyroid glands. Patients have hypocalcemia from hypoparathyroidism, and the absent thymus leads to frequent infections resulting from a lack of T cells.
Slide 74: PTH- Parathyroid hormone regulates calcium
  • PTH dependent
  • Primary hyperparathyroidism
  • Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia
  • PTH Independent
  • Malignancies – PTHrP mediated – solid tumors e.g. lung cancer, T-cell leukemia
  • 1,25 OH vitamin D mediated – lymphomas, sarcoidosis and other granulomatous disesases
  • Multiple myeloma, leukemia, lymphoma
  • Endocrinopathies – thyrotoxicosis, pheochromocytoma,
  • Medications - Vitamin D intoxication, Vitamin A intoxication, Thiazide diuretics, Lithium.
  • Milk alkali syndrome
  • Immobilization
  • Idiopathic
Slide 75: Primary hyperparathyroidism
  • Serum calcium is elevated
  • Correction for measured calcium is needed only if serum albumin is outside the normal limits. Most calcium is albumin bound. So, abnormal albumin level can alter the measured calcium levels.
  • Formula for corrected calcium:
  • Calcium = Serum calcium + 0.8 (Normal albumin – patient Albumin)
  • For example, if albumin is 3.2
  • Corrected ca=11.2+ 0.8(4-3.2)
  • =12.8
Slide 77: Parathyroid scan
  • A parathyroid scan is used to determine the location of one or more overactive parathyroid gland(s)
  • The imaging test is usually an ultrasound or a nuclear scan called sestamibi scan.
  • The images from the scan help to make the surgery minimally invasive.

  • IV Bisphosphonates ( inhibit osteoclast bone resorption) – IV zoledronic acid 5 mg or pamidronate

Slide 84: MNG
  • Increased uptake of iodine is seen in the following patterns:
  • Diffuse pattern: Graves disease, secondary hyperthyroidism (see Figure 3B)
  • Nodular pattern: toxic multinodular goiter (see Figure 3C)
  • Single “hot” nodule (which produces more thyroid hormone and, therefore, takes up more iodine): toxic thyroid adenoma (see Figure 3D)
  • Decreased uptake of iodine (see Figure 3E) is seen in:
  • Hashimoto thyroiditis
  • Atrophic thyroiditis
  • Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis
  • Secondary hypothyroidism
  • Iodine deficiency
  • Exogenous hyperthyroidism (patients taking thyroid supplements)
Slide 85
  • The TRH receptors on the anterior pituitary and the TSH receptors on the thyroid are both G protein–coupled receptors.
  • Receptors. Once they reach the target cell, thyroid hormones cannot passively diffuse through the cell membrane like steroid hormones can, even though T3 and T4 are lipophilic. Instead, they are internalized via specific transmembrane thyroid hormone transporters. Unlike steroid hormones, T4 and T3 do not bind to cytosolic receptors but instead go directly to the nucleus, where the thyroid hormone receptors are located. These receptors are found in cells throughout the body. Once inside the nucleus, T4 and T3 bind to specific receptors to modulate gene expression
  • Thyroid hormones have major metabolic effects. At the cellular level, T3 and T4 upregulate the Na+/K+-ATPase, which increases cellular oxygen consumption, heat production, and basal metabolic rate.
  • Thyroid hormones upregulate β1-adrenergic receptors in the heart, which increases the heart’s response to sympathetic activation. This leads to an elevation in pulse rate and cardiac output.
Slide 86: Negative feedback
Slide 89
  • A thyroid uptake scan – NOT in pregnant / lactating women
  • shows DIFFUSE uniform uptake of technetium or iodine in Graves’ disease, AND 24 HOUR UPTAKE IS INCREASED
  • NODULE - localized uptake in toxic nodular/multinodular goiter,
  • THYROIDITIS- or decreased or absent uptake in thyroiditis
  • Presence of detection of thyroid stimulating immunoglobulin or TSH receptor antibodies (TSAbs; 95-99% positive) – elevated in Graves’ hyperthyroidism
Slide 90
  • Thyroid Hormone Effects
  • Thyroid hormones are transported in serum bound to carrier proteins
  • Free thyroid enters cells in the periphery and T4 converted to T3 by 5-deiodinase enzymatic activity
  • Receptors are intracellular and binding results in non-genomic (cAMP) and genomic effects
  • Genomic effect: thyroid receptor can bind DNA in absence of T3 – then T3 can bind

Slide 2: Objectives

  • Identify the visual pathways and vision disturbance caused by pituitary tumor
  • Understand the Hypothalamic-Pituitary axis and it's disturbances
  • Identify basic radiology findings of pituitary tumors

Slide 3
  • 34 yr man c/o blurred vision , headache for past 4 months.
  • Labs- normal electrolytes, renal function
  • Eye visit – shows partial defects in visual fields
  • MRI pituitary – 12 mm pituitary macroadenoma pressing on optic chiasm
Slide 4: Master gland
  • The pituitary gland, controls many of the hormones that circulate in our bodies
  • The pituitary gland is roughly the size of a pea and projects out anteroinferiorly from the hypothalamus.
  • The pituitary is located just inferior to the optic chiasm (where the optic nerves cross) and sits in the sellar space within the sella turcica (Turkish saddle), a saddle-shaped depression in the sphenoid bone of the skull.
  • The pituitary consists of two distinct lobes that project from the hypothalamus by a thin stalk called the infundibulum
Slide 5
  • The anterior pituitary gland, also known as the adenohypophysis, is formed from the Rathke pouch, a finger of ectoderm that buds off from the roof of the developing mouth. In contrast, the posterior pituitary gland, also known as the neurohypophysis, is made of nerve axons that extend from the hypothalamus. At the same time the Rathke pouch is developing, another pouch of neuroectoderm extends from the developing brain to become the posterior pituitary.
  • The two adjoining tissues form the mature pituitary gland. However, their histology is different.
Slide 6
  • The two lobes are the anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) and the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis).
  • The anterior pituitary is a true gland, with cells that synthesize and release hormones. It is richly perfused with capillaries.
  • The posterior pituitary is a neural extension of the brain. It is connected to the hypothalamus through the infundibulum, which contains the hypothalamo-hypophyseal portal tract
  • The tract carry oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) from the nerve cell bodies in the hypothalamus, where they are made, to the nerve endings in the posterior pituitary, where they are stored
Slide 7
  • Hypothalamic Hormones Regulating the
  • Secretion of Anterior Pituitary Hormones
  • Hypothalamic neurones synthesize and secrete
  • peptides (releasing hormones):
  • Corticotrophin Releasing Hormone (CRH)
  • Thyrotrophin Releasing Hormone (TRH)
  • Growth Hormone Releasing Hormone (GHRH)
  • Gonadotrophin Releasing Hormone (GnRH)
  • Somatostatin (also GH-Inhibiting Hormone)
  • Dopamine (also Prolactin-Inhibiting Hormone)
Slide 8
  • Five Cell Types of the Anterior Pituitary Gland
  • Corticotrophs (20%): produce corticotrophin, also called adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)
  • Thyrotrophs (5%): produce thyrotropin, also called thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH)
  • Somatotrophs (45%): produce growth hormone (GH)
  • Gonadotrophs (5%): produce the gonadotropins, luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)
  • Lactotrophs (25%): produce prolactin (PL)
  • Adapted from Scheithauer BW, et al., 2001
  • Chromophils (Acidophils [GH/Prolactin] + Basophils) and Chromophobes (Undifferentiated)

Slide 13: Visual Field testing
  • CN2 = Optic Nerve – this nerve carries visual impulses from the eye to the optical cortex of the brain by means of the optic tracts.
  • CN3, CN4, CN6 = Oculomotor, Trochlear and Abducens Nerves – responsible for extraocular movement.
  • Testing
  • Acuity with Snellen Chart – in office

Slide 18: Optic nerve related visual field defect
Slide 20: LR6
  • The abducens nerve innervates the lateral rectus (LR) muscle, which abducts the eye to move it outward. In the case of a CN VI lesion, the affected eye will not be able to abduct beyond the midline. So for example, with a palsy of the left CN VI, the left eye does not move laterally when the right eye is brought medially to gaze left.
Slide 21: 6th cranial nerve palsy, right eye
Slide 22: 3rd cranial N
  • CN III supplies all of the extraocular muscles with the exception of the lateral rectus (LR) and the superior oblique (SO). A CN III palsy therefore results in unopposed action of these two muscles. The result is that the eye is pulled down (loss of inferior oblique) and out (loss of medial rectus) . There would also be ptosis, or drooping, of the upper eyelid, due to loss of the levator palpebrae superioris as well as the mydriasis
Slide 23: 3rd cranial nerve palsy, right eye
Slide 24: 3rd cranial nerve palsy, right eye pupil involvement
Slide 25: SO4
  • The trochlear nerve innervates the superior oblique (SO) muscle, which moves the eye downward, especially when the eye is adducted, ie, looking to the nose. When CN IV is damaged, the eye moves upward (elevation) and outward (extorsion) because of the unopposed action of the inferior oblique muscles. This causes the patient to experience vertical diplopia when looking down and in, such as walking downstairs or reading a book. For example, if the right trochlear nerve is damaged, then the right eye will be resting in an upward and outward gaze

  • Microadenoma - < 10 mm

  • Pituitary function tests

  • CT of brain with coronal cuts when suspecting a bleed
Slide 30: Treatment – Replace hormones- Cortisol
  • Hypopituitarism / Pan hypo
  • Lactation failure
  • GH def-Short stature in kids
  • Secondary adrenal insufficiency—fatigue, low BP, dizziness
  • Secondary / hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism – Infertility
  • Secondary hypothyroidism
  • Posterior pituitary
  • ADH deficiency – high volume of dilute urine
Slide 31
  • The most critical hormone to replace is cortisol, because its deficiency can cause hypotension and death. In such patients, the priority is stabilization of the circulatory system. Treatment in this setting requires the administration of intravenous (IV) saline, dextrose if the patient is hypoglycemic, and IV hydrocortisone.
Slide 32: Treatment of pituitary adenoma
  • Based on size
  • Microadenoma , less than 1 cm -can be monitored
  • Macroadenoma- Surgery usually.
  • Based on secretion
  • Prolactin secreting – usually medical therapy is first line
Slide 33: Indications for surgery
  • Visual Impairment:
  • Surgery is a primary treatment for adenomas that are pressing on the optic chiasm or optic nerves, causing visual field defects or other visual abnormalities.
  • Pituitary Apoplexy:
  • If the pituitary gland experiences a sudden hemorrhage (pituitary apoplexy), surgery may be needed to relieve pressure on the brain and potentially improve vision.
  • Secreting Adenomas:-- except for prolactinoma
  • Surgery is often the first-line treatment for secreting adenomas, such as those causing acromegaly or Cushing's disease, when other treatments like medication have not been effective.
  • Large or Invasive Tumors:
  • Tumor Growth:
  • Persistent Symptoms:-If headaches, facial pain, or other symptoms persist despite other treatments, surgery may be an option.
  • Failure of Other Treatments: -If medical treatments (like medication or radiation) are not successful in controlling the adenoma or its symptoms, surgery may be considered
Slide 34: Treatment
  • Medical stabilization:
  • This includes administering Pre/ post operative high dose corticosteroids, monitoring fluid and electrolyte balance and pituitary hormonal defects post op
  • Surgical decompression: surgical removal of the tumor or decompression needed to improve vision
  • Prognosis:
  • Early detection and treatment are crucial for a positive outcome.
  • Visual symptoms may improve with medications or surgery, with full recovery occurring in about 40% of cases.
  • About 80% of individuals require long-term hormone replacement therapy.

  • Both images show sagittal views of a pituitary dedicated MRI

Slide 36: Sella and optic chiasm, cavernous sinus
Slide 37
  • Trans-sphenoidal hypophysectomy - procedure most commonly used to remove a pituitary gland tumor. Trans-sphenoidal means through the sphenoid sinus – the air sinus cavity at the back of the nose.
  • The pituitary gland is within the sella turcica or the hypophyseal fossa. This structure is present near the center at the base of the cranium. The anatomical boundaries of the gland have clinical and surgical significance. Sella turcica is a concave indentation in the sphenoid bone. The reflections of the dura bound the fossa laterally and superiorly.The diaphragma sellae is a dural fold with a central aperture, and it covers the sella turcica as a roof incompletely. The adenohypophysis is separated from the optic chiasm by the diaphragma. It is continuous with the dura. The pituitary stalk and the blood vessels travel via the central aperture.he lateral walls of the pituitary fossa are made up of dura mater, and it contains the cavernous sinus. The cavernous sinus consists of the internal carotid artery, sympathetic fibers, cranial nerves III, IV, V, and VI.

Slide 40: Diabetes insipidus/ AVP- deficiency
  • Usually post pituitary tumor resection, other causes include trauma, autoimmune. Postoperative diabetes insipidus (DI) is a common complication following pituitary surgery, with an incidence ranging from 10% to 30%. DI results from the pituitary gland's inability to release enough antidiuretic hormone (ADH)
  • Large volume(4-8L/day) of Dilute urine ( Low Osmolality)
  • This results in dehydration and Hypernatremia ( high sodium) → altered sensorium/ vomiting etc.
  • In Hyperosmolar Diabetic state – Large volume of solute high urine ( Glucose and sodium etc)– OSMOTIC DIURESIS
  • Usually hyponatremia to normal Na seen

Slide 47: Testing – Water deprivation Test
  • The physiological basis for the WDT is that dehydration causes an elevation in plasma sodium concentration, which stimulates AVP release. AVP is carried from the circulation to the kidneys, where it binds to V2 receptors, causing elevation in urine osmolality. If the stimulus to AVP secretion is sufficient (plasma osmolality >295 mOsm/kg), urine osmolality should rise to over 700 mOsm/kg.
  • P.Osmolality (mOsm/kg) =
  • 2[Na+] + [Glucose]/18 + [BUN]/2.8
Slide 49: Water deprivation test

| Condition | Urine Osmolality After Dehydration | After Desmopressin |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Normal | Increases | No significant change |

| Central DI | No/low increase | Marked increase |

| Nephrogenic DI | No/low increase | Little or no change |

| Primary Polydipsia | Gradual increase (may reach normal) | Minimal change |

  • Deamino-D arginine vasopressin abbreviated DDAVP, a derivative of ADH – selectively acts on V2 receptors
Slide 50

| Table 1 Diagnosis of diabetes insipidus using water deprivation | | |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Test | Central DI | Nephrogenic DI |

| Water-deprived plasma osmolality | ↑ | ↑ |

| Water-deprived urine osmolality | ↓ | ↓ |

| Urine osmolality after DDAVP | ↑ | No change |

| Urine volume after DDAVP | ↓ | No change |

Slide 51: Serum AVP and Co peptin
  • Copeptin is secreted in equimolar amounts with AVP from posterior pituitary in response to osmo and baroreceptor stimuli
Slide 52: Treatment of central DI
  • Fluid intake as dictated by thirst
  • AVP is a nonapeptide hormone, with a short plasma half-life of 5 to 10 minutes. The main physiological action to induce postreceptor synthesis of aquaporin 2 water channels and the insertion of preformed aquaporin 2 water channels into the apical cell membrane is therefore very transient
  • AVP is therefore unsuitable for therapeutic use in the management of CDI, but the synthetic analog desmopressin (dDAVP [deamino D-arginine vasopressin, desmopressin]) has been modified to prolong half-life from 5 minutes to 6 to 8 hours and to eradicate the vasopressor activity. This allows dDAVP to be administered twice or 3 times daily.
  • dDAVP is available in a parenteral ( hospital setting), oral ( o.1 to 0.2 mg tab- start at bedtime)
  • and nasal spray.

Slide 59: Pituitary apoplexy/ infarction
  • Medical and surgical emergency – ACUTE condition where the pituitary gland experiences a hemorrhage or infarction (tissue death). This usually occurs within a pre-existing pituitary tumor, often an adenoma. This requires prompt diagnosis and treatment to improve outcomes.
  • Causes:
  • Bleeding into and ischemia of the pituitary
  • Risk factors:
  • These include MACROADENOMA , prior radiation, pregnancy (Sheehan syndrome), trauma, surgery, and anticoagulation therapy.
Slide 60
  • Symptoms:
  • Sudden and severe headache.
  • Visual disturbances (visual loss, double vision).
  • Nausea, vomiting.
  • Altered mental status.
  • Signs of meningeal irritation (stiff neck).
  • Hormone insufficiency.
  • Ophthalmoplegia (paralysis of eye muscles).
  • Diagnosis:
  • Imaging: CT scans and MRI are used to confirm the presence of hemorrhage or infarction in the pituitary gland.
  • Blood tests: Evaluate hormone levels and electrolytes
  • Immediate treatment with steroids ( don't wait on labs etc) and emergent surgical decompression
Slide 61: Sheehan syndrome
  • Sheehan syndrome, also known as postpartum pituitary necrosis, is a condition where the pituitary gland is damaged, often due to significant blood loss during or after childbirth. This damage leads to a decreased production of pituitary hormones, resulting in various symptoms.
  • Causes:
  • Postpartum hemorrhage/ hypovolemic shock:
  • Severe blood loss during or after childbirth is the primary cause, leading to ischemia (reduced blood supply) and necrosis (tissue death) of the pituitary gland.
  • Symptoms:
  • Sheehan syndrome can manifest with a range of symptoms due to the deficiency of pituitary hormones, including:
  • Inability to breastfeed (agalactorrhea): Prolactin, a hormone necessary for milk production, is often affected. -- First symptom
  • Amenorrhea (absence of menstruation): Gonadotropin hormones, which regulate menstruation, are also deficient.
  • Hypothyroidism: Thyroid-stimulating hormone deficiency can lead to hypothyroidism symptoms like fatigue, cold intolerance, and weight gain.
  • Adrenal insufficiency: ACTH deficiency can lead to low cortisol levels, causing fatigue, weakness, and other symptoms.
  • Hypogonadism: Gonadotropin deficiency can affect sex drive and reproductive function.
Slide 62: Hypophysitis
  • Hypophysitis-- pituitary gland inflammation, is a rare condition that can lead to hypopituitarism (decreased hormone production) and pituitary enlargement.
  • Causes and Types:
  • Primary Hypophysitis: -due to autoimmune conditions- ex: lymphocytic hypophysitis, IgG-4. Other types include granulomatous, xanthomatous, and plasmacytic hypophysitis.
  • Secondary Hypophysitis: This is caused by other systemic diseases or conditions affecting the pituitary gland, such as infections or tumors.
  • Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor-Related Hypophysitis
  • Headaches are a common initial symptom.
  • Visual disturbances due to compression of optic nerves or cranial nerves can occur.
  • Hormonal deficiencies can lead to symptoms like adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, hypogonadism, and growth hormone deficiency.
  • Diabetes insipidus
Slide 63: The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism, Volume 107, Issue 1, January 2022,
Slide 65
  • Treatment- Steroids given as a therapy as well as to replace deficient cortisol hormone
Slide 66: Empty sella
  • After pituitary surgery, hypophysitis or idiopathic.
  • Very little pituitary tissue is left
  • If idiopathic- no hormonal defects usually
  • If non- idiopathic, may have hormonal deficiencies
Slide 67: Hyponatremia SIADH
  • Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH secretion ( when euvolemic) – unregulated ADH secretion resulting in water retention------>Hyponatremia.
  • Causes- medications- diuretics, opioids, NSAID, alcohol, malignancies ( ectopic ADH secretion)
  • Labs- Low serum sodium and , normal thyroid and adrenal function
  • Chronic – asymptomatic– Treatment is water restriction, rarely vasopressin receptor antagonists like tolvaptan, salt tablets
  • Remember ADH and AVP are synonyms
  • Too much ADH- hyponatremia
  • Too liitle ADH- hypernatremia
Slide 68: SIADH- Diagnostic criteria
Slide 70: SIADH treatment
  • Acute worsening, seizures- treat aggressively with 3% hypertonic saline – to bring up Na by 4-6 meq/L in First hour and then slow down.
  • Chronic, mild symptoms like dizziness/ confusion, Na > 125 – go slow, goal correction to 4-6 meq over 12-24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome

Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 14e

Chapter 41: Pancreatic Hormones & Antidiabetic Drugs

MEDICATIONS FOR TREATMENT OF TYPE 2 DIABETES

Several categories of glucoselowering agents are available for patients with type 2 diabetes: (1) agents that bind to the sulfonylurea receptor and

stimulate insulin secretion (sulfonylureas, meglitinides, Dphenylalanine derivatives); (2) agents that lower glucose levels by their actions on liver,

muscle, and adipose tissue (biguanides, thiazolidinediones); (3) agents that principally slow the intestinal absorption of glucose (αglucosidase

inhibitors); (4) agents that mimic incretin effect or prolong incretin action (GLP1 receptor agonists, dipeptidyl peptidase 4 [DPP4] inhibitors), (5)

agents that inhibit the reabsorption of glucose in the kidney (sodiumglucose cotransporter inhibitors [SGLTs]), and (6) agents that act by other or illdefined mechanisms (pramlintide, bromocriptine, colesevelam).

DRUGS THAT PRIMARILY STIMULATE INSULIN RELEASE BY BINDING TO THE SULFONYLUREA RECEPTOR

SULFONYLUREAS

Mechanism of Action

The major action of sulfonylureas is to increase insulin release from the pancreas (Table 41–7). They bind to a 140kDa highaffinity sulfonylurea

receptor that is associated with a betacell inward rectifier ATPsensitive potassium channel (Figure 41–2). Binding of a sulfonylurea inhibits the efflux

of potassium ions through the channel and results in depolarization. Depolarization opens a voltagegated calcium channel and results in calcium

influx and the release of preformed insulin.

TABLE 41–7

Regulation of insulin release in humans.

Stimulants of insulin release

Humoral: Glucose, mannose, leucine, arginine, other amino acids, fatty acids (high concentrations)

Hormonal: Glucagon, glucagonlike peptide 1 (7–37), glucosedependent insulinotropic polypeptide, cholecystokinin, gastrin

Neural: βAdrenergic stimulation, vagal stimulation

Drugs: Sulfonylureas, meglitinide, nateglinide, isoproterenol, acetylcholine

Inhibitors of insulin release

Hormonal: Somatostatin, insulin, leptin

Neural: αSympathomimetic effect of catecholamines

Drugs: Diazoxide, phenytoin, vinblastine, colchicine

Efficacy & Safety of the Sulfonylureas

Sulfonylureas are metabolized by the liver and, with the exception of acetohexamide, the metabolites are either weakly active or inactive. The

metabolites are excreted by the kidney and, in the case of the secondgeneration sulfonylureas, partly excreted in the bile. Idiosyncratic reactions are

rare, with skin rashes or hematologic toxicity (leukopenia, thrombocytopenia) occurring in less than 0.1% of cases. The secondgeneration

sulfonylureas have greater affinity for their receptor compared with the firstgeneration agents. The correspondingly lower effective doses and plasma

levels of the secondgeneration drugs therefore lower the risk of drugdrug interactions based on competition for plasma binding sites or hepatic

enzyme action.

In 1970, the University Group Diabetes Program (UGDP) in the United States reported that the number of deaths due to cardiovascular disease in

diabetic patients treated with tolbutamide was excessive compared with either insulintreated patients or those receiving placebos. Owing to design

flaws, this study and its conclusions were not generally accepted. In the United Kingdom, the UKPDS did not find an untoward cardiovascular effect of

sulfonylurea usage in their large, longterm study. The sulfonylureas continue to be widely prescribed, and six are available in the United States.

FIRSTGENERATION SULFONYLUREAS

Tolbutamide is well absorbed but rapidly metabolized in the liver. Its duration of effect is relatively short (6–10 hours), with an elimination halflife of

4–5 hours, and it is best administered in divided doses (eg, 500 mg before each meal). Some patients only need one or two tablets daily. The maximum

dosage is 3000 mg daily. Because of its short halflife and inactivation by the liver, it is relatively safe in the elderly and in patients with renal

impairment. Prolonged hypoglycemia has been reported rarely, mostly in patients receiving certain antibacterial sulfonamides (sulfisoxazole),

phenylbutazone for arthralgias, or the oral azole antifungal medications to treat candidiasis. These drugs inhibit the metabolism of tolbutamide in the

liver and increase its circulating levels.

Chlorpropamide has a halflife of 32 hours and is slowly metabolized in the liver to products that retain some biologic activity; approximately 20–30%

is excreted unchanged in the urine. The average maintenance dosage is 250 mg daily, given as a single dose in the morning. Prolonged hypoglycemic

reactions are more common in elderly patients, and the drug is contraindicated in this group. Other adverse effects include a hyperemic flush after
